paragraphs.text: The Book of Questions [of Saint Augustine] on the Old and New Testaments: One Hundred and Twenty-Seven Questions
I. WHAT IS GOD?

God is that which no notion can reach, for he is more than anything that can be said or thought. Still, let us say something which, though inadequate, fits in some measure with what seems worthy of God. Each nature forms its idea of God according to its own capacity, so that the opinions about what God is differ as much as one nature differs from another. Since he is above all things, he must surpass the minds of all. Human beings, stretching the eye of the mind as far as they can, see what God is by opinion, not by definition. The angels, who are higher than human beings, certainly perceive something more of God; the archangels more still. The cherubim and seraphim, the powers said to be next to God, perceive greater things of God, yet even they do not fully grasp what God is, for no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father.

God, then, as he appears to human beings, is spirit, simple in nature, light unapproachable, invisible, beyond reckoning, infinite, perfect, in need of nothing, eternal, immortal in every way, the one from whom all things took their beginning. He is to be revered, loved and feared. Nothing is outside him; rather, in him are all things that exist, above and below, highest and lowest. He is almighty, all-holding, truly rich in all things, since there is nothing that is not his. He is good, just and merciful. He is good, because he made things exist which did not exist. He is just, because the things he made were left to the free choice of their own will so that they might make progress. Since they are not so perfect that they cannot fall, he decreed that the seeds of the law should be in them by nature, and added the help of the revealed law, so that its authority might help human beings to advance. He is merciful, because he does not readily repay sinners but bears with them, so as to pardon them when they turn back. He is also severe, so that fear may preserve what he has well established and negligence may not bring life to ruin. And not to pass over what is more wonderful still, so great is his mercy that he endures insults from those he made and is the first to call them to peace. Is this not a greater power than to have created the creature? Yet if he were to remain always in this forbearance, his excessive goodness would harm the creature. So he wills sometimes to be loved and sometimes to be feared, lest those who stray from him perish. That is why he says, so that his patience should not be thought something to be despised (which would harm not him but wholly us): "I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever?"

So, since God is good, all that he made is good. Where then does evil come from? Evil is nothing but the transgression of the good, when things not permitted are presumed upon, or things permitted are done in a disordered way, so that what was commanded for one place is done in another. This happens when what is allowed with a wife is done with a prostitute; when what should be offered to God is offered to the devil; when someone takes not what is his own but what belongs to another; and when, though it is lawful to put a transgressor to death, an innocent person is killed. So no nature is shown to be evil. The will, however, is an accident of nature, arising from causes, and it is moved wrongly when it oversteps its measure and does things that do not belong to its nature. The causes of transgression arise from the senses, when we see or hear something wrongly. What brings about this error is that man is not God, who alone cannot err.

Human nature, then, has been left to its own choice, so that it can do what it wills. If it improves the good of its nature by exercise, it deserves honor; but if it weakens its own strength, such a person is held worthy of disgrace, for he does what is against himself. It is no small thing that has been granted to man: when he follows what is right, he may rejoice in himself because he sees that he has become better by his own effort; or else he must blame himself if, when he could, he made no effort to improve himself by good things. If man did not have power over himself, he would have been subject to necessity, so that he would have neither the glory of good works nor the punishment of evil ones, but would have been just one of the cattle.

We were made capable of either course: we sin through negligence if we hear and see wrongly, that is, contrary to nature and reason, what we ought to hear and see rightly, and we guard the good of our nature through vigilance. Since we cannot always be on our guard, because, as I said, we were made capable of either course, we are not yet condemned if we sin, unless we sin again, as men now lost. Whoever has sinned once must restore himself so as not to sin again, lest he remain no better than the one who overcame him. Then, if he does not sin again, he will be counted the stronger, for though thrown down once, he has triumphed twice. This is justice: since there is a struggle in the world, the one who strives harder not to sin is crowned.

There is nothing evil, then, in God's work, even if some people call certain things evil, such as poison or darkness. Poison is called evil because our bodies cannot bear its force, as if they could bear fire or water! Iron or lead will be called evil because it falls far short of gold. And they condemn darkness by comparing it with light, though they know it is necessary in its place, just as lead or earthenware is. For darkness at least gives rest after labor.

So everyone who struggles in the world ought to strive not to go off beaten in some hard trial and become guilty, recovering himself barely or late, lest death perhaps come in the meantime and he leave this life in sin. For one who resists with all his strength, if he happens to be thrown down, falls like a man, and no one is angry with him; instead they encourage him and restore his spirit. They saw that he was determined to win, and they hope that one whom the enemy overthrew only after a hard fight can go on to victory. But the one who is easily overcome has no will to resist; he is not so much overcome as consenting. He sins more grievously, and such a person who wants to sin can hardly be admitted to pardon. Whoever takes care not to sin does not sin grievously even if he does sin. Lesser sins sometimes creep up even on the careful; the smaller they are, the subtler they are, and because they are despised they are not avoided. The greater ones are visible from far off, so whoever sins in greater matters is guilty by his own will.

Since we said above that sins arise from the senses when we look at or hear something against the command of the law or against reason, consider some examples. If, seeing the sun, we think it should be worshipped because of its beauty, then we see wrongly, because it insults the common Creator when what is due to him alone is given to a creature, since he has forbidden this by the law. Or when we see well-formed and comely bodies, or covet something of our neighbor's, and look at them otherwise than the law commands, then sin occurs, which is called evil. But perhaps someone will say, "Nothing beautiful should have been made, so that we would not sin." Then our safety would depend on the ugliness of others; nor should there be iron, so that no murders were done with it; nor should lamps be used, so that thieves would not use their light to break in. So things of great use to everyone would be lacking because of the idle talk of a few, though it is clear that we always look at everything and yet do not always covet it. The fault is not in those things but in us when we are negligent. This negligence clearly arises from time to time because we are not what God is. Likewise, we hear wrongly if, on hearing that idols are gods, we agree, or if we lend an ear to those who sing indecent songs. We hear rightly when we are delighted to hear about God, that he is one. But if anyone hears something contrary to the law and assents to it, he sins: this is what it is to hear wrongly.
II. WHY GOD MADE THE WORLD

He made it because he is a maker; otherwise let it be denied that he is a maker, if he is not. But his very works show that he is. He made it, then, so that what did not exist before might exist, since without doubt it is better to exist than not to exist. But someone says, "Was there some empty space where he could make it, or what was there before, in which he made it?" The chosen vessel settled this in a few words, for when speaking of God he said, "In him we live and move and have our being." That is, all things are in God, because he is everywhere, and before all things he alone existed, eternal and invisible to every creature.

Lest we seem to have passed over the mystery, or rather to be ignorant of why the world was made, we say that the devil in his apostasy drew many angels, that is, spiritual powers, with him into transgression, when in impious presumption he sought to claim a kingdom for himself. The prophet Isaiah signifies this when he says, "How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, who rose in the morning!" That is, the one who appeared brighter than the rest. He was a kind of leader of many, among whom he shone more brightly, and in their company he went down into an impious contest. Seeing many spiritual powers below him, and being superior in the paradise of God in his knowledge of the heavenly mystery, he was puffed up by this very pride and wanted to be called God. It was the same pattern we see some imitate in this present life: men who, elated at the sight of the soldiery gathered around them, with their followers supplying the tinder of conspiracy, have tried to claim the empire for themselves.

This is why God, in order to destroy the devil's presumption not by force but by reason, created matter, a confused mass of things, from which he would make the world. When the things that had been mingled together were separated, they produced this ordered beauty we see. When the substances had been divided from one another and joined in an orderly structure, it was called the world (mundus), because each thing, separated from the others, appeared in clean and tidy order. Man was set here, created from things above and below, that is, from the heavenly and the earthly, so that he might show the lordship of the one God, not only by his voice but also by his image, since he was made as one by the one God, so that the rest might spring from him. The one God made one man in order to teach that all things come from one, and therefore that God is one, so that the higher creation might learn the truth, to its own shame, in man, who was formed from the earth.

From then on the devil became man's enemy, for he saw that man had been made to accuse him. So by his cunning he contrived to lead man into the same transgression into which he himself had fallen, so as to make his accuser a sharer in his own condemnation. He promised him godhead through transgression, the very thing he himself was cast down for aspiring to. And since every nature is free from guilt, names come from what is accidental (first the thing, then its designation). So "Satan" and "devil" are names formed from his conduct, and they signify not his nature but his will.

So that God's purpose in creating man might stand, and the devil's deed by which he deceived man might add to the sum of his guilt, Christ deigned to come from his holy seat to earth, both to free man from the sentence passed on his transgression and to show the devil's coming destruction, so that no one would imitate what he had done. That is why the apostle John said, "For this reason the Son of God came: to destroy the works of the devil." If the devil were evil by nature, it would be either madness or injustice to threaten him with punishment. For who would blame someone he sees doing nothing other than what his nature allows? Can one be angry with fire because it burns, or with water because it cools, when they do this not by will but by nature? So the devil too, if he were evil by nature, would have no will. He could not discriminate, but would plunge himself blindly into everyone in one and the same way.

But in fact he acts with a kind of judgment. He spares those who do his will; he pretends not to notice certain novices; he puts obstacles and hindrances in the way of those who want to flee to God's help; he lays traps for God's servants; and he is especially hostile to those most eager in God's service. From this it is plain that the guilt lies in his will. For this reason the apostle Peter says, "Be sober and keep watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." He does not seek out the Gentiles, he does not seek out the Jews, he does not seek out those of wicked life and conduct; he seeks the servants of God and of Christ, whom he knows to be his enemies, because they condemn his deed and his presumption.

Indeed, once the law was given, his envy burned more fiercely against those who were under the law, since he knew that the teachings of the law convey the one God and a good way of life to human beings. Now if he is thought to do these things by nature, he cannot be held guilty, because he does what belongs to his nature and what he is able to do, and does not do what he cannot do, because it does not belong to his nature. So he is to be neither praised nor condemned: not praised, because what he does is harmful; not condemned, because he does it not by will but by the impulse of his nature. We know of people who suddenly went mad and did great harm with swords, clubs, stones and bites, some even killing; yet when they were caught with much effort and brought to trial, they were not held guilty, because they had done these things not by their will but unknowingly, driven by some force or other. For how can someone be held guilty who does not know what he has done? So too with the devil: if he does not know the good, why should he be judged worthy of condemnation for not doing what he does not know? Rather, if that were possible, he would deserve praise for doing what he knows.

We, however, are rightly held guilty, because we do something other than what we know we ought to do. And since we see throughout Scripture that the devil is held guilty, and read that Gehenna has been prepared for him on that account, we know that he is to be condemned by the laws, because, though he knew the good and could do it, he did evil. For God, who is just, would not condemn him for failing to do a good he did not know, or for doing the evil that was all he knew. So I think it has been shown that no nature ought to be called evil, because all evil, as has become clear, comes from the will, which affects nature through the senses.
III. WHY WAS IT NECESSARY TO SET OUT THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD AND THE ORDER OF CREATION THROUGH MOSES, AND NOT BEFORE?

It did not need to be written down earlier, because there was not yet such great error among human beings on this matter. But error grew among the human race, until even the children of Israel in Egypt heard the opposite of this account taught by the philosophers of the Egyptians. Moses too had been trained by them in all the learning of Egypt, which asserts that a certain Saclas made this world through evil angels, and that he is regarded as the prince of this world, that is, Satan. Marcion followed this view and plunged to his death. The Manichees, more foolish than the rest, say that man, though not this world, was made by the same Saclas. Since it is clear that the world was fashioned for man's sake, they say that the world was made by God, though out of what belonged to another, but that man was created by the adversary, as if in one person's house someone else had installed the master. So Moses needed to expose and remove this error by showing that God is the author of both the world and the man that were fashioned. Having gained authority through the signs and wonders he performed, he showed beyond doubt that what he taught, with signs as his witnesses, was true. Who would not believe a man whose deeds were accompanied by such great signs? That is why those who hold views contrary to this teaching are known to be in error: they try to support their assertions with bare words.

So, to teach that nothing is coeternal with God, Moses sets out the very order of created things. By recording that lesser things were made first and greater things afterward, he ensures that none of them is thought to be unmade. The things that come later in time are greater in power. So if the earlier things think they can claim precedence on the ground of time, they are refuted by the very weakness by which they are subject to the later ones; and if the later things presume on their power to claim first place, they are humbled by coming later. Thus nothing among them appears not to be subject to a beginning. First, indeed, heaven and earth were made; then light, whose function is to be day; after that the firmament, which was called heaven, and the gatherings of the waters, which he called seas, so that the earth might appear and be habitable. By the earth which he says was made after heaven he does not want us to understand the earth alone; he signified matter, that is, all the lower things that developed into the whole visible form of the world. And he maintains that the heaven made in the beginning is not this bodily heaven but that heaven above which is spiritual. So when he says that heaven was made first and then earth, he indicates that all invisible things in heaven and all visible things on earth were created by God. He takes in the highest and lowest of all nature, so that whatever lies between may be believed without doubt to have been made. He states that the lights, which God established to govern the world, were made on the fourth day, so that the greater they are in power, the later they are in time. Man he set up on the sixth day, to bring an inhabitant into a house already made.

This is why the words that displease some people were said: "And God saw the light, that it was good." Since it was being said that all things were made by an evil being and could not be believed to be good, Moses, to prove that the things made were good, showed that what God made pleased God himself, so as to convict anyone they displeased. For how could he who said, "Let there be light, and there was light," not know the light? Does anyone make what he does not know? The light, once made, pleased him who made it. What craftsman does not rejoice in his work? If, after it was said, "God saw the light, that it was good," there are still [?] people who say "it is evil," what would have happened if it had been left without testimony?

So, after describing the making of the world and the origin of the first man, Moses traced the line of descent of Seth, who was given in place of Abel, and came in order down to Abraham, the father of the Jews. He did this to show that Abraham believed in this God, who is the maker of the world, and that this God gave the law in which the coming Christ was promised, who would free the human race from the dominion of the devil. From this our faith is shown to be reasonable, for the recorded lineage bears witness to it, since the race of Christians exists from the beginning. From Seth, the son of Adam, one comes to Enoch; from Enoch to Noah; from Noah to Abraham; from Abraham one descends to David; and from David, of Mary, by the Holy Spirit, Christ is born. So all those of earlier times who had faith in the one God whom the Savior preached are rightly to be called Christians, for the Savior was promised from the beginning as the one who would come. That is why it says in Revelation: "the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world." So Christianity has always existed. All those I mentioned above, from the first man created in the world, through whom the line extends to the Savior, had faith in this God, of whom Christ spoke when he said, "Now this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Someone may object, "If Christianity existed before, what knowledge came through Christ?" The coming of Christ brought this advance in understanding: he revealed the mystery of the one God who had been proclaimed, showed what belongs to which person, and, to fulfill the righteousness of the law, added what had been held in reserve.
IV. WHY DID HE NOT GIVE THE LAW AT THE BEGINNING?

At first the law did not need to be given in written form, because it is in some way implanted in nature itself, and knowledge of the Creator was not hidden, being handed down from generation to generation. Who does not know what befits a good life, or is unaware that what he does not want done to himself ought not to be done to another? But once the natural law had faded, crushed by the habit of sinning, it had to be made manifest, so that all might hear it in the Jews. It was not that the law had been wholly erased, but people were for the most part without its authority: idolatry was pursued, there was no fear of God on earth, fornication was practiced, and people were greedy with covetousness for their neighbor's property. So the law was given, so that what was known might have authority and what had begun to be hidden might be made manifest. For we find that before Moses sins were not only not hidden but were even punished. That is why many are found to have been righteous: knowing that God is an avenger, they were afraid to sin. When this began to be neglected, the natural law had to be revealed, so that all might know by plain reasoning that the Lord will call human deeds to account. It is true that we read of punishment through the flood and on Sodom and Gomorrah, but forgetfulness had covered these over with age, so through Moses they were recalled to instill fear, to correct conduct, and to restore faith in God. That is why the apostle says, "The law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous, for idolaters, fornicators," and the like.

Now let us consider, with those who laugh on hearing of God's judgment to come, whether it is fitting: whether it will help or harm, whether it is backed by truth or lacks reason. The law was indeed given to the world, but we see that it has no force in the case of many, and so things do not appear just. Why is it that here sinners are secure through their power, others make a mockery of the laws, the poor are oppressed, charges are trumped up against the righteous, those who do good are reviled, the godly are in want, the wicked flourish, the unjust and corrupt are honored, the greedy and the robbers grow rich, and the judge is for sale? Would it not seem unjust if the Creator of all things did not call these to account? Those unjustly oppressed here should be raised up, those who were in want for living rightly should be rewarded, and those who were reviled for the sake of righteousness should be honored. But those who through their power despised the laws, or evaded and mocked them in pursuit of wickedness, and gloried in these things so much that they seemed to insult justice itself, should be humbled and put to shame and subjected to torments in the sight of those whose misfortunes and contempt they enjoyed. Then those very people, glad at their punishment, may give thanks to God, with whom alone there is no respect of persons.
V. WHY WAS ABEL'S SACRIFICE ACCEPTED AND CAIN'S REJECTED?

From the very words of this reading it can be gathered that the story is not veiled by any literary artifice. For the language of Scripture itself shows Abel to be prudent and devout, but Cain careless and thoughtless, and for that reason less devout. Abel, then, chose the better part of what was pleasing to offer to God the Creator, so that out of the things God had created he might offer him the choicest. By this he gave proof both of his own dedication and of God's worth, showing both his own reverence and God as the Author of all. Cain, like a rustic, could not see this beforehand. For he sank his whole soul into the earth and could not lift the eyes of his mind to heaven to see what was worthy of the Creator; and so he offered God gifts of any sort at all.

This same fault of a crooked mind is found among the Jews too. For they were often rebuked for thoughtlessly bringing to God's altar gifts that would not have seemed fit even for men, as the Lord says: "You offer me the blind and the one-eyed; I will not accept these from your hands. Offer them to your governor or your prince, and see whether he will accept them", since everyone agrees that the greatest gifts ought to be offered to an exalted person. That is why Cain's gifts were rejected, and God said to him: "Why are you grieved, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still. Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it."

You see, then, that it was the dividing that incurred the sin. Since he did not consider what was worthy of God, he kept the better things for his own use. So he was not rebuked for offering, but for offering unworthy things. Nor was he condemned for it; he was warned to correct what he had done. For God says, "Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it", that is, "Since I do not accept it, the gift you offered has turned back into your possession", so that he would know what to do in future. From this his envy flared up so that he killed his brother. The one who had first shown righteousness was killed by an unrighteous man, and an evil example was given to mankind. For he was so blinded by jealous rivalry that he not only failed to give thanks, though he had not been made guilty and had even learned how to put the matter right, but he also added another, graver deed, for which he deserved to be condemned.

The case of the thoughtless fratricide Cain is like that of the wicked servant who, after his master had forgiven him, became ungrateful, went out and began to choke his fellow servant, so that he was condemned without excuse both for the past crime that had been forgiven him and for the cruelty he had committed against his fellow servant. Yet Cain was not condemned at that moment. Confounded and guilty, he was sent away over the earth under terror, so that if he repented he might be forgiven. Indeed, fearing that someone would kill him for this deed, he said to God: "My guilt is too great for me to be let go. If you drive me out today from your face, I shall hide myself from the face of the earth too, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth; and whoever finds me will kill me." Terrified by the words of God, the just Judge, Cain fears that God will scorn him, so much so that he thinks he must flee even from the sight of men, sure that whoever lives under God's anger can be killed even by a man. But what did the Lord answer him? "Not so," he says, that is, "I did not send you away, though you do not deserve to live, so that someone might kill you, but so that you might groan and tremble as the one who first gave an evil example on the earth, while the ground yields no fruit for your labours." And so, he says, "whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance." This sentence shows that Cain deserved to be condemned. For when he saw a law given under such a threat, so that no one would imitate his deed, he began to fear all the more, knowing what evil he had committed.

So he threatens sevenfold vengeance on anyone who aspired to this crime. Anyone who saw that Cain had been made guilty by this deed, even at a time when the law had not yet been made known, was to know that he would be punished sevenfold if he did not avoid it. Knowledge of the law would add six blows beyond what Cain had deserved, so that, with Cain's blow, seven punishments would be counted. By this number too are those to be rewarded who leave everything and follow the Lord, and in the age to come they will have eternal life. This is the sign that God put on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. For a law was laid down concerning fratricide: if anyone committed murder, since every killing of kin is murder, he would be seven times as guilty as Cain had been, so that others, frightened by this severity, would hold themselves back from this crime.
VI. Did Lamech kill Cain, as is supposed?

Those who think that Lamech said this about Cain are mistaken: "I have killed a man to my bruising, and a youth to my wound." For Lamech was born in the fifth generation from Cain, that is, from Methushael, Cain's great-great-grandson. Lamech mentions this to show that one who sins after the law has been made known must be bound more severely. And so, if after Cain vengeance was taken sevenfold on whoever imitated him, how much more must vengeance be taken on one whom neither Cain's deed and his rebuke nor the sentence passed after him frightened into turning his will away from so impious and cruel a crime! So after Cain, Lamech committed murder, and according to what was said above he no doubt paid sevenfold vengeance. And he showed what would happen after Lamech to anyone who followed his example, saying: "but for Lamech seventy times seven." [?] Because repentance does not follow the evil deed, let him be struck with the blows of seventy-seven plagues. That is why the Saviour commanded that even one who sins seventy times seven should be forgiven, provided that he turns back.

But it should not be thought that someone other than Lamech committed murder after Cain, merely because he said, "Vengeance has been taken for Cain," as though it had already been done. For how could Lamech say of himself that vengeance had been taken on him, when the murder he had confessed to was still recent, unless every deed is agreed to carry its sentence with it? For when there is no other prospect than what is known to be due to the completed deed, the future is regarded as already done. Thus it was said to Adam: "On the day you eat, you shall die the death." Yet they certainly did not die at once, but after a long interval of time. Because the hope of immortality had already been lost, however, future death was spoken of as present, since from then on it began to be expected. Lamech, then, confesses that he killed a youth, and Cain, as has been made clear, could not have lived to that time; or if he did, which is impossible, he was an old man.
VII. What are the ten words given on the tablets, and how many words did each tablet have?

He called ten sentences "ten words", just as the Saviour too used "word" to mean a thought when, among other things, he said to the Jews: "I too will ask you one word; answer me: the baptism of John, where was it from, from heaven or from men?" He called this thought a "word". In the same way, ten words are said to have been written on the two tablets, and these are ten thoughts. Thus he says: "You shall have no other gods besides me", and this is the first word. Then he adds: "You shall not make for yourself any likeness of the things that are in heaven above or on the earth below or in the water that is under the earth." Then, third, he adds: "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not cleanse one who takes his name in vain", that is, you shall not take up the name of the Lord your God in a lie, so as to swear falsely by it. Next, in fourth place, he says: "You shall keep the sabbaths of the Lord your God, and you shall do no servile work on it." These are four of the ten words; they belong properly to the Lord, and they were written on the first tablet.

Then the second tablet contains these. The first word is: "Honour your father and mother"; the second: "You shall not kill"; the third: "You shall not commit fornication"; the fourth: "You shall not steal"; the fifth: "You shall not bear false witness"; the sixth: "You shall not covet anything of your neighbour's", and so on. The apostle Paul proves that these were written on the second tablet when he says: "Honour your father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise." How could it be the first, unless the second tablet began with it? He said "with a promise" because he immediately added: "that you may live long on the earth and that it may be well with you." This is the promise made to those who keep the commandments. So you have the commandments set out, their number made complete, and what and how many were written on each tablet.
VIII. Why, when Moses came down from the mountain with the tablets, was his face so radiant that it could not be borne?

Having received authority against sinners, he came down from the mountain in honour, with a glorious face. For the law was given against sinners. So because Moses had not sinned, he appeared so glorious that sinners could not look at him. This showed that sinners do not deserve to look on the glory of God. For after the image of the molten calf and the breaking of the tablets on which the law had been given, Moses went up the mountain again with tablets, and when he came down having received the law on them, his face became glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look at his face, nor could Aaron, because he too had sinned. Instead he spoke to them with a veil placed between, so that they would remain unworthy of God's glory for as long as they persisted in their sins.

Hence the apostle says: "When one turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away", so that, washed by God's gift, they might become worthy to gaze on the glory of God. For by breaking the tablets he had received earlier, he signified that the Jewish people were rejected, because in their eagerness for sin they would become unworthy of God's promise. And the fact that the law was given a second time signified another people to come, for whom the law given on the mountain would be of profit.

IX. If God made all things good, and very good, why does he say to Noah, "Bring with you into the ark some of the clean and the unclean," since, strictly speaking, what is unclean cannot be called good?

Because words carry many kinds of meaning, they give rise to questions. If they are referred to the matter under discussion, there will be no question, because the facts will reveal themselves in their proper order. For sometimes we call "common" what is undivided, and sometimes what is unclean; "common" is used in two senses. Thus the apostle Peter says: "Nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth." And the apostle Paul says: "Whatever is not of faith is sin", and elsewhere he says: "The law is not of faith", and yet it is not sin. You see, then, that one and the same word does not always mean the same thing.

So too, when something is called "unclean", we must consider why it is so called. Sometimes a thing is called unclean in comparison with better things; sometimes the word refers to foul deeds, and then evil is meant. So no substance is evil, because things thought unclean in their substance are unclean only in comparison with the most beautiful things. For even bread [?] is called unclean; oil and lead are unclean in comparison with gold, and the raven in comparison with the peacock. And although they are members of a single body, some members are called honourable and others dishonourable, though it is known that they are not evil. So all things are good in their own nature, because they are useful.

X. Since God told Abraham that the children of Israel would come out from the power of the Egyptians in the fourth generation, why does the law say the opposite: "In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt"? This seems flatly contradictory.

As far as the words go, it seems contradictory; but if the sense is sought, it will be found not to differ. For the law speaks in such a way that it can be understood by the careful and diligent, so that the reason of truth reveals itself not to the incurious but to the attentive. God certainly said "in the fourth generation", and Moses wrote "in the fifth generation". Yet Moses recorded both, and it is impossible that he, through whom such great power worked, should deceive. So the sense must be investigated, because divine Scripture says nothing idly or thoughtlessly. There are, then, two parts, which each of them mentioned. God signified the four generations that were born in Egypt. Moses, however, added to these the one from which they had their origin when they entered Egypt, and said: "In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out." For he included both the generation that entered Egypt and the four that were born there. From Abraham to the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt there are eight generations. For they lived in Canaan two hundred and fifteen years from the promise made to Abraham, and two hundred and fifteen in Egypt.

These are the years the apostle covers when he says to the Galatians: "The law came four hundred and thirty years afterwards." These four generations, then, were born in Canaan: one in Isaac, the second in Jacob, the third in Levi, and the fourth in Gershon, Kohath and Merari. When the children of Israel had entered Egypt, Kohath begot Amram, and this is the first generation born in Egypt. Amram begot Aaron, Moses and Miriam, the second generation born in Egypt. Aaron begot Eleazar and his brothers, the third generation. And Eleazar begot Phinehas in the fourth generation. These are the four generations born in Egypt. That is why God said to Abraham: "Your seed will be strangers, and they will oppress them with slavery; but I will set them free, and in the fourth generation they will come out from there." See whether it is not plain that God meant nothing other than what took place in Egypt. Moses, however, in order to include also the generation that entered Egypt with Jacob its father, from which these four took their origin, said: "In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt."
XI. If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless not Esau, whom he wanted to bless, but Jacob, whom he did not want to bless?

The will of a righteous man is good as far as his conscience is concerned; but as regards foreknowledge, it is immune from adversities [?]. For God alone judges the future. So Isaac, a righteous man, judged as far as was fitting for his present human condition, and thought that his elder son should rather be blessed. But God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger deserved the blessing. He did this to show that in blessing the gift is not man's but God's, and that God's blessing follows the dignity of the office, not the merit of the man. Thus God said in Numbers to Moses and to Aaron the priests: "You shall put my name upon the children of Israel; I the Lord will bless them." So the tradition pours grace into people through the ministry of one who has been ordained, and the priest's will can neither hinder nor help; what counts is the merit of the one who asks for the blessing.

Let us see from this how great the dignity of the priestly order is. It was said of the wicked Caiaphas, the killer of the Saviour, among other things: "He did not say this of himself, but being high priest that year, he prophesied." This shows that the Spirit of graces does not follow the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the ordination of the tradition. However good a man's merit may be, he cannot bless unless he has been ordained to carry out the office of the ministry. But it belongs to God to give the blessing its effect.
XII. Why did Abraham receive circumcision as the sign of his faith?

If you are willing to pay attention, you will see that what you think is contrary to reason is not unfitting. Believing that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed, and from whom holiness was to arise, he received the sign in that part through which the begetting of children takes place and comes to an end, so that it might be holier. And if to some this seems a disfigurement, let them notice that Abraham rejoiced in it and that his sons gloried in this testimony. Achior, for instance, one of the chiefs of the Gentiles, saw that there was such power in the God of Abraham that by a woman's hand he beheaded with his own sword Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, whose might the whole earth trembled at. He circumcised himself of his own accord, believing that by this very act he had gained dignity for himself. Does not someone who has lost an eye or some limb for the name of Christ display it openly? Does he not thrust that very part before people's faces so that he may appear glorious? For to lose something for a time for the sake of faith is to make a gain.

So Abraham too, in receiving the sign of his faith, was not disfigured but improved. Spiritually, this signified that the fog of the flesh would be cut away from human hearts through faith in Christ. For fleshly error stood in the way, casting darkness over human hearts so that they did not know the Creator. Abraham, because Christ, who would wipe away this darkness, was promised from his seed, was circumcised for this reason: he believed that he would have a son who would cut off this error. See now whether it was not fitting that he received such a sign, and in that part.
XIII. If God's judgment is just, why were the infants in Sodom burned together with their parents?

To show how utterly impious the crime of the Sodomites was, their sin went so far as to bring about the death of their own children, so that no trace of their offspring would remain. Was it not a provision for them, so that they would not live long and follow their fathers' example? For since they were killed for another's guilt, they are free from Gehenna. The parents are guilty both for themselves and for their children, because their whole progeny was wiped out so that their deeds might be blotted out. For if children rejoice in their parents' good things and in being commended by their privileges, then they cannot complain of a death inflicted for their parents' evils; as they share in the gain, so they share in the loss. Likewise in Egypt the sons were punished for the crimes of their fathers, but in order to bring about the fathers' correction. Since for other reasons they had refused to believe in and worship the Lord who was in Moses, they were to be terrified by this plague into confessing with amends, so that they would not feel his anger more heavily.

This death of the children, then, is the fathers' crime. In whatever way the children gave up the life they owed, they will be their parents' accusers, because the parents could not overcome their own faithlessness even with their children's blood. So the parents' evils overtook the children for the present time, not for the future. And is it not some kind of benefit to be not glorious, yet not guilty either? For if some, placed at the very end of life, strive with prayers to come to the faith of the truth so that they may win, if not a crown, at least pardon, how can anyone complain about those who were dealt with in such a way that they had nothing for which to beg pardon, and yet were not held in high honour, since they had not laboured at all? Now compare the torment of a single moment with punishment lasting a long time. Consider also that many labour and, because they cannot persevere, not only lose the fruit of their labour but are punished as well. Add, too, that those born of wicked parents and brought up or living among the most wicked find it hard to train their minds to follow God's discipline. See, then, whether the children of the lost were not rather well dealt with.
XIV. Why did God, who is proclaimed to be just, promise to visit the sins of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation?

Anyone who doubts that the Lord neither does nor says anything unjust is out of his mind. So if the Lord's words are not suppressed, and everything that bears on this question is set out, what seems obscure will become clear, and what is thought anything but just will be seen to be righteous. For whoever suppresses the words that bear on a question is either unskilled or evasive, more eager for slander than for teaching. Now God did indeed promise to repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, but upon those who hate him, that is, upon those who carry on in their fathers' wickedness and serve idols as their fathers did. For he is an enemy of God who claims for a creature the honour due to God's name. Just as the children of the righteous, being righteous themselves, ennoble the line of righteousness in their own persons, since they are exalted both by their fathers' righteousness and by their own, so too the children of the very wicked, being very wicked themselves, increase the wickedness, because they are both the children of evil men and have copied their wickedness, to the ruin of many.

So God seems to have spoken to strike terror, but what he said is true, and it is reasonable. For who would not detest an evil man who is also the son of an evil man on two counts, just as he judges that a good man who is the son of a good man deserves honour on two counts? He promised to repay to the third and fourth generation for this reason: so that if a son does not follow his evil father's faithlessness, but the grandson turns out to imitate his grandfather's evil, the grandson may know that he will not be exempt from the severity of the sentence; or if the grandson perhaps follows in the footsteps not of his grandfather but of his father and loves God's covenant, the great-grandson may not be unaware that the sentence reaches all the way to him, should he emulate his great-grandfather's faithlessness.

By making the law this plain God wanted to deter ungodly fathers, so that, recognizing how much evil the pursuit of idolatry brings forth, they might be called back to reverence for the Creator, if only out of love for their children; or else so that the children, fearing to incur their fathers' sins, would obey God's law. But they, intent on wickedness, began to interpret this differently, saying, “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge,” so that, feeling safe from punishment because their sins would be repaid upon their children, they themselves had no devotion either of spirit or of flesh. Hence it is said to them, not “The son shall die for the father” nor “The father for the son,” but “The soul that sins shall itself die,” so that they might learn that they would not go unpunished, and that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the children in this sense: because the children followed their parents' ungodliness and copied evils that ought to have been wiped out, they are punished more severely.

After God had shown what evil idolatry brings forth, he immediately added what blessings follow those who love him, saying, “and showing mercy to thousands of thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments,” so that he repays a father's goodness not only as far as the great-grandson but to thousands of thousands. For example, if someone of the seed of David, who certainly lived a thousand years earlier, loves the Lord, God's mercy is added to him, so that in his need he deserves to receive mercy on two grounds that plead for him: he is himself a worshipper of God, and he is of the seed of one who loved God. And in this God's clemency is praiseworthy, that to those who hate him he repays to the third and fourth generation and not to thousands of thousands; so that if the evil is drawn out to a fifth generation, it begins again from there as from a new head, and is counted from that point to the third and fourth generation.

But someone will say, “It seems just that more should be repaid to the one who originates evil than to the one who imitates it.” A fitting punishment is inflicted on the originator; but the extra that Scripture says is repaid to the children is the penalty of the fathers. And if you ask, sinners become more guilty with the coming of the law, as with Lamech, and after Lamech. Some, however, think that the sins of the fathers were repaid upon the children in this way: they were led into captivity because of their fathers and remained there until the fourth generation. But if that is true, God repaid the sins of the fathers not only upon those who hate him but also upon those who love his name, for Daniel was carried away, and the three youths, and Baruch and Ezekiel, and Ezra was born there. So it is plain that what we said above fits the question before us.
XV. SINCE THE LAW PROCLAIMS THE RIGHTEOUS MAN, AND HE IS TRULY RIGHTEOUS WHO HAS FULL RIGHTEOUSNESS, WHY DOES SOLOMON ON THE CONTRARY SAY, “DO NOT BE OVERLY RIGHTEOUS”?

Excessive righteousness falls into sin, but tempered righteousness makes people perfect. For the one who is overly righteous is not without malice, since if you answer sinners point for point, there will be no lack of occasions for you to sin. Indeed, God's own righteousness is tempered. With sinners he sometimes forgives, sometimes is angry, and sometimes repays them less than they deserve; for he bears with them, so that there may be some who make progress. The law, since it cannot soften itself, must be tempered by us, so that it may benefit those who live under it. So the one who imitates God is not overly righteous.
XVI. WHY WAS THE ANGEL WHO WANTED TO KILL MOSES ON THE WAY APPEASED BY THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE INFANT?

What Moses had done without forethought he corrected when the threatening angel appeared. Then, once the angel saw that what had been passed over through negligence was attended to, he ceased from his anger. Moses saw the angel so hostile to him and ready to punish because the fault of an exalted man is a grave sin: the more highly his person is regarded, the more his slight offence becomes a most bitter sin. He was on his way to the children of Israel, sent by the God of Abraham, and yet he did not bear the sign of Abraham's righteousness, in which he knew the Jews gloried; so he would have been called either a deceiver himself or someone not sent by the same God who had chosen Abraham. For while living in Midian he had not circumcised his sons. Either he ought not to have taken them with him to Egypt, since he was going there to lead the others out, or at the very least he ought to have taken them circumcised, for the reasons we have given above.

So Zipporah, Moses' wife, not being unaware why the angel appeared hostile to her husband, took her son and circumcised him, and the angel withdrew; this Scripture tells in condensed form. The anger was appeased by the same cause by which it had been kindled. For Scripture tells some things in condensed form, wanting them to be understood from the reasoning set before us, as in what the Saviour said to the Jews among other things: “Why do you also set aside the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition? For God said, ‘Honour your father and mother,’ and ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.’ But you say, ‘Whoever says to father or mother, “Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you,”’ and he has not honoured his father or his mother.” Without doubt the Saviour said this in condensed form, so that it would be understood that the priests of the Jews, being devoted to greed, had despised God's law. In an ungodly conspiracy they advised sons who cursed father or mother to offer something as a gift to God, by which the sentence pronounced against those who curse would be annulled; and so the sons, made secure, despised their parents against God's commandment. In the same way Moses, seeing the angel hostile to him, understood the cause and showed his wife what had to be done, so that the angel who sought to kill him would withdraw from him. This is understood in this case, just as what we said above about the priests.
XVII. WHY DOES IT CALL THOSE ACCURSED WHO HAVE LEFT NO OFFSPRING IN ISRAEL, WHILE THROUGH ISAIAH IT SAYS THAT IT DOES EUNUCHS NO HARM THAT THEY CANNOT BEGET?

Because it had begun to be understood otherwise than it was given, the prophet Isaiah afterwards showed in what sense it had been said. It had been laid down by way of a sentence because God was offended: those who deserted God were struck with this, that when they took wives they would leave no offspring. But human error seized on this so as to think that people were guilty before God if they did not want wives, or if, having taken them, they could not beget, as often happens, as though God sought nothing but offspring; and for this they are rebuked through the prophet Malachi. So Isaiah, to console those whom a wrong understanding had saddened, taught that it does no harm if someone either cannot have children or does not want them, provided he keeps God's law. The curse applied to those who, though able and willing, were barren because divine judgment stood in their way, so that they would not have the fruit of the creation of God, whom they spurned; so that when they saw that they either could not beget or could not keep those they had begotten, they would recognize that it was the wrath of an indignant God, and would turn and make amends.

For holy men too, when they longed for children and did not obtain them, thought that their sins stood in the way, and grieved, not knowing that it was God's providence, for which they were being reserved. Indeed, by God's provision Hannah conceived and bore Samuel, Elizabeth bore John, and the wife of Manoah bore Samson. But the spiritual understanding in this matter is that those are to be held accursed who have not left offspring that sees the Lord, that is, “who has not instructed a son or a servant or a neighbour to teach the fear of God on the earth.”
XVIII. WHY DID SAUL, WHEN HE SINNED, ASK THAT PRAYER BE MADE FOR HIM SO THAT HE MIGHT BE FORGIVEN, AND YET COULD NOT OBTAIN IT, WHILE DAVID, WHEN HE SINNED, ASKED AND RECEIVED PARDON?

It is not fitting to call God's judgment into question. Rather, human weakness and ignorance ought to let God's judgment teach it in matters it does not understand, so that from God's verdict it may grasp the truth, and see that nothing else ought to have been done than what it sees the Lord did, knowing that he is no respecter of persons. If he accepted David's plea and rejected Saul's, we must not think that the Lord did anything wrong. Knowing in what spirit each of them spoke, he accepted the petition of the one whom he saw asking pardon with a troubled heart; but he disregarded the other, because the pain of repentance had not touched his soul. For God listens to the heart more than to the voice. Hence it is said, “Man looks on the face, but God on the heart.” This is why we are deceived: pretence in words and looks gets the better of us, for we cannot see what is in the heart.

Therefore we must follow the judgment of God, who examines each person according to the heart, where each one's true intention lies. We find that the Saviour did this too. He did not accept the scribe who offered himself, but he called Levi as he sat at the tax booth, because the scribe's heart did not follow his words, whereas Levi, though silent, had in his heart what the scribe had in his words. And Jesus, who, as it is written, knew what was in man, chose Levi. Besides, David did not want another to be humbled on his behalf, as Saul did; he himself, a suppliant with a troubled heart, prayed for pardon.
XIX. WE MUST ASK WHETHER ADAM, WHEN HE WAS MADE, HAD AN IMMORTAL OR A MORTAL BODY.

God made man so that he would flourish in immortality as long as he did not sin, making him the author of his own life or death. If he guarded himself from sin, he could rejoice that he was immortal by his own effort; but if he became careless, he would have himself to blame for having begun to be mortal. For as long as he remained under the Creator's law, he was worthy to eat of the tree of life, so that he could not die. His body was not of such a kind that it seemed impossible for it to be dissolved; rather, tasting the tree of life held back the body's decay. Indeed, even after his sin he could have remained indissoluble, if only he had been allowed to eat of the tree of life. For how could he have had an immortal body when it was sustained by food? One who is immortal needs neither food nor drink. Food supplied strength, but the tree of life, like a medicine, kept away all decay. For man it was like an impregnable wall.
XX. WHAT DOES IT MEAN WHEN IT SAYS, “MAN ATE THE BREAD OF ANGELS,” SINCE ANGELS NEED NO FOOD, BEING SIMPLE BY NATURE AND STRONG WITH SPIRITUAL POWER?

The bread it calls “of angels” is the manna. Manna means “What is this?” For when the children of Israel saw something white like coriander seed falling on the ground, they said to one another, “What is this?”, which in Hebrew is “manni?” So this bread or food was not created by the world's law through a mixing of the elements, but came from above, provided by a spiritual design. Nor indeed was it kept in the heavens, since it was created by God's power at that moment to nourish bodies. It was called the bread of angels because it was created by the power by which the angelic nature subsists and lives; for without God no one has life. So because it is said to have come from heaven, it was called the bread of angels. He spoke this way to recall how great and how many are God's benefits toward man, so that, recognizing this, they would give thanks to God, who governs his servants with such care that, if need be, he provides them, while they are still in the flesh, with the things by which angels live.

Among other things the apostle said, “And the rock was Christ,” so that, because water flowed from the rock by Christ's power, Christ is called the rock. In the same way, because the manna came from heaven by his power, Christ may be called manna, that is, bread; and what was done then may be regarded as a figure of what is now offered in the church. So the bread of the Christian peoples, whom Scripture signified by “angels,” was eaten by “men,” that is, by the Jews. And because grace is greater now than it was among the prophets, and liberty has been given through Christ, for “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty,” by comparison of the times and of the graces Christians are called angels, with whose bread, which is Christ, the Jews, whom it called men, were fed. Christ belongs rather to those to whom he has been revealed and who are deemed worthy to be called by his name. So the question above can be understood in two ways: the bread can be called the bread of the heavenly angels, and also the bread of Christians, in the sense explained.
XXI. WHAT IT MEANS THAT GOD MADE MAN IN THE IMAGE AND LIKENESS OF GOD, AND WHETHER WOMAN IS THE IMAGE OF GOD.

Man was made in the image of God in this sense: the One made one, so that just as all things come from the one God, so the whole human race comes from one man. The likeness is this: just as the Son is from the Father, so the woman is from the man, so that the authority of a single origin is preserved. But the Son was born of God the Father ineffably and incomprehensibly, whereas the woman, as we read, was made from the man bodily, so that through her birth might arise. The Son of God, on the other hand, was born so that creation might come into being through him. In this, then, they are unlike: God was born of God, but woman of man, because there simplicity is found, and nothing but the simple could be born of the simple, spirit of spirit, God of God. Therefore the man is the image of God. For so it is written: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him.” Hence the apostle too says, “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God”; but, he says, “let the woman cover her head.” Why? Because she is not the image of God. Hence the apostle says again, “A woman is not permitted to teach or to have authority over a man.”
XXII. WHAT DOES SOLOMON MEAN WHEN HE SAYS, “JUSTIFY YOUR SOUL BEFORE YOUR DEATH,” WHILE THE PSALM SAYS, “NO ONE LIVING WILL BE JUSTIFIED IN THE SIGHT OF GOD”?

He justifies his soul before death who, in the hope of the life to come, attains faith, so as not to die ungodly. Solomon is speaking of someone who lives under the law and does not turn rightly. If such a person amends his mind so as to walk in the ways of righteousness, he justifies his soul before death. Solomon gave this counsel because of the coming judgment, so that no one careless of himself should die in his sins. David, however, spoke of the perfection of righteousness, because no one will be justified before the Lord, so as to be worthy of the promise, unless he has died in righteousness. For as long as he lives, he does not yet possess full merit for the things to come. Hence the Saviour says, “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”
XXIII. WHETHER SOULS ARE PASSED ON BY TRANSMISSION, AS BODIES ARE.

I think it unseemly to say that souls are generated together with bodies, so that soul is born from soul; this does not befit even the soul itself. Or if indeed the heavenly powers were each made individually and the rest were born from them, could it also seem credible that the other souls are born from the one soul of Adam? But that is not fitting, because to God alone was it possible to beget something simple, and this was not granted to others. This is so mysterious in the case of the Saviour that it is thought incredible not only by Gentiles and Jews but even by those who call themselves Christians; for both the Photinians and the Arians reject this faith.

For suppose the soul is generated from soul at the time the body is sown. We read that a rib was taken from Adam, yet not that a soul was born from a soul; and if the rib had a soul with it, then that soul was not born but detached as a part. But this is not written either. For the prophet Zechariah says among other things, “who forms the spirit of man within him.” Nor does Isaiah disagree with them when he says, “Thus says the Lord God, who made you and formed you in the womb.” If, then, it is formed in the womb, it is given to a body already formed. Since it fills all the members of the body, it is said to be shaped in the body; and just as water, though it has no shape, appears shaped when poured into a vessel, so the soul, though by nature incorporeal and simple, is as it were shaped into the body as it gives life to each member. Moses taught this more plainly when he said, “If anyone strikes a woman who is with child and she miscarries, if it was formed, he shall give life for life; but if it was unformed, he shall be fined,” to prove that there is no soul before the body has form. So if the soul is given to a body already formed, it is not born at the body's conception, drawn off along with the seed. For if it comes into being with the seed, and soul from soul, many souls perish every day, when seed is lost through some discharge and does not lead to birth.

But if we look more closely, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us consider the making of Adam, for in Adam an example has been given, from which we may understand that the body was already formed when it received the soul. God could have mixed the soul into the clay of the earth and formed the body that way. But it was formed according to a reasoned order, because the house had first to be built and then the inhabitant brought in. Certainly the soul, being spirit, cannot dwell in what is dry; that is why it is carried in the blood. So when the body's features have not yet been put together, where will the soul be? Or does it wander outside until it is sent in, although reason teaches that it is given in order to animate the body, not to wander about idle? But let those who think otherwise say from whom it is given: from the male or from the female? If from the female, that does not fit, because the example shows otherwise. For they claim that the soul too was given from the man along with the rib, which we have shown to be weak on many grounds. Hence it might perhaps seem to be given from the woman, chiefly because of the Saviour, who we know was born of a woman, from the Holy Spirit, without carnal union. But if they think this, they give more to women, for they transfer the man's authority to the woman. Though they say that the origin of both body and soul is from the man, they turn around and say that the better part, the soul, comes from the woman, and the lesser part, the body, from the male, although it is obvious that the order of the example handed down by God cannot be changed.
XXIV. WHY, SINCE MAN AND WOMAN ARE ONE FLESH, IS THE MAN THE IMAGE OF GOD AND NOT THE WOMAN AS WELL?

Man and woman are indeed of one substance, both in soul and in flesh, but the man is greater in rank, because the woman comes from him, as the apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man.” For it is origin, not substance, that made the man greater. In one body, too, there are greater and lesser members, not by nature but by order.
XXV. WHY DID JOSEPH, AFTER HIS PROPHECY, MAKE THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SWEAR THAT WHEN THEY WERE SET FREE BY GOD THEY WOULD CARRY HIS REMAINS OUT OF EGYPT?

It is plain that Joseph did not give this command to the children of Israel idly. One who was able to prophesy must be believed not to have spoken without foresight. He was especially devoted to God the Creator, and he knew that the Egyptians revered him because of his administration, by which he had governed Egypt in a time of great want. So he sought to remove an error after his death, being certain that the folly of the crowd venerates the dead as gods more than the living, and he did not want the honour owed to the Creator to be paid to him. Here, then, he showed that he was free of the empty superstition of the Egyptians, when he ordered his remains to be carried away so that it would not lead to an insult to God. We find that the apostles followed this example too. When Paul and Barnabas saw that people wanted to offer sacrifice to them, knowing that this was hateful to God, they tore their garments, saying, “What are you doing? We too are men like you,” and so they restrained the crowds.
XXVI. WE MUST INQUIRE ABOUT ELISHA WHETHER HE OBTAINED WHAT HE IS SAID TO HAVE ASKED OF ELIJAH, A HARD THING.

Holy Elisha was eager to work mighty deeds, drawn on by his master's example. When he was given the chance to ask for whatever he wanted, he was greedy for the good and asked that the spirit might be in him twice over compared with what was in his master. Elijah, the man of God, said to him: "You have asked a hard thing." In his eagerness he had not considered that the disciple is not above the master. Yet Elijah, knowing that he had not asked this out of ambition for present glory, answered: "Nevertheless, if you see me taken from you, it will be so for you." The meaning here must be weighed carefully. Somewhat indignant, he had said, "You have asked a hard thing," and then he added, "Nevertheless, if you see me taken up, it will be so for you." Since he had seemed to refuse him, was he not showing that it would happen to him as was fitting, and not as he himself had asked? Scripture wants much to be understood between the lines, so that the sense gathered from its words may not be contrary to the reason of religion. A hard request ought certainly to have lost even the reward that was due. But because he asked in this way out of eagerness for the good, God, who knows what gift should be given to each, did not allow him to be deprived of what he deserved.

Let us see, then, whether Elijah's merit would allow Elisha to deserve to receive his gift doubled. Through Zechariah the Holy Spirit said what John's merit would be: "He will come," it says, "in the spirit and power of Elijah." So it shows John to be Elijah's equal. And the Lord says: "Among those born of women no prophet is greater than John the Baptist." He did not say "he is greater than all," but "no one is greater than he," that is, "he has an equal, but he has no superior." Elijah, then, is his equal, and certainly less than no one. How then is Elisha greater than Elijah, when John, than whom no one is greater, is Elijah's equal? For when Elisha came to cross the waters, he did not receive from them the honor of being able to cross until he had named the God of Elijah. By this his hard request might be seen to be rebuked, since he was heard only in Elijah's name. So no one would think that he had received what he had harshly asked, as though the dispensation of the Spirit granted to Elijah were not enough for what that time deserved.
XXVII. Whether the medium raised up Samuel, and whether he was seen by her and spoke to Saul, as the narrative in the Book of Kings relates.

I consider it an outrageous thing to give assent to this according to the words of the narrative. How could it happen that a man holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life should be drawn up by magic art? Or, if he was not drawn up, did he consent? Either belief is contrary to what we should hold of a righteous man. If he was brought unwillingly, righteousness has no support. If he came willingly, then he lost the merit of the spiritual life which he had sought while placed in the flesh. That is utterly absurd, because one who departs from here righteous remains righteous. This is rather a trick of Satan, by which, to deceive as many as possible, he pretends that he holds even the good in his power. As the apostle says among other things: "Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light." To produce error, in which he glories, he disguised himself in the appearance and name of a righteous man, so that he might falsely persuade the worshipers of God that the hope they preached profits nothing, since he pretended that the righteous who depart from here were in his power.

But some are misled by the fact that he did not lie about the death of Saul and his son, as though it were a great thing for the devil to foresee the fall of a body before the day came. After all, certain signs commonly appear in those who are about to die, inasmuch as God's protection seems to have been withdrawn from them. How much more can the devil foresee it, whom the prophetic oracles testify was exalted in angelic majesty, and of whose greatness the apostle says: "Or do you not know the heights of Satan?" What wonder, then, if he could foresee a death close at hand, since this is the very means by which he deceives and wants to be worshiped as having God's power? For Saul had become so dull-witted and mad that he fled to a medium. Corrupted by sin, he turned to the very things he had condemned.

But someone may think that, for the sake of the narrative and what is expressed in its words, these things should not be passed over, lest the account of the narrative be empty. He will indeed do right, provided he refers it not to the truth of the matter but to what Saul saw and understood. Once he had been rejected, he could not have a sound understanding. The historian described Saul's mind and Samuel's appearance, setting down what was said and seen, and leaving aside whether it was true or false. What does he say? Saul heard in what garb the figure had been raised up, and "he perceived," it says, "that it was Samuel." The historian reported what Saul perceived. And because Saul did not perceive rightly, he worshiped someone other than the Lord, contrary to Scripture. Thinking that it was Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that Satan had the fruit of his deceit. For this is what he strives for, to be worshiped as God. If Samuel had truly appeared to him, that righteous man, who had preached that the Lord alone is to be worshiped, would certainly not have allowed himself to be worshiped. And how could the man of God, who was with Abraham in the place of refreshment, say to a pestilent man who deserved the burning of Gehenna, "Tomorrow you will be with me"?

On these two points the improvident Satan betrayed the subtlety of his deceit. First, he allowed himself to be worshiped under the guise and name of Samuel, contrary to the law. Second, he falsely claimed that a man weighed down by sins would be with the most righteous Samuel, though there is a great distance between sinners and the righteous. The statement could seem true if the name of Samuel were left out, because Saul was going to be with the devil. For he passed over to the one whom he had worshiped. So the devil, though he always hides under a veil, betrays himself when he invents things abhorrent to the persons through whom he tries to deceive.
XXVIII. What should be said in reply to those who say that this world moves naturally from eternity and is subject neither to a beginning nor to destruction.

That the world exists from eternity and is subject to nothing cannot be proved and is impossible. We see that it is bodily and exists in great diversity, whereas nothing can be divine and eternal unless it is simple, so that no diversity is seen in it but there is unity. The world does not even keep the changes of the seasons constant. So it is varied not only in its seasons, and composed of contrary substances, but also in the very changes of the seasons. An eternal thing, however, abhors diversity, and since it is incorporeal it cannot be grasped by touch or sight. But this world can be acted upon: water fights against fire, and fire, if there is more of it, overcomes water; and earth, though dry and cold by nature, is burned like any bodily thing. It is therefore unfitting to call the world eternal. Since we see that it is subject to being acted upon and fails with age in each of its parts, we believe that it will also come to an end.

And what does one who thinks the world eternal hold about man? Man certainly had a beginning within the world. Without man, then, whom did the world's yearly fruitfulness benefit? Or did it produce without any providence? And how did an eternal thing produce corruptible and mortal things, when what comes from the eternal ought to be eternal? With what audacity is something called eternal when it is visible and can be perceived and touched? And how can something be called eternal when it depends on the changes of the seasons, and the seasons themselves sometimes fail to do their work? For eternity is neither corrupted nor changed.
XXIX. Why was circumcision commanded on the eighth day?

Circumcision was commanded on the eighth day after birth because, by the count and cycle of seven days, the eighth day turns out to be the first again, coming as it were after the sabbath, so that it is now reckoned not the eighth but the first. The salvation to come through Christ was predestined for the first day, which is called the Lord's day because on it the Lord rose, and it comes after the sabbath. For this reason a figure of this salvation was given in circumcision, so that the renewal to come might be recognized in the law of circumcision. And because people were to be saved through faith, which was confirmed on the first day by the Lord's resurrection, a figure of this was given in circumcision on the first day, and circumcision was also a sign of Abraham's faith. So the reason is complete: the sign of past faith, signified on the first day, was a figure of the future faith established on the first day.
XXX. In Proverbs it says: "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech." How is he righteous if he is a sinner?

All truth is righteousness. Whoever confesses what is the case is righteous, for he speaks the truth; but sinners who defend their offenses cannot be justified. So a man of this kind is rightly called righteous, because by declaring his sin he is surely asking for it to be forgiven, imploring God's mercy. For he knows what is said in the law: "Confess your sins, so that you may be justified." And what is it to confess at the beginning of one's speech, if not to admit one's sin voluntarily and not under compulsion? Who, even among those who fear God, is without sin, when offenses are mixed in even with our thoughts and we sometimes sin unwillingly? The verse can, however, also be said or understood of the one called a catechumen, who approaches the faith in order to be justified. When he asks to be changed, he undoubtedly confesses himself a sinner, so that he may be justified.
XXXI. Whether it was a serpent by nature that spoke with the woman, or whether the devil, called a serpent because of what he did, led her astray.

As far as the narrative is concerned, it is a serpent by nature that is spoken of, which was wiser than the other beasts that the Lord God had made on the earth. Indeed, God also passed sentence on the serpent. It would be no wonder if the devil were wiser than beasts, for the apostle says of him among other things: "Or do you not know the heights of Satan?" But the serpent was so truly a serpent by nature that it was told: "On your breast and belly you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life." These things are far from Satan's condition, since he is neither bodily nor mortal. And if one looks more closely, it will be seen that the sentence did the serpent no harm; it was simply ordered to remain in the state in which it was made. It had become Satan's servant in subjugating man, to whom God had subjected all things. Therefore God, keeping it in the subjection by which he had made all things subject to man, checked the serpent's arrogance, because it had begun to serve pride. For man seemed to have been placed under the serpent, since he had taken its counsel and despised the law he had been given. That serpents are prudent the Lord confirms in the Gospel, saying: "Be shrewd as serpents."

Since it is clear, then, that a serpent truly spoke with Eve, it remains to determine whether it could have been so prudent and shrewd as to deceive her by guile. Though it was more prudent than the other beasts, it was not more prudent than humans, since no animal is rational except man. It is therefore impossible that the serpent devised this subtle plot. Though it is called prudent, it is not so beyond its nature; it does not deliberate, devise or form plans. So there is no doubt that it was the devil who got the better of the woman through the serpent. Mingling himself with the serpent, he acted through it as through an instrument, so that the woman, knowing the serpent to be prudent, did not detect the guile of the hidden devil. Thus the sentence, though given bodily, fell spiritually on Satan, because a sentence binds the guilty party. It was not given by a man, who might perhaps destroy an innocent party through error or malice, but by God, who certainly cannot be deceived so that his sentence fails to bind the one who is guilty. Satan is invisible, but he carried out his deceit through a body; so the sentence appears to have been given bodily, in order that it might bind spiritually the one whose deed caused it to be given. For the utterly shameless Satan, cast down from the most sacred seats of heaven, rolls about on the earth, forever groaning.

But someone may perhaps say: "And in what language, do you suppose, did the serpent speak to the woman?" With the serpent's mouth, of course.
