Even today there is no lack of people who understand the barking of dogs, the howling of wolves, the trumpeting of elephants and the crowing of cocks. Why then could the woman, still newly made, not all the more know and understand the hissing of serpents, when we know many people who can tell the calls of birds apart? It is also established that the devil uses the tongue of the creature whose body he has entered; otherwise he could not have deceived the woman. So he spoke through the serpent with the serpent's mouth.
XXXII. We read in Solomon: "The rich man and the poor man met; but God made them both." How then is it that there is no partiality with God?

Far be such an impious claim from the minds of the faithful! To teach that the poor man is not to be despised nor the rich man honored, Scripture shows that God is the maker of both. He made them not in their poverty and riches, but in what they are. Though they differ from each other in their means, they do not differ in the substance of their nature. Circumstances bring about certain outcomes in the world, making some prosperous in riches and others unlucky in poverty. But that is no reason to despise those whom God has not humbled, or to look up to those for whom the truth has not testified. Those who are plainly to be despised are the corrupters of morals and those who commit sacrilege against God's law; those to be honored are the ones who love God and cultivate discipline.

For those of good conduct are counted rich in God's sight, and the more contemptible they are in the world, the more honored they are in heaven. God gave the earth to all, commands his sun to rise on everyone, and pours out his rain without distinction; but the injustice of the times, chance circumstances or want deny some people what God gave to all. So those who enjoy the favor of the times in increasing their wealth, if they know themselves and understand God's will, should minister to such people. Then, discerning God's will, they will be rich not only in the world but also in heaven, and the riches of a short time will not shut them out of the eternal ones. As for those whom they think despicable because of their poverty, if they contemplate God's coming judgment, they will be forever rich there, where the rich of this age will be in need and will regret that they were not poor.
XXXIII. Solomon says: "The years of the wicked will be shortened." Yet we see a good many wicked people who live long.

It would indeed be fitting that all the wicked should not only lose this light sooner, but not enjoy life for even a single moment, since they forget their Creator and ascribe all authority over life to the creature. But Scripture is speaking of those wicked people who lived under God's law and were nevertheless more inclined to idols. They are worse than the other wicked, because they know the Lord and despise him, and obey servants instead. The apostle proves that this was said of them, saying: "Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law." The Gentiles, however, are not counted among the living.
XXXIV. In Solomon it says: "God did not make death," and in another place: "Good and evil, life and death, poverty and wealth are from God."

No one doubts that all good things are from God. The evils he spoke of are evils to us when punishment is exacted from us. Punishment, even when justly inflicted, still seems evil to the one who suffers it. So too God speaks to sinners through the prophet, saying: "I will do evil to you," that is, "I will drive you with punishments." Life and death are from God in this sense: he gave the law, which promises life to those who keep it, but death to those who despise it, namely the death that is called the second. Since he judges what each person deserves, both acquittal to life and condemnation to death come from him. He is not, then, the inventor of death but its judge, for the author of death is sin. How could God, who does not know how to sin, make death? But because he repays sins, death is said to be from him, although it does not come from him but from the one who sinned.

By the same reasoning poverty and riches are from God. Some people who have the fear of God spurn luxury, flee a prodigal life, and do not turn their eyes away from the needy or the poor; people of this kind increase their goods. For it is written in Proverbs: "Discipline takes away poverty and disgrace." But those who do not have the fear of God live too loosely and despise the needy, and, as it is written, they will be in want, being not only careless and improvident about their own affairs but also despisers of the law they were given. It is in this way that God makes people poor and rich. When offending against the law brings need, this is said to be done by God, since he is the law's author; and when some keep the discipline of the law out of fear, they are made rich by God, the author of the law.
XXXV. On what ground does David call Saul the Lord's anointed and defer to him, after God had departed from Saul?

David was not unaware that the office of kingship is bestowed by God. He therefore honors Saul as one still holding what had been bestowed, so as not to seem to wrong God, who decreed honor for these offices. For the king bears the image of God, as the bishop bears that of Christ. As long, then, as he holds what was bestowed on him, he is to be honored, if not for his own sake, then for the sake of his office. Hence the apostle says: "Be subject to all the higher powers. For there is no power except from God; those that exist have been ordained by God." This is why we honor even a pagan who has been placed in power, though he himself is unworthy, since he holds what God has ordained and yet gives thanks to the devil. The power requires it, because it deserves honor. That is why the dream of the coming famine was revealed to Pharaoh; and why Nebuchadnezzar alone, though others stood beside him, saw the Son of God in the fiery furnace. This was certainly not by his own merit, since he wanted to be worshiped in an idol, but by the merit of the royal office.
XXXVI. If "the soul that sins shall itself die," how is it that Achan son of Carmi sinned and thirty-six men were killed on his account?

Scripture spoke in a different sense from the one proposed. It was not speaking of this death that is common to all, but of the one that is called the second. This second death receives sinners. But Achan's sin was not repaid upon those who died in the battle; rather, it harmed them by keeping them from prevailing over the enemy with the help of divine protection. They were not weakened because of Achan; but since they were not defended by God's help at all, they were unable to fight bravely and so were killed. They were few against many, and that is why they are known to have been defeated. There is, then, no injustice in God's will. It is in his power whether he wishes to help: if he is present, he is merciful; if he does not wish to be, he is just. He is not in debt to such people, so as to be bound to them. That is why Joshua son of Nun was grieved and tore his garments, understanding that the Lord had not withdrawn his help without cause.
XXXVII. What does it mean that death sent upon Jacob came upon Israel, when Jacob himself was called Israel?

He gave one people two names, so that their merits could be understood from the names. Certainly the man surnamed Israel was earlier called Jacob. Wrestling with the Savior, he understood that the one he saw in bodily form was God, and so he was called "a man seeing God." The people he calls Jacob, then, signifies in this place and in this matter the carnal people, in the way that names are given to children by their parents. But these, that is, the Jews, were not called Israelites because of their evil works, since they sacrificed to calves and in groves in Samaria by the zeal and command of King Jeroboam. The people who offered victims in Jerusalem in the Lord's temple through God's priests was called Israel. So Samaria was handed over to captivity and death for its impiety, but Jerusalem was spared because it had kings who loved God. But when Jerusalem too followed the impiety of Samaria, the sentence passed on Samaria seized her as well.

That is why it was said: "God sent death upon Jacob" — that is, upon the people of Samaria, who lived carnally, as we said above — "and it came upon Israel," that is, upon the people of Jerusalem, because it followed idolatry in imitation of Samaria. So it was carried off into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, just as Samaria had been by Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians. Put plainly: the sentence passed on the wicked found the good as well, once they ceased to be righteous. The death sent upon Jacob, as was shown above, reached Israel, without passing Samaria by. But when the cause for which it was sent upon Samaria was found in Jerusalem too, the death sent there came also to the place where the same cause remained. For punishment follows the cause and makes no distinction of persons.
XXXVIII. If the horse and the mule have no understanding, how much less does the earth, a thing without sense? What does it mean, then, that the earth is said to bless God?

It is not to be understood as the words sound. The earth is a work which, though mute, is said to cry out the praise of its Creator; for it urges those who look at it to bless its Maker, just as every well-made vessel praises its craftsman. We read in the Psalms, after all: "Will the dust confess you," it says, "or declare your truth?" In every senseless substance, then, it is not will, which it certainly does not have, but works that bless their author. But if you wish to take this spiritually, understand earth to signify man, according to the prophet's saying, "Remember, Lord," he says, "that we are earth." The works of creation urge man to break forth in praise of his Creator.
XXXIX. What does it mean when we read in Solomon: "There is hope," he says, "in darkness; a dog is better than a dead lion"?

Darkness signifies paganism and ignorance. So he wants it understood that there is more hope in a pagan than in an apostate, through what he added: "A dog is better than a dead lion." For just as the lion is stronger than all wild beasts, so Christianity is stronger than all sects. If anyone abandons it, then, he loses salvation, so that he becomes worse than a pagan. A pagan may come to believe and gain the salvation that the apostate has lost. And even if the pagan does not believe, the apostate is still worse, because it is worse to have lost salvation than never to have had it. The Saviour shows that "dog" signifies a pagan when he says: "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."

XL. WHAT DOES THE PROPHET MEAN WHEN HE SAYS: "REJOICE, BARREN ONE, YOU WHO DO NOT BEAR; BREAK FORTH AND CRY ALOUD, YOU WHO ARE NOT IN LABOUR, FOR THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ONE ARE MORE THAN THE CHILDREN OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND"?

Since the children of the earthly Jerusalem have fallen away from God, joy cannot be ascribed to her, but only grief. So, to the shame of this Jerusalem, the prophet says that the Jerusalem above ought to rejoice, the one the apostle calls our mother. Without groaning and pain she has far more children than this one, who gives birth in the flesh with tears, namely to the Jews, while the other gives birth spiritually, through faith, to Christians. He calls her desolate, or deserted, because she is life itself, which Adam first deserted when he followed death. So when people are reborn, they return to the life they had deserted. This life is Christ, for he himself said: "I am the life." God the Father is also life, for the Lord says: "As the Father has life, so he has given the Son to have life." Without doubt the Holy Spirit is also life, as the Lord says: "For he will take," he says, "of what is mine." Whoever has received from life is life, and so the three are one life. This is the life through faith in which we are reborn. She is our mother, as we also read in Genesis: "For she," it says (that is, life), "is the mother of all the living." And who are the living, if not those who believe?
XLI. WHETHER THE SPIRIT THAT WAS BORNE OVER THE WATERS IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD AS THE HOLY SPIRIT, SINCE IT IS SAID: "THE SPIRIT OF GOD WAS BORNE OVER THE WATER."

If some people think it is the Holy Spirit because we read that it is the Spirit of God, the claim is weak and empty. Not only does the order of the account not allow it and reason reject it, but the words themselves prove too weak to establish the case. We often find these same words signifying something else in the law. Among other things the Lord God says: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." And further on: "But I will blot out everything, from man to beast," because he was about to bring a flood upon the earth. Can the Holy Spirit be understood here? Was he not speaking of souls? For not only our souls are called spirits, but those of beasts as well. Thus it is written: "And all flesh died in the water, in which was the spirit of life." And in the prophet Ezekiel, where God promises that men will be restored, it is said: "Thus says the Lord to these bones: I will stretch skin over you and put my spirit in you, and you shall live." Was he speaking of the Holy Spirit and not of the soul?

All heavenly beings are indeed spirits, but they differ from one another. God too is spirit, but in a very different way. So every spirit belongs to God, yet none is God except the Spirit who is from him, and what marks him out is that he is called "Holy." Men too are called sons of God, and Christ is called the Son of God, but there is a great gap between them, because he is the true Son and they are adopted. In the same way there is a difference among the spirits of God. The Holy Spirit is from God and of one substance with him, while the other spirits are said to be of God but are creatures. Nor does the order of things allow us to understand that the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, since reason teaches that a spiritual creature was over the waters, one which has another, higher creature above it, for one creature differs from another in brightness. The nearer anything comes to the throne of God, the brighter are its ministries. That is why the angel Raphael says, among other things: "I am one of the seven holy angels who stand and go about before the majesty of God."
XLII. WHY DID THE ANGEL SENT TO SPEAK TO MOSES APPEAR IN FIRE AND IN A BUSH ON A MOUNTAIN?

God is exalted, so it was fitting that he should appear on high, in a place close to heaven. And because fire always seeks what is above, growing upward toward heaven, the Lord of the heavens ought to appear in that which strives from the ground toward the heights. It was on account of sins that he appeared in a bush. He had come down to give the law because of sins, and thorns signify sins ("I waited for it to produce grapes," he says, "but it produced thorns"). And the law did not come to punish at once, but first to make sin known. That is why the fire did not burn up the bush: the giving of the law did not make sinners guilty for what they had done in the past. And because sins do not belong to nature but arise by accident, the bramble, the stuff thorns are made of, does not have a root armed with thorns. So there was good reason for the Lord to appear to Moses in this way.
XLIII. SINCE WE KNOW THAT ABRAHAM WAS FORBIDDEN BY GOD TO SACRIFICE HIS SON, WHY WAS JEPHTHAH NOT FORBIDDEN WHEN HE OFFERED UP HIS DAUGHTER, BUT INSTEAD PAID HIS VOW TO GOD WITH HUMAN BLOOD?

There is a great difference between the case of Abraham and that of Jephthah. First, Abraham was born legitimately, whereas Jephthah was illegitimate, for he was the son of a prostitute. Next, Abraham's way of life was excellent, while Jephthah was a captain of robbers. Abraham was a righteous man, proved in testing, but there is no testimony at all to Jephthah's righteousness.

So Abraham was commanded to offer his son to God, so that people might see how much Abraham trusted God, since at his command he did not hesitate even to kill his own son. For there could be no doubt that the one who, against all worldly hope, had been able to make the boy be born of a barren old woman could, against all worldly reason, raise him from the dead. By this deed Abraham's righteousness was made complete. God showed that he had not asked for the boy's blood, but wanted his servant Abraham to grow greater through this deed. He wants those who love him to suffer something, so that he may be seen to promote them justly.

Jephthah, on the other hand, a criminal and thoughtless man, promised God a gift with a foolish vow, saying: "Whatever meets me in front of the door of my house when I return from the slaughter, I will offer to God." Was he forced to make this vow? Did he understand how a vow ought to be made? What if a dog or an ass had met him, which God had forbidden to be offered? Or someone else's son, or his wife? Would he then have paid his vow rejoicing at another's grief? So what this reckless and impious [?] man had vowed to the ruin of another was turned back upon him by divine judgment. And Jephthah was so senseless that even afterwards he did not see that his vow had been foolish, which would have let the error he had begun be corrected by him as well. He ought to have understood that God takes no delight in such a sacrifice, and to have prayed for forgiveness of his folly and offered something else that was not against the law. But the fool proved himself faithful as a parricide, though it is clear that foolish faithfulness not only does no good at all but does harm. So in his daughter's death he himself was the one struck down, and that is why God took no notice of such a sacrifice. For if he had forbidden it, he would have seemed to want Jephthah to offer him something else, when he knew that, being unworthy, Jephthah ought not to offer anything. His daughter, however, gained by it: dying innocent through her father's wickedness, she escaped the punishment of hell, which, had she perhaps lived long, she might not have been able to do.

That a triumphant victory attended Jephthah was not due to his merit, nor to the people's. We do not read that they pleaded with God to give them a defender. Did God send Jephthah, or speak to him? No. But because the foreigners were praising their gods for having made the children of Israel subject to them, and were reviling the God of Abraham, God took vengeance on the foreigners for the honour of his name: if not for the sake of these people, then at least for the merit of Abraham and for his own majesty. Or, because the spirit of the Lord leapt upon Samson while he was consorting with a prostitute, are we to call him worthy, when this was clearly done to destroy the foreigners?
XLIV. AGAINST THE JEWS.

It is written in the prophet Isaiah: "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations." But perhaps the Jews may say: "The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all." We do not object, provided, however, that the circumcised are attached to the law, as has always been the case. For the law belongs to those who were commanded to be circumcised after the manner of Abraham. On this view, then, nothing new can be seen in this text of the prophet, since from the beginning of Judaism no one coming from any nation was forbidden to join himself to the law. Nothing new can be thought to have been said by the prophet; rather, it would have been said to no purpose, if the Gentiles were always admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, for those who submitted themselves to the law are shown never to have been turned away. If, then, these things are so, the prophet seems to have needlessly announced something that, once handed down, had always been kept.

And could anyone be found so dull as to say that so great a prophet spoke of something needless and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this without forbidding it. For the Jewish people sinned against the Lord by seeking help from idols, and though the prophets often rebuked them for it, they refused to set out on the path of repentance and return to God. So God, to reproach them, made it known that he would open his house to all nations for prayer. In this way he showed that he would cast off the Jews and put others in their place. For if the nations had always been admitted to the law, as was said above, how could the prophet speak of this as something to come, unless he meant something other than what had been laid down before? He could not speak of something that happened every day as though it were still to come. Hence it is clear that this saying spells the ruin of the Jews. Through it the prophet showed them that they would be removed and that others would be called to receive the gift of God's grace that had been promised to the Jews.

What was promised, the prophet Isaiah teaches when he says: "There shall come from Zion one who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them." This covenant, then, is the abolition of sins. For this is the new covenant that was promised through Jeremiah, who says: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will accomplish a new covenant for the house of Israel and the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord." This was their transgression: when they made the image of the calf, they broke the covenant. That is also why the tablets on which the law had been given were broken at the foot of the mountain: they had deserved to receive heavy commandments.

But because God is merciful and compassionate, he promised through the prophets that he would change the law and give another covenant, different from the one he had given before. Not only what was burdensome would be changed, but also the things that had been given as a figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision. In this way people who had long been weighed down would be relieved in every respect and would humbly give thanks to God. And because the Jews persisted in their fathers' transgression and would not turn their minds from idols, God solemnly declares that the Gentiles, together with the remnant who kept faith, would enjoy the covenant he had said was to come. So the faithless Jews would be tormented by a double burden: for a time they were weighed down by commandments, and in the future they will pay the penalties they deserve, because they were found faithful neither in the old covenant nor in the new.

So he said that he would give a new covenant in order that the old one, which had been given to the fathers, might cease. And therefore whoever serves God under this covenant keeps neither the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions between foods, but has only the fear of God in faith, because he is justified not by the law but by faith. As the prophet Habakkuk says: "For the righteous shall live by my faith." So such a person no longer uses many commandments to win God's favour, but only a few. Isaiah again says the same thing in this sense, for he says: "Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant of them shall be saved. For he completes the word and cuts it short in righteousness, because God will make a shortened word throughout the whole world." To the remnant, who persevered in faith in the promise while the rest did not believe, he shows the shortened word of the law, that is, the new covenant he promised. It would not be called a covenant unless it too were ratified by the testimony of blood, just as the old covenant was, so that both bear the same name. But the old has many commandments and the new has few, as he promised. He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations, so the sons were to be justified in the same way the father had been justified. The things that began after Abraham's faith would cease, and those who took up the faith by which Abraham himself was justified would be sons of Abraham, as the Lord said. Indeed, it is neither surprising nor unheard of that people should be justified without concern for the sabbath, circumcision, and the other commandments of this kind.

For it was not by these things that Enoch pleased God and was taken up. Nor was Noah found to be the only righteous man at the flood because he kept them. Nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: for "Abraham believed God," it says, "and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Only then was he circumcised, so that it would be a sign in him that he had believed, though old, that he would have a son. It is not circumcision, then, that commends Abraham, but faith. And so faith is enough for believers to be justified, so that they are sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision. They have no need of circumcision, because what they believe is not the thing that Abraham believed. The Jews, however, were commanded to be circumcised so that they would bear the sign of Abraham's faith, not of their own. The purpose was that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. But if they believe, they will be his sons for justification as well.

For what good is it for a powerless man to be called the son of a powerful one? Is it not rather a hindrance? It is a disgrace for the son of a man of rank to be without honour. Indeed, circumcision of the flesh has so little merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that he will punish all who are circumcised in the foreskin if they are not circumcised in heart. But he is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart while uncircumcised in the flesh, since no one has ever pleased God without circumcision of the heart. All who are circumcised in the flesh, then, signify the race of Abraham according to the flesh. But those who are circumcised in heart signify the race of God according to faith, because they have been cut off from all worldly error and confess God as their father. What good, then, is circumcision of the flesh, when a Jew who lacks faith cannot attain the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is uncircumcision, when no one attains Abraham's righteousness unless he has followed the example of Abraham's faith?

It is pointless for them to boast of circumcision of the flesh, then, since they see that it has no merit before God. And if, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, then the Gentiles are better than the Jews, because the Gentiles have faith while the Jews have circumcision. Whom, do you think, would Abraham more readily acknowledge as his sons: those who resemble him according to the flesh, or those who resemble him in faith? But it is faith that bears witness to Abraham, and so he glories not in the flesh but in faith. He therefore accepts as sons those he sees imitating the thing in which he glories. For how can he call them his sons when he sees them shrink from the very thing by which he pleased God and was justified? He could judge them to be not sons but enemies. For by scorning the faith through which he was glorified, they show that they envy him.

Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found to be unbelieving and refuse to accept the new covenant, since we know that they were not faithful even under the old. They were always rebellious and insolent toward God, and that is why they received commandments designed to press down their unbending necks. They never wanted to hope for good things from God, even though they had known his great benefits and wondrous mighty works. That is why, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: "I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries, because they did not carry out my ordinances and they rejected my commandments." And further on: "And I gave them commandments that were not good, and ordinances by which they shall not live." He shows why commandments so many and so harsh were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great blessings, justice required that they be pressed down by more severe commandments. He called these commandments "not good," though they are just, because they served not for their justification but for their ruin. A punishment, even when deservedly inflicted, is not good for the one who suffers it. Yet after this, because God is kind, he promised to give a new covenant, in which an abridgment of the law would justify believers as Abraham was justified. New moons, the sabbath, circumcision and the other commandments would cease, though not those that belong to the natural law, such as the laws against murder, adultery and the like. And so believers would be justified just as Abraham was. For when he renewed the faith of Abraham, he willed all these things to cease, so that the time would be like the time when Abraham believed.

But perhaps the Jews may say: "If the things given by Moses are said to cease through the abridgment of the law, was circumcision given by Moses, so that it too should cease? Through it we bear the sign of our father, since we are sons of Abraham, and it ought not to cease, because it testifies to our lineage." Circumcision did indeed have to be kept in its own time, that is, before the promised new covenant was given. But once the burdens of the law were ordered to cease by the gift of God's grace, what need is there to be circumcised? A new law, that is, a spiritual one, was given for this very reason: so that carnal things would cease and those who accepted it would receive its sign. In the old covenant they had the sign of Abraham, with whom the old covenant began. In the same way, in the new covenant they would have the sign of the Saviour, who established the new covenant. For just as the Hebrews took their name from Abraham, so Christians take theirs from Christ. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the new covenant that God promised. They bring to nothing the kindness and mercy of God. He no longer wished his people to be counted under the name of a man, and so he graciously established them under the name of his Son.

With what audacity, then, do the Jews say that we use not our own law but theirs, when David says: "I will praise you among the nations," and again: "Feast, you nations, with his people"? And the Lord says to the prophet Jeremiah: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations." Judaism certainly has its own designations, for that people is referred to as Jacob, or Samaria, or Jerusalem, or Judah, or Israel. But it is plain that he refers to the nations in a different way from the Jews.

Jeremiah, then, is our prophet. For although God showed in all the prophets that the Gentiles would share in his gift, he speaks specially to Jeremiah, because he gave him to us as a prophet. Jeremiah foretold the new covenant, which would benefit the Gentiles more than the Jews, and this now seems to have been made plain. For while the new covenant is preached throughout the whole world, a believing Jew is found so rarely and with such difficulty that all the churches of the new covenant are called churches of the Gentiles. As was said in the prophet Hosea: "I will call those who were not my people 'my people,' and her who was not beloved 'beloved.'" So he has rejected the Jews and calls the Gentiles together by the same merciful grace with which he graciously called Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. So the one who graciously called Abraham has graciously called the Gentiles as well.

Why, then, do they say, "The law is ours," when it is clear that God's gift belongs to all who are willing? Let them stop this rash usurpation, for the grace of God is common to all. And how can they shamelessly deny that our Christ was promised in the law, when they see in him all the signs that the law foretold? According to the promise made to Abraham, all nations that believe in him are justified. According to Isaiah's prophecy, he was born of a virgin in Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah and the seed of David, as had been promised. As Jeremiah prophesied, he preached the new covenant that God had promised would come. After displaying all the signs of his mighty works, he humbled himself in accordance with the sayings of the prophets. He suffered everything that had been foretold, and he rose on the third day, as is written in the prophet.

And if they ask about the time of the promise, as it was revealed to the prophet Daniel, they will find it fulfilled at the time when Christ was born and suffered. From the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian, emperor of Rome, the seventy weeks were completed, which are four hundred and ninety years. This reckoning becomes clear when one goes through the reigns and the successive rulers of the empire. Tertullian also worked it out in the book he wrote Against the Jews. We have not repeated his calculation, so as not to do him an injustice, since he reckoned it correctly.

And who could be in doubt about this number, when some three hundred years are now found beyond it? It is shameless, then, after so many years have been added, to say of the Saviour's coming, "He has not come." In the time of the apostles, or during the very time when the Lord lived among men, malice opposing the truth could hide itself. It saw all the signs of the promised Christ in the Saviour, yet it could claim to be in doubt about the time, so as to conceal its faithlessness. But later, when many years began to accumulate beyond the promised number, what shamelessness it is to deny that he has come, when the prophecy is known to have been fulfilled in both its signs and its times! For when something is exactly full and does not overflow, a contentious person can say that it is not full. But if it overflows, the contentious person's mouth is shut.

So too in the Saviour's time the Jews could say, though falsely, that the reckoning from the time of Darius to the Lord Christ had not been worked out correctly enough to say that he was the one promised. For we make mistakes about the years, months and days of the emperors' reigns and have not calculated them precisely. But once the times had grown beyond the prescribed number of years for the promised Christ, no excuse can be offered for saying that the one who came is not the Christ, unless, God forbid, one says that the one who promised lied. For when the time of the promise has passed and someone denies that the one who was promised has come, what is that but accusing the one who promised of lying? But all the signs that were foretold, and that are known to have been found in Christ, show that the one who promised is truthful. The Jews, however, are ashamed to correct themselves and give no thought to the coming judgment. For nothing is worse than to deny the truth of what one knows is no lie.
45. ON THE IMAGE

"Let us make," he says, "man in our image and likeness." Some think this should be understood in the light of another passage, namely the one where we read that God said: "Come, let us go down and confuse their languages." On the surface the two seem alike, since in each one person is speaking in the plural. But they differ in meaning, because the reasoning behind them is different. In the first passage he speaks of creating man, whom God wills to be created in his image and likeness. But the saying "Come, let us go down and confuse their languages" concerns stopping people from understanding one another. So God can be taken to have spoken to the angels there, like an emperor to his army. He included them in his words because he was going to act through them, as their creator. That is why he says, "Let us confuse their languages." But when he says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," he cannot be said to have spoken to angels. The image of God and of the angels cannot be said to be one, any more than the image of an emperor and of his attendants can be, for beings who share one image cannot be unlike in dignity or nature. Finally he added: "And God made man; in the image of God he made him." So it was God who spoke and God who made: not another or a different God, but the same God.

For when one spoke to one, this pointed not to a different nature but to a different person. Though God is one, there are three persons. And God is one because, whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit, the substance is that of the one God, since what comes from him cannot be anything other than what he is. So it is the person of God the Father who says, "Let us make," and the person of the Son who makes man in the image of God. Whether this is the Father's image or the Son's own makes no difference, because both have one image. The Son, then, made man through the Holy Spirit. For just as the Father is said to act through the Son, so the Son acts through the Holy Spirit, as he himself says: "For I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." Therefore the three have one image, because whether it is Father, Son or Holy Spirit, God is one. And so one man was made in the image of the one God. Man is the image of God in this respect: just as there is one God in heaven, from whom all spiritual things have their being, so there was to be one man on earth, from whom all others would have their bodily origin.

Some, however, think that man was made in the image of God in respect of dominion, because he said: "And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the whole earth." Yet these things are seen to be subject not only to the man but also to the woman, who, it is agreed, does not have the image of God. This view is unreasonable on two counts. First, if man has the image of God in his dominion, then God is said to have spoken the words "Let us make man in our image and likeness" not to the Son but to the heavenly dominions that the apostle mentions. Second, dominion is given to the woman as well, so that she too would be the image of God, which is absurd. For how can it be said of woman that she is the image of God, when she is plainly subject to the man's rule and has no authority? She can neither teach, nor be a witness, nor give a pledge, nor judge: how much less can she rule!
46. ON SAMUEL

There are some among us who, partly because they are busy with worldly affairs and partly because they pay too little attention to the sacred Scriptures, fall into the error of thinking that Samuel was a priest, that is, that he was descended from Aaron. The Lord God ordained that priests should be born from Aaron's line, not made, and no one except Aaron's sons was allowed to place incense on the altar. Some of these people go further astray: they deny that Samuel was of the family of Aaron, that is, they say he was not born a priest, yet they still claim that he performed the priesthood. These must be answered first, for it is worse to deny that Samuel was born a priest and still claim that he performed the priesthood than to say that he was a priest descended from the sons of Aaron. In the second case there is ignorance; in the first, foolishness. Once those who think he was born a priest learn that he was not one of Aaron's sons, they will see clearly that he was not a priest, for they did not know that no one was permitted to perform the priesthood except a descendant of Aaron. They know the facts well enough: it is plain that when Korah, who was not one of Aaron's sons, wanted to place incense on the altar, he and his companions were swallowed up when the earth opened. And King Uzziah, who was certainly not of Aaron's line but of the tribe of Judah, presumed to perform the priesthood; as he stood before the altar he was struck with leprosy on his forehead, and so he died.

Then there are those who say that Samuel was not born a priest but still claim that he performed the priesthood. What they say is foolish enough, and persuading a fool of what is good takes the greatest effort. How dull they must be, to say it is night while the sun is shining over the earth! They read, and read in more than one place, that God decreed that no one should dare to perform the priesthood except Aaron and his sons, and yet they stubbornly insist that Samuel was a priest. They do not understand that if Samuel was not born a priest and still performed the priesthood, he must be called presumptuous, since God had laid down that priests were to be born, not made. I do not think it safe to hold such a view of Samuel. How could it be that a praiseworthy man, commended by God's own testimony, would do what he knew was not permitted? He knew for certain that punishment for such presumption had been inflicted once and again. Nor could he have aspired to it by God's decision, for he knew God to be unchangeable. If by chance he had heard such a thing from him, he would rather have believed that he was being tested, knowing that God could in no way rescind his own sentence. He would sooner have believed that this was being done to him under God's appearance and name by the adversary, in order to deceive him, than that God could change his judgment.

Indeed, when Balaam had been forbidden by God to go to Balak and afterward asked again whether he might go, God was angry with him and rebuked him through the example of the donkey: the donkey saw the angel barring the way and refused to continue the journey it had begun. When God had forbidden Balaam to go and he asked again whether God wanted him to go, he judged God as though he were a man, who changes and shifts because he cannot foresee. But Balaam is commended by no divine testimony, for he was a soothsayer. Samuel, on the other hand, was a man dear to God and knew that God's judgments are fixed. How then could he believe that something should be done other than what he knew God had established?

"But after Eli and his sons the priests had died," they say, "Samuel began to perform the priesthood." Scripture does not teach this, and reason does not allow it. Those who say it suppose that there was then no one else to perform the priesthood, so that after these three had died the priesthood would have ceased had Samuel not offered the people's gifts. This assertion is hostile to God, for it judges him improvident, as though he had unknowingly established something that could not last. Why would he have decreed that no one but the sons of Aaron should perform the priesthood for ever, that is, until the time of Christ's coming, if he knew that it would fail? If he did not know (God forbid!), he was improvident, and then it is possible that Samuel became priest when the others failed. But if God is provident and foreknowing, what he established remained; and if what he established remained, Samuel did not perform the priesthood, because priests were not lacking [?]. Under the old law God decreed that priests should be born; under the new, the Lord commanded that priests be made.

Let them now choose one of two things: either prove that Samuel was born a priest, or that he was made one. But they agree that he was not born a priest, because they know he was not one of Aaron's sons. If, then, Samuel was not born a priest, and we neither read nor can prove that he was made one (for God had not ordained that priests be made), it is settled that Samuel was not a priest at all.

But our opponents shut their eyes and say: "Even if he was not a priest, he still acted in the priest's place, since we read that he offered sacrifice to God. Who would dare deny what Scripture shows?" Samuel did offer sacrifice to God, but that does not show that he acted in the priest's place. The one whose offerings the priest places on the altar is always said to offer them. Saul offered in this way, that is, through a priest, just as offerings are made now; David offered, Solomon offered, and the rest offered likewise. Did they all act in the priest's place? Though the priest carries out his own office, the one in whose name the priest acts is said to offer, for the gifts are credited to the one whose gifts are offered. And how could someone who was not a priest act in the priest's place? Can a deacon act in the priest's place? A prefect can act in place of a prefect, and a praetor in place of a praetor, but a private citizen cannot act in place of any official. How much less can someone who is not a priest act in a priest's place!

With what intention would anyone dare to aspire to what he knows is not permitted to him? If a priest is lacking somewhere, a priest from another place can be asked to come and act in his place; but a prophet, however holy his life, cannot do what he knows has not been granted to him at all. Living well is one thing; receiving the authority of an office is another. Just as a priest should not think that his priesthood makes his life commendable, so someone of holy conduct and life should not on that account claim the priesthood for himself. The priesthood is good, yet it will be evil for one to whom it has not been granted and who presumes to take it. If we look at what is written about holy Samuel, we shall see what testimony Scripture gives him: "And it became known to all the people," it says, "that Samuel was faithful as a prophet of the Lord." And in the psalm: "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name." Who does not notice that by this distinction the persons are divided according to their rank? Moses and Aaron are recognized as having obtained the priestly dignity, while Samuel is held to have proved worthy of God among the prophets, who called upon God in prayer to protect his people, as we read. And priests were so far from lacking that when the ark was brought back, carried by Levites, the men of Beth-shemesh offered sacrifices to God while Samuel was absent. And when Saul had been made king, Achimas, the great-grandson of Eli the priest, was the one who carried the ephod.

"But from this," they say, "it appears that Samuel was a priest: he was clothed in an ephod." As if deacons today did not wear dalmatics, as the bishop does! We read that David too was clothed in an ephod, and a double ephod at that. Samuel was still a small boy when he was girded with an ephod. Could a small boy offer the people's gifts to God? You see, then, that "ephod" is one word but does not always mean one thing. The priests carried the ephod; they did not wear it. But kings, and the Levite Samuel, were clothed with an ephod. So "ephod" sometimes means a garment, and sometimes a kind of small chest that the priests carried in order to inquire of the Lord.

As far as can be seen, it has been proved that Samuel was not a priest but a prophet. Now we answer those who, not knowing that Samuel was not one of the sons of Aaron the priest, suppose he was a priest; for it was not right that anyone descended from Aaron should not be a priest. I want them first to recognize that if Samuel was a priest, then without doubt Elkanah his father was a priest too. It would also have been fitting for his sons to be priests; but because they were not priests, he appointed them judges over the children of Israel, as Samuel himself was. For so we read: that he judged the children of Israel. Elkanah, Samuel's father, since he was not a priest, "went up," it says, "from year to year from his city Ramathaim to worship and sacrifice to God almighty, the Lord of hosts. And there were Eli and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord."

What could be plainer than that Elkanah came to offer his gifts before the Lord through the priests at the proper time? Moses had laid down that three times a year they should offer their gifts and tithes where the ark of the Lord and the priests were. Besides, Elkanah had two wives at one time, which is not permitted to priests. Elkanah was in fact one of the Levites, as the order of generations in the book of Chronicles shows. At that time the Levites did not yet have a fixed order of ministry around the priests and the ark of the Lord. It was David, during his reign, who arranged the courses of the priests and Levites, so that they should begin to render service in the Lord's ceremonies from twenty years old and upward (though in the Law it was from twenty-five and upward). From the sons of Aaron, that is, from the line of Phinehas and Ithamar, there were to be twenty-four courses of priests, each serving its turn at fixed times. Levites were appointed to be doorkeepers of the tabernacle, bearers of the ark of the Lord, keepers of the watch, guardians of the vessels, and receivers of the various offerings. Twenty-four courses were also instituted of singers, harpists, and other musicians, so that these too, that is, all the Levites, had their turns of service, since they needed time off as well, to look after their own households.

Not only do these things support the point made above, that Samuel was not one of the sons of Aaron, but so does what his mother said to the Lord: "If you give me a son, I will lend him to the Lord all the days of his life." She would not have said this if he had been born a priest, for then he would have been bound to serve the altar anyway. She said it because he was a Levite, and no law had yet been laid down for the Levites; each acted as he wished, so that some went astray and presumed to do what was not permitted. Jonathan, the son of Moses' son, though he was counted among the Levites, presumed to perform the priesthood for the tribe of Dan. That is why we read in the book of Judges: "Everyone did what pleased him, because there was no king in Israel." So Hannah made her vow, saying, "I will lend him to the Lord," so that he would not go astray with the rest.

So that the question may be discussed more fully, let us also consider what is said of Elkanah, that he came from year to year to offer his gifts and tithes. How could he offer tithes when he owned nothing? The Levites did not receive land, since they got their living from the tithes given by the people. But it is possible, and can be understood this way: he may have had property that belonged to his wife, or that he had bought. Not only the Levites but others too took wives from other tribes, so that even the priests took wives for themselves from other tribes. Jehoiada the high priest, for example, married a woman of the tribe of Judah, the daughter of King Joram.

47. ON THE READING FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH: "AND SEVEN WOMEN TOOK HOLD OF ONE MAN, SAYING, 'WE WILL EAT OUR OWN BREAD AND CLOTHE OURSELVES WITH OUR OWN GARMENTS; ONLY LET YOUR NAME BE CALLED UPON US. TAKE AWAY OUR REPROACH.'"

It is settled that the seven women signify seven churches. Though the Church is one, it is called sevenfold, just as one body is made up of a sevenfold number of members. For not only we, but also the heavenly beings above, are members of the Church, whose head is Christ. So whether the churches are called one or seven makes no difference. The Church is called one because it has one head, which is Christ; and seven because, just as the members are different, so are the spiritual powers. Among these we too are counted, and their capacities differ, which is why they are also said to be in need. They are different precisely so that no single one can do everything, but all together are the body of Christ, since he is the head of the body, the Church, from whom the whole body subsists, that is, from whom all things in heaven and on earth have their origin.

So in this church which is on earth, mention is made of all the churches, because when the mystery of the Creator is preached to this church, the same teaching is also made known to the heavenly ones. When it is imparted to those below, those above must hear it too. Hence the apostle says: "To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach among the Gentiles the incomprehensible riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the Church." Through this Church, then, those above are taught, for, as it says, "truth has sprung up from the earth." So that the higher beings may be mentioned, seven churches are named here within one people, and the prophet presents these seven churches as suppliants before the Savior made man. For they understood that Christ was born in order to take away reproach, first from those living under his law, and then from the rest. They remembered that it was written: "From Zion will come one who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob."

These seven churches, then, took hold of one man, that is, of Christ when he was born, saying: "We will eat our own bread and clothe ourselves with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach." What is it they are asking? If they use their own bread and are clothed in their own garments, that is, if they are alive and not naked, what do they lack? Bread signifies life, and clothing signifies devotion to God, since whoever is without God is called naked. Hence the apostle says, "You who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ," and again, "if, when we are stripped, we may not be found naked." Why then do they ask to have their reproach taken away, unless this signifies, in the number of the seven churches, the people who lived under the law and awaited the promised Christ to abolish sins? So they say, "We will eat our own bread," that is, we will feed on the words of the law, which teach one God, for "man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God"; "and clothe ourselves with our own garments," that is, we are registered under the name of our Creator, for each person is said to be clothed with what he both is and professes.

After all, senators and officials are recognized by their clothing for what they are. But since these things are not enough to win God's favor, he also decreed that through the mystery of the knowledge of the one God a person should become an heir of the kingdom of heaven. For through faith a person is washed of sins and freed from the second death, which, by the sentence passed on Adam, held people in the underworld; and with nothing to hold him back he goes on to the paradise of God the Father, where the Lord told the thief he would be with him. The people mentioned above, signified by the seven churches, had been under God's law and in devotion to him from the very beginning of the world; yet they needed purification from both their own sin and their forefather's, for "all," it says, "have sinned and lack the glory of God." That is why the churches mentioned above pray that their reproach may be taken away by calling on the name of Christ, because those who bear his sign, by which he conquered death, cannot be held by the enemy. And not only these churches pray that Christ's name be called upon them, but also the spiritual churches above, dwelling in the heavenly places. For though they are spiritual and heavenly powers, they are still subject to reproach if they are estranged from their Creator, and they will not be members of the body if they wander about without knowing their head.

That the meaning is none other than what we have explained, the prophet testifies in what follows, saying: "But on that day God will shine in counsel upon the earth," and he added: "for the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters, and will purge the blood from their midst." What could be clearer? On that day, that is, the day when God's promise was fulfilled and the mystery of faith was made known to mankind, people were enlightened, so that those who had been guilty of death, purified through knowledge of the Creator, might become heirs of eternal life. The prophet spoke of everyone together, to show that all needed God's gift, so that both sinners and the righteous might be known to have awaited God's mercy: sinners because of their own sins, that they might be snatched from the jaws of death; the righteous, so that, absolved of their forefather's sin and with the sentence passed on Adam, by which all were held by death, blotted out, they might receive freedom and enter the kingdom of God, no longer slaves but sons of God.
QUESTIONS ON THE NEW TESTAMENT
48. GOD IS SURELY PERFECTION AND NEEDS NOTHING. WHAT NEED WAS THERE, THEN, FOR CHRIST THE SAVIOR TO BE BORN OF GOD, AND FOR GOD TO HAVE A SON THROUGH WHOM HE MIGHT MAKE ALL THINGS?

When God willed that things which did not exist should come into being, and knew that such a work was not worthy of his majesty, he first begot from himself a Son (for he is simple and incorporeal in nature) who would differ from him in nothing, so that the work produced would correspond fittingly to his greatness. What more could he do than beget another self who is perfect? This, then, is the perfect work, than which nothing more excellent can be imagined. All other things are lesser; for as much as Christ excels all of them, so much is their creation inferior to his begetting. There is another point as well. God, from whom are all things, wishing to make the creation, first begot, that is, brought into existence, the Word that he held in mystery within himself. He called this Word "Son" in order to show that he had come forth from him and was consubstantial with him, so that the law by which children come from their parents would make this believable. Through this he revealed to the creation the mystery that had lain hidden in him from eternity.
49. WHY WAS THE SAVIOR BAPTIZED, SINCE HE WAS BORN HOLY AND WAS CALLED CHRIST THE LORD AT HIS VERY BIRTH, WHEN BAPTISM IS FOR PURIFICATION AND FOR SIN?

It is true and evident that the Savior had no need of baptism, since Christ was not made but born so, as the angel said to the shepherds: "Behold, today is born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord." And so John, knowing his holiness, tried to keep him from baptism, but the Savior insisted that it must be done, certainly not because of sin, but in order to fulfil all righteousness. It was fitting that he who taught that people become children of God through baptism should himself be an example to the future children of God; and he who promised that the Holy Spirit would be given to believers ought to show this visibly in himself, so that, having seen it, believers might be confident in hope that they receive the Holy Spirit invisibly. For the Savior, being born of the Holy Spirit, certainly had a purified body. The anointing was given to his flesh spiritually in the womb: the Holy Spirit purified what passed from the Virgin Mary into the Savior's body. This is the anointing of the flesh of the Savior's body, and that is why he was called "Christ" even at birth. What God granted through anointing with oil, by the ministry of the prophets, to those anointed as kings, the Holy Spirit granted to the man Christ, with purification added; for the earlier anointed ones received through anointing only the power to rule, but the Savior, born as a man, both received the power and was born purified. It would have been unfitting for the Son of God to be born in a body subject to sins.

So, taking up the cause of mankind and teaching that people become children of God through regeneration, he had to be baptized, in order to show in himself that this is valid. What is said is easily proved and believed when it is seen being done by the teacher. In the same way it was fitting for the signs of power to be performed, so that, now appearing as the Son of God through the mystery of regeneration, he might bring healing to bodily ailments and be an example to his future brothers, since it is through regeneration that each person receives the power to work mighty deeds.
50. IF THE SAVIOR WAS BAPTIZED TO BE AN EXAMPLE, WHY, WHEN HE HIMSELF WAS CIRCUMCISED, DID HE FORBID OTHERS TO BE CIRCUMCISED?

Circumcision was a command for a time now past. It was meant to keep its authority until Christ, running only until the birth of Christ, who had been promised to Abraham, and then to cease once the promise was fulfilled. Isaac was promised as a figure of Christ, for God said to Abraham: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed," and that seed is Christ. Christ restored the faith that Abraham had received, so that all nations might be blessed in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, as had been promised to Abraham. Circumcision was therefore the sign of the promised son, that is, of Christ. Once he was born, the sign of the promise had to cease. Yet the promised one himself, when he came, received the sign of his father, so that he would be known as the one who had been promised to justify all nations through faith in the circumcision of the heart. For just as father Abraham's son, born in the flesh, bore circumcision as a bodily seal, so those who are born spiritually have circumcision of the heart as their spiritual sign. It was therefore right that after Christ there should no longer be circumcision in the flesh.

51. How should we understand the angel Gabriel's answer when Mary said to him, "How shall I know this, since I do not know a man?" He replied: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you."

Mary was unsure how she could conceive, and the angel tells her that it is possible: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." That is: "Do not doubt because you know no man. When I said you will conceive, I meant that the Holy Spirit will come upon you and work so that you conceive without a man." "And the power of the Most High," he says, "will overshadow you." "The power of the Most High" is without doubt Christ, for the phrase belongs to his person. So the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin and sanctified her, and by his work he formed from her a holy body, in which the power called the Son of God would be born. His overshadowing of the virgin means that something of the immensity of the Godhead came to be in the virgin's womb, as much as human nature could hold. Because it came, as it were, from that radiance, it could be called the overshadowing of the power of God, and yet it was the power of God and indeed God, for nothing that is from God is not called God. In bodily things, by contrast, something can be in the flesh and still not be called flesh, as with hair, bones and the like.
52. If Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, that is, was made flesh from Mary by the Spirit's working, why is it said: "Wisdom," which is surely Christ, "has built herself a house"?

This question should be understood in two ways. First, the house of Christ is the Church, which he built for himself with his own blood. Second, his body can also be called his house, just as it is called his temple. If it is called the temple of God because God dwells in it, there is nothing absurd in also calling it a house, as we read in the Law. But if the body, which we think can also be called a house, was made by the working of the Holy Spirit, one may ask why this work is credited to the person of Christ. The answer is that what the Son does, the Father does, because both have one power. In the same way, what the Holy Spirit does, the Son of God does, because their nature and will are one. Whether the Father acts, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is the Trinity that is at work, and whatever the three have done is the work of one God.
53. If all things were made according to reason, why is the Saviour said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January?

No one could be so dull as to deny that God does everything according to reason. Christ came down from the holy seats to bring salvation to the world, and he also meant to teach that the world itself and its seasons were established by him. So he chose to be born as a man, in order to make a diminished human race grow toward God, at the time when the light, that is, the day, begins to grow again after it has greatly diminished. In this way the time of his birth fits the logic of the divine teaching, which began to multiply men from the shadow of death into life.

54. If Christ was made Son to God from the seed of David according to the flesh, that is, if he was already born Son of God in both natures because he was born holy, how was it that after his baptism the Lord God said to him: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"?

Christ is the Son of God from eternity according to the spirit of holiness. According to the flesh, he was born Son to God from the seed of David. So in both respects he is to be regarded as Son of God not by being made so but by being born so. What he hears at his baptism is for the sake of the mystery, not for his own sake, for he hears it on behalf of all who are baptized. He himself is simply shown forth, so that his mighty works may make it plain that God is in the man. The others, however, are confirmed, because they begin to be sons of God from the moment they receive the Holy Spirit. The Lord's body was indeed born holy. Yet the man Christ would not have been confirmed as Son of God by the sacrament of regeneration if he had not received the Holy Spirit, according to the decree, the gift of rebirth. The Jews too were called sons of God, but by devotion, not by the sacrament that now works so that, once they have received remission of sins and the Holy Spirit has come upon them, people are called sons of God. The Saviour, then, was both born Son of God according to the flesh and afterward confirmed in the mystery. What was born holy from the Holy could not fail to be born to God. But so that the purpose of the mystery might be fulfilled, when the Spirit came upon him he was not diminished but increased.
55. Why did the Lord submit to the cross at the time when the Jews kept the Passover, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April?

The Saviour did everything at its proper place and time. To show that he had rightly created all things at the Father's bidding, he chose to redeem and reshape the world by his passion at the same time at which he had created it, that is, at the equinox. That is when the world began and when day began to grow longer than night. Because he was acting within the Roman realm, he had to suffer on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the date the Romans keep as the equinox. That was when this part of the world was first lit and the day began to lengthen, and so it was then too, through the Saviour's passion, that it was led from darkness to light. No fault can be found with the Creator for restoring his fallen creation at the time when he had made it. Nor can anyone criticize the beginning of creation of a thing that has fallen, when its restoration returns to that very point. He willed that the joy of renewal should fall on the same day as the joy of its dedication.
56. Why does Matthew record Joseph's father as Jacob, while Luke records him as Heli? Either Joseph has been ignorantly described as having two fathers, or else no one knows who his real father was.

There is no doubt that Joseph's father was Jacob. The line runs from David through Solomon and continues straight down to Jacob, whose son is Joseph. Heli, the son of Matthat, belongs to the line that runs from David through Nathan, another son of David, and continues to the time when the Saviour came. So each evangelist followed from David the line of descent of one of the two brothers, and between them they made a kind of fork. Matthew came down from David through Solomon to Joseph. Luke went up from Heli, who lived in the Saviour's time, through the branch of Nathan, David's son. In doing so he joined the lineages of Heli and Joseph and showed that both were of one family. By linking Heli with Joseph, he shows that they do not differ in descent but are brothers, and so the Saviour is the son not only of Joseph but also of Heli. For on the same ground on which the Saviour is called Joseph's son, he is also Heli's son, and the son of all the others who are of the same tribe. That is why the apostle says: "Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ." Luke was moved by divine prompting to go up from Heli through the branch of Nathan to David, then through Terah his father up to Shem the son of Noah, and further back beyond the flood to Seth the son of Adam, who was given in place of Abel. On the same ground on which the Saviour was called the son of Joseph and of Heli, Luke made him the son of Adam. Then, going beyond Adam, he declared that Christ is the Son of God before all flesh.

Some think that Heli took Jacob's wife according to the law's command that if a man died without sons, his brother or kinsman should take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. On this view Heli fathered Joseph for Jacob, whose wife he had taken, and this is how the lines are joined, so that Joseph may fairly be said to have Heli as his father. This view is not probable, and it serves no purpose.

What was said above, however, both joins the lineage through two brothers who were sons of one father and shows that Christ is Son of God before every generation. The evangelist puts it like this: "And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, who was of Heli." That is, Jesus was thought to be Joseph's son, and he was the son not only of Joseph but also of Heli. Luke does not say that Joseph was Heli's son. He means that Jesus was Heli's son in the same sense in which he was called Joseph's son, because Joseph and Heli were sons of brothers, Solomon and Nathan, the sons of David. Then, going up through David to Abraham, Noah and Seth, and to Adam himself, and beyond Adam, he teaches that Christ is the Son of God. When he says, "who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the son of God," he certainly calls Christ the son of Adam in the same sense in which he was called the son of Joseph. As Mary said to Jesus: "Son, why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow and grief." Beyond Adam, Luke joins Christ to God the Father. So the one who was called the son of these men, from Adam down to Joseph and Heli, was to be understood as the true Son of God before all of them. This refutes Photinus, who maintains that Christ existed only from Mary and not before. Christ was called the son of men whose son he was not, while men denied that he was the Son of God, whose Son he truly was.

Suppose, improbably and to no purpose, that Joseph is called Heli's son in the way described above. Then Luke will appear to have said "who was the son of God" not of Christ but of Adam. For he lists the fathers of each son in order until he reaches Enos, whose father he names as Seth. He names Adam as Seth's father, and God as Adam's father. I do not see what use there is in insisting on this. But suppose that, as we said, these men in their order are each called fathers of Christ, just as he was called Joseph's son, since it is written: "Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ." Then in that same order we read that he is the son of Seth and the son of Adam, and beyond them all he is declared the Son of God, so that he is said to exist before the very men whose son he is called.

57. Why is it that the words "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way" are written in the prophet Malachi, and yet the evangelist Mark says they are written in the prophet Isaiah?

Mark could not have been unaware of what he was writing. He was well read in Scripture: he had been steeped in the sacred writings from childhood and trained in the Law, and above all he was a follower of the apostles. Knowing that sayings should be traced back to their source, he attributed these words to Isaiah, who had first expressed this meaning when he said: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God." Indeed, right after Malachi's words the evangelist adds "The voice of one crying in the wilderness," so as to join the words of both prophets, which share one meaning, under the name of the earlier prophet.

58. How can John deny that he knew Christ before the baptism, when Christ came to be baptized and John said to him: "I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" How could he not know the one whom he tried to stop, humbling himself before him?

John was endowed with such holiness from his very cradle that we must believe he could neither be deceived nor deceive, nor fail to know his Lord, who had enlightened him in the womb through the Holy Spirit. So both statements are true: he recognized him when the Spirit came down upon him, and he did know him before he came to be baptized. He knew him, but he did not know whether he was the one who would bestow the gift of God promised to the fathers. This is what he says he learned at the moment he saw the Spirit come down upon him. John says that God had instructed him in this way: "The one on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." The apostle bears witness to the same thing: "For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers." This is the sense in which John did not know the Lord. Though he was not unaware of his greatness, it was hidden from him that the faith of Abraham was to be fulfilled through him.

59. If baptism is a heavenly mystery, why does the Lord say to Nicodemus, when he was in doubt about baptism: "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"

Anyone who thinks baptism rests on a fleshly principle is not spiritual. Nor can anyone obtain the heavenly gift who does not believe that he is changed not by water but by faith. The water is seen, but the Spirit, who is not seen, does the work, so that faith may be in it. As water washes away bodily dirt, so the Spirit washes the soul clean of sins. Visible things benefit visible things, and in the same way the Spirit benefits spiritual things. So a spiritual principle is at work in baptism, for there is more in it that is heard than is seen.

Nicodemus was hemmed in by fleshly reasoning and so was in doubt about this. To draw him to faith, the Saviour used a fitting example. To establish an invisible reality he gave an example from the visible world, yet one that is grasped by hearing alone, not by sight. No one denies it, and yet it is earthly, because it accomplishes something belonging to this world. So the Lord said to Nicodemus, to persuade him: "The wind blows where it wills, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit." The sound of the coming spirit, that is, of the wind, is heard but not seen, as was said. In the same way, the principle of baptism is heard in what is said, but how it is accomplished through the Spirit is not seen. It is heard when the one who pronounces the words declares what is to happen, so that what is heard is believed to happen, though no account is given of how it is done.

But when even this example did not lead Nicodemus to faith, he hears the Saviour say: "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" The earthly things he spoke of were the ones he had put forward as an example. That is: "If you do not believe it can happen when I give you an example drawn from earthly things, the spirit that is the wind, simply because you cannot see how it happens, how could you believe if I gave you heavenly examples, which you certainly do not know?" A person can be persuaded of what he does not know by means of what he does know. For example, God says of Christ that he is his true Son. How that is cannot be comprehended. But from what we know about how sons exist according to the flesh, we believe that God said "Christ is my true Son" to show that Christ is from himself. In the same way, the Saviour wanted to commend something that can be explained neither in words nor in thought by means of something perceptible that the ears can hear. That is, by the example of the spirit that is the wind, which the senses grasp and the ear hears though it does not know where it comes from, he wanted to make credible the work of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be grasped.

We read the same thing in the Acts of the Apostles: "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven like the rush of a mighty wind, and it filled the whole house," and so on. Here, plainly by the example of the wind, Luke conveys that the Holy Spirit came from heaven and resounded just as a mighty wind does over the earth. Jeremiah too calls the wind a spirit when he says: "The wind blows in every region." Because the wind is in this world and is carried about to many places, we do not know where it comes from or where it goes. But the Holy Spirit comes from heaven, as we read, to enlighten believers.

How then do some think that the Saviour was speaking of the Holy Spirit when he said, "The wind blows where it wills, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes," when it is clear that the Saviour said this as an example? He goes on to add: "So it is with everyone who has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit." What could be plainer than that he meant the wind by "spirit"? They think the wind is not meant because he says "It blows where it wills," as if every creature were not left to its own choice within the law laid down for it. We too go where we will and do what we will, acting under law, and for that reason we shall also have to give an account. Or is it thought possible, and does it not seem foolish, that in wishing to convey the working of the Holy Spirit he would offer that very Spirit as the example? I consider the question settled in every respect.
60. If "the Law and the Prophets were until John," how is it that the Saviour sends a man to the priests to offer gifts for his cleansing from leprosy?

This did not really belong to that time. It was done to condemn the Jews. They did not understand that the summit of truth, in this better time, had come for the gain of their own salvation, so truth stooped to accuse them. They regarded the Saviour as an enemy of the Law, because in his mercy he wanted to free them from the burden of the Law, as the prophet Jeremiah had foretold when he said, among other things: "And I will give them a new covenant, not like the one I gave their fathers." So that he would not appear to be an enemy, as they thought, by preaching new things, the Saviour sent the man who had been cleansed of leprosy to the priests to offer gifts for his cleansing, as Moses had commanded. And to make clear that this would serve to accuse them, he said, "as a testimony to them": at the judgment this act would stand as a witness against those who called the Saviour an enemy of the Law. The apostle Paul followed the same course.
