Though he was preaching that circumcision was no longer necessary, he circumcised Timothy himself because of the scandal it would cause the Jews, for he preferred to do something superfluous rather than have false brethren stir up an uproar. This in fact served the Jews' error: they were satisfied for the moment, and by this they would go on erring forever.

61. When the Jews accused the disciples of breaking the Sabbath by rubbing ears of grain in their hands and eating them, why did the Saviour cite the example of David, who ate the bread that only the priests were allowed to eat? This does not seem to excuse them. Rather, it seems to make them guilty along with David, especially since David did not do it on the Sabbath.

The Saviour wants to expose the hypocrisy of the Jews with many examples. He shows that greater things had been done under the Law and that no one had dared to bring charges. He shows not only that the Sabbath had been broken under the Law more than once, but also that the priestly bread had been taken unlawfully, with the priest himself allowing it, and, what is more, that these things were done by men of high authority. First, Joshua the son of Nun, by divine command, did not keep the Sabbath, and when he did so the walls of Jericho fell of their own accord. How much good it did to keep not the Sabbath but faith! The Maccabees too, after they had first been slaughtered, fought on the Sabbath and triumphed over their enemies. And the priests, in order to serve in the Lord's ceremonies, disregarded the Sabbath in the temple. David, already anointed king, had by God's power stripped the slain Philistine of his arms. Then, while on a journey and pressed by hunger, he received bread from the priest. It was not lawful for him to eat it, but only when there was no necessity; it was lawful if necessity required it. So the priest, seeing his need, did not refuse, and David, chosen by God, took it without hesitation.

The same reasoning applies to the Sabbath, which is why circumcision is not forbidden on the Sabbath. Things that are not dangerous are commanded to be kept in such a way that no harm is done if they are set aside out of necessity, because they were commanded not for salvation but for reverence. But what is wholly unlawful is always unlawful. No necessity softens it so that doing it does no harm, for what the laws forbid because it is criminal is always unlawful. The things we mentioned above as sometimes lawful are like the fasts prescribed by law: breaking them out of necessity does not make one guilty, if it is because of the stomach or the weakness of fever. The crafty Jews knew this, yet they accused the disciples of breaking the Sabbath, as was said above. The Saviour did not want to confront them prematurely with the time of the Law's fulfilment, lest they leap further into madness. Instead, from the past, on the basis of which they thought the Sabbath should all the more be upheld, he showed them to be slanderers. They were put to shame not only over the Sabbath but also over the priestly bread, as was shown above.
62. Why is it that when the sons of Leah, who were of the tribe of Judah, were killed, Rachel is said to weep for her children?

As far as the history is concerned, the sons of Rachel, of the tribe of Benjamin, had long before been wiped out and erased by the other tribes for their own crimes, namely the deeds of the Sodomites and the outrage they had committed against the Levite's concubine. This is why she is said to refuse consolation: she knows there is no hope for those who are known to have perished. The sons of Leah, by contrast, were killed in their earliest years for the Saviour's sake. So he does not want the lament to be attributed to them, because they were killed innocent and for God's sake, and God without doubt gave them eternal life by the grace of reward. Therefore the lament belongs to the sons of Rachel, who were erased both in the present and in the future. The others were lamented according to the flesh but consoled according to the spirit, whereas the sons of Rachel lived according to the flesh and will be consumed by spiritual flames. The evangelist testifies that Rachel's lament was fulfilled when Leah's sons were killed because it was then that she began to lament her own sons, when she saw her sister's sons killed in such a cause that they became heirs of eternal life. For when misfortune has befallen someone, another's happiness makes him mourn his own ill fortune all the more wretchedly.
LXIII. How did the Chaldean magi understand from the appearance of a star that Christ, King of the Jews, had been born, when it is usually an earthly [?] king who is marked out by a star as a sign?

These Chaldean magi studied the course of the stars not out of ill will but out of curiosity about the world. For, as we are given to understand, they followed the tradition of Balaam. When Balak summoned him to curse the people of God, he began to bless them at God's command. From his account, then, they had learned that by God's providence one would arise from Jacob who would reign. For he prophesied (this is no secret): "A star shall rise out of Jacob," and so on. So the magi, following this tradition and seeing a star outside the order of the world, understood that this was the star which Balaam had prophesied would be the sign of the King of the Jews. This in fact happened to confound the enemies of religion. The truth received testimony from the very quarter that usually attacks it, for astrologers are enemies of the truth.
LXIV. How is it proved that the Saviour rose from the dead after three days and nights?

In this matter, if you look for the number by counting days and nights in sequence, you will not arrive at an understanding. Moses too fasted forty days and forty nights, and yet the full number is not found. Since he went up by day and came down by day, he certainly did not complete the whole number. But where there is a day a night is also counted, and where there is a night a day is also counted, so that, taking the part for the whole, forty days and forty nights are spoken of. So it is with what the Saviour said: because there are three nights, three days are also understood. For night is such that it depends on the day, lest this perhaps seem novel or contrary to reason. For there is no doubt that the light, from which the day was named, was created before the evening, which is followed by night.

It is not absurd to assert that the Lord's passion began at night. As light, that is day, is the image of life, so night, that is darkness, is the likeness of death, as the scriptures clearly show: "sons of light" and, on the other side, "sons of darkness." Nor is it surprising that, while everywhere else day comes before night and light before darkness, here alone what follows is placed before what precedes. Or perhaps in such a case the order of things is confused and changed, so that night rather than day seems to be the forerunner of death (which is why the reckoning begins from the night). For he could not enter in upon the prince of darkness except by night, and so the Lord of light, that is of eternal life, was in some measure subjected for a time to the prince of darkness or of death, in order to free from death both those who had gone before and those who would come after. Death would not have been wholly emptied, nor the gloom of darkness ever dispelled, had it not seen the Lord. When so great a light entered the secret place of death where it held sway, death vanished; for no one can be wholly conquered unless he is caught either by his own means or among his own. Rightly, then, in such an affair night alone holds first place, so that it might lose its power. And so that the unbelieving Jews might remain in perpetual night, and so that night, not day, should be the author of so great a crime, indeed sacrilege, the day is placed after the preceding night, against the order of things, just as the God and Lord of all things was placed under the prince of wicked death in order to release all from the snares of death.

If this still seems contradictory to anyone, let him consider carefully, lest he begin to find this harder to accept: that God, putting on the person of a servant, I will not say of a man, gave himself over to death. Why then do you look for order here, where you see everything turned upside down? For what is the light that was in the darkness, which the darkness did not grasp, by which he was grasped? Whoever knows he is being seized in order to be struck reckons that time as part of his death. Then there is the following day, on which he was heard and crucified; there is the night that leads into the Sabbath; there is the Sabbath itself; and there is the evening after the Sabbath, in which the Lord rose and which includes the Lord's day. (This is what Moses commanded the Jews in a figure, that they should enter the Sabbath at evening.) For night is not counted without day, nor day without night. By this reckoning the Lord rose after three days and three nights.

LXV. If the evangelists spoke with one voice and one understanding, how did it come about that three of them, namely Matthew, Luke and John, say that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, while Mark, on the contrary, says that the Saviour was crucified at the third hour?

It is not good to wrap the truth in obscurity. The three evangelists had one meaning, but Mark wanted to point out something they had passed over, knowing it to be necessary. Nor could he be mistaken: he followed the examples of those who had authority, he learned what he wrote with great devotion and diligence, and he was not without the Holy Spirit. What he wanted to show by this, then, must be explained. It must be observed that the Saviour was crucified not by Pilate but by the Jews. As far as Roman law was concerned, they declared the Saviour innocent. Pilate said to the Jews, "I find no case against him," and when they said, "Crucify him," he answered, "Why, what evil has he done?" Then, when he persisted and wanted to rescue him from their hands, he was subjected to their slander, as they said, "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar." So it came about that he handed him over to their judgment. It was not Pilate, then, who passed sentence, but the Jews.

Indeed, it says, they had been prompted by the chief priests to say, "Let him be crucified." Mark wants this sentence to be understood as having been given at the third hour. They persisted in it with unceasing cries, yet it was after an interval of about three hours, during which he was taken to Herod and brought back, that they crucified the Saviour. For everyone who is condemned is counted as dead from the moment he receives his sentence. Mark therefore made it plain that the Saviour was not crucified by a judge's sentence, since it is hard to prove innocent someone who is punished by a judge's sentence. He allowed himself, then, to disagree in wording in order to teach that what was completed at the sixth hour had begun at the third, not through the laws but through the persistent malice of the Jews.

LXVI. The evangelist Mark says that the demons recognized Jesus and confessed him, but the Apostle, on the contrary, denies that the rulers and powers of this age knew the divinity of the Lord Jesus. Mark says, among other things, "For they knew who he was"; but the Apostle says, "whom none of the rulers of this age knew; for had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." If the demons knew, how were the rulers ignorant?

Some think that "the rulers of this age" meant the leaders of the Jews, in line with what the apostle Peter said: "For you know, brothers, that you did this evil in ignorance, as did your rulers also." So they were rulers of the Jews, but not of this age. He says "your rulers," not "rulers of the age," since the Jews themselves said that they had Caesar as king, under whose power they had been brought. The rulers in question, however, are those the Apostle meant in another place when he said: "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world." So the question is rightly asked: if these did not know Jesus, how could the demons have recognized him?

But what he says the demons recognized in Christ is one thing, and what he denies that the rulers of this age recognized is another. The demons did indeed know who he was, but only as the one who had been promised through the law. They saw in him all the signs that the prophets had foretold, including that the redeemer of Israel would come from the seed of David, born of a virgin. But the mystery of his divinity they did not know, any more than their rulers did. Indeed, the devil questions the Saviour, though craftily, saying, "If you are the Son of God," and so on. Seeing divine power at one moment and human weakness at another, he was tormented, unsure what was true. So the scriptures agree with one another according to what has been revealed. It is impossible for men of one Spirit to disagree.

LXVII. What does it mean that the Saviour, as he hung on the cross, says, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing"? If they do not know, what is there to forgive, especially since King Abimelech says to God, "Will you destroy an ignorant nation?"

Not everyone who is ignorant is exempt from punishment. The ignorant person who can be excused from punishment is one who found no one to learn from. He asks forgiveness for these men because they had someone to learn from and took no trouble to do so. People like this are not entitled to be ignorant. So they will receive pardon if they are converted.
LXVIII. The Lord certainly taught that we should pray for our enemies. Why is it, then, that the souls of the slain, on the contrary, seek to be avenged and demand vengeance from God?

The souls of the slain cry out demanding to be avenged in the same way that Abel's blood cried out from the earth. So it is the facts of the case that are said to cry out, though they cannot speak. What else does shed blood do but demand to be avenged, crying out not with a voice but by its very nature? In the same way a work is said to praise its maker simply by delighting whoever sees it. For the saints are not so impatient as to press for something to happen which they know will come at its appointed time, a time that can be neither hastened nor delayed. By this saying he meant to show that God will avenge the blood of his saints, lest, because he now seems so patient, the impious war waged against the saints be thought to go unpunished. In this way he would strike terror into those who persecute God's servants and encourage those who suffer for him. The soul of one who suffers is relieved when it hears that it will be avenged by one who is mighty. It counts it in its favour to hear that its death displeases the judge, for then it knows for certain that it is innocent. God is indeed merciful and patient, but within measure. He waits for the impious to believe and for sinners to amend. If they do not, they will be punished, because they despised God's long patience.

He gives an example of this even in the time when mercy is preached, so that he may not seem insensible rather than patient, someone moved neither by anyone's pain nor by compassion. Hence he says through the prophet, "I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever?" And the Lord says, "Will not God avenge his servants who cry to him day and night?" They cry out, of course, in the way we described above. If, then, a Christian takes vengeance for a time, not harshly and without bloodshed, he does not sin; yet he will do better to leave it to God the judge.

LXIX. If the law had already ceased when John or the Saviour was preaching, how does the Saviour say, "I have not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfil them"? If it has been forbidden, how has it not been abolished, when it has lost its authority to be practised?

Everything that was said about Christ has been fulfilled. The Lord himself fulfilled the law and the prophets in this way, by doing everything that had been written about him; he abolished nothing but confirmed it. For the law and the prophets lasted until him. The prophets spoke about him, so what they said about him cannot be extended beyond him. Nor could any prophets of this kind be found after him, because they have nothing to speak about: the one they spoke about has already come. They included everything in their books, revealing his incarnation, his life, his passion, his resurrection, the manifestation of his divinity and his future judgment. And so the prophets ceased once the work of the dispensation had been fulfilled.

The law, however, ceased in two ways, and not entirely; for even what has ceased can remain in force if the condition is kept. One part ceased with respect to its sentence, another with respect to the law itself. When John preached the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, the sentence of the law, which held sinners guilty, ceased. The burdens of the law also ceased, which had been imposed because of the hardness of the Jewish heart, in matters of foods, new moons and weasels. For when mercy came, punishment ceased. But whereas the burdens of the law ceased forever, the sentence ceases and is abolished only for those who persist in the benefit they have received. For those who go back to the old man the authority of the law is renewed, because, forgetful of the benefits, they return under the sentence of the law.

Circumcision and the Sabbath, however, remained valid until the time when the commandment of the new law would be preached. They were given on condition that they would cease when the law of faith came. Hence the Apostle says, "Christ is the end of the law." Daniel too signifies this when he prophesies about the Lord's coming and the times of the weeks, saying that anointing, judgment, sacrifice and the city itself would cease. When the spiritual law came, the carnal things had to cease. Then God was served with the body, now with the soul; formerly visibly, now invisibly; then in the flesh, now in the mind, because God, who is spirit, must surely be served in spirit. So the law was not abolished because it ceased; rather, when its time was fulfilled, something succeeded it. Nor is its administration or its judgment called into question if pardon is granted to sinners. On the contrary, this proves all the more that it was rightly and justly given, since no one denies that those over whom it ruled were sinners: for "the law," he says, "is not laid down for the righteous."

So let no one think that justice deserves condemnation because mercy is to be preferred. If there were no reverence for justice, mercy itself would bear no fruit, for unless people keep justice after receiving mercy, the pardon will do them no good. The law said: "You shall not make yourself an idol, nor worship the things in heaven above or on the earth below"; and "You shall not swear falsely"; and "Honour your father and mother"; and "You shall not kill, nor commit fornication, nor steal; you shall not bear false witness, nor covet anything that belongs to your neighbour." Are we to say that these have ceased? Far from it. Without them, who could be judged fit even in this life? It is the other things we mentioned above that have ceased: new moons, Sabbaths, the food laws, sacrifices, circumcision and the rest. Hence the Apostle says, among other things: "Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you want to have no fear of the authority? Do good, and you will receive its praise." Keeping these things makes people good, but not perfect. Hence the Saviour says: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." By adding greater things to these, the Saviour certainly did not abolish the law but fulfilled it. The intent of the law concerns human welfare. Take, for example, "an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth": its purpose was that a man, afraid of suffering what he was forbidden to do to another, would keep himself from wickedness. But the Saviour, adding a higher justice to this intent, says: "But I say to you, do not resist evil; if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the left as well," so that by not repaying evil a person may be perfect. To pay back in kind is just, but not complete; but to let an injury pass is full and abundant justice. To retaliate brings joy for a moment, but to forgive brings gladness in the future.

This, then, is how the Saviour fulfilled the law: those whom it taught righteousness he made more righteous, which the law could not do. That is why the law rejoices, because its disciples have become more skilled. He would plainly have destroyed the law if he had taught that one may sin with impunity. Instead he suspended the sentence so that whoever does evil may have time to repent. If he does not, the sentence returns upon him with interest, because he did not recognize that he had been pardoned so that he might amend his life.
LXX. The Lord certainly commanded us to become enemies of the devil. Why, then, does he say in the Gospel, "Come to terms quickly with your adversary"? Who is man's adversary but the devil?

No one doubts that the devil is man's enemy, and especially the enemy of the believer, for he sharpens his fiercest weapons against God's servants. But just as he is the enemy of the good, so the law is the adversary of the wicked. For who would not oppose someone who despises him? So the Lord is speaking to the sinner, telling him to come to terms with the commandments that condemn him for his disobedience, to submit to their will and become a friend instead of an enemy. For whoever despises the law is its enemy, since he resists its will. Therefore the Lord urges the sinner to reconcile the law to himself by doing good, so that on the day of judgment it may not accuse him before the judge and he may not be condemned and pay the penalty for spurning the law. To everyone who wants to do evil, the Lord's discipline looks like an enemy. Unless he comes to terms with it, he will be sent into the Gehenna prepared for the devil, who is truly the enemy of the human race.

LXXI. Jacob was called "a man who sees God," and Moses saw God face to face, and Isaiah too says, "I saw the God of hosts with my own eyes." But on the other hand John the evangelist says, "No one has ever seen God." This, it would seem, is a contradiction.

As far as the truth of the faith is concerned, no one has ever seen God at all, neither the Father nor the Son. When he is said to have been seen, this refers to understanding, for he was seen as in an image. We who have never met the emperors still see them in a likeness, though not in reality. In the same way God was seen, so that the one who appeared might be understood to be God, by reason and not in his substance, because in his own nature God cannot be seen. And to lay open more truly the hidden sense of the question before us, let us try to explain the evangelist's meaning. John wanted to bring out something hidden which he knew belonged to saving doctrine. That is why he says, "No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known."

Let us consider the evangelist's meaning. To show that it is true that no one has ever seen God, he teaches that the Son has declared it, and the Son certainly cannot be deceived, because he is in the bosom of the Father. And what is the bosom of the Father but the true Father's loving affection toward the Son through the unity of their nature? Therefore no one has seen God except the only Son. The apostle John heard the Son of God say this, among other things: "Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father." So, to bring about the condemnation of the Jews, who would neither hear nor believe that Christ was the Son of God, the evangelist shows that this Christ is the one who had appeared to the fathers as God, while the one who is the Father is never seen except by the Son. For in denying that God the Father was seen while affirming that God appeared to the fathers, the Son of God wants to reveal himself, since it was always he who was seen by the fathers as God. Hence, among other things, he says to the Jews concerning the Father, "You have never heard his voice or seen his form." So you see, there is no contradiction in God being both seen and unseen.

LXXII (LXXVI). In the Gospel John says, "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." So truth did not exist before. How, then, can the law be said to have been given by God if there was no truth in it?

We must not pass over this so casually. We must consider what "the law was given through Moses" means. The law given through Moses contains plain commandments, but Moses also wrote history, and that too is called law. Let us see, then, what in his commandments will not be true. Perhaps what it says: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit fornication, you shall not steal"? The rest are of the same kind. As for his history, it is clear that it was not truth before the coming of Christ, because what the things under the veil meant was uncertain. But then it was made plain through Christ whose person it is that says in Genesis, "Let us make," and who it is that makes, and who it was that was seen in the bush and by the patriarchs, and who was at work in the rock that gave water in the desert, for, he says, "the rock was Christ." In this way truth comes through Christ, since Christ showed what the hidden or doubtful things meant. Among other things the Lord says, "Moses wrote of me." This was hidden before, and so there was error: the one thought to be God the Father was the Son, and the one taken for an angel was recognized as the Son of God. Again, a promise had been made to Abraham, and as long as it was not fulfilled it remained uncertain. But when it was fulfilled at the coming of Christ, it became truth, for then what had been promised was given, and people began to know what the promise had been. The good faith of one who promises is proved true only when he fulfils his promise.

73 (77). Among other things, the evangelist Mark says of Christ: "Entering a house, he wanted no one to know, and he could not be hidden." What does this mean? If he wanted it and could not have it, his will seems to have been weak.

It is utterly impossible for the Saviour's will not to be fulfilled, and he cannot will what he knows ought not to happen. So we must say that he willed what actually took place, for his will is never outside his nature. Just as his nature cannot be faulted, neither can his will. What the question raises took place, we read, in the region of Tyre. There he entered a house and wanted no one to know. Now we must ask how and why he wanted no one to know. We should notice that this happened in the territory of the Gentiles, and the time for preaching to them had not yet come. When he sent out his disciples he commanded them: "Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."

So he did not want his disciples to give away that he was in the house. Yet he did not refuse to be sought out; he gladly allowed it. Although the time for preaching to the Gentiles had not come, it would have been ungracious to turn away people who came to the faith of their own accord. And so it happened that the Saviour, though not given away by his disciples, was given away by others who had seen him go into the house. People began to know that he was there, so that those who wished to obtain his benefits might come in to him. He did not want his own followers to announce that he was in the house, but he did want to be sought out, and that is what happened. He was not hidden, because others pointed out that he was in the house. Then the Canaanite woman heard about him and came in to him, begging him to drive the demon out of her daughter. She would not have obtained this favour if she had not first submitted herself to the God of the Jews. So the Saviour's will was fulfilled, as we have explained. The evangelist, aiming at brevity, summed the events up, and by examining them we have found what lay hidden.
74 (78). We read in the Gospel of John that the Saviour said he was not going up to the feast, and then he went up. This seems to show inconstancy.

You always hide the sense by cutting the passage short. What you call into question happened when he was in Galilee. Because the Jews were in an uproar, his brothers, who did not yet believe in him, were pressing him to go up into Judea for the coming Jewish feast, so that he would meet with violence there. He answered them: "You go up to the feast, because the world does not hate you. But it hates me, because I expose its works. I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled." Then his brothers went up to the feast, but he stayed in Galilee. Afterwards he too went up to the feast.

What contradiction is there here? He did not go up at the time when he said he would not, but later, and he did not go up as if to a feast but as if to a contest. The others all went up gladly, as if to enjoy the pleasures of the feast day. It is certain, then, that he did not go up to the feast. The Saviour's feast day was the day on which he redeemed the world by his passion. So he says: "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in him." His feast day is the day on which he conquered death.

75 (79). If we live by our own choice, why did the Saviour say, "No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him"? And the Apostle agrees with this: "It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy," and: "He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." How is the choice of the will free when it is led to good or to evil at another's nod?

The matter stands otherwise than you have put it. These passages do not have the sense you allege. They can in no way unsettle the case for free will. In fact, if you look closely at what they mean, you will see that they rather confirm the doctrine of free will. These words were spoken against the malicious Jews. Out of jealousy and with deceitful pretence, they claimed that Joseph was the Saviour's own father and that Joseph's sons were his brothers, so that he would not be believed to be the Son of God. Then the Saviour said: "No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." And how did the Father draw people to the Son, if not through the works he did through him? For he said: "The Father who dwells in me does the works himself." The purpose was that these works should draw people to faith in Christ. The mighty deeds the Saviour did were themselves persuading people that God was Christ's Father, and so whoever said he had another father was not drawn to Christ by God. God worked through Christ so that people would give credence to his words when he said he was the Son of God.

This is the drawing: not force, but God's testimony in Christ. Whoever believes it is said to be drawn by him to Christ, for no one believes in the Saviour except someone who says that God is his own Father. Nor did the Apostle say the words you have called into question in order to attack free choice. He said them to forbid anyone from reopening God's judgement, and he was proclaiming that God is just, for God knows on whom he ought to have mercy. He who searches the heart sees clearly whether the mind of the one who asks deserves to receive. So he says through the prophet: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." It is just for him to harden the heart of a hypocrite. Someone may call the true false, not by mistake but out of malice: he understands the good, pretends not to know that it is good, and so turns it into evil. That person should be given exactly this, that he really does not understand the good, so that he is not saved, since he does not want to be. It is not just for someone to be saved against his will when he spurns salvation, not through ignorance, but through malice or envy. So these passages confirm free choice rather than destroy it: each person is answered according to his own wish.

76 (72). We read in John's Apocalypse: "Go and take the book from the angel's hand and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." What is this book that makes the stomach bitter even though it is sweet?

All the divine books are bitter, but only to the faithless and the carnal. Idolaters find it unpleasant to hear one God preached in Christ. Photinus shudders with horror at it. Sabellius blushes too when he hears that the Father is the Father and cannot be called the Son, because all things are from him, and that the Son is called the Son because he is certainly not the Father himself but is from the Father; he is not the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom they are. Arius too is refuted when he reads that Christ is the true Son of God, for without doubt he could not be called true unless he were properly from God. Marcion, who thinks that flesh must be denied to Christ, is proven wrong when he learns that the Word became flesh. The wicked Manichee is also rebuked when he sees it written by the evangelist that the Saviour not only graced a wedding with his presence but also honoured it with wine. For the Manichee shuts the way to marriage and urges promiscuous intercourse.

These things are contained in the book which the apostle received to eat up. This book is the gospel entitled "According to John." It is bitter not only to those who think wrongly, but also to the undisciplined, who refuse correction and so go from bad to worse. This revelation was given when the apostle John was on the island of Patmos, banished there by the emperor Domitian for the sake of the faith. Then he was in the Spirit, so that he could see heavenly things. While the things that are to come because of impiety, lewdness and the rest were being shown to him, he was given a book that was sweet in the mouth but made the stomach bitter. Among people who seem to belong to one body, it would be sweet to some. These are signified by the mouth because their profession of faith is sound, and what is true is sweet in the mouth. But it would be bitter to those who live or think carnally in heretical depravity; they are signified by the stomach. For the book will accuse them on the day of God's judgement. So after the revelation he was ordered to write the gospel, for the reasons we have given above. In the same way the prophet Ezekiel was told to take a book that would be sweet in his mouth, when he was sent to rebuke the faithlessness of the people.

77 (73). Among other things Simeon says to Mary, the mother of the Lord: "This child is set for the fall and the rising of many in Israel; and a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." What does this mean?

Simeon was a holy man, approved by divine oracles. Through the Holy Spirit he declared what would come upon people because of Christ. It would be a fall for those who thought they stood firm by keeping the law and knowing it well, but fell through distrust of Christ's works and were cut off from the promise made to the fathers. But for those who had almost no standing under the law yet believed in Christ, it would be a rising in Israel. So those who had once been unworthy and useless would become worthy of God, and those who were thought to be something would be rejected. This is what the Lord says in another place: "For judgement I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." And indeed it was not the teachers of the law, not the Pharisees, not the scribes who followed Christ, but fishermen, unlearned country people. This is why the Lord says: "Father, I thank you that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones."

He went on to say: "And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." By this he certainly meant that even Mary, through whom the mystery of the Saviour's incarnation was accomplished, would doubt at the Lord's death, but in such a way that she would be made firm again by the resurrection. For at the Lord's death everyone doubted in a kind of stupor. Who would not waver on seeing the one who called himself the Son of God so humbled that he went down even to death? And because, as I said, all doubt was to vanish at the Lord's resurrection, he said the sword would "pass through," not fall upon her or graze some limb in passing. When a sword is thrown and passes close by someone, it frightens him but does not strike him. In the same way doubt caused grief but did not kill, because it did not settle in the mind. It passed through, touching the disciples' hearts like a shadow. So Cleopas and Amaus, going sadly along the road [?], said among other things to the Lord himself, not knowing that it was the Lord: "We thought that he was the one who was beginning to set Israel free." They doubted, but as soon as they recognized the Lord the doubt passed. The same is said of Joseph: "The iron passed through his soul." This means escaping death, because to doubt about God or Christ is death, and so whoever stops doubting escapes death.
78 (74). What does it mean that the prophet Isaiah says of Christ, "who did no sin," while the Apostle on the other hand says, "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us"?

As far as the sense is concerned, the two questions are different. But the words are partly alike and partly at odds. "Made" and "did not do" are contrary, while "knew no" and "did not do" are alike. The prophet spoke in the person of Christ: that he did no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth. The Apostle speaks of the person of God the Father: that he made him who knew no sin, that is, Christ, to be sin for us. This is to be understood in two ways. First, he made him sin when he willed him to become incarnate, so that he whom the lot of sin did not touch took a body from sinful flesh; because of that body he is said to have been made sin. Second, he made him sin when he offered him for sins, for under the law a victim offered for sins was called "sin."

So Christ did not commit sin, as the prophet says, but he plainly was himself made sin, as has been shown. And what is it for him to offer Christ for us, if not to give those who wanted to kill him the power to do so? This was permitted because it would be of benefit: it gave him reason to descend to the underworld and strip Tartarus of its souls. For it was an overwhelming and unheard-of sin to kill one who had not only committed no sin of any kind, but had even given life to many. Made guilty by this sin, the devil lost his boldness to raise objections. Something similar is read in the letter to the Galatians, where among other things it says: "He became a curse for us." Made so by whom, if not by the Father? By God's judgement the cross of Christ is the curse of the Jews, for the Saviour's death cries out their sin. So he allowed himself to be crucified, so that his passion might benefit us, and so that, departing from here with his sign, we might in no way be held by the second death. For death fears even the servants of the one who conquered it.
79 (75). Why did the Saviour pay the didrachma only for himself and Peter, and not for the other apostles as well, since they had all left everything they had and followed him?

The didrachma is understood as a poll tax, not a tax on property. The Saviour owned nothing in the world, though he is the Lord of the world; when he died he was buried at another's expense. And we, to whom the world is foreign, are eager to increase our wealth. Then at death we attest, not only by word of mouth but in writing, that we have seized hold of the world, and so by our own declaration we are condemned by him whose world it is. Hence the Lord says: "Whoever does not leave everything and follow me cannot be my disciple." So whoever holds his possessions in such a way that he does not put his hope in them, and is ready to throw them away for the sake of the faith, walks the road that leads to Christ our Lord.

The didrachma, then, was to be collected from those who carried on some business or worked at a trade. The Saviour cared for none of these things, nor did his disciples, so the tax certainly should not have been demanded of him. But the devil, the enemy, was always lying in wait and looking for an opportunity to see if he could bring the Saviour low. He took hold of the minds of the didrachma collectors to make them do his will. So they came to Peter, who was first among the apostles, and said that his master ought to pay the didrachma, although he and his followers were free of such burdens, since they did nothing in the world that belonged to the world. The aim was that, since he had nothing to pay with, he would either offend them or else have to humble himself and beg someone to pay for him. Then the Lord, to show that the devil is short-sighted and always scheming against himself, told the apostle Peter to go to the sea, open the mouth of the fish he caught, and find there the amount owed for the tax. When it was paid, the Lord not only gave the collectors no offence and did not lower himself by seeking help to pay; he also displayed a sign of the greatest power, by which he might draw to himself those whom the devil held captive. So the devil was tormented by his own scheme and cunning. The collectors of the didrachma said to the apostle Peter: "Does your master not pay the didrachma?" In saying this they called on the master to pay for all his disciples.

When the Saviour ordered the coin to be given for himself and Peter, he is seen to have paid for everyone. Just as all were contained in the Saviour because he was their master, so after the Saviour all are contained in Peter, for the Lord appointed him to be their head, so that he would be shepherd of the Lord's flock. Among other things he says to the disciples: "Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation." And to Peter he says: "See, Satan has demanded to sift you all like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when at last you have turned back, strengthen your brothers." What doubt can there be? Did he pray for Peter and not pray for James and John, to say nothing of the others? Clearly all are contained in Peter, because in another place too he says: "I pray for those whom you have given me," and: "I want them to be with me where I am."
Now let us see what the didrachma is, that is, what its weight or amount is, or of what substance [?] …
80. Surely everyone is a son either of God or of the devil. So a person is always a son, but sometimes of God and sometimes of the devil. We must ask, then, what we are born as.

After the children of Israel had been brought out of Egypt and had sinned many times, the Lord in his anger pronounced sentence: none of them would enter the promised land except Caleb and Joshua son of Nun, who was formerly called Hoshea. But he said that those born in the desert would enter, because they did not know good or evil. Not knowing good or evil is a kind of natural simplicity, which has been trained neither to good nor to evil; that is, it is ignorance without malice. For we are born without understanding, but our nature has this good in it, that it is capable of learning the truth. The son of the devil is the one who, once born, is steeped in evil things, so that he devotes himself to what is hostile to the Creator: he claims there are many gods and that sacrifice must be made to them as rulers of the world. If he comes to his senses, thinks in keeping with his nature and turns to the Creator, he will be a son of God.

So those who are born are neither sons of God nor sons of the devil. For what does the Saviour say to the Jews? "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires." You see, then, that people become sons of the devil by their works and their profession, while those are sons of God who confess that God is Christ's own Father and live rightly. God established our race so that, though born without understanding, we have the capacity to learn either good or evil. So we acquire either evil or good for ourselves. Then we may rejoice in ourselves when we are rewarded for acting rightly, or blame ourselves if we follow wicked ways and are condemned.

81. The Apostle says: "We are Jews by nature." He shows, then, that Jews are born of Jews. I am not speaking of proselytes, who clearly become Jews. After all, those who were born in the desert were not circumcised. If, then, Jews are born of Jews, why are Christians not also born of Christians? Pagans, too, are born of pagans.

Not everything that is born is the same as what it is born from. Gold is born from the earth, yet it is not earth; so too are gems and many other things. Food grows from a tree, and an egg comes from a hen. That pagans are born of pagans has this cause: every pagan is in ignorance, and the one born of him is without understanding, so both are ignorant. But there is this difference between them: the father is without doubt a blasphemer and therefore a son of the devil, whereas the newborn infant does not know how to blaspheme, just as he does not know how to bless; yet he is a pagan, because he is without understanding. A Jew, on the other hand, is born of a Jew because he is begotten in devotion to the Creator. As Adam said of Cain: "I have brought forth a man through God." Pagans have no devotion to the Creator and give thanks to demons in everything they do. In the same way, the Jews humbly praise God the Creator in their every act. They deserve contempt only in this, that they do not acknowledge Christ, through whom all things exist. It is in this way that a Jew is born of a Jew, and not, as some think, because circumcision makes a Jew. Circumcision is the sign of Judaism, not Judaism itself, because in Abraham circumcision is not righteousness but the sign of righteousness. It was given so that those born of Abraham would have a sign proving that they were sons of Abraham. Yet they were called by this name from Judas Maccabeus, so that not only those descended from Judah but all the others descended from all the sons of Jacob were called Jews, because Judas had been their leader. And so those born Jews receive the sign, so that it may be recognized what they are.

2. A Christian, however, does not beget a Christian by birth, because the one who begets was not born a Christian but was made one. The one who is born must likewise be made this [?], in order to be it. For one is not born a Christian by substance, but by faith, which comes to those already born. Ignorance is born with the flesh, but faith is implanted afterwards by a spiritual principle. Yet it is objected: “If the one who begets has indeed been made a Christian, he ought then to beget what he himself is, so that the dignity he received would be passed on by descent. After all, senators beget senators.” But the dignity of senators has no merit before God, nor does nature itself, that is, the substance, gain any benefit from it; that dignity consists only in reputation and talk. So the title does indeed pass down by fleshly descent, but it confers nothing beyond a reputation of dignity, just as those who are consuls or are honoured with statues rejoice in something empty. But when people become Christians, dignity is added to their very nature, so that the very being of a person holds the everlasting gift of incorruptibility, and this not in reputation only but also in reality [?] and in effect before God. It is as if some eloquent poor man were praised and yet lacked bread and other necessities. True praise is when the dignity one has sought so benefits him that he lacks nothing, because his very nature is granted to live of itself, and to live well, without needing anyone's support. That is truly to become rich and glorious.

82. No one doubts that pagans are subject to the elements. What, then, does the apostle mean when he says, “We too were in servitude under the elements of this world”? If the Jews too were in servitude to the elements, how did they differ from the pagans?

It is plain that adding, removing or changing a syllable distorts the meaning. Everyone knows that pagans worship the elements, whereas the Jews served God, not the elements, but “under the elements,” on account of new moons and sabbaths and circumcision and other such things. These are carnal, for whatever is visible is carnal and belongs to the elements. But because it was by God's command, it was God who was served, so that they might pass from things visible to things invisible, and through this care make progress toward grasping greater things, so that, practised in these, they might become worthy of the spiritual promises. In the respect I have just described, then, the Jews served under the elements; in another respect they had the spiritual law, which forbids sin and urges love of the Lord God, who had been promised to come to them to forgive sins.

83. If salvation and true and perfect knowledge come through Christ, why did he not come earlier, so that our forebears, who lived in ignorance, might also have learned the truth? Indeed, after Christ's coming many more have been saved than before. So if he had come earlier, far more would have been saved. If this is so, it seems blameworthy.

No one who shows mercy ought to be maligned. It lies in the giver's power when, and how much, he wishes to show mercy. Such a person should be encouraged and appealed to with prayers, not called away from his good work by quarrelling. Perhaps there would be no objection if some return were made to him for this mercy. Would anyone find fault with a doctor who spends his medicines and services for nothing, or will he be blamed for his slowness by people who never sent for him?

We have said this according to reason, but the Saviour's goodness does not take account of such things because of human weakness; it follows its own nature in showing mercy. Therefore he came when he ought to have come, following the reason of his own will, not of our merits. For if you weigh merits, he ought not to have come at all. So he came when he knew that help ought to be given and that the gift would be welcome. If someone facing need is helped beforehand, it will indeed be welcome, yet he will hardly be able to know what has been done for him; but if you bring help to someone in the very midst of need, he will know what a benefit he has received. One rescued from distress will give greater thanks, as when you offer bread to someone who is hungry; but if you offer it when he is not hungry, it will certainly not be so welcome.

So it was right that the Lord did not come earlier. First he left the human race to use its own will, though not without witness to himself, for he willed that his divinity be understood and feared from the very fabric of the world and from the yearly gifts which he decreed should be provided for human use through the service of the elements; and indeed knowledge of him was present on earth through the line of the first man, and then through Enoch and Noah. But when, through a kind of weariness of the human race, the knowledge of God began to fade among people and their ways became corrupt, he deigned to choose Abraham, in whom there would be a pattern of renewed knowledge of God and of good conduct. And since reverence was still sluggish, he later gave the law in writing through Moses, so that it would not fade and would inspire more fear; for fear is greater where authority is manifest. And because, once the law had been given, the nations despised it and would not submit to it, and those who received it did not keep it, the Lord, moved by mercy, sent his Son, who would offer himself for them, destroy death, grant forgiveness of sins to all, and present them justified to God the Father. For he could not descend to the underworld except through death: neither order nor reason required that one who had not died should enter the gates of Tartarus.

If someone wants to outwit barbarians in their own land, does he not change into their dress so that he is taken for one of them, and so find out how to overthrow them? That is what was done to the devil. Since he had overthrown man by wicked means so that he would remain in death, a remedy was found by which he would lose those he wrongly held: he was to be infiltrated, and the one he thought he had killed as a man he would find in the underworld to be God. When this happened, he was found guilty and lost all those he held, and from then on the way to heaven was open.

See how much the Saviour's coming has profited, so that people, knowing from what danger they have been freed, may give him thanks without ceasing! But perhaps someone will object: “If many before the law and after the law, weighed down by sins, gave themselves wholly to the flesh and deserved to remain in Tartarus, there were without doubt others who, out of devotion and reverence for the Creator, restrained their lives by the law of nature. Were not these too held in the underworld once this life was over? But if he had come earlier, after Adam's death, then by freeing Adam, who had sinned first, he would have opened the way to heaven for the rest, so that those who had lived well and known the Creator would have been received into heaven at their death. So it is a loss that Christ did not come earlier.” That it is a loss is plain; but ask whether it is just or unjust. Losses are often just, and then one may not complain of them. Does a thief who is caught and condemned by law to repay fourfold dare to complain? So the loss which the human race suffered was justly inflicted, and for that reason it was permitted.

For this reason too the Saviour ought not to have come at the very beginning. For when [?] the devil grew proud, man was made by God and set up as his enemy, so that, protected by God's help, since he was no match for him on his own, he might resist him by keeping the command he had received. But the devil, with his usual subtlety, pretended not to know what God had commanded and found Eve unsteady; then, by promising her that if they touched what was forbidden he would grant them divinity, he deceived them. Then the devil triumphed over the defeated man, and man, once conquered, subjected his descendants to sin. Therefore it would have been unjust to snatch the spoils from the victor by force, for whatever God does, he does justly; and besides, man had sinned grievously. For by consenting, against the Creator's command, to become a god, he committed idolatry, and in this he sinned against God. So he ought not to have been helped at once, especially since he did not repent. Nor would mercy have been welcome if he had not known what he deserved. For although God can do all things, he does what accords with reason, so that he may remain beyond reproach.
84. Since we observe the course of the moon in reckoning Easter, why do we find fault with pagans for observing lunar days and their measure?

Far be it from Christians to be said to worship the stars; they have been granted spiritual worship, so that, looking down on things that are seen, they may be joined to things invisible and above the heavens, and so rise above all these things, since they will be with the angels of God. Those who worship the stars will be either with them or beneath them; for how can anyone be above the things he worships? The pagans, then, do not observe the reckoning of the moon; they worship the moon itself as a goddess, and, believing they have grasped the effects of its courses, what should be done or avoided on certain days, they have resolved to subject their life and conduct in a fixed order to its rule. And because they have dared to usurp these things outside God's ordinance, we often find them deceived. God established these lights as signs of the seasons; so we too keep the number of the moon, but we do not worship the moon itself. So we observe the reckoning of Easter from the fourteenth moon, which for us, according to the law, is the first. God established all things complete; and so we are permitted to celebrate Easter within the seven days from the fourteenth to the twenty-first, so that, within these seven days, the days from the Preparation to the Lord's resurrection may be included. Thus the thirteenth does not fall on the Passion, nor the fourteenth or fifteenth on the resurrection, so that Christ's passion does not come before what is for us the first moon, nor his resurrection on any day other than the first day, on which the world began.

All the times of the world are counted by the cycles of a single week, in which God put together the members and adornments of the world. He fashioned the world in six days and rested on the seventh, which he called the sabbath. In these seven days the whole order and number of the world is contained; ever returning upon themselves, they multiply the number of the times. After the sabbath the count always begins again from the first day up to the seventh, that is, the sabbath, so that we may learn that the Lord's resurrection took place on the first day of the world's beginning, which is called the Lord's day. For the Lord made it the one day which, having run its course to the number seven by evening, begins again, so as to be the first after the week. This was so decreed from the beginning on account of the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, passion and resurrection; for in the Lord's body almost the whole world rose again and was renewed.

It is settled, then, that we do not worship the moon, but keep the number that was established through the moon's course. But the devil, who is Satan, so that he might lend some authority to his deceit and colour his lies with counterfeit truth, established mysteries for the pagans to observe in the first month, the month in which he knows the Lord's sacraments are to be celebrated, for his power is no small one. He did this to hold their souls in error for two reasons: first, because falsehood came before the truth, the truth might seem to be falsehood, as though falsehood's antiquity prejudged the truth; and second, because this observance is kept by them in the first month, in which the Romans have the equinox just as we do, so that they even say expiation is made by blood, just as we say it is by the cross. By this cunning he holds the pagans in error, so that they think our truth looks more like an imitation than the truth, as though it had been invented out of rivalry by some superstition. “For what was invented later,” they say, “cannot be thought true.” But because the truth is certainly with us, and has been from the beginning, signs of mighty works and wonders bear witness to it, so that with power as witness the devil's wickedness becomes known. Since power alone readily convinces people of these things, it has been set against the devil's cunning and his getting in first, to expose his pretence. For no one, not even among our enemies, would dare to deny that the truth is there where power appears.

85. Since it is agreed that from David to the deportation to Babylon there were seventeen generations, why does the evangelist say fourteen, leaving out Ahaziah, who came after Joram the son of Jehoshaphat, Joash the son of Ahaziah, and Amaziah the son of Joash?

We should believe that the evangelist followed nothing but the meaning of the law, and so these men were rightly removed by him from the count of the others. For their wickedness was so continuous that there was no break in their evil. The evil that began with Joram ran on unbroken until Uzziah the son of Amaziah, so that there was support from no side by which any of them could remain in the list of kings through his father's merit. Joram, though he did evil, was allowed to remain in the count through the merit of Jehoshaphat, and Uzziah was kept in the count through the merit of Jotham; but the wickedness of those three against God was unbroken. Solomon too was allowed to remain in the line of kings through his father's merit, and Rehoboam the son of Solomon, though he did evil, was left in the list of kings through the merit of Asa. But those three, who did evil, were shut in between evil men; so they were erased. For it is a worse example, leading to the ruin of a line, when wickedness spreads without interruption. And to put it properly: they were passed over because Joseph is not descended from them. For the evangelist traced the descent from Abraham of those from whom Joseph takes his origin, Joseph to whom Mary was betrothed when she gave birth to Christ.
86. What proves that Mary the mother of the Lord was of the tribe and seed of David?

We cite the word of a reliable witness. Among other things the angel says to Mary: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” How could a reliable witness call David his father if Mary were not of the seed of David?
87. If God is one, why does the hope of salvation lie in three, and not in two or four, or indeed in the one himself? And why was the Trinity not preached from the beginning?

There is almost nothing new here; for the Trinity is preached in such a way that one God is believed in. So nothing has been added; rather, the mystery of the one God has been revealed. It ought not to have been made known at the very beginning, because a thing must first be proclaimed and only afterwards what was proclaimed revealed, so that you may know that there is the Father, from whom all things are; that the Son is spoken of, through whom all things are; and that the Holy Spirit is named, through whom all things, which are from the Father but through the Son, are regenerated to faith in the one God. These, then, are indeed three, but one divinity. Reason, therefore, makes them three, neither more nor fewer. For every number goes up to nine, because the three, since they are in one another, make the number nine: three are in one and three in one. Whoever sees one sees three, since the one differs in nothing from the other. So three are one, and three times three are one; that is, as far as number goes, perfection lies in the number nine, because all things come from one. For when one is added, from which or in which the three that are counted as nine exist, they become ten or twenty. Yet the count always comes up to nine and one is added, because nine are one, so that there may be the full perfection of unity.

88. If grace is greater and understanding clearer in the New Testament than in the Old, why did the prophet Isaiah see the Lord of hosts, who is Christ according to the interpretation of John the evangelist, seated on the throne of majesty (for among other things John said, “Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty and spoke of him”), while in the New Testament Stephen, the first martyr, says that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God? Why is it that here he appears as a subordinate after his triumphs, and there as Lord before he had conquered?

The Lord showed himself as the case required. To the prophet he appeared as a king rebuking the people, and he showed himself as what he was; for the cause of his divinity was then at peace. But that he appeared standing to Stephen was due to the slander of the Jews. In Stephen the Saviour's cause was suffering violence; so, with God seated as judge, he appeared standing, as one pleading a case, and because his case is good, he stood at the judge's right hand. For everyone who pleads a case must stand.

Among other things the Saviour says of the Holy Spirit: “When he comes, he will convict the world of sin and of righteousness and of judgment: of sin, because they do not believe in me; of righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will see me no longer; of judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.” He seems to have stated the reason for convicting the world, but it needs explanation.

Since neither the Jews nor the worldly powers believed the Saviour (for he willed to make himself known not only to human beings but also to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, as the apostle teaches in the Epistle to the Ephesians), he made it clear that after his passion the Holy Spirit would prove that he had spoken the truth. And this is what “to convict the world” means: to show it that what it refused to believe is true. It refused to believe that the Saviour had come from God. But the Saviour, keeping righteousness, did not fear to return to the one who had sent him, and by going back he proved that he had come from there, because no one ascends to God except one who has descended from God. So when the powers saw him ascending, they were confounded, seeing that what they had scorned as false was true. Thus this righteousness convicted them, by which he was proved righteous, because he returned to where he had come from. And he convicted them of sin in that they not only refused to believe him but even killed him. And he rebuked them concerning judgment by showing that the ruler of the world had been found guilty and crushed by him in whose faith they had not shared. For when they saw souls going from the underworld into heaven, they recognized that the ruler of this world had been condemned, so that, found guilty in the Saviour's case, he lost what he held.

These things were indeed seen when the Saviour ascended, but when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples they were made openly and plainly manifest. The true rebuke came when, after the passion, in witness to the Saviour, the faithless saw publicly the dead rising, the lame running, lepers cleansed, paralytics made strong, the blind seeing, the deaf hearing, the mute speaking, the demon-possessed set free, and the sick restored to health and giving thanks. In this way the Holy Spirit convicted the world, because in the name of the Saviour, whom the world had rejected, he worked mighty acts of healing of every kind.

90. If the devil is Satan himself, why does the Saviour say to the Jews, among other things: “You are of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar, as is his father also”?

“Devil” is not a proper name but a common one. Anyone in whom the works of the devil are found must without doubt be called a devil; it is the name of a deed, not of a nature. So in this passage the father of the Jews means Cain, whose imitators the Jews wished to be when they killed the Saviour. He says that Cain did not stand in the truth because he stained himself with the murder of his kin and made himself guilty of death. It was he who set the pattern of fratricide. It is of him that he says that when he speaks a lie he speaks from his own, to show that each person sins only by his own will. But because he is an imitator of the devil, he added: “because he is a liar, as is his father also.” For the devil, in order to bring death upon the first man, pretended not to know what God had commanded; likewise Cain, when questioned, pretended not to know where his brother Abel was, whom he had killed. So in this passage he called Cain a devil, and his father the devil whose works he followed; for the son of the devil is a devil. But that devil who is also Satan has no father in his wickedness; he is himself the author of his own evil. For he sinned first, and so all who imitate him will be called his sons, and he their father. Just so, in faith we have Abraham as our father, because he first believed God, and so we are named after him; for we are called faithful, as he was.
91. It must be asked how, without arguments, Photinus is to be refuted on the point that Christ existed before Mary.

Let us first ask John the Baptist, whom the Savior himself declared to be his witness. Among other things he says of the Lord: "He who comes from above is above all; he who is of the earth speaks of the earth; but he who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony." See: John calls everyone, himself included, earthly in comparison with the Lord. He testifies that the Lord came from heaven, but that all the others are from the earth, that is, from the regions below. The Lord himself says the same, among other things: "For I have not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me," meaning the Father. And again, among other things, the Lord speaks to this effect: "And now I tell you that I will ask the Father. For the Father himself loves you, because you love me and believe that I came forth from God the Father and came into this world. Now I am leaving the world again and going to the Father." Then the disciples, seeing that he had spoken plainly, said to him: "See, now you are speaking openly and not using any figure of speech. Now we know that you know all things and have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God." These words need no interpretation. This is the sum of our religion: that we believe Christ was with God in heaven before he took flesh, as a Son with the Father.

Suppose he said he had come forth from heaven and from God and come into the world because of his righteous life and heavenly teaching. Then all the prophets and apostles ought to have said the same of themselves. And since he said, "Now I am leaving the world again and going to the Father," someone might perhaps say this meant that the teaching which had come from God left the world and returned to God. They have nothing else to say. But suppose that coming from heaven, coming forth from God and coming into this world refer to power and teaching rather than to the person of the Savior. Then, when he says, "Now I am leaving the world again and going to the Father," that power and teaching would be returning to where it came from. Yet we see that both the power and the teaching remained in the world after the Lord's departure. So you see that the Lord was not speaking of power and teaching. He was speaking specifically of himself.

But perhaps you say that these are the words of the power that worked in Christ. Then this very power calls God its Father. See, you run straight into what you fear. For if the power of God is the Son of God, it is surely the power of which the apostle says, "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." This power came forth from God and returned to God again. And this same power, which is Christ, testifies that it casts out demons by the Spirit of God. That Spirit worked through the apostles. So you may know that the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord worked, went on working here in the world in the apostles after the Lord's departure. This makes it all the clearer that the Lord was speaking of his own person when he said that he left the world and returned to God. Or if you think this power is not Christ, there will be two powers and two Sons of God. Then what becomes of the passage we read: "the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father," and again, "For God so loved this world that he gave his only Son for it"? You now see that the power of God which worked in the world in a body is one and the same, and that it may be called both the power of God and the Son. And let us see what the apostles believed, and in whom. When they heard the Lord say, "See, now I am leaving the world again and going to the Father," they answered him: "See, now you are speaking openly and not using any figure of speech. Now we know that you know all things and have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God."

Now let us consider what the disciples were in doubt about. Was it the miracles, and whether they came from God? They had seen Lazarus raised on the fourth day when he already stank, a man blind from birth given his sight, a woman freed from her flow of blood by touching a fringe, and the nature of water changed into wine. Or was it the person of the Lord? Plainly no one doubted the miracles, since some said he was Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. When the Jews wanted to stone him, Jesus answered them: "I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?" The Jews said to him: "We are not stoning you for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, though you are a man, make yourself God." If even the Jews did not doubt that these were the works of God, would the apostles have doubted it?

All the doubt, then, concerned the person of the Savior. It was something unheard of, which had never entered human understanding, and people were astonished to hear him say that he had come forth from God and that God was his own Father. That is why the disciples admitted that the plainness of the Lord's words had satisfied them, and said to him: "Now we know that you know all things and have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God." If he did not truly come forth from God, the faith of the apostles is emptied. But that cannot be, for the Savior approved it. He answered them: "Now you believe," that is, "seeing such great signs, you did not believe." So it was proved to the apostles that Christ had come forth from God and had come, so that because of this coming forth there would be no doubt in believing him to be the Son of God. No one has seen God except the one who is from God, and he has seen God. No one knows the Father except the Son. This means that he was truly with God and came forth from him and came. No one else could come forth from God except the one who was with God in the beginning, since no one else knew or had seen God. Therefore it is not hard for us to believe that he is the true Son of God. As John says in his first letter: "And we are in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true one and eternal life." The apostle says, "who did not spare his own Son," and the evangelist says, "because he called God his own Father."

If Christ, then, is the true Son of God, how is he merely a man? He would not be called true unless he had been properly begotten of him. Otherwise let Photinus say why he is believed to be truly the Son of God if he is not the true Son. Or what need was there to believe him the Son of God, if he were just one of the other saints who are worthy to be called sons of God? Is there perhaps some unworthiness in him that would keep him from being believed a son of God as the others are, so that this is said in order to make people believe what seems incredible about him? But if he is superior to the others, what need is there to say, "Believe that Christ is the Son of God"? It can only be that we are commanded to believe something different about him than about the others. Many are called sons of God because of their holiness, but he alone is to be believed the true Son of God. That is why he is also called the only Son. Which of the saints ever dared to call himself a son of God, let alone the true Son, except the Savior, who knew that his birth came from God? And how could he allow himself to be worshiped if he did not know that he was from God? For it is written: "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." Indeed the angel rebuked John when he wanted to worship him, saying, "Do not do that, for I am your fellow servant; worship God." And although scripture testifies that God alone is to be served, the apostle says, "Whoever serves Christ pleases God." Why? Because God and Christ, Father and Son, are one.

The apostle declares himself a servant of Christ, and he says to the Corinthians, "Do not become servants of men," and to the Galatians, "Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead." He shows openly that Christ is God and man. His point is that his apostleship came not from a man but from Christ, as God, and from God the Father. Then, a little further on, he says: "For I did not receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ." What could be plainer? He says that he did not obtain God's teaching through a man, but was taught by God himself. We received God's teaching through men, but the chosen vessel shows that he obtained nothing from the apostles, that is, from men. If God's teaching is never learned through a man simply because it is God's, what credit could the apostle claim for himself, if he learned it just as the other peoples did?

Why else would he also say, "I did not receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ"? Who could doubt that in this passage Christ is meant as God? But that is no wonder, since among other things he says to the Romans: "theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever." What does "from them is Christ according to the flesh" mean? He would not say this unless Christ also existed according to God. According to the flesh he is from the fathers, but according to his divinity he is from God, and so Christ is God over all. "But perhaps it may be said to refer to the person of the Father." Yet in this passage the name of the Father is not mentioned at all. So if anyone denies that it is said of Christ, let him name the person to whom it applies. And why should it not apply to Christ, at whose name things in heaven, on earth and under the earth bend the knee? This is what it means to be God over all, for besides these there is nothing else. Let Photinus tell us now whether these bend the knee to a man, or whether God decreed that the heavenly powers and the holy angels should worship a man. Far from it! God decrees nothing foolish, especially since it is not permitted to worship anyone but God, and how much less in heaven! A king is reverenced on earth as God's vicar, but Christ, once he had fulfilled the dispensation he carried out as vicar, is worshiped in heaven and on earth.

For we read that the Word became flesh, that is, was made incarnate of Mary through the ministry of the Holy Spirit. We read that this Word was with God in the beginning and was God, and also that it is called the Son of God. How then is he not before Mary, when he was in the beginning and was God? Even if in your blindness you deny that this Word is God, you do not deny, and you know well, that this Word is called the Son of God and was with God in the beginning. By what reasoning, then, do you say that he exists only after Mary, when you read that he was in the beginning? In the Apocalypse we read of Christ: "and his name is the Word of God."
