This word "Word" can be interpreted in many ways. For nothing that is from God is not called God. But out of regard for the authority of the one God, scripture called what was born of him the Word. Just as we know that our words come only from ourselves, so by this reasoning we would believe that Christ is from God.

Nor indeed should it have been put any other way, if he was to be believed to be from God and not outside him. In the same way he is also called the power and the wisdom of God, so that by the same reasoning he may be understood to be from him. If scripture had said "God and God," it would not have shown that he was from him. It would have made two gods, which is contrary to unity. This is the principle in the divine books: when Christ is said to be God, it does not go beyond the bounds of the one God.

And how foolish is that punctuation of yours, Photinus, by which you divide the opening of John's Gospel so that the Word is not called God! You read it like this: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was. The Word was in the beginning with God." What is the point of this division? What sense does it give? What principle of piety does it show, except sheer hostility to the Son of God? What could anyone mean by saying, "and the Word was with God, and God was"? Is this the wisdom of our law, to teach that God exists? What tongue, what nation, what land, what sect denies that God exists? And to what purpose does it say, "and the Word was with God"? Or how is this Word to be understood, unless scripture explains what it is? The Gospel was not written on account of God, whom no one doubts, but on account of the Word, which raises questions. It is a mystery of God, and it must be believed precisely because it is not plain to everyone. That is why scripture takes pains to teach what the Word is, saying: "and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God." This reading agrees with reason, and it is sound and complete. It shows that this Word, which was with God in the beginning, was God. So in the sacrament of the mystery of the eternal God, hidden for ages and generations, we are to believe that God the Word was with God the Father.

Carnal people, who want scripture to speak according to the limits of their own understanding, fall into doubt about this. That is why faith has been established, so that by following the sense of scripture it may earn its reward. When Solomon asked God for wisdom, the Lord answered him: "See, I have given you a wise and discerning heart, such as no one had before you, and after you no man like you will arise." What shall we say? Is what God promised true? Yes, indeed it is. So no human being will ever be like Solomon. What then shall we think of Christ, who among other things says: "The queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and see, something greater than Solomon is here"? Now choose whom you will believe, Photinus: God or Christ, the Father or the Son. If you believe the Father, you convict the Son. If you believe the Son, you accuse the Father. If Christ is merely a man, he put himself above Solomon for nothing and against God's promise. But if he is understood to be God as well, he rightly ranked himself above Solomon, and God's promise stands unblemished, since no man like Solomon has arisen. Christ shows himself greater precisely because he is God.

O the madness of Photinus! He refuses to acknowledge that Christ existed before Mary, though he hears Christ testify with his own voice that he is before Abraham. When the Jews were arguing with him about time and said, "You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?" he answered them: "Truly I tell you, before Abraham I am." He did not say "I am better." He answered the question that was asked, and said that he existed earlier than the Jews supposed. Photinus plainly cannot escape the curse of the law, since he puts his hope in Christ while calling him merely a man, though he reads: "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man." But the apostle knew that Christ is God, and that therefore our hope is in him both now and in the future, and so he says: "If we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are the most pitiable of all people." So the one in whom we are taught to put our hope is not merely a man, for hope in a man is vain. We have said these few things out of many. If Photinus were of sound mind, this last point alone would be enough for him.
92. How are we to understand the Savior's saying: "I give you peace, my peace I leave you; not as this world gives do I give to you"?

Whoever receives the Savior's peace will draw the world's hostility upon himself. Unless he breaks with the devil, he will not have peace with Christ, for no one can serve two masters. So the one who faithfully serves God's law is at odds with the world. Protected by Christ's peace, he holds back the weapons of all his adversaries. For who would dare to attack someone he knows to be a friend of the king? Yet the world gives peace differently from the way the Savior promised to give it. The world gives peace either out of fear or because it is begged for. But the Savior is stronger than all and fears no one, and he gives peace without being asked. This peace, then, brings salvation, and it is given to be a defense against enemies. Both are called by the one name of peace, but the peace of God and the peace of the world are very far apart. The world's is fragile, God's is strong. The world's is fleshly, God's spiritual. The world's is earthly, God's heavenly. The world's comes from necessity, God's from free will. Christ needs nothing, and he offers peace to the weak and unarmed: the Lord to servants, the good to the wicked, God to human beings.

So he rightly says, "not as this world gives do I give to you." By saying this he wanted us to understand the kindness of his good will. Everyone else gives peace for his own benefit, but he gives it to benefit not himself but those to whom he gives it. So the world gives peace differently from the way the Savior gave it. The world's peace does not teach a good life, does not urge patience, does not call to justice, does not encourage mercy, and does not promise eternal life. But whoever has received Christ's peace will be a stranger to the vices of this world, which wage war against the soul.

93. We must ask whether the apostles had the Holy Spirit during the time when they were with the Lord. Among many other things the evangelist says, "The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified." In another place the Lord says: "If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You see him and know him, because he remains with you and is with you." What does this mean? He denies that the Spirit was given before the passion, yet he promises to ask the Father to send him. He also adds that the Spirit was with them and remained among them. Then after the resurrection we read that he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit," and at Pentecost we read that the Holy Spirit came down upon the apostles. I see so much confusion in this matter that I do not know what to hold.

Not everything put forward here concerns one and the same matter. These passages briefly describe the forms of several different matters, because the Spirit is one but has many gifts. So whenever we read of the Holy Spirit, we should also understand which of his functions is meant in that passage. It is not false that he was both with them and still to come, as long as you refer this to his nature rather than to his person. Christ promised that another would come from the Father. Since their divinity is without difference, the Holy Spirit should not be thought absent while Christ was present, and when the Holy Spirit came and appeared, Christ too should be thought present. That is why, while promising that the Spirit would come, he says, "you see him, because he remains with you and is with you." He wanted the apostles to be confident that after the Lord's ascension they would have no lesser or inferior shepherd or king to protect them. For there is no doubt that the Spirit was not given to believers until, as the evangelist testifies, the Lord had conquered death, risen and been glorified. These are the words of the Lord himself in his triumph: "For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will receive not many days from now." He appears to have said this at the time when he was preparing to ascend to the Father.

We also read that a few days after his resurrection the Lord breathed on the disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." This is understood to mean the authority of the church. Everything in what the Lord handed down is done through the Holy Spirit. So when the rule and pattern of this discipline were handed on to them, they were told, "Receive the Holy Spirit." And because this truly belongs to the jurisdiction of the church, he immediately added: "Whose sins you retain, they are retained; if you forgive anyone's, they are forgiven." This breathing, then, is a certain grace poured into the ordained through the act of handing on, which makes them more worthy of respect. That is why the apostle says to Timothy: "Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given you through the laying on of hands by the presbytery." So it had to happen once, so that from then on this handing on would be believed never to be without the gift of the Holy Spirit. In the Savior a pattern was given visibly, so that no one would doubt that from then on the Holy Spirit is given invisibly to believers after baptism. In the same way, in the case mentioned above, a pattern was given at the beginning, so that from then on the Holy Spirit is believed to be poured into the church's act of handing on. As for the apostles working miracles while the Lord was still with them, they were given power for that, just as the prophets had been before.

3. So the forms of three functions were displayed in the apostles through the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first belongs to the jurisdiction of the church, in regenerating people and in its other offices. The second, given at Pentecost, is general, for the Holy Spirit fell not only on the apostles but on all believers. The third form was granted at the beginning only to the apostles, or to those who were ordained, for working signs and miracles until the seeds of faith had been sown so that it might grow. The miracles done through the apostles are the seeds of faith. They were appointed as overseers of this truth, to bear witness through signs and wonders that our faith is not irrational. There is no greater proof of truth than power. This is what condemns all earthly philosophy, which has always devoted itself to words alone. It lacks the witness of power that would show that what it built with words is firm. So the Holy Spirit is given once, generally, to all believers, and through him they are shown to be sons of God as long as he remains in them. But when signs and wonders are worked, he does not remain in the person. He comes when called, or suggests what is needed, and then withdraws. In the same way, in the act of handing on, that is, in ordination, he grants grace from outside, and also brings protection to those devoted to the faith.
94. We must ask whether Judas Iscariot, the Lord's betrayer, ended his life with a noose before the Savior's passion.

When the Saviour had been handed over, as the day of Preparation was dawning, all the chief priests, scribes and elders gathered at the house of Caiaphas the high priest, where they knew Jesus was to be brought, so that they might hear him. Both Matthew and Mark the evangelists attest this. They also attest that none of these men left the governor's residence until the impious work was finished, since all their urgency and zeal for keeping the Passover was directed at the Saviour's death. They were busy with putting the Lord to death from morning until the ninth hour. How, then, can it be shown that Judas gave them back the price of blood he had received before the Lord was crucified, and said to them in the temple, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood"? It is certainly established that none of the chief priests and elders were in the temple before the Lord's passion, since they mocked him even as he hung on the cross.

Nor can this be proved from the fact that it is related before the passion. Many things are shown to have happened earlier and yet are placed last. Again, when the context allows, something that happened later may be placed earlier. For it is quite clear that the fiftieth psalm is earlier than the third. So it sometimes happens that later events are anticipated. Thus Mary is shown to have anointed the Lord's feet with ointment at a supper six days before the Passover, after the resurrection of her brother Lazarus. Yet because of its significance the evangelist anticipated it, saying among other things: "It was Mary," he says, "who anointed the Lord with ointment." He reports this before Lazarus died, and if we did not find that it happened afterwards, we would not know when it happened.

But might it not have happened after the ninth hour? The impious and most cruel Judas, seeing the Saviour slain, and on that account the veil of the temple torn, the earth quaking, the rocks split and the elements terrified, may have been seized by that very fear and been grieved, knowing well that he had betrayed a just man, at whose passion God the judge was so angered. But even after the ninth hour, I think, the elders and chief priests were busy, for they were to keep the Passover that same day in the evening, and on the Sabbath it was not lawful under the law to carry money. For this reason I cannot establish on what day, or rather at what time, Judas Iscariot ended his life with a noose.
95. WHERE THE OBSERVANCE OF PENTECOST CAME FROM, AND ON WHAT PRINCIPLE

There is no doubt that everything in our religion is strengthened by the witness of truth and marked out by the precedence of the old law. For we know that all things in the past were done and designed as a figure of our future faith, so that we would have no doubt that we hold the truth when we see that the things we now hear and believe were predestined before the ages and commended not only by words but also by the power of signs. But the task now is to understand them in the way in which they were designed, so that we may properly discern where the day of Pentecost was derived from and on what principle. For the Lord's scriptures open their meaning to the careful and devout and close it to the negligent. Nor was it fitting that things reserved for the deserving and worthy should be seen by everyone indiscriminately.

Pentecost, then, which is counted as the fiftieth day from the Passover, has this principle. After a week the Lord's day comes first, the day on which the mystery of the Passover was fulfilled for the redemption and salvation of humankind; for after the course of seven days one must always return to the first, to show that the age of the world is completed in the number seven. In the same way, after seven weeks the day of Pentecost comes first. Indeed, Pentecost never falls on any day but the Lord's day, so that everything that belongs to human salvation may be known to have been both begun and completed on the Lord's day. For the world was made on the Lord's day, and after the fall it was renewed again on the Lord's day. A figure of this renewal was first given in circumcision, which was a sign of the faith to come. For the day called the eighth, after the week, is the first in the mystery. "This is the day that the Lord has made." He made one day, from which the others would take their course. Therefore he rose on the very day that he made; and, by the reckoning given above, it was on that same day that he gave the law on Mount Sinai through his servant Moses. Just as the lamb in the sacrament of the Passover was a figure of the Lord's passion, so the giving of the law was a figure of the preaching of the gospel. For the law was given on the same day, that is, at Pentecost, as that on which the Holy Spirit came down on the disciples, so that they might receive authority and know how to preach the law of the gospel. This event is confirmed by a twofold testimony: it is shown to have been predestined, and by the manifest outpouring of the Holy Spirit it is proved to be divine and heavenly; for unlearned men spoke the mighty works of God in various tongues.

The law was given to the children of Israel through Moses on the third day of the third month, as recorded in the book of Exodus. That day is the fiftieth from the fourteenth of the first month, the day on which the Passover was kept in Egypt; that is, it is Pentecost. That is why the Holy Spirit came down on the apostles at Pentecost to preach the law of faith: so that the deeds of the ancients might be held as images of things to come, for the security of our faith, since what was proclaimed from the beginning cannot seem false. For this reason the time of forgiveness and renewal is described in the fiftieth psalm, so that the same providence might be recognized in the fiftieth day as in the first. Hence also the manna was given from heaven to the Jewish people on the first day, which is the Lord's day. This is proved by the six consecutive days on which they gathered it, while on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, they rested. The manna is a type of spiritual food, which through the Lord's resurrection became a reality in the mystery of the Eucharist.

It now remains for us to prove that what we have said is to be understood as we stated above. The fourteenth day of the first month, on which the Passover was celebrated in Egypt, was a Wednesday; hence the law too was given on a Wednesday. This can be understood from the fact that the fifteenth day of the second month after the departure of the children of Israel appears to have been a Sabbath. For that reason the flock of quails was sent to them not during the day but in the evening. In the morning, however, manna rained down on them from heaven, that is, on the Lord's day, which is found to be the first day as the week begins again. Indeed, they gathered manna for six consecutive days, and on the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, they rested. So count from this day to the third day of the third month, on which the law was given, and you will find that the law was given on a Wednesday. For from the fifteenth day of the second month, which was a Sabbath, to the third day of the third month, when the law was given, there are nineteen days. Keep these nineteen, then go back from the fifteenth day of the second month, the Sabbath, which is reckoned the fourteenth counting from the first, and come back to the first day of the second month: you will have another fourteen. Add these to the nineteen mentioned above, and you will find that the first day of the second month was a Sabbath. Then add seventeen more days back to the beginning of the first month, because the thirteen days of the first month that came before the Passover must be subtracted, since the Passover was kept on the fourteenth day of the first month. So when you have subtracted the thirteen and added the seventeen, you will find that the fourteenth of the first month was a Wednesday.

So that you are not wearied by reading, or made to examine each part of the question minutely, I give a summary, so that you may be certain of the number of days from the Passover to the giving of the law, and may more easily learn from it on which day of the week the Passover was kept. The law was given on the third day after the second month, so there are two months and three days. Subtract from these the thirteen days that came before the Passover, and fifty days will remain. That the law was given on a Wednesday is easily seen from this: the manna was given on a Sunday, since they gathered it on six consecutive days, and that Sunday was the sixteenth day of the second month. Counting from this Sunday to the eighteenth day, on which the law was given, you will find a Wednesday. And from a Wednesday, whether you count forward or backward to the fiftieth day, it is a Wednesday. Therefore, since the Jews kept the Passover in Egypt on a Wednesday and received the law on a Wednesday, but set out from Egypt on a Thursday, the dedication of the law is Pentecost.
96. AN INQUIRY WHETHER PASCHA MEANS "PASSING OVER", AS THE GREEKS THINK

The Apostle could not be mistaken when he said, "Christ our Pascha has been sacrificed." This is certainly not his own word but the law's, for Moses says: "And when your children say to you, 'What is this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the Lord's Pascha.'" What more testimony is needed? The law speaks, the Apostle confirms; it only remains for the objector to be rejected as stubborn. For it is clear that the passing over came after the Pascha. They put some of the blood of the sacrificed lamb on the doorposts and the lintel, so that the angel passing through by night would not strike a house where the sign of blood was. So it was the blood that brought salvation, not the passing over, because it was the blood that kept the passing over from doing harm.
97. HOW THE IMPIETY OF ARIUS CAN BE ANSWERED SIMPLY FROM THE LAW

If reason is given any credit, the very meaning of the names "Father" and "Son" would show their unity by nature. For he would not be called the true Son of God unless he had come into being from the substance of God the Father. The truth and justice of God would not allow him to be called a true Son if he were not from him. He is not true if he is not from him. But Scripture says: "He is true"; therefore he is from him. Whoever denies that Christ was born of God slanders Scripture, which calls him the true Son precisely to show that he was born of God. If he is not from God and yet is called the true Son of God, Scripture is deceptive. But if Scripture does not deceive, then whoever does not confess that Christ came into being from God both empties Scripture and denies that Christ is the true Son of God. For it is not will that makes a true son, but birth. "But," they say, "it lies within God's power to make false things true." On the contrary, God's power is this, and this is why he is worthy of all praise: with him the true is true and the false is false. To call the false true belongs to a liar, and that does not befit God. God can indeed do all things, but he does only what agrees with his truth and justice.

It is clear, then, that Christ is called the true Son of God so that he may be understood to be God's own Son, that is, born of his substance. Hence the apostle says: "He who did not spare his own Son," and in another letter: "Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God." If, then, he did not think it robbery when he said he was equal with God, he showed himself to be the true Son of God. For he could not be equal to God unless he were from him. Those are equals who are either both true or both false. What has a beginning and what is eternal admit neither equality nor unity. By saying that he was one with the Father, Christ made himself equal to God. "For not only," it says, "was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God," that is, on a par with him. Is it not plain that this equality comes down from the fact that he was born God's own Son? By calling himself God's own Son, that is, his true Son, he made himself equal to God.

This is why he says: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also." Because they are of one substance, whoever sees one sees both. "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life"; that is, the Father begot a Son equal to himself. And all that is the Father's is the Son's, and all that is the Son's is the Father's; and no one can snatch anything out of the Father's hand, nor out of the Son's. And he added: "I and the Father are one," and: "The words that I speak to you I do not speak of myself; but the Father who dwells in me, he speaks; and the works that I do, he does. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me; or else believe because of the works themselves." Because what is begotten does not come from itself but from the one who begot it, he says that whatever he does is the Father's doing. All this confirms that Christ is called the true Son of God so that he may be believed to have been born of him, and so that his being may not be thought to lie outside the nature of the one God. His humility, then, is his highest exaltation. When he seems to subordinate himself by saying, "The words that I speak to you I do not speak of myself; but the Father who dwells in me, he speaks; and the works that I do, he does," he proves that he has his origin from God and that he is God's power, since he says that what he is, he is not from himself but from him. By these words Christ is commended, not lowered. For one who speaks from himself is not a true son.

You see, then, that the Arians misunderstand Christ in the very place where he ought to be rightly understood. They disparage him and call him false on the very grounds that prove him to be the true Son of God. For he asks to be glorified by the Father and promises to glorify the Father to whom he makes the request, so that where he seems to humble himself, he exalts himself. When the Father bears witness to the Son, he attests his own praise; and when the Son proclaims the Father, he displays his own glory. The magnificence and nobility of the Father is the noble birth of a true Son. Therefore whatever is said to be the Father's is without doubt the Son's as well, and what is said to be the Son's is the Father's as well. The Spirit is called the Spirit of God, and the same Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ. The church is called God's, and it is called Christ's. God is worshiped, and Christ is worshiped. God is served, and Christ is served. The saints are called priests of God, and they are called priests of Christ. God is said to be the temple of the holy city, and so is Christ. The holy city is said to be lit by the light of God, and likewise by the light of Christ. The throne is God's, and it is Christ's too. God is judge, and so is Christ, for the prophet Isaiah saw Christ, the Lord of hosts, seated on the throne of majesty, which the Arians do not deny. We read of God the Father that he is King of kings and Lord of lords, and the same is read of Christ, the true Son of God. Thus everywhere the Father and the Son are made equal in divinity, so that the number of persons does not go beyond the measure of the one God.

Between the Father and the Son there is no difference except this alone: the Father is unbegotten, while the Son is begotten; that is, the Father is from no one, while the Son is from the Father. And this is indeed something lofty in the Son, for from it we learn the eternity of his nobility, and that he is the true Son of a true Father. For where else does that saying in Genesis come from, when God says: "Let us make man in our image and likeness"? If their image and likeness is one, how are they not also one in nature? In spiritual beings, where there are certainly no shapes, nothing can be like another except through substance. So where two have one image, how will they not also have one substance? We read that their image and likeness is one precisely so that we would believe that the one differs in nothing from the other; that is, that Christ is the true Son of God, because what is born is not unlike the one who begets. Indeed the Jews, understanding that he was calling God his own Father, said to Pilate: "We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." The Jews understood, and Christians say they do not understand? Those who did not believe understood, and those who say they believe make sure they do not understand? Let them at least accept this: the prophet Isaiah, to show that Christ is God not indeed from himself but God from God, says among other things: "They shall follow after you, bound in chains, and they shall worship you and make supplication to you, for God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior."

To a sound mind these things are plain. By them the Father is proved to be in the Son, and the Son is shown to be God of the same substance as the Father. For if God is in him, and there is no God besides him, and he himself is God, what else can he be said to be than what God the Father is, differing from him in nothing? That is what it means for two to be one. God is in him because, although he is God, he is not God from himself; he is from the Father, because he is the Son. There is no God besides him, because he is the only Son of the Father. And he himself is God, because God and Christ have one and the same substance. No ambiguity remains, then: the Father and the Son must be believed to have one substance. For a true Son belongs to a true Father.

Of the same kind is that passage of the prophet Jeremiah, who says among other things: "This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men." Can one with whom no other can be compared be called inferior? Or can he be called a God other than the Father, so that what is ascribed to God would turn to the Father's injury? For if no other God can be compared with him, and he is apart from God the Father, see whether what follows ought to be said, for it is dangerous: he will be called greater than the Father. Thinking that they honor God the Father by separating the Son from him, they detract from him; impiously blinded in mind, they set the one they want to make lesser above the one to whose authority they think he must bow. But Scripture, to teach that the Son differs in nothing from the Father (and he would differ if he were not a true Son), said that no other was to be compared with him, because no other substance can be found like the substance of God, which is also the substance of Christ. Christ could not be taught to be from God in any other way than by saying that no other was to be compared with him. Knowing that God the Father can in no way be called subject to anyone, the prophet, to show that his Son is equal to him, said: "No other shall be compared with him," because he is equal to God the Father, who is God of all; for he is his true Son. So the prophet says: "This is our God," that is, the God of Israel. If he is this one, he is the one God; for of him Scripture says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." And certainly the one meant here is not the Father, but his Son.

You see, then, that the person of the Son does not prejudice the one God if he too is called the one God, since Scripture testifies to this. How can this be, unless the Father and the Son are one, because the unity is signified not in persons but in nature? So they are not two in substance but one, not two in divinity but one God; so that whether the Father speaks or the Son speaks, it may be said that the one God has spoken. For if the Lord himself, speaking among other things of male and female, says, "They are no longer two, but one flesh," how much more are the Father and the Son not two gods but one substance! That the Father and the Son are called two is due to the birth; that they are not, on the other hand, two gods is due to the one divinity. By what dullness, then, do they proclaim Christ created, that is, made, when they read that God made nothing without Christ? If nothing was made without him, he himself will not be something made. For if he is something made, then something was made without him. But far from it, since nothing was made without him. Born of God, he did not begin; he came forth. For birth is nothing other than a going forth, and a going forth is a manifestation. So he was not made but brought forth. To show that Christ came forth or proceeded from the essence of God, his going forth was called birth, so that, since what is born is not unlike the one who begets, there would be no doubt that Christ is of one substance with God, and so that the mind that says, "There was a time when he was not," would be condemned. For one who is read to have proceeded from God, which signifies that he was always with God, cannot at any time not have existed. No one has proceeded from a place where he was not.

The Arians are accustomed to interpret the Son of God this way, saying: "Christ is called the true Son of God because God made him in such a way that he is true." As if there were something that God makes false! And what will become of all that we said above about the unity of the Father and the Son, so strongly supported and confirmed? If it is thought that one should think otherwise here, then many things established by divine oracles could be overturned by a single unworthy testimony. Still, this claim must be cut away, so that iniquity may not flatter itself even on this point. "He made him," they say, "in such a way that he is true," so that will takes the place of birth and making takes the place of begetting. "For so much," they say, "must be granted to the power of God, that he can make things that are not as though they were."

Since, then, they use this crafty cunning against the Son of God, we must answer them from the very things on which they rely (for on the other points they have already been refuted), so that they may be seen to be refuted on the whole matter. As far as its sense goes, this proposition is of no weight; but as far as its words go, it creates a fog so that its meaning does not quickly appear. It is like an Egyptian placed in the dark, for a bad cause cannot be defended with sound sense. So to defend impiety they use sacrilegious words. If, then, it is God's power to make Christ his true Son even though he was not born of him, then he made him such as he himself is, so that making supplied what begetting would have given. If, then, you say there is no difference between God and Christ, it might perhaps be thought that you do not assert this maliciously, and that what is said in words is also meant in sense: that because he is called a true Son, he is understood to be true, in that he is of one substance with the Father, though not by begetting but by making, since God can do everything, as you say, so that what is made is as if it were unmade.

But if, following the line of reason, you say that what is bounded by a beginning cannot be equal to and of one substance with what is eternal, you reveal the deceit of your malice. To evade the sense of the word, you say with a false voice that Christ is the true Son of God, while denying that he is equal to God the Father. For he is not true if he is unequal. Can the Son be called true if the Father is not also called true? If the Son is true, the Father will also be true, and equality proves this truth. But if they are unequal, neither of them is true. Yet since the testimony of the Scriptures, by which Christ is shown to be the true Son of God, cannot be made void, he must be believed to have been born of God the Father; for to confirm this truth, we read that he is both on a par with God and equal to him.

But you who proclaim the inestimable power of God say: "God cannot beget, because his nature is simple." By this you insult God the Father himself, for you make him a liar, denying the Son whom he declares to be his own and true, and you expose your hypocrisy, since you proclaim God powerful falsely. For if you proclaim the power of God in claiming that something true has been made out of something false, so as to mock what is truly true, how much more ought you, if you were of sound mind, to embrace that by which what is called true is proved true, and the testimony that God the Father gave of his Son is confirmed as true! For the Lord says: "With God all things are possible," so that whatever seems impossible to men is possible to God. If the reasoning of the flesh is consulted, then neither did a virgin give birth, nor did Jonah live in the belly of the whale, nor will the dead rise, nor did God beget a Son, since a simple nature cannot beget, because nothing in the world is begotten without mixture. All these things must either be believed together or rejected together. If the reasoning of the world is to be held to, it should have authority in all these cases. But if there is a reasoning proper to spiritual things, then he must be called carnal who, tainted by worldly reasoning, denies that anything can happen otherwise than he knows.

They are also accustomed to put forward another question with their evasions. They say: "Did the Father beget the Son by will or not?" so that when they hear, "Certainly by will," they may at once reply, as enemies of the Son of God: "Then the will comes before the Son, so that from this he appears not to be eternal, since he did not take his beginning simply through birth but came into existence afterward." Yet if they think this, the will will come not only before the Son but also before the Father, since generation is what makes both Father and Son. Unbelief follows the senses of the flesh in everything. It treats God's case as if it were a man's, as though he had first deliberated and considered whether to beget, as if subject to weakness; whereas in God there was neither begetting without will nor will without begetting. The will itself is the begetting. It is a common way of speaking to say, "God made" and "man made"; but God makes in one way and man in another. So it is in other matters too: we must speak of God in a way worthy of him.

They are also accustomed to raise another question about God the Father himself, saying: "Did begetting come to him as something added, or is it his nature always to beget?" They bring this up so as to make God a liar, since he testifies that he begot Christ, and to make Christ not a true Son but an adopted one. "For if he begot," they say, "he ought always to beget; so, since he does not always beget, he should not be believed to have begotten Christ either." As if one were to deny that he made the world because he does not make other worlds! What irreverence, what lack of discipline it is to lay down a law for God: "If he begot, either he begot many, or he could not beget one," not believing even the Lord himself, who declared that he is the only Son of God!

Now that we have shown above what is equal between the Father and the Son, let us see whether what is written about the Holy Spirit agrees with it, so that the Trinity, which we hold in the profession of faith that saves, may admit no difference of nature, just as it admits no difference of faith. Since there is no salvation without any one of them, the three are seen to have one power, which gives salvation to those who believe in them. Since we have cited the words of the Father as testimony to the Son, let us now use the words of the Son as testimony to the Holy Spirit, by which he declares that the Holy Spirit does not differ from him; so that, as the Father is witness to the Son and the Son to the Holy Spirit, the Trinity may be understood to be of one nature. Among other things, then, the Lord says: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth." When he says that another Paraclete is to be sent, he certainly shows that he himself is a Paraclete. For we read in the letter of John: "We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who intercedes for our sins." And again the Lord says: "I am the truth." Here is the open unity of the Holy Spirit and the Son of God: what the Son says of himself, he says also of the Holy Spirit.

Now we must add what Scripture sets out in this sense. We read in Isaiah that he saw the Lord of hosts seated on the throne of majesty, whom the evangelist John understood to be Christ, saying among other things: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty and spoke of him." The apostle says that this is the Holy Spirit. For in the last part of the Acts of the Apostles he says: "The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers, saying: You will hear with your ears and not understand," and so on. These words were spoken by the Lord of hosts. This is the one God, and whether he is understood as the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit, there is no contradiction, because their divinity and power are one. If, in the edict of a single praetorian prefect, the other prefects are also said to give the order because of the authority of their single office, how much more, under the rule of the one God, if one of the three has spoken, will it not be inappropriate to say that the three have spoken! For their nature and will are one.

They are also accustomed to disparage the Holy Spirit, claiming that he is to be understood as inferior because he is placed third in order. Yet there is such simplicity in the divine Scriptures that you sometimes find the third placed first. They are placed as the occasion requires, and this wrongs none of them, because their divinity is one. Indeed, we read in Isaiah, where the Lord says: "I am the first, and I am forever, and my hand founded the earth, my right hand established the heavens," and further on: "I have spoken, I have called, I have brought him, and I have made his way prosper. Come near to me and hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when these things were being made, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." Who do you think it was who founded the earth? He himself says that he was sent. Was it the Father? Far from it. So it is the Son who says that he was sent by God and by the Holy Spirit. See, these things are matched between the Son and the Holy Spirit: just as we read that the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son, so Christ too was sent by God and the Holy Spirit. For this belongs to the Father alone: that he is not said to be sent.

Take the words of the apostle, who includes the Trinity in another order. In the second letter to the Thessalonians he says among other things: "May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ." Whom do you think he calls Lord, if not the Holy Spirit? And what wonder is that, since this same apostle says that the one Isaiah saw seated on the throne of majesty, the Lord of hosts, is the Holy Spirit, as we showed above? And the apostle John indicates that God is understood in the Holy Spirit, saying among other things: "By this we know that God abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us." If, then, he abides in us through his Spirit, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is from God. Nor is there any doubt that what is from God is God. This is why the apostle says: "No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God." How can he know the things that are in God unless he is of the same divinity? An inferior nature cannot know what is in a superior one; how much less could a creature know what was in its Creator!

In the First Letter to the Corinthians, too, the apostle sets aside the order found in the handing down of the faith. In recounting the workings of gifts and ministries he begins with the Holy Spirit, adds the Lord Jesus, and puts God third, who, he says, works both in the Holy Spirit and in the Lord, just as the Lord also says: “The Father who dwells in me does the works himself.” Because both the Holy Spirit and Christ are from God the Father, their working is the work of God. In fact he calls the Holy Spirit Lord as well, and he calls the Lord God as well, on account of the unity of their nature. So, having said in this passage that God, who is also Lord, works all things in all, he concluded further on: “All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one as he wills.” What could be plainer than that the three share one working, since the three are said to work when one works? Why, unless because they are of one divinity? For there is no doubt that the gift of graces is properly the work of the Holy Spirit. But to teach that God and the Lord and the Holy Spirit are one because there is no difference in their nature, he showed that the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of the three. And to make it plain that, as far as the person is concerned, it is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, he says: “All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one as he wills.” He says “as he wills” because his will is the will of God. For he did not say “as God wills,” but “as the Spirit wills.” A creature has to compel itself to do God's will, but the Holy Spirit wills it by nature.

To make it shine out clearly that the Holy Spirit works all things, the Lord says, among other things: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God,” and so on. He calls the Holy Spirit the finger of God to prove that he is from God. Indeed he declared that the Jews, who said he cast out demons by Beelzebub, had blasphemed against the Holy Spirit. Likewise, because Moses performed signs through the Holy Spirit, the magicians admit it, saying: “This is the finger of God.” In the Acts of the Apostles, too, we read: “While they were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” See: it is the Lord who is being served, and the Holy Spirit claims this for himself, which makes it plain that he is Lord just as God the Father is. And it was Christ who called Saul from heaven and sent him to preach, yet the Holy Spirit likewise claims this for himself when he says: “for the work to which I have called them.” Again, everyone knows that the Savior appointed bishops for the churches; for before he ascended into heaven he laid his hands on the apostles and ordained them bishops. Yet the apostle ascribes this to the Holy Spirit when he says: “Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops to rule the church of the Lord Jesus.” And among other things Peter says to Ananias: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit?” And further on he says: “You have not lied to men but to God.” It is plain that the Holy Spirit is called God, since Ananias, who lied to him, is said to have lied to God. If he had not wanted the Holy Spirit to be understood as God, he would have said, “You have not lied to men but to the Holy Spirit,” so as to mark him out as neither God nor man. And why be surprised? For the apostle sometimes calls a man the temple of God and sometimes the temple of the Holy Spirit, because they are one in nature. If the Holy Spirit were not understood to be God, how would he dare to say further on: “For God's temple is holy, and that temple is you”?

Because one God is proclaimed throughout the Scriptures, while his mystery is worshiped in the Trinity, Scripture proceeds in such a way that, under the confession of one God, what is from him, that is, his Son and his Spirit, is understood to share the same honor that God himself has. For the sacrament of God was revealed precisely to show that his glory abides in the Trinity. For this reason, what is from God is not called God with full and explicit authority, so that it may not be thought to act as a second being apart from him who is one. Instead Scripture leads us to understand and believe that the salvation of the creature rests in the Trinity because the three have one divinity. For Creator and creature, Lord and servants, the eternal and what had a beginning, could not be joined together and set in one order, especially when no one has salvation without any one of them. For whatever is God, whether the Son or the Holy Spirit, is wronged if it is reckoned as lying outside the honor and glory of the one God. So the Scriptures show that Christ is God and show that the Holy Spirit is God, so that those who see may know what it is that is being shown. It is as if someone were to show a gem without announcing that it is a gem: just because he does not announce it, will what is seen not be a gem? In the same way, through the passages discussed above, the Scriptures show what we ought to believe, enclosing our understanding within faith in one God by the mystery of the Trinity.
98. On the Gospel of John.

You have heard what the holy Gospel declares, where the Lord says to the Jews: "You are born of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature, because he is a liar, and so was his father." None of the faithful should doubt that the devil had no one who caused his apostasy. He himself is the prince of all error. He saw that God had made him with no small power, and he dared to lay claim to deity, so that, seeing that the others were beneath him, he might set himself above them as God. The names by which he is called, "devil" and "Satan," are taken from what he does, not from his nature. Every evil is shown by its deed, so that in a crime there is no substance, only a will conceived from certain causes. When he saw that he was more powerful than the others, he grew proud and set out to exercise dominion.

How, then, can he be said to have a father who would be held responsible for his wickedness? And how is it shown that he was a murderer from the beginning? The answer is that Scripture calls the one who imitated him by his name. Since the devil's name comes from his work, anyone who does an evil work may rightly be called a devil. So in this passage the Saviour called Cain the devil, because Cain copied his works. Out of envy for his brother he committed murder and left behind an example of the cruelty of killing one's own kin. In the same way the devil, out of envy for man, who was made in God's image, heaped up the malice of his work and set a pattern for error. This is why Cain also proved to be a liar. When God said to him, "Where is Abel your brother?" Cain, steeped in his father's malice, burst out with a lie: "I do not know." He pretended not to know where the man was whose life he had taken. Fury had so blinded him that he answered God as if God were a man from whom he thought he could hide.

The Jews, then, became imitators of Cain and went so far as to kill the Lord himself. They chose to have Cain the fratricide as their father rather than God, and so they became guilty of all the blood that has been shed. By killing the Author of life they became the chief authors of all wickedness. They even bound their own children to this evil, saying, "His blood be on us and on our children." To persuade Pilate that there was nothing wrong in what they asked, they said that if it was unjust, it should fall back on their children. To satisfy their rage they would not spare even their own children.

That the devil is not evil by nature is easily learned from this: punishment would not be threatened against someone who had not acted knowingly. It is unjust to punish someone who does nothing other than what belongs to his nature, and it is even worse to demand from someone what you know he cannot do. So the one who deserves punishment is the one who does evil when it is clear that he knows the good and is able to do it. This can also be seen from the Saviour's words. As was quoted above, he says: "Your father was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth." If the devil is a liar by nature, how can it be said that he did not stand in the truth? The one who does not stand in the truth is the one who does not remain in it. It is clear, then, that the devil was in the truth but did not persevere in it. We also read the Lord saying through the prophet: "If they had stood in my substance," that is, "in my law"; and the Apostle says to the Galatians: "Stand, and do not be held again under the yoke of slavery." What could be plainer? He is commanding them to remain in God's commandments from then on. If the devil had kept them, he would have stood in the substance and law of God, for the law is a foundation for those who keep it.

Why, then, do some people think either that God made the devil evil, or that the devil has an origin of his own, that is, that he arose from nothing? Both ideas are plainly opposed to God. Whoever says that the devil was made in order to be evil thinks that God's goodness is imperfect, because one who is perfectly good does not make evil. Whoever does not believe that God is the author of the devil's origin denies God's lordship. Although all things belong to God, such people suppose that something exists that does not belong to God at all. They must suffer punishment when they see all things judged by God through Christ.
99. What is meant by "Let no temptation seize you except what is human."

I think it is with foresight that the teacher of the Gentiles, our Apostle, wishes temptation to seize us, but only human temptation, because divine temptation brings destruction. The Jews were seized by this kind of temptation and perished by the serpents: though they lived under God's law, they doubted his providence. That is why he urges that it should be human and not divine temptation that seizes us. A person is said to tempt God when he acts in God's name but hopes for salvation from idols, because he does not regard God as proven. Whatever is not proven is put to the test, and whatever is put to the test is called into doubt. Divine temptation is therefore deadly, but human temptation brings salvation. Just as it is ruinous to doubt God, so it is most wholesome to give up hope in man for the sake of God's law. So the Apostle says with foresight: "Let no temptation seize you except what is human." When men tempt us for the sake of God's law, we should be found strong while carnal men doubt us, and we should be approved by God. Those who are not approved by God are tempted so that they may be corrected.

Temptation, then, is of two kinds. Sometimes we are tempted as people who believe, and sometimes as people who distrust God, and the temptation of believers is human. Men afflict us because of our faith: they tempt us to see whether they can lead us away from it. Those who distrust God, on the other hand, are tempted so that the distress will make them repent and return to the way. This is what happened to the Jews: when they distrusted God's providence, they were tempted by serpents, so that the pain would correct them. God tempts people of this kind in order to correct them. There is also another kind of temptation, by which God's servants Abraham, Job and Tobit were tempted. Abraham went through the trial of offering his only and dearly loved son so that he might bear a richer fruit of righteousness for eternal glory. Job lost all his possessions so that he might be increased and enriched with wealth in heaven and on earth. Tobit suffered blindness and advanced so far by it that he was honoured in this life when his sight was restored, and everlasting glory is kept for him in the life to come. The righteous are tested so that they may advance. In temptation, therefore, we ought to be strong in mind, knowing that it serves not to diminish us but to increase us, if only we bear it calmly through Christ.
100. On the Gospel of Matthew.

You have heard, dearest brothers, what the Gospel declares, where the Lord says: "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you." If we look at the meaning of these words, we shall see that the Lord spoke them to encourage believers. Because believers spurn worldly wisdom, they look like little ones to the wise of this world, who want to be called wise though nothing testifies in their favour. So God thought it unfitting to show the truth to the worldly wise. But to the humble, who presume nothing of themselves and submit to God's will, justice requires that the things of salvation be revealed. The person who is prudent in God's eyes and mindful of his salvation is the one who puts God's law above his own knowledge, for he sees that this law rests not on the noise of words but on mighty works. Without doubt the person who entrusts himself to something that is backed by no sign is foolish and empty.

This is why God promised the kingdom not to the learned of this world but to the faithful. He pledges eternity not to those who scrutinize the stars but to those who act rightly. He gives glory not to dialecticians, who try to shut out the truth with tricks and petty subtleties, but to people of good will, who take more care over how they live than over how they speak. God rejects those who would rather display brilliant eloquence than do good deeds. Anyone who thinks he can adorn the things of God with words wants to turn God's glory toward himself. The matters themselves ought to please on their own merits, so that it is the meaning that is praised, not the style. If meaning gives rise to the written word, and words were invented to signify things, why should the things themselves not be set out in plain meaning, so that they move the mind more easily toward salvation? That is why the Lord chose fishermen as our apostles: simple, unlettered men who, without any cunning, showed God's truth in themselves by keeping the faith and living well. So the apostle Paul says: "When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with lofty speech or wisdom." Among other things he also says: "For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power." Since words are open to contradiction, power was to stand as witness to God's law, and all lofty speech gives way before it.

I have set these things out, dearest brothers, for the sake of simpler people, so that they do not think themselves unworthy of God's grace because they have little training in the learning of the law courts. In fact their simplicity counts all the more to their credit. The worldly wise, in the pride of their learning, do not see what these people believe, for they are wise not in words but in judgment. They know that God rests in good works and looks for faith, not polished speech. They read the Lord saying: "On whom shall I rest, if not on the humble and meek, and the one who trembles at my words?" So, to be made worthy of the promised rewards, we ought to do what the Lord commands, confident that the Lord loves those who keep his words. This is what he said to his disciples: "If you love me, keep my commandments." By serving the Lord in these things, may we become heirs of his kingdom through [?] Christ our Lord.
101. On the boasting of the Roman Levites.

In trying to obey the commands of charity we may perhaps lay ourselves open to criticism, since we are writing about a matter that no one has ever doubted. Because we do not want to offend friendship, we tangle up an effort that should have served to bring something hidden to light. Still, a certain man has asserted, with great folly, the claim we will set out below, and the same charity has laid this task on us too. If no one answered him for a long time, he might go on to worse things, and after long practice in empty ideas he might become impossible to correct. This is the zeal of charity, which does not seek its own interests.

A certain man, then, who bears the name of a false god, led by folly and by the boasting of the city of Rome, insists on making Levites equal to priests and deacons equal to presbyters. I will not say that he ranks them higher, because that would be even more foolish and might seem beyond belief, and we would be taken for slanderers rather than correctors. I do not think anyone knows by what law, custom or precedent he dares to attempt this. Deacons have not been given a seat in the church, and he makes them equal to those who, as prelates of God, sit with dignity in the house of God and in the honour of Christ. What audacity, to make presbyters' own ministers their equals! What empty and rash presumption, to compare with priests the men who carried the tabernacle and all its vessels, who chopped the wood and carried the water! For that was the Levites' work. It is as if officials were made equal to prefects, or slaves to their masters. Scripture records the Lord saying to Moses: "Take the tribe of Levi from among the children of Israel and set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall serve him." What could be plainer than this example, which the church still observes today?

Even the deacons of the Roman church, who seem somewhat bolder than others, do not presume to claim the dignity of sitting in church. They do not perform every service in its proper order only because there are so many clergy there. Otherwise they would certainly carry the altar and its vessels and pour water on the priest's hands, as we see done in all the churches and as the Lord established through Moses. Or are they better than Elisha, who poured water on Elijah's hands?

He defends deacons against presbyters as though deacons were ordained from among presbyters, and not presbyters from among deacons. Because they are ministers of the Roman church, they are thought to deserve more honour than deacons in other churches, on account of the splendour of the city of Rome, which seems to be the head of all cities. If so, they ought to claim this for their priests as well. If the lower ranks are raised up because of the city's splendour, how much more should the higher ranks be exalted! Whatever is granted to officials adds to the authority they serve, just as a slave's honour adds to his master's praise. Yet before God, the just judge, each person keeps the honour established for each office of the churches. Whoever is a deacon holds the honour of the diaconate in all the churches, for it is no small honour to serve a prelate of God, at least in the church. The priest, for his part, is held worthy of the whole of ecclesiastical honour. A higher order also contains the lower order within itself: a presbyter performs the office of deacon, exorcist and reader as well.

The apostle Paul shows that the presbyter is to be understood as a bishop, since he instructs Timothy, whom he had ordained presbyter, about what kind of man he should make bishop. What is a bishop if not the first presbyter, that is, the high priest? In fact, a bishop calls presbyters nothing other than his fellow presbyters and fellow priests. Does a bishop also call his ministers fellow deacons? Certainly not, because they are far beneath him, just as it would be insulting to call a judge a chief clerk. In Alexandria and throughout Egypt, if there is no bishop, a presbyter performs the sealing.

The case of Caiaphas shows how great the dignity of the priestly order is: though he was a very wicked man, he prophesied. Why? "Because," Scripture says, "he was the chief of the priests." The book we call the Acts of the Apostles also shows that there is a great difference between a deacon and a priest. When people in Samaria had come to believe through the preaching of Philip, a deacon ordained by the apostles, "they sent," it says, "to Peter and John, so that they might come and give the Holy Spirit to those who had believed by the laying on of hands."

I believe they defend these claims because they do not know the Scriptures or have forgotten the law. Whoever thinks these claims should be upheld ought to remember what happened to the Levites when they thought the same way. When they presumed that there was no difference between priests and Levites, God judged them: Korah and those who sided with him were swallowed up when the earth opened, and a torrent of fire consumed two hundred and fifty men together. King Uzziah was covered with leprosy when he presumed to do the priests' work. These examples were meant to frighten everyone else, so that they would not dare to presume what has not been granted to them. Yet now we see deacons rashly doing the priests' work at banquets and wanting the response in prayer to be made to them, though this is permitted to priests alone. The order of deacons is to receive from the priest and so to give to the people.

Do you see what empty presumption leads to? In their pride they forget themselves, because they see that they are ministers of the Roman church. They do not consider what God has decreed for them and what they ought to observe. Their constant attendance in the household and their official position wipe this from their memory, for that position now has great power through recommendations, whether bad or good. People either fear them, in case they speak against them, or pay them for favours. These are the things that make them disregard the principle of their order. People flatter them and defer to them improperly, and so they rush headlong into thinking that more is permitted to them, especially since they see that priests are not shown the same deference. So they think they rank above the priests.

"But," he says, "a presbyter is made on the testimony of a deacon," as though this were a mark of superior greatness. Yet we read that the apostle Peter said to the people: "Choose from among yourselves men whom we may appoint to serve the ministries of the church"—I do not want to say "tables." See, deacons were made on the testimony of laypeople! And the Apostle wants the one who is to be ordained bishop to have the testimony even of Gentiles, for he says: "He must also have a good testimony from those outside." Everyone, then, may give testimony, and yet not everyone is worthy of this honour. Anyone can judge, but not everyone can be what he judges. Someone who cannot paint can judge a good painter to be good, and a flute player can be judged better than another by someone who practises a different art. In the same way, someone of lower rank can be a witness when a presbyter is made.

There is another thing that puffs them up and makes them think they are owed a great deal. "It is we who escort those who are to be ordained," they say, as though candidates seemed worthy of honour only while flanked by deacons at their side. Suppose that is true. The bishop sends the deacon like an official, to render service to the one being ordained. An emperor, too, is installed with the service of soldiers, so that he may be seen to be emperor, but the army is neither better than the emperor nor his equal. Haman, though distinguished by military honours, was sent by the king to serve Mordecai, so that this service would show how worthy Mordecai was. In the same way deacons are sent to serve those being made presbyters, so that everyone may understand that these men have been made worthy to be priests. Deacons rank above everyone except the priests, to whom they owe service.
102. Against Novatian.

His disciples said to Jesus: “Lord, do you want us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” And the Lord answered them, saying: “You do not know what spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them.” Although it would certainly have been fitting to punish the Samaritans for not receiving him, the Lord nevertheless set the sentence aside, because he had come to bestow mercy, so that they might correct themselves and be amended in future. The prophet Elisha, too, was angered at the boys who were insulting him, and with God as judge he took vengeance on them, so that they were devoured by bears in a place where there is said to be no forest. The Lord, however, spared the harlot who was brought before him, namely the woman whom the elders of the Jews said they had caught in adultery, so that, since his merciful preaching was just beginning, he might teach that she was not to be condemned but forgiven. For the law given through Moses, because its justice was directed toward punishment, exercised severity at its beginnings: it punished with death the man who went out on the sabbath to gather wood; it likewise took vengeance on the son of the Egyptian woman who had blasphemed against God; and in the affair of the molten calf it struck down the children of Israel.

Each law, then, showed its full character at its very beginnings. The old law, being readier to punish, appeared harsher at its outset, so that by striking fear it might make its hearers careful and attentive. The new law, on the other hand, because it is merciful and inclined to compassion, displayed the gentlest and most clement beginnings, so that by that very delight it might draw everyone toward forgiveness. Afterwards, however, the law that had seemed harsher not only softened its rigor on account of the frailty of the human race but also showed itself humane and merciful, and the law that had seemed clement sometimes punished. For Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck down by God; Elymas the magician, an unbeliever who opposed the law of God, was blinded by the judgment and power of the Lord; and King Herod, because he did not give honor to God, was struck by an angel of God and died swarming with worms. So that people would not suppose, because mercy is preached, that sin goes entirely unpunished and that one may sin with impunity, the Lord instilled fear, showing that pardon for sins is given for this purpose: that those who have been brought to life, as it were, from the dead should afterwards abstain from what is contrary, and that every effort be made that no one depart this life in guilt, since all will come to judgment. For each person is charged with the sentence under which he dies. Since, therefore, the new law has the fullness of mercy, it punished the people mentioned above, so that it would not be held in contempt by lovers of sin. The old law, on the other hand, though it was given for punishment, nevertheless forgave some, so that it would not be thought wholly cruel; but it punished more, because its character is quick to avenge.

There is no doubt, then, that the grace of the new law is greater than that of the old. If, therefore, its grace is greater, how can it be denied that it is able to grant what that law granted which had the lesser grace? For the old law was more inclined to severity. So if it is proven to have forgiven the penitent, how can it be that this law, which is clement, does not receive the penitent? For the Jews too were called sons of God, and on the authority of the apostle Paul we read that they were baptized through Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Since they were about to receive the law, they are without doubt understood to have been purified, so that thereafter they might give an account of the law they had received, and that any who sinned might be restored through penance, as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Repent, you who go astray, and turn back.” But perhaps someone will object: “Penance was indeed preached, but not forgiveness.” If, then, penance was preached by God, there is fruit for those who do penance; for the Lord would not have urged this to no purpose. Moreover, the Lord, knowing that forgiveness of sins ought to be granted to those who turn back, commanded this, since he said: “I do not desire the death of the dying, so much as that he should turn back and live.” So there is, as has become clear, fruit of penance for those who turn to God. Excluded, therefore, is the impiously contrived assertion of Novatian, by which he twists the sense of the Lord's words, saying: “The Lord says: ‘Whoever denies me, I too will deny him’,” meaning that if any Christian has denied Christ, for whatever reason, he can no longer return, or at any rate, if he does return, he is by no means to be received.

And where, then, will the command to do penance stand, when the Savior, after pronouncing this sentence, did not deny the apostle Peter, who had denied him? Why? Because, with penance following, Peter wept most bitterly over his fault, knowing full well that those who turn back are forgiven and restored through penance. But Novatian pretends that penance is to be done. Because he does not dare to deny openly that penance should be granted, being bound by the law, he subtly strives to make it void. For when he says that “whoever has denied will in no way have pardon, but will himself be denied in the presence of the angels of God,” how is he not professing with deceit that penance is to be done? His fraud appears plainly from what he adds, saying: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either here or in the age to come.” Although sinning against the Holy Spirit is one matter and denying the Lord Jesus is another, Novatian nevertheless, in order to deny pardon for this sin, wants denying the Lord and sinning against the Holy Spirit to mean one and the same thing, so that by this evasion he may cut off the fruit of penance. For if denying the Lord is the same as sinning against the Holy Spirit, no pardon is to be hoped for by those who deny, nor any fruit of penance, since the Lord's oracles declared that this sin would be forgiven neither here nor in the age to come.

From this it is clear that Novatian speaks deceitfully when he says that penance is to be done; for why should anyone repent if it is denied that the offense can be wiped away? The groaning, weeping and lamentation of penance achieve this: that a person earns both pardon and restoration. David, indeed, repenting and confessing his sin, earned pardon and was restored to his former state, for he both remained king and afterwards prophesied. This is clearly proven: in the fiftieth psalm he repented, and afterwards, when he suffered persecution from his son, he prophesied; for the third psalm, according to the history, comes after the fiftieth. But perhaps it was right to forgive a king, while the lowly ought not to be forgiven—though it would seem that the more powerful are the harder to forgive. For God does not show partiality. The more exalted someone is, the more serious a crime his sin becomes, even if it is slight. Just as humility in a petitioner of high rank is lofty and splendid, so too his fault must be counted as a crime. For apart from the sins that are agreed to be unlawful for everyone, not everything permitted to the lowly is permitted to the powerful. For a man of rank it is unseemly to engage in trade, and it is a mark of disgrace to enter a tavern; for senators, too, moneylending is infamous. If, then, they are to be censured when found in these slight matters, how much more are they to be held guilty if they sin! From this, then, it is clear that David sinned most gravely, and indeed in a twofold way; yet when he turned back he obtained pardon for both murder and adultery, and, what is more, through his weeping he was restored. For when he was rebuked by the prophet

Nathan, he did not dare to conceal his sin, but confessed it, saying: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Then the prophet answered him and said: “The Lord has taken away your sin, and you shall not die, because you have repented.” And since he is found to have prophesied afterwards, there is no doubt that he was restored. Ahab, too, rebuked by the prophet over the death of Naboth, went about weeping, tore his garments and girded himself with sackcloth; and the word of the Lord came by the hand of his servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said: “Have you seen how Ahab has been moved before me? I will not bring the evil in his days.” And for the Ninevites who wept over their sins, life was restored when death was at hand. See how great is the benefit of penance!

But perhaps someone will object: "Yes, those have been granted pardon, but not the crime of idolatry. However grave those sins may be, the crime of idolatry is greater." Yet Novatian's assertion has already been demolished in no small part, since two grave crimes are seen to have been granted to penance. If fornication ought not to be pardoned, as Novatian thinks, how much less murder or adultery! But his emptiness shows itself here, since these graver sins are proved to have been granted pardon. We must therefore now inquire whether God has promised that pardon can be granted to idolaters. For whatever has not been rightly granted here cannot be granted in the future either. Here, as the Lord said, sins are either bound or loosed; in the future there will be nothing but reward or condemnation. Everyone who is rightly rejected here cannot be chosen or judged worthy in the future.

Let us hear, then, what the Lord says about idolaters to the prophet Jeremiah: "Go," he says, "and say: Return to me, dwelling of Israel, says the Lord, and I will not set my face against you, for I am merciful, says the Lord, and I will not be angry with you for ever. Only acknowledge your offense: you have acted impiously and turned your ways to strangers under every leafy tree." See what God promises to those who turn to him after a fall: he will forgive the sins of those who come back after apostasy. And again God says through Jeremiah: "My delicate ones have walked rough ways; they were led off like a flock seized by enemies. Be steadfast, children, and cry out to God; you will be remembered in your captivity. For as your mind was set on straying from God, so, once you have turned back, you will seek him ten times as much. For he who brought evils upon you will bring you everlasting joy along with your salvation." O the clemency of God! How he calls on the fallen to rise again! How he urges them to return to him after the error of idols! Like a kindly father he promises his children the everlasting joy of salvation if they amend themselves. Likewise, in the same prophet, among other things: "And I will restore them to this land and build them up again and not abandon them; I will replant them and not pluck them up." He had threatened, "Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be uprooted." So that those who sinned against God would not despair of themselves, as though those who had sacrificed to idols, once uprooted, could never be replanted, he encourages them: if they repent, they can be restored to their former state. For the sentence stands only if the offense is not amended.

Thus it was preached to the Ninevites that their city would be overthrown after three days. Why after three days, unless so that they might either repent and have the sentence lifted, or persist in their ways and perish all the more justly? This is what he said through the prophet: "I do not desire the death of the dying man so much as that he turn and live." So it came about that the Ninevites, who were about to die for their sins, were pardoned once repentance followed. Why indeed do we find that the ark was built over a hundred years under Noah, unless so that people, seeing and hearing what was coming, might amend themselves? For God wills that no one perish. Hence we read in Solomon: "For the Most High has had mercy on the penitent"; and again: "You have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men for the sake of repentance."
