In this spirit too the Lord, grieving over the faithlessness of the Jews, says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!"

Throughout the whole law, then, the Lord constantly urges sinners to turn to him, since he does not want his work to fall into perdition. Indeed, the law was given for no other reason than that men might turn from error to truth. Yet in the New Testament the author of the law appears more merciful still. At the time when he deigned to reveal the mystery of his Son, our Lord, he chose to be more generous and abundant in mercy, so that there might be more grace when the Son preached than there had been when the servants preached. And rightly so, for it was fitting that he should bestow greater gifts through the Son than through servants. So to believers who turn to him he grants pardon for all their sins at once, without any lamentation of penance. Hence the apostle Paul says: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance." But if they sin afterwards, they can earn pardon through penance. Since they sinned after receiving mercy freely, they may reach forgiveness no longer freely, but through groaning and weeping.

For it is impossible for a man not to sin. Hence the apostle John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness." So David earned pardon and restoration when he confessed his sin. The apostle is certainly speaking to Christians, for he says in what follows: "My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; and if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ." He says this so that, if we sin after baptism, we may humbly entreat the advocate to plead with the Father for us. If penance had a place among our forebears, how can it have no place in this age, when the clemency proclaimed is greater? Will he who had mercy on enemies, calling them to grace, not have mercy on them once they have become friends, when they bring their payment? For contrition of heart is the payment of the penitent. If Novatian's view were true, men would grieve that they had been turned from enemies into friends. Or what kind of being would God be, if he gave mercy to enemies who did not repent but refused it to friends who even plead for it? Besides, does the Lord not know that the devil exalts himself and rages more fiercely against the friends and servants of God? Hence the apostle Peter says: "Be watchful, be sober, for our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour."

Since the Lord knows, then, that we have a dreadful and powerful adversary, if we are overcome by him he wants us to flee to his help. He grieves that we have been struck down, so that, restored by his power, we may fight back bravely. Just as no flesh would be saved unless those days were shortened, as the Lord says, so too, if penance is denied to men, no one can be saved. "For no one," it says, "will boast that he has a clean heart." And elsewhere: "No one is without stain, not even an infant one day old." Who can escape, if penance is denied? And what becomes of the Lord's saying that there will be joy in heaven over a sinner who repents?

"But the greater crimes," he says, "fornication and idolatry, ought not to be pardoned." Then what becomes of the Lord's saying, in which he promises that all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven men, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven them? He says that absolutely every sin can be forgiven except one. Now choose, Novatian: of whom do you take this to be said, of those who do not yet believe or of those who already believe? If of unbelievers, how can remission of sins be granted at all, since it is agreed that all people, before they believe, sin against God and against the Holy Spirit? Some, for instance, call the Lord's deeds magic and ascribe the work of the Holy Spirit to demons. But if you take it to be said of believers, your assertion is ruled out, because all sins will be forgiven: "And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man," he says, "it will be forgiven him." So whether one sins against God or against Christ, it will be forgiven; he has included every sin except that against the Holy Spirit. Therefore he does not mean the sin committed against God to be understood as also a sin against the Holy Spirit; if it were, he would certainly not have made this exception. Since, then, he means a different sin when he speaks of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (for this saying concerns the person, not the nature, of the Holy Spirit), all sins will be forgiven: to those who already believe, through penance, and to those who will believe, through baptism.

The sin of the Jews against the Holy Spirit is another matter, and one that belonged to that time. That is why he shows that it is not forgiven them, either here or in the future. They did not sin against the Holy Spirit through error, but through malice. They knew and understood that the works they saw in the Savior's deeds were of God, yet, to turn the people away from faith in him, they pretended that these were the work of the prince of demons. That is why the Lord says to them: "You have the key of knowledge, and you neither enter yourselves nor allow others to enter." This sentence, then, was pronounced against the malicious, for whom no remedy can be found to save them. No crime is graver than this: to pretend that something is false when one knows it is true. The Jews seemed to be under God's law, and the promise of Christ had been made to them. Yet when they saw his mighty works and understood that this was what God had promised, they were so blinded by envy that they denied it, and not only denied it but persecuted him to the death. It is not fitting, therefore, that this sin should ever be forgiven these men, who, with their own conscience as witness, dared to fight against the God to whom they claimed to be devoted.

People sin against God or against Christ for various reasons. A man may envy another's good fortune and, in grief at his own lowly state, rise up against the Creator. Or he may suffer some sudden misfortune and, roused to anger, become insolent toward his Father. With Christ, it is his incarnation that provokes insult. Men who do not know the mystery of the incarnate Christ blaspheme, thinking it unworthy that the Son of God, whose nature is incorporeal and simple, should be said to have been born in human fashion. They blaspheme, then, because they do not know the mystery. For this reason a hand must be held out to them when they turn, because they stand against the truth while believing they are acting for the truth. Such a man, even when tortured and torn with hooks, maintains that what he follows is true. But the Jews mentioned above thought one thing and did another, and they are tortured endlessly, without judge or executioner, by their own conscience as witness. He who became an enemy of the truth through error rejoices, once converted, that he has come to know the truth. The malicious man, however, has nothing to correct: if he turns, he will begin to call true what he knew all along was not false.

But there is no reason at all for anyone to insult the Holy Spirit. His work gives no offense, since it shows itself in the power of signs and wonders. Who would dare to attack him on seeing the dead raised? Who would be angry with him through whose working he sees paralytics running, the blind receiving light, the deaf hearing? How could anyone not love him on seeing him cast out unclean spirits, cleanse lepers, and heal every infirmity alike? Yet the Jews chose to insult him, calling his work the work of demons, so long as they could vent the envy and hatred they bore toward the Savior. That is why he shows that this sin is not forgiven them, either here or in the future.

But Novatian says: "Let it be proved that the greater crimes, namely idolatry and fornication after the washing of baptism, are expressly forgiven. For this is why all sins are forgiven at once in baptism: so that afterwards, if people commit anything grave, they may by no means obtain pardon, since after the Holy Spirit has been received, nothing against the Holy Spirit ought to be committed." Who would deny that one ought never to sin, if only that were possible? But God, knowing how frail the human race is, has always supplied it with saving remedies, so that after sinning people might have a way to restore themselves. If the gift of the Spirit forbids penance to be given to sinners, there is no providence in the New Testament, and the ancients, to whom this medicine was by no means denied, will seem to have been better provided for. Then how is there greater grace in the new than in the old? It would be the act of an enemy to know that men cannot be brought to salvation in any other way than through penance, and then to give the Holy Spirit on such terms that, if he is insulted through some fear or through error, no satisfaction remains to restore the man. That would be to look for an occasion to destroy man, not to save him. But far be it, for the Lord says: "The Son of Man came not to destroy souls but to save them." If God commanded us to forgive one another, seventy times seven times, the sins we commit against each other when the offender turns, how much more does he himself pardon those who turn, when the sin is against him! For he wants every sinner to be converted.

Hence the apostle shows that the fornicators and the unclean were forgiven, when he says: "lest perhaps when I come I mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication they committed." This shows that some had done penance, and over these he does not grieve but rejoices. But he indicates that others had not done penance for their fornication, and for that reason he says he mourns them as people cut off from life, because they had not done penance. If penance for this crime had to be done throughout this life, he would not say that he mourns them because they had not done it, but because they are not doing it. Knowing, however, that penance is both begun and completed here, he says "they have not done it." What he wanted was that when he came to them he might be at peace with them in communion. There you have proof that fornicators are to be admitted to communion once their penance has been completed. They cannot be admitted to communion while they are still doing penance; but they must be admitted once they cease doing it by the judgment of the church.

It remains for us to prove whether idolaters in particular can be forgiven. We read in the Apocalypse of the blessed apostle John that penance for idolatry is proclaimed. There the bishops, whom he calls angels (that is, messengers, as the blessed apostle Paul also says: "You received me as an angel of God"), are admonished to grant penance to sinners, and not to let those who cause scandal in the church, though they are themselves of the church, go unadmonished. So he says: "And to the angel of the church of Pergamum write: This is what he says who has the sword sharp on both edges: I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is; and you hold fast to my name and did not deny my faith in the days when Antipas was my most faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells. But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the eyes of the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed and to commit fornication. So you too have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Likewise, repent." He says that the teaching of the Nicolaitans is the same as that of Balaam, namely idolatry and fornication, and for this he commands penance to be done. And that he is speaking to members of the church he shows when he says: "This is what the Spirit says to the churches."

That penance bears fruit he indicates thus: "To him who conquers," he says, "I will give the hidden manna to eat." That is, through penance one conquers sins. For what is it to repent but to grieve over what is past and thereafter to keep from what one has committed? "And to the angel of the church of Thyatira write: This is what the Son of God says, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like [?] brass: I know your works, your love and faith and service and patience, and that your latest works are better than the first. But I have this against you: you tolerate the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet and teaches and seduces my servants to commit fornication and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, and she would not repent of her fornication. See, I will throw her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent of their deeds; and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works. But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching and do not know the depths of Satan, as they call them, I say: I lay on you no other burden; only hold fast what you have until I come. And to him who conquers and keeps my works to the end I will give authority over the nations."

In a single letter addressed to the church of Thyatira he confounds and demolishes the twofold error of the Novatian heresy. He promises fruit to those who repent of idolatry, and he shows that within one church the wicked do not contaminate the good, though they were certainly in one communion. He was not writing to people outside the church, for he says: "He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches." In the same way the apostle Paul says: "We know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law"; and elsewhere: "For what have I to do with judging those outside?" So he calls some members of one and the same church to penance and praises others, saying: "But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching" (that is, the teaching of idolatry), "hold fast what you have until I come." In other words, "persevere to the end," because he who perseveres to the end will be saved. In the same way, he who perseveres in evil will be condemned. And so, just as the righteousness of the righteous man will not save him on the day he goes astray, so the wickedness of the wicked man will not harm him once he turns. That is why it says: "Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be uprooted"; but if he turns, he shall surely live. The same holds for the Lord's saying: "Whoever denies me, I will deny him." But if he turns, he cannot be denied by the one he confesses.

Hence it is said in the psalm: "No living man will be justified in my sight." For a man is judged according to the state in which he dies. That the wicked would be in the church together with the good until God's judgment, the Lord himself also indicated when he said: "The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which gathers fish of every kind. When they had come to shore, they sorted the good into their vessels but threw the bad away. So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will come out and remove from the kingdom of God all causes of scandal and those who do iniquity." The same point is signified in the man found among the guests without a wedding garment. He shows that this man alone was thrown out of the assembly of the church, because the crime of his unworthiness did not pollute the others. And since his unworthiness was marked by his lack of a wedding garment, it was evident to the others: they could see that he was dressed differently from them.

Hence the apostle Paul says: "In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay." He wrote this on account of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, though they belonged to the church, held perverse views about the resurrection, just as some in the church of the Corinthians denied the resurrection. But Novatian claims that this great house is to be understood as the world, not the church, so as not to be forced to admit that within one church there are wicked along with good, unclean along with clean. This, I think, is easily overturned. In one house everyone is under one name; however much they differ in conduct, they are all reckoned by profession under the one name of their master. But this world contains people of different professions, so much so that they profess to have different gods and lords. You see, then, that this could not have been said of the world, but only of the church, in which those living under one name differ in their conduct. I perceive that Novatian was not unaware of this. But because he had no just grievance for his secession, and so as not to be openly put to shame, he contrived certain arguments for himself through a bad interpretation of the law, by which he tried to excuse and cover the envious intent of his spite.

Finally, he replied to what we have said: "I do not deny that penance must be done for idolatry committed, but I do not dare to forgive it, because this crime must be forgiven by the one against whom it was committed." But he gave this answer with guile, and he is exposed by his own interpretations, in which his deceit shows itself. For when he says, "It is written: 'Whoever denies me, I too will deny him,' and he whose words these are cannot lie," he shows that the penance he says must be done is empty and fruitless. If the sentence has been pronounced, and he who pronounced it does not deceive, why do you force a man to torment himself with lamentations and groans, when you either deny that this produces any effect or admit that you do not know whether it does? Anyone who gives advice to someone surely gives it in order to point out what benefit can come of it. But because you, Novatian, profess this deceitfully, you tell people to do penance only to make sport of their minds. Knowing that penance cannot be openly denied, you act subtly: you cut penance off not in word but in effect. You certainly say that everyone who has sacrificed to idols sins against the Holy Spirit, and you argue from the words of the law that this sin is not forgiven him, either here or in the future. How then can you say that penance must be done for this offense, unless you are deceiving, as I showed above?

But you usually try to cover up this fraud with another trick. You say that the apostle Peter meant the same thing when he said to Simon: "Repent of this wickedness of yours, in case it may perhaps be forgiven you." But the apostle Peter saw how poisonous and bitter the man's wickedness was, and that is why he gave him an uncertain answer. For what mortal ever sinned in such a way as to want to buy the gift of God with money? That answer, then, was given to malice, not to error. Malice is what has no remedy, because it is neither error nor a sin that necessity can excuse, so as to reach pardon through weeping. So if any are found in such a case, let them hear what Simon heard. And the apostle Peter shows why he answered doubtfully when he says: "For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." If, then, in so grave a case, one that seems to be without remedy, the answer given was doubtful, there is no doubt that those who sin against God through error or some necessity can be forgiven, if they do fitting penance. For the Author of the Church has granted this to the Church's law: both to impose penance and to receive back after penance.

There is another thing that Novatian finds fault with. "Why," he says, "do they give the body of the Lord to those whom they know to be sinners?" As if those who are judges could themselves be accusers! But if such people have been accused and their guilt made plain, they can be cast out. For what judge would take on the role of accuser? The Lord himself put up with Judas, whom he knew to be a thief who carried off what was put into the purse, and he did not cast him out, since he had not been accused. We ought to follow this example, so that it is not permitted to cast out anyone who has not been publicly exposed. Nor is it fitting for a righteous man to accuse anyone. Hence it says of Joseph: "Since he was a righteous man and did not want to expose her, he resolved to put her away secretly." So Judas, though he was among the disciples, did not defile them by contact with him, for they had no part in his thefts; and in receiving the Eucharist among them he did not pollute the innocent. Nor did the Lord deny his body to the man he knew to be a robber, because, according to the apostle, whoever receives unworthily takes a sword upon himself. That is why he did not turn away even from Judas's kiss. Sinners defile those who consent to their evil deeds. Hence it is said: "When you saw a thief, you ran along with him."

This is why the apostle rebuked the people of Corinth for not reproving or shunning the man who openly had his father's wife, so that he might mend his ways. He said: "Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?" Since there was no leader or overseer of the church, it fell to the people to reprove the man they saw living among them so shamefully and obscenely. For this reason the apostle rebuked them as if they consented to his crime. In this matter there was no need of an accuser or witnesses, for he openly kept his stepmother as his wife. [?]

So, as far as our own case is concerned, we have set out our reasoning, not to accuse others but to defend ourselves. But I appeal to the conscience of Novatian, who is always accusing us: does he know that all those he has with him are holy? He is so angry with us that he even denies we are Christians, although he knows that we were baptized in the same faith that he himself lays claim to. Surely it is profession and life that make a Christian. If, then, you see a man professing what you profess, and not unlike you in his life, why do you deny that he is what you are? Certainly whoever says "Lord Jesus" says it in the Holy Spirit, for he speaks the truth, and all truth is from God. Why do you not agree with one who speaks the truth, but deny him instead? You contradict one who confesses God, not out of reason but out of rage. Do you not show yourself an enemy of God when you resist one who professes the truth about him? Does a pagan who hears someone say that idols are gods deny that he is a pagan? Why do you deny that a man is a Christian when you hear him profess the words of the true faith, though you read: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation"? But you, like an enemy, blinded by anger, fight against God by denying that those who confess these things have salvation, though the Lord says: "Whoever confesses me, I too will confess him." Does he say, "If Novatian confesses me"? Yet you build your case as if you were defending this: that the one saved is not simply a Christian, but one who is also a Novatianist. But if confession made of Christ gives salvation, then wherever and among whomever that confession is kept whole, it has salvation. So if the tradition of this confession has been corrupted among us, or its meaning altered, you are right to accuse us. But if it remains in us as it does in you, then in denying us you show that you deny yourself as well.

But you accuse the ministers of the faith. Suppose it were true, though you cannot prove it. Still, is what those who heard them heard true or false? For if a man of bad character speaks the truth, it does not stop being true because a man of bad character said it, since conduct is one thing and profession another. Does not the persecutor, out of hatred for the Christian name, persecute the profession and not the conduct? He knows that this is what matters first of all for religion, and so when we confess that we are Christians, the sacrilegious man believes us as we confess what he does not want to hear, because he hates it. But you, though you share the same profession and the same seal, do not believe us when we confess what you yourself confess. If you knew that we had been reborn in some other way than you were reborn, you would rightly refuse to believe that we are what you are. Why do I suffer persecution from the sacrilegious, if I am not what you are? For if I professed about myself what you say about me, I would not suffer persecution. In the end, it is I who must be believed about myself, not you. The judge asks for my profession, not for yours about me. Why then do you deny what I confess, when in this matter it is not someone else's testimony that is required, either for me or against me, but my own profession? I wish you were being tortured for the Name facing me, so that it might become clear whether you would deny against me the truth I confess, or which of us would be believed. You put this forward deceitfully, to make it seem that you have just grounds for schism. For you are well aware that in this matter it is my testimony about myself that is required, not another's, and that what is held true is what I confess, not what someone else denies.

It is clear, then, that those are free of guilt who, out of love for Christ, do not inquire into the deeds of men but hasten to obtain faith in him, approving in the ministers only what they know is useful to themselves, namely that they may receive the tradition of the faith that concerns Christ. For anyone who thinks that something more than the ministry of a man is needed in this matter does an injury to the tradition, because he thinks too little of the grace of God. When he denies that God's gift can benefit one devoted to him unless the merit of a man is present, he makes the man either greater than the tradition itself or equal to it, though a man's merit is far removed from this office. As the apostle Paul says about this very matter: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth."

How then is anything in this matter to be hoped for from a man, when the words to be handed on have already been given? Let us see, then, what good it will do if he is of good merit, or what harm if he is of bad merit. The one who comes desires to hear the words of God; by putting his faith in them he believes he receives salvation. What difference does it make here whether the one who hands on the solemn words lives a good or a bad life, when what is sought is the devout faith of the recipient, that he may believe with his whole heart what he hears? If the one who hands them on lives a bad life, will he be an obstacle to the recipient, so that he does not believe what he hears must be believed, as if the minister's sin entered the recipient's heart to keep him from believing? Or is God, who is just, going to reject one devoted to him because of the sin of a man whom God himself allows to remain in orders? Not even a man judges like that, though he is known to be often deceived or swayed by favour. If it were so, and the man were pleading his own case, would he not say to God: "I do not know who this man is on whose account you reject me. I came to him for your sake, because he was called your bishop. It was you I sought, you I longed for, you I believed in; I hoped for nothing from the man. Why then should his evil deeds harm me, when I would not have known him if I had not been seeking you? If his good deeds could benefit me, it might perhaps seem just that his evil deeds should harm me too. But just as his good deeds would have done me no good if my belief had been doubtful, so his evil deeds ought to do me no harm when my belief is sound. For I put my faith in his words, which are said to have been given by you, which breathe of you, speak of you, and make promises about you. I believed nothing about him himself or his deeds; I joined myself to the faith that comes from you."

On this reasoning, the believer's case stands intact. Think of bishops as like advocates. If an advocate lives a bad life, will judgment be given against his client? The advocate's duty is to plead his client's case according to the order of law. Can his life, if it is shameful, harm his client's case? The person of the advocate can neither harm nor help; the answer given will depend on what the case is. So it is with those who wish to become Christians. They come to the bishop and tell him their vows, and he pronounces the words of the Church's law. If the vows are true, they are accepted by the Judge. How could the bishop either harm or help here, since he does not even know his client's case? For God the Judge alone knows with what intention each person comes. So it belongs to the bishop to carry out the office entrusted to him, and to the Judge to accept or reject the client's case. For it is he who is found to have said: "Daughter, your faith has made you well."

You see, then, that each person is saved not by anyone else's help but by his own faith. For God has decreed this for faith: that if it does not doubt, it will obtain whatever it wishes. Yet you, not as a friend but as an enemy of Christ, have gathered a people under your own name, so that they are not Christians unless they are Novatianists, though the apostle condemns anyone who calls himself a follower of Paul or of anyone else. But you, judging yourself greater, have set your own name above the name of Christ, as if he were not enough to protect his own Church.

103. Since it is clear that in Leviticus the Lord gave commands about offering sacrifices, what does it mean when, in anger, he says to the people that he did not command their fathers to offer libations, sacrifices or burnt offerings? For this is what he says through the prophet Jeremiah: "Thus says the Lord: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the meat, for I did not speak to your fathers or command them, on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices."

If you consider the matter carefully, there is no question to raise here. Do not suppose that the Lord lied or changed his mind, commanding something and later denying it. For he is found to have given no command about the kind of sacrifices, libations or burnt offerings of which he declares he said nothing. Notice that there are two kinds of sacrifice: one that was commanded to be offered for particular cases, and another that is called voluntary. For the sacrifice prescribed for the various cases, whether for sins or for the firstborn, there was a command stating what was to be offered, of what quality, and in what manner. The voluntary sacrifice, however, was certainly not commanded, since it was left to free choice: if anyone wished to make an offering, he could offer whatever seemed good to him, for these were votive sacrifices. And because they offered these carelessly and thoughtlessly, without considering that whoever makes an offering to someone more powerful ought to offer choice gifts, they are told: "I did not command you about these; but if you wish to offer them, you ought to offer what is worthy."

This is how Cain too is found to have sinned, when he did not consider that what is better ought to be offered to God. For while they claimed to be offering these things to appease God, by that very act they provoked God to indignation, so that in the thing they said they were doing well they sinned, offering God unworthy burnt offerings. That is why he says in the prophet Malachi: "If you bring for a victim what is blind or lame or sick, that is not good. Offer such things to your governor or your overseer, and see whether he will receive you, says the Lord Almighty." Hence too in Isaiah God complains about the same thing, saying: "What are the sheep of your burnt offering to me? You have not honored me with your sacrifices. I did not make you for this, that you should toil over incense or buy me incense with silver, nor have I desired the fat of your sacrifices; but in your sins and iniquities you have stood before me." It is clear, then, that the complaints arose because, when they offered voluntary sacrifices, they did not honor God with them, offering what was unworthy, even though nothing compelled them to offer. For if these had been commanded, they might have seemed to offer whatever they had out of necessity; but since they offered them of their own free will, they ought to have offered such things as would show their devotion to God. But because their minds strayed in the desire for idols, they did these things without thought. They are therefore reproached on two counts: they dared to make offerings to God while acting wickedly, and what they offered was unworthy, whereas wicked deeds are not redeemed by sacrifices but by lamentation and mercy.

That is why David, when he had sinned, says: "Had you wished it, I would surely have given sacrifices; you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise." Likewise Samuel says to Saul, who, after despising the Lord's command, thought God could be appeased by sacrifice: "God does not want sacrifice more than that his voice be heard." And Scripture says: "I desire mercy rather than sacrifice," because, though they were unjust and merciless, they thought God would become favorable through offerings, just as even now some who scorn justice think they win praise by offerings. An offering, then, is good if justice is kept and mercy is not neglected, because what we ask for ourselves we ought also to grant to others.
104. On the Gospel of Luke.

Knowing that a Jewish war would be waged against him, the Lord told his disciples to provide themselves with swords. When this had been done and the war had begun, led by Simon Iscariot, the apostle Peter, seeing the enemy rising against them, drew his sword and cut off the ear of the priests' servant. Then the Lord told Peter to put his sword back in its sheath: "For everyone," he said, "who takes the sword will perish by the sword." Why did he order swords to be got ready, when he forbade striking, and even declared guilty of death whoever struck with the sword, although the apostle certainly does not seem to have struck unjustly? As far as the matter goes, he struck a man he saw armed against him. Surely he ought to have resisted ungrateful servants who had armed themselves to kill their Lord.

If you examine each part of the case whose reasoning you want explained, you will find other things to ask about in these words. For what need was there for one who relied on spiritual power to order material swords to be got ready? And why should he, who earlier had ordered that they carry neither bag nor money nor staff on the road, now order them to have what he had previously forbidden?

Let us begin, then, by explaining why he ordered swords to be got ready and yet forbade striking. He directed that weapons be procured for the coming war not only on account of his enemies but also on account of his own disciples. For something new and astonishing was about to happen: that he who was performing new and unheard-of signs should suddenly be so humbled as to be subjected to scourging and to death. So, lest he should seem to suffer these things without foreknowledge, as though his power had perhaps deserted him, he foretold all of it in such a way that there could be no doubt about it, but that he was preparing himself against these things with full foreknowledge. And because he was humbled of his own will, he ordered that his enemies not be resisted more fiercely, showing that he was still the same as he had been, to such a degree that, even after he had been seized, he restored the ear that had been cut off and gave back what the sword's work had severed. He did not do this like a physician of the flesh, but as the creator of the body he refashioned his own mutilated work; for physicians cannot restore limbs cut from the body. So that the power of God might be seen not to be diminished in him but to remain in him as it had been, and that he might confirm what he had said, "I have power to lay down my life and I have power to take it up again" — for this reason, then, he had swords got ready, yet he did not order anyone to be killed.

It remains now to ask why, seeing what the apostle Peter had done, he said that whoever used the sword would perish by the sword, when Peter does not seem to have struck unjustly. For, as Luke indicates, he struck with the Lord's own permission, and having been stopped in this way he heard these words. It was permitted so that they might be seen to be able to avenge themselves but unwilling to do so, and so that the power might be shown to remain in him as before; thus in both respects there could be no doubt that they were able to avenge themselves, while his enemies would know for certain that the power to do these things had been given them by him. For he did not appear as one defeated, but as one handing himself over to their will. Why, then, was the sentence pronounced that whoever takes the sword will perish by the sword, unless because no one except a judge is permitted to kill anyone with the sword? The apostle Peter was permitted only so far as to cause pain, not to kill. By hearing this, so that he would not strike again, he learned moreover that once people have become Christians they may not kill; for those who are established in mercy are not permitted to use harshly the law of justice entrusted to the world. As for his earlier apparent command to the disciples going on the road that they should take nothing for the journey, that was for the sake of peace, for the grace of their mighty works, and for the gentleness of their teaching. For what need was there for them to take anything on the road, when everything was to be offered to them because of the signs they worked? But when the time came at which he allowed himself to suffer, and on that account a brawl, or rather a war, was impending, he ordered the disciples to be armed—not so that he who was willing to suffer might fight back, but, as I have said, to show that he foreknew this event and that his passion was in his own power, while humbling himself for the sake of human salvation, which will be discussed in its proper place.
105. That the Gospel agrees with prophecy.

At the Lord's first coming it was foretold that the sun would be darkened at his passion at the very hour at which it is shown to have happened, that is, at midday; for it is written thus in the prophet Amos: "And on that day, says the Lord, the sun will set at noon, and the daylight will grow dark over the earth." So on that day the sun was darkened from the sixth hour until the ninth hour, and thus the prophecy of the prophet just mentioned was fulfilled. For an image of what will happen at the Lord's second coming was shown at the Lord's passion, since at the end, when the Lord begins to come to judge the world, the lights will be released from their duty, as the Lord says: "In those days the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light." The prophet Joel did not pass this over either, so that, since it is signified by Joel, it may be believed without doubt that it will be fulfilled. For he said: "The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes." This, as far as appears, fits the second coming better; for then he will be openly manifested to all, as Scripture says: "Then every eye will see him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him, and those who crucified him."

So if both comings include this, that the sun will be darkened in those days, what day is it in which, as Scripture proclaims, the sun and moon will be increased? For Isaiah says among other things: "And on every high mountain and in every lofty place there will be running water on that day, when many have perished, when towers have fallen. And the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold in that day, when he heals the bruising of his people," and so on. What day can be understood as the one on which the Lord promised to heal the bruising of his people? This, I think, is the day that Zechariah, the father of John, pointed to when he said: "Blessed is the God of Israel, for he has visited and wrought redemption for his people, and has raised up a horn of our salvation in the house of his servant David, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old; and he has delivered us from our enemies and from the hands of all who hate us, to show mercy to our fathers." And Simeon says among other things: "This child is set for the fall and the rising of many in Israel." This fall is that of the scribes and Pharisees and the chief men of the Jews, whom the prophet signified by "towers."

While these fell through unbelief, others rose by believing, who earlier had seemed weak and sick through negligence. Hence the Savior says: "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind"—so that those who, through their observance and knowledge of the law, seemed to have sight would be blinded through unbelief, while the blind, that is, the unlearned or the tax collectors, would see by believing. The prophet foretold that the Savior would bear their infirmities. And so this came to pass in the Savior's time, as we read in the Gospel, for he himself took our infirmities and healed our wounds.

All these things were completed and fulfilled in the Savior's passion; for in this way the salvation of the human race was both redeemed and secured, among those above as well as among those below, since the prophecy of Zechariah mentioned above includes both. Here, among those above, people were freed from being crushed by their enemies through the intervention of mercy; and there, among those below, when they were rescued from Tartarus. For all who had hoped in the promised Christ were awaiting his coming, so that, once death was conquered, they might be freed from the underworld. That is why he said: "to show mercy to our fathers." But if anyone understands this salvation to be included in the second coming too, nevertheless at both comings, and especially the second, the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon will not give its light. How, then, are we to understand that the sun and moon are increased on the day when the Lord visits his people, when we read that at both times—when the liberation of the people began and when it was completed—the sun and moon are not diminished but darkened? Unless, plainly, we understand the sun and moon as figures for the saints, just as elsewhere we read that the saints are likened to lights, as the apostle Paul proclaims, because among other people the saints appear in this world like lights; and in the Gospel: "Then," he says, "the righteous will shine like the sun." For the Lord calls righteous works light, since he says: "Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven."

Those, then, who leave all they have and follow the Lord for the sake of righteousness and holiness are compared to the sun and moon, honored sevenfold, as the Lord says: "There is no one who leaves house or wife or children or fields who will not receive sevenfold in this age." Since those who are honored sevenfold in the present, it may be understood that in the future too they are to be believed seven times brighter than the rest, so that their resurrection is compared to the sun and moon, while that of the others is like the stars. The glory of the saints, then, which is honored sevenfold here, attains another sevenfold in the resurrection, so that whoever here has the brightness of the moon will receive the brightness of the sun in the future, and whoever here is compared to the sun is to be believed destined to receive sevenfold as much.

So the prophet Isaiah, by comparison with the sun and moon, foretold that the merits of the saints would be increased, and not without reason. For if the Lord himself is called the Sun of righteousness, and the saints will be like him, as the apostle John says, "For when he appears, we shall be like him," it is fitting that the saints are signified by the sun. Yet the prophet just mentioned shows the sun to be seven times greater than the moon. For when he shows that the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the sun sevenfold, he indicates that the moon is increased sevenfold, to the measure of the sun, so that it becomes such as the sun is. Although the subject here concerns the saints, under the figure of the lights he has partly disclosed their magnitude: after the increase of the sun and moon, the sun is again greater by as much as the sun had been, so that however far one saint differs from another in the present, so far will he differ in the future too, after the reward is given.
106. On the Book of Genesis.

In the beginning God made heaven and earth. If he made heaven and earth in the beginning, and heaven is the firmament, as appears from what follows, then this is not true, because light was made first and only then the firmament. Yet it could not mean some other heaven, since it is describing the making of the world, completed by God's work. People were deceived by various opinions about the cause of the world, and for this reason Moses, with God inspiring him, showed how the world came to be. Some thought it had no beginning. Others thought it did have a beginning, but had been fashioned by certain angels. Some thought it was likewise made, but by a certain Saklas, who was the god of the hostile power. A few, however, following the line handed down from the source of truth, declared that God was its maker. Because of the variety of these people, who were led astray by false opinion, Moses was compelled to show the true cause of the world. Otherwise the children of Israel, though rescued from the power of the Egyptians, would not have been freed from their false understanding. For the Egyptians, more than any others, pursued the study of error; from ancient times they had devoted themselves to vain philosophy beyond all other peoples. Indeed Moses, because he was regarded as the adopted son of Pharaoh's daughter, was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

What, then, does it mean when it says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth? If it does not mean the firmament, as we showed above, let us see what it does mean. We think that Moses wished to remove every error about the lower creation and about the materials from which the world was made. So he indicated that in the beginning the very substances of which the world consists were made. Had he been silent about this, those substances might perhaps have been thought eternal, as though they were coeternal with God. As it is, whoever accepts his testimony on this matter cannot doubt that the world was made, since he acknowledges that the substances which served as the material of the world were laid down at the beginning. So in the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, the upper and the lower substance. The upper is the substance of which heaven consists. The lower is a kind of dregs-like concretion, which went to form the dry land, called earth, and the darkness. Hence he says in the prophet Isaiah: I am God, who made light and created darkness. That is, he made water, darkness and earth.

These substances, then, were created together before time. For time belongs beneath the firmament. The firmament, as some think, is ice formed from the waters. It is called the firmament because it was made firm when the waters were congealed by divine power, and it is called caelum, 'heaven', from 'concealing' or 'hiding'. Water is the greater element, and so it is mentioned first, and also because part of it went to form the vault of the world, while the earth is the floor. David too, through the Holy Spirit, acknowledges that these things were created, for he says: And let the water that is above the heavens praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and it was made, he commanded and it was created. After these elements, then, and before the world was put together, God made light, so that his works might go forward in light. This light, in its appointed measure, completed the course of a day. Then night came, matching the measure of the day. In the same way, when its span was complete, the night was lit up by the arrival of the morning light. Thus the first day was completed when the second began, for the night is counted with the day, so that together they are called one day. Because darkness is subordinate to light, it lacks the authority to make up a count. Thus thirty days are called one month, though they include the nights as well. So the service of light, by which it completes the span decreed for it, is called day, while the substance of darkness, before it is lit up, is called night. The span between sunset and sunrise is night. For darkness does not make night in the way that light makes day, since darkness simply remains in its own nature. Rather, the approach of light makes day and its departure makes night. It is not without reason, then, that night is subordinate to day.

When light had been made, then, and a course of twelve hours had been completed, followed by an equal span of night, there was an equinox on the first day. From then on the day began to grow longer than the night for three months, which are the season of spring. Then, from that increase, the day shortens over another three months, which are the season of summer. Again there is an equinox, so that from then on the night grows longer than the day for another three months, which are the season of autumn. Then the night begins once more to shrink from the length by which it exceeds the day, until the end of the fourth season, which is winter. And the equinox of the first season comes round, the time when God created the world. This is understood to be 22 March, when the first day of Passover falls, that is, the first day of the first month. For the law commanded that on the tenth day of the first month, in the evening, they should make ready to keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, that is, counting from the eleventh. For the evening of the tenth day already dawns into the eleventh, so that the first month began on 22 March. In the beginning the moon, when it was made, was at its fourteenth day, since all things were made full. Add the three days counted from the evening of the tenth; these are the three days that came before the luminaries. Thus the world was made on 22 March, since the moon's count runs from the eleventh to the fourteenth, the day to which the whole first month of Passover is assigned. So the solemn day of Passover is kept neither apart from 22 March nor apart from the fourteenth moon, because the world was made on the eleventh, and on the fourteenth moon it was made brighter with a greater light.

Between the beginning, then, and the brightness by which the world was lit up, our Saviour both suffered and rose again. For he suffered on the fourteenth moon and rose on the first day. That day is therefore called 'the Lord's day', because he made it, and when it is multiplied it makes months, seasons and years. The reason the feast is not celebrated in one and the same way each year is the course of the moon as it wanes and waxes.

But the earth was invisible and unformed. It is plain that the earth, after it was made, was invisible and unformed. It was invisible because it was covered with waters. It was unformed because, being fluid, it was not fit for cultivation.
And darkness was over the abyss. He says that darkness was over the abyss, that is, over water that was boundless on every side.

And the Spirit of God was borne over the water. He means this water as its surface, and he shows the Spirit of God above it, because the Spirit was borne over it. In this way he indicates that darkness was over the boundless depth, but the Spirit of God was over the waters, for where the Spirit of God was there was no darkness. As far as it could, the Spirit lit up the water, but it could not light up the abyss, that is, the immeasurable depth. In other words, it lit up the upper waters, while beneath them lay the darkness over the abyss.

He calls this the 'Spirit of God', not because he wants it understood as the Holy Spirit. Rather, he wants spiritual realities to be understood as standing above material creation. He calls the spirit that was borne over the waters God's spirit to show that the whole belongs to God, and so to overturn the perverse claim some make that there is something that does not belong to God. For it would be contrary both to order and to reason to say that the Holy Spirit was over the waters, since he is above all creation. What is of God is above all powers and principalities, and likewise above all spiritual powers. Let no one be troubled that it is called the Spirit of God, since it is established that all things are God's. For God says, among other things, when he was about to send the flood: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh. And in Ezekiel, among other things: Thus says the Lord to these bones: I will stretch skin over you and put my spirit in you, and you shall live. Do these words refer to the work of the Holy Spirit and not to the soul? So this spirit is indeed God's, as everything else is, but it governs material substances; its rank is to preside over them.

When light had been made, then, and the course of the day had been regulated and completed, on the second day he made the firmament, that is, heaven. In this way the light within the firmament might regulate the day, like a lamp in a house. This firmament was made from the substance of water mentioned above. For now the world is being put together into its form. Out of the confusion of things, once the substances had been separated, the individual parts were to be fitted together that would go to make up the members of the world. The substances which we said were made first are the materials of the world. And it is called mundus because things that had been confused were separated from one another and brought out into form, and so caused the world they went to build to be called mundus. So the firmament, that is heaven, was made in the midst of the waters, to divide the water above the firmament from the water beneath it. By God's power the firmament was to stand in the midst of the waters, with water beneath it, within it, above it and around it. It was to be vaulted on the outside and fortified within, so that the waters, whether outer or inner, would not break into its hollow. Thus it would be like a fortified and strengthened house, so that those who live in it might be safe.

On the third day he commanded the water under heaven, that is, within the space enclosed by the firmament, to be gathered into one gathering, so that the dry land, which is the earth, might appear; and so it was done. A broad stretch of the earth was hollowed out to form something like a basin, into which all the water within the firmament might sink, and then the dry land appeared. For as the water withdrew, the earth, which had before been invisible, was bound to appear and become visible. Then the dry land was called earth and the gatherings of waters seas. And he commanded the earth to bring forth grass for fodder and fruit-bearing trees with seed upon the earth.

Then on the fourth day God commanded that lights be made in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth: the greater light to begin the day, the lesser light to begin the night, and the stars. These serve for the conception, birth and nourishment of the things that are begotten in the world. They are needed as signs of the seasons, with fixed marks, and also to adorn the whole world. A house is adorned if its vault has ceiling panels picked out in gold, and in the same way the stars, shining with varied light, give the world its adornment. So the splendour of the sun was added to the light that had been made first, so that these are joined and indivisible. To the night, which was dark, a light was given. And because the moon was at its fourteenth day when it was made, he says: the lesser light to begin the night. For once made, it shone the whole night through. So 'to begin the night' is said by taking the part for the whole, since the moon does not always shine in the evening. The greater light, which we call the sun, remains at the beginnings of the day, because it was fused together with the earlier light.

For three days, then, the world was without these lights, because there was not yet anything for their services to benefit. But when the earth brought forth grass for fodder and fruit-bearing trees, there was need for things to nourish and preserve what had been brought forth. All generation of these things is brought to completion through the agency of the lights. So it was not fitting for the lights to be made first, lest the things brought forth from the earth be thought to have arisen through their effect. Instead it was fitting to make those things first and these afterward, so that no one could doubt that the former were made without them.

Then on the fifth day he commanded the waters to bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds flying above the earth along the firmament of heaven; and so it was done. And among other things it says: And God saw that they were good, and said: Increase and multiply. He added the words And God saw that they were good because some people call these creatures evil, so that such people might be put to shame, if nothing else. For when they please God their maker, they surely ought to displease no one. Fools are in the habit of saying: 'He saw them and they pleased him because he did not know beforehand.' You dullards, how could he not have known, when what he willed was brought forth? Does anyone will what he does not know? Can one who is able to make something be said not to know what he is making? And what is more, he did not make them himself but commanded them to be made. Did the element he commanded have the power to make them by itself? No, but since all things are possible to him, at his command what could not do this began to be able to do it, and so it served to his praise. For his power is twofold here, in that he commanded a thing without sense to bring forth things with sense.

Then on the sixth day he commanded the earth to bring forth living souls, four-footed creatures and beasts of the earth; and so it was done, and they were brought forth. And God saw that they were good, and indeed very good, because they are all necessary.

On that same day, then, God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have power, it says, over all things that have been made upon the earth. First God made the substances out of which he would put the world together. When it had been put together, decked with every adornment and furnished with what it needed, he then made man to enjoy it and everything in it. He had commanded everything on earth to be brought forth from the waters and the earth. To make man, however, he is described as taking the clay of the earth in his hands, to teach that man differs greatly from the things he had made. He means it to be a mark of man's honour when he describes him as made by God's hands, and made in the image and likeness of God, that is, of the Father and the Son.

We have said elsewhere what 'in the image and likeness' means, yet this passage and the subject require us to say it again. These are the words of the Father to the Son: Let us make man in our image and likeness. In every work, however, the persons of both are understood, the one who speaks and the one who obeys. This, then, is the image of God in man: that one man was made as a kind of lord, from whom the rest would spring, holding God's rule as his vicar, for every king bears the image of God. And therefore woman was not made in God's image. For it says: And God made man; in the image of God he made him. Hence the apostle says: A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God, while a woman veils hers because she is not the glory or image of God. The likeness of God in man is this: just as the Son is from the Father, so the woman is from the man. Yet they are plainly unlike in this respect, that she was made, whereas he was begotten.

Some, however, think that the Lord made all things at once. 'If he made them by a word,' they say, 'why should he not be said to have made them all at once? Making things piece by piece is the human way, if he is believed to have made them so.' So they say it does more honour to God's power if all things are believed to have been made by him in a single day. In fact, however, we see great providence in this work and in its order. He could certainly have made everything at once, but a manifold reason prevented it. And setting all these arguments aside, we must put our faith in divine Scripture, which says, and says often: For in six days the Lord your God made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them. In the first place, things had to be made in this way so that they might perceive and know that they had been made. For they did not see themselves all come to be at once, but one today and another tomorrow. So they recognized that they were bounded by a beginning, and since they recognized one another as coming one after another, they could not suppose themselves eternal. If all things had come into existence at once, they would have had no sense of their weakness, but would have thought that they had no beginning. For things that suddenly come into existence together by God's word do not perceive that they are being made, except by seeing one thing before them and another after. And lest what was made first should think itself unmade, it sees greater things made after it and believes of itself what it sees in another, superior thing. Thus light, which is called day, has heaven and earth before it, that is, water and dry land. Since the water, the dry land and the darkness had been made in a state of confusion, they could not claim eternity for themselves, for none of them dared to claim a settled state and a distinct character of its own. Again, the sun and moon, though they are most brilliant, have many things before them. So it was done in this way, so that when the later things see themselves as superior and the earlier ones see themselves as inferior, none of them claims eternity for itself.

Moreover, the work completed in six days contains within itself the age of the whole world, so that the works of the six days are a figure of six thousand years. What was to come in each age is contained, in order, in the works of the six days. Thus the earlier days appear without splendour, because, I think, in the earlier ages there was not yet to be so great a knowledge of God on earth. Cattle were made before man because our ancestors were to live uncultivated and rustic lives, like cattle. Man was made on the sixth day because in the six thousandth year the coming of Christ made man no longer subject to death. Man was made the image of God because by God's gift he would be conformed to the image of the Son of God. As the apostle John says: We know that when he appears we shall be like him. And the chosen vessel says: conformed to the image of the Son of God. The tree of life, which was placed in paradise, was an image of the future grace of God, which is the body of the Lord; whoever eats it will live forever. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the law given through Moses. By making known sin, which had before been hidden, it gave the knowledge of good and evil, for it showed what was good and what was evil. And the fact that he rested on the seventh day from his works signified that when the six thousandth year was complete, he would rest in the seven thousandth, when the world would at last cease from all worldly work. 20. We have said these few things out of many in order to open up a way of understanding in line with what we have shown above.
CVII. ON THE ORDER OF DAY AND NIGHT.

As far as the account of the world is concerned, we read of darkness before light. For the things that went to make up the fabric of the world, and that appear to have been made together, are considered to have been without light: that is, water, earth and darkness, out of which the world was put together. So it says in the Wisdom called Solomon's: "out of unseen matter", that is, dark matter. The sacred books testify that both darkness and water were made, by the voice of the Lord himself through the prophet Isaiah: "For I am God," he says, "who made light and created darkness." Likewise through David the Holy Spirit shows that the waters were made and that the earth was established upon the waters. This agrees with the authority of the Gospel and with apostolic tradition, in which we read that all things were made. So as to leave nothing out, the apostle says: "whether things in heaven or things on earth."

In this part, then, which concerns the earth, we read of darkness before light. This concerns the order in which we read them, not their dignity, for light is certainly far better than darkness. In the account of the world, however, light received a name, so that it was called day and the darkness night. The reason is plainly this: when the darkness is lit up and the light passes, that time, until the light returns, is called night, and the time in which the darkness is lit up is called day. So when we say night, we look for a day to come, and when we say day, we expect that night will come. But when these functions cease as the world passes away, we will speak only of darkness and light. For it cannot be called night when the darkness is perpetual, nor day when the light has stopped setting. Where there is eternity these names cease, because they began with the world. Indeed, before the light was made that was called day, we read that there was not night but darkness. Only after the darkness had been lit up and the light had passed was it called evening and night.

So, as appears, night is subordinate to day. Darkness should not be thought to rank first just because we read of it before light. Heaven too comes before the sun, and yet the sun is greater in brightness. The earth comes before man, and so do the cattle and the other living creatures, yet they are subject to man. Night, therefore, should not be preferred to day because darkness is read of first, since it is clear that light ranks above darkness in dignity and day comes before night in time. For, as was shown above, light was made when there was darkness.

"And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night; and there was evening and there was morning, one day." If there had been no day, there would have been no night either. There was darkness, and when it had been lit up and the day had passed and completed its course, evening came. And when it had grown light again after the evening and the night had passed, the first day was complete, so that night followed day. It is both fitting and reasonable that the inferior nature should in all things be subject to the superior.

How then will night be said to come before day, when you read its name after day? It would not have been called night or evening unless the light, once made, had produced a day. When that day had passed, evening came, which is night. The day itself became evening, so that you may know that night is part of the day. For a day is completed when it has passed, and not [?]. This is how we speak: "The year has 365 days," certainly not leaving out the nights. When we say days, we count the nights along with them. Under the authority of day we also mean night. If night went before day, day would be counted under the name of night. Who would say, "I shall see you after five nights," and not "after five days"? Nor do we remember reading anywhere of night being mentioned before day. "Moses," it says, "was on the mountain forty days and forty nights." In the psalm: "The sun," it says, "shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night." And to give an example from the very beginnings: "Let there be lights," it says, "in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth: the greater light to begin the day and the lesser light to begin the night." If the moon can be ranked above the sun, then night can be ranked above day too. But just as the moon is beneath the sun, so night is beneath day. In the Gospel, too, we find nights included under the authority and number of days. Among other things the Lord says: "There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom." And the evangelist adds: "And it came to pass after eight days," and so on. Are the nights not included in this number? In another place it says: "These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. The next day he saw Jesus coming." Did it say "the next night"? It goes on: "The following day he wanted to set out for Galilee." And a little later: "And on the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee."

See how everywhere day is shown to hold authority, with night subject to it. If the number were counted under the name of night, night would come before day. Because the Romans hold the rule, the Spaniards, Gauls, Africans and the other peoples subject to them are called Romans under their name. In the same way night, because it is subject to day, is included under its name. Some people are misled because the Jews are commanded to begin the sabbath in the evening, and they do not consider why it was commanded so. On the previous day the Jews must buy their food, prepare for the sabbath and go to wash. Could they do these things at night and then begin the sabbath at daybreak? The Lord certainly rose in the evening, and yet it is reckoned to the day. The resurrection is celebrated by day, and that day is called the Lord's day. So you read: "This is the day which the Lord has made." Yet there is no Lord's night, because the day holds the primacy. Whether to the past day or to the coming one, night is always subject, because it is inferior both in order and in nature. As the apostle says: "You are children of the day and of the light, not of the night and of darkness." If we draw a comparison from the consuls, we shall see that the one elected first is named first. People commonly ask: "Who will be consul with him?" If night were before day, then, it would also be named first. The count begins from the day so firmly that if we say, for instance, "Tomorrow is the sixth day before the Kalends," we reckon from morning until the next morning comes, counting it once a day and a night have passed. The moon too was made in the morning at the beginning, as a fourteen-day moon. Once made, it had to shine the whole night, and on the next morning it began its fifteenth day. Why then is there any doubt that beginnings are counted from the day?

Because some people dispute it, we have been forced to speak at length about an obvious matter, though the reading explains itself and plainly shows day before night. All that we have said above concerns the origin of the world. But if we wish to speak at a deeper level and raise our understanding with spiritual vigor, we shall find it incongruous to claim that darkness was created before light. If the nature of light is heavenly and that of darkness earthly, it is surely absurd to think that light was made after darkness. Moses says that light was made, but he means made in the part where the world now is, not that it was created then. All spiritual things were created before carnal ones, so that the light which was in the regions above came to be in those below, like a lamp in a house. And on what grounds is darkness said to come before light, when it is always seen to come after light? Heavenly and spiritual things are believed to be of the nature of light, and earthly and carnal things of the nature of darkness. So the nature of darkness appears to subsist by the power of light, since everything lowest belongs to what is highest. If we look into it, we find darkness in the sun itself. If you are near it, it appears so bright that it cannot be looked at. At some distance it is still very bright, but it can be looked at. Far off it is less bright, and the farther away you go, the more a kind of failing appears that announces darkness. In this way one comes to see that darkness takes its origin from light. So he who made light created darkness in the same way as, in making water, he created earth along with it: just as earth is the solid part of water, darkness is the failing of light.

God alone suffers no failing. He is everywhere, or rather he holds all things within himself, and yet he is so brilliant that no one sees him unless he chooses to temper himself. Indeed the Savior, when he was in the body, was not enclosed in it, and yet he was not seen in his glory unless he wished to be. When he was transfigured on the mountain and appeared in great brightness, that glory had been hidden, as it were, in his body, and he revealed it when he chose. How then was he hidden, when he was not enclosed? If he came in with his body to the disciples through closed doors, how could his divinity fail to penetrate all things? That is, it cannot be enclosed, because it suffers no failing. Since God is absent nowhere, he is nevertheless said to be where he appears and wishes to be seen. All things are in God, because he surpasses them all, as the apostle says: "For in him we live and move and have our being." Yet he himself is in nothing except in whom he chooses. By a certain mystery he is in all things, and by a certain providence he appears in whom he chooses.
108. On the Hebrew language: from whom it took its name.

Everything that comes from God has a rational basis. For each thing a cause supplies its beginning, which is its origin. So the thing does not seem to be named or to exist without reason, and its name points to the thing that is understood as the head of that name. So the rationale of man is the cause by which he exists. He is made of four elements, earth, air, water and fire, with God, of course, as maker. The fifth is the mind, which acts like a charioteer and drives the compact, shaped body as its commander. From this first man we all took our beginning, and we are called by his name. We are called homines because of humus, the ground, from which our father takes his outward origin. So cause and reason bring it about that those who come after someone are called by his name and signify him in themselves.

Let us see, then, whether some are right to think that the Hebrews are named after Eber. Judging by the name alone, it does seem to come from there, and Eber is earlier than Abraham. If this were true, those of Eber's line after him ought to have been called by the same name, for Abraham was born seven generations after Eber. So if people before Abraham, or Abraham himself, were called Hebrews, the Hebrews are no doubt named after Eber. But if we do not read of anyone before Abraham being called a Hebrew, only of people after him, then surely the Hebrews are named not after Eber but after Abraham, since Abraham's sons are known to have been the first to bear this name. In Genesis, Joseph and his brothers are called Hebrews. People knew it was Abraham who had come down from Syria into Canaan and multiplied. Because of his faith he was loaded with every kind of wealth and called king, prophet and father of many nations, and with three hundred and eighteen men born in his household he struck down five kings. Since these things were not done or said in a corner where they might stay hidden, people called those of his seed Hebrews. So it was owing to Abraham's rank and merit that he became the head of those descended from him. By God's judgment he was made the founder and origin in the land of Canaan, so that his descendants would differ in their faith and way of life from what he himself had been before he came into the land of Canaan. Having been renewed himself, he was to found a new people devoted to God. This is why the apostle Paul declares himself a Hebrew of Hebrews, for the name was regarded as a mark of dignity. It was a testimony to noble birth to be named after the one who had pleased God in many ways and who was the people's origin.

Let this view be rejected if it does not agree with reason. Let it be scorned if it does not fit, and overturned if it is out of keeping with Abraham's merits, and let us be refuted as his flatterers. But what is this hostility toward Abraham? What rivalry makes enemies disparage him, and who are they, if not those who are called his sons? What is it about Abraham that displeases them, so that they think this glory does not belong to him? And what is it about Eber that pleases them, so that they say he holds this primacy? If his way of life could be examined, he might well be found to have worshipped idols, like Terah and Nahor and Nahor's father. These men were evidently not far removed from him, and Joshua son of Nun testifies that they worshipped idols.

Or else let those on the other side show on what grounds this honor should be claimed for Eber, in case we are suppressing some merit of his. But there are no such grounds, for the Scriptures are common to us both, and what is due to each person is there for all to see. If they think the claim can be defended from the name alone, that is weak and unconvincing. It could rightly be claimed for his name only if some reasons stood as witnesses to confirm it. Others with the same name could otherwise claim for themselves what is not theirs. So the true view is the one established not by the name alone but by clear reasoning. No one doubts that by God's favor the human race was visited in Abraham and that he became a saving pattern for mankind. In him, therefore, was restored what had been lost through the weakness of human frailty. He was set up as a kind of image, so that the human race might return to God after his likeness, and so that he might recover for mankind both the worship of God and the language that had first been given for human use. In the beginning the image of God was in Adam, so that knowledge of God might be on earth. In the same way, after the ruin of the human race and its forgetting of the truth, that image was re-formed in Abraham, so that faith in God, begun anew from him, might grow and bear fruit. So it is not absurd that the people that began from him should take its name from his name.

Some may still be troubled by the name Eber, because it sounds closer to "Hebrews", since they are called Hebraei and not Habraei. But let them consider in turn that they are called Hebraei, not Heberei, for he was called Heber, not Hebrer [?]. If they think they can attack us on this point, the same objection falls on them, and neither of us will win on this ground.
