Victory goes only to the one who sets out his reasons in order and shows that what he claims is true. One who is equal on one point must be judged the loser if he is found wanting on another. The letter was changed for the sake of sound, so that they are called Hebraei instead of Habraei, because it sounds better. In the same way, those named after Judah are called not Iudai but Iudaei. Wherever a form seemed awkward, a letter was changed so that the word would sound well. We say meridie ("at midday") instead of medidie, and there are many such cases. So it is fitting, as has been shown, that both the language and the people should be named after Abraham.

This, then, is the language which we say was given at the beginning to Adam and the others. We believe that, because of the presumption of building the tower, it was scattered and confused into many languages. It was no longer this one language, but many arose from it through the alteration of certain words. So it lost its own form, yet it did not perish, but was wholly mingled with the other languages. This was done at that time so that people would not understand one another and dare greater things. So it is understood that as many languages arose then as there were men. They were scattered to the places where they settled, and each established his own language.

But suppose it is thought not to be the very language that Scripture says was then the only one. In that case it remains that it was gathered piece by piece from the other languages and put together into the form of a single language for Abraham to use. Since he was the father of many nations, he would then have had a speech composed from many languages and been renewed in every respect. Yet we read that those whom the book of Genesis describes as having one voice and speech migrated from the east, and from there God scattered them again over the face of the whole earth. So surely no one remained there who kept to the language first given. Indeed, this language has no territory among men as the other languages do, and no nation except the Jews, because it was given to the first man in paradise. After the languages were confused, the language now called Hebrew was found nowhere. If, then, it has no place or nation anywhere, and Abraham was a Syrian by birth, where did this language come from for Abraham and the rest of his seed? Either it is the earlier language, or else it was fitted together from many. For we see that quite a few languages have features similar to it.

But the second view does not agree with reason as well as the first, that it is the original language itself. Reason shows that this did not happen without purpose. Abraham had to have the very language that the first man had. Then Moses, when he came to describe the creation and the man God made, could use the language in which God spoke and named the man Adam, and in which Adam's wife was named Eve. So the language in Moses' book was the one spoken by the people he describes, and he could truly teach that in Abraham the first cause and God's gift were restored in every respect.
109. On Melchizedek.

We read about Melchizedek in the book of Genesis, and likewise in the letter to the Hebrews. It says: "Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, met Abraham as he returned from the slaughter of the kings, brought out bread and wine and offered them to him, and blessed him, saying: Blessed are you, Abraham, by God Most High, who made heaven and earth, who delivered your enemies into your hands." And to show how this Melchizedek should be understood, the letter adds: "Without doubt the lesser is blessed by the greater." He certainly did not say this about the office handed down in the Church. Who would doubt that the rule handed down by the Lord, by which those subject to the Lord are blessed, is greater than those who are blessed by it? The Lord's mystery is at work in the words that contain him and call him to mind. But here the apostle wanted to show the merit and power belonging to Melchizedek's own person.

Who, then, is this man, and how great is he, if Abraham is called the lesser beside him? Abraham, after all, clearly bears among all the faithful the mark of noble standing and of faith! So this Melchizedek is surely not understood to have blessed Abraham the way human priests do, giving a blessing on someone else's behalf in set words. He gave it as his own, a blessing he received not through words but in his very nature, so that it belongs to him. Priests, whom we call bishops, have a rule laid down in set words and handed down to them, which they pronounce over people to bless them. They bless not only those they wish to bless but sometimes also those they do not, because the giver of the rule himself knows to whom the most sacred blessing should be given or poured out.

But the one who has blessing in his very nature, whom Scripture calls priest of the highest God, gives the blessing by his own will. The words of the blessing and his nature are in harmony with his will. He does not err by willing to bless where he should not, or by refusing where he should. To whomever he has given the words, he has also given the effect. Our priests, however, pronounce the name of the Lord and the words of blessing over many people every day, but in few does the blessing take effect. And sometimes they bless people better than themselves. Even a holy person bows his head to receive the blessing, because it does not belong to the priest; it was devised by God. Eli the priest blessed Hannah and the effect followed, certainly not by the priest's merit but by Hannah's own, for God looked upon her pure heart.

So Melchizedek is said to be greater than Abraham not only because of his priestly office. He also ranks above him in nature, so that he must be understood as more than human. It is quite impossible that one ranked so far above the friend of God should be thought a man. Abraham was so faithful that for love of God he did not hesitate even to kill his dearest son. By what righteousness, by what works, could anyone deserve more than Abraham deserved? There was nothing more he could have done to show his merit than what he did. First of all, he did not know God and had seen no sign to persuade him. Yet when God said to him, "Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house," he did not delay but obeyed at once. In this he fulfilled the will not only of God who was present but also of the Lord who was to come. For the Lord says: "Whoever loves home or parents or brothers or relatives more than me is not worthy of me." What sort of man, then, was Abraham, and how great his merit, if he fulfilled the Savior's commands before they were ever preached!
The apostle earnestly teaches that hospitality is to be pursued. This

Abraham practiced so devotedly that the apostle seems to have learned from him to preach it. Then, though advanced in years, he believed that his descendants would be multiplied like the stars of heaven, a belief that seems foolish to the wise of the world. So even before the wise of this age were sentenced, they seem to have been condemned by him, since it was said later: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise." At God's command he was circumcised, which certainly is not done without pain, and he did not resent it, so that he might give later generations a pattern of patience. He was promised a son by his wife Sarah, who was already an old woman, and he did not doubt. In this he showed those who would come after that we must yield to God's authority so completely that we do not hesitate even when he commands or promises things that seem unreasonable. We must look to his person rather than to his words, so that his person may confirm what seems weak or impossible in the words and make it appear possible. It is God who promises, and we must believe that he can do what seems impossible to men. What offense can there be when humanity thinks more highly of God than it does of itself?

This is why Abraham does not hesitate to kill the son God had given him when the same God commands it. He does not delay, and he does not wonder at God's will in ordering the death of the son whom he had given as a great grace of kindness and wonder. He is certain that man must not question God's will, and that God's command and deed are not without providence. To carry it out with complete devotion and without delay, he does not tell his wife, the boy's mother, knowing well that women are more fragile where their sons are concerned and might hinder this devotion with tearful pity. The boy himself is also kept unaware until the hour of slaughter. In this way Abraham obeys God's command with wholehearted compliance, regarding the act not as the murder of his own child but as a burnt offering made on the authority of a just judge.

What greater things, then, could Melchizedek have done than these, by which he might surpass Abraham, who, as we see, was plainly disobedient in nothing? Moses, to whom we read that the Lord spoke face to face, was unwilling to go when he was sent to his nation and his brothers. Likewise the prophet Jonah broke the command given him to preach to the Ninevites and set off for another place, where he had not been sent. Job, outstanding as he was in every respect, was nonetheless shaken by the loss of his children; he tore his garments and shaved the hair of his head. But we do not read that Abraham was saddened by the death of his dearest son, the son he himself had been ordered to kill, nor do we read anywhere that he trembled when God commanded him.

From this, then, it appears that Melchizedek is beyond man, since there was no way he could be better than Abraham unless he surpassed him by nature alone. An impassible nature possesses blessedness through its very substance, whereas what is humanly born acquires blessedness through deeds. Since it lacks the perfection of deity, it advances through training and struggle so as to become better, when it conquers more often than it is conquered. If it could act so as never to sin, which is impossible, it would become better than God (God forbid!). For a nature that is able to sin as well as not to sin, if it always conquered, would have to be ranked above the nature that does not sin only because it is impassible. It would not seem a great thing not to sin because one cannot; but it would be magnificent if one could sin and did not.

This, then, is the difference between the substance of God and that of man: God's substance is always blessed in the security of its invincible eternity, while man's substance becomes blessed in another way, through toil. So the blessedness of the impassible must be of one kind, and the blessedness of one who is worn down by tribulations so that he may one day rejoice must be of another. Impassible blessedness consists in being always blessed, while the passible rejoices after great trials that it has escaped death. It suffers sorrow so that it may rejoice, and because its nature is passible it is never permanently secure. The impassible, however, is always blessed, because it neither knows sorrow nor suspects that it could be made sorrowful. Even human nature, though it attains blessedness through toil, will not come through untouched or without scars. How could a nature that has often fought and has sometimes been defeated not be wounded? But the impassible remains forever untouched, unharmed, inviolable.

So Abraham would not be called least in comparison with Melchizedek unless Melchizedek's nature were superior to Abraham's. What we have said so far may perhaps seem a matter of ingenuity; but if we look to the law, many more and weightier things will be said. For "this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham as he returned from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, is first, by interpretation, king of righteousness, and then king of Salem, that is, king of peace. He is without father, without mother and without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life; but, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever." To commend these things in the places where he had pointed to them, he added concerning him: "See," he says, "how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the firstfruits." To show with what power Melchizedek acts and how great he is, he praises Abraham by calling him chief of the fathers. In other words, Abraham is better than all the rest, but least in comparison with Melchizedek.

Is it not obvious that this is not a man but something better? What does it mean when it says of him that he is king of peace and king of righteousness? Come closer and see. Seeing the sun from far off, you take it for a lamp, and looking at silver you think it is tin. Can any human being be called king of peace and of righteousness? Peace is preached to men, and so is righteousness; but he is called king of peace and righteousness precisely so that righteousness and peace may be known to have their origin in him. What is ruled by him cannot be said to be above him. Men are trained by righteousness, their teacher, and by peace to win God's favour. This teacher of men, then, has Melchizedek as its king. How much better than man Melchizedek is, when the governess of men is under him! This is to be king of kings.

So when he is called king of righteousness and peace, it means that he is their author. Just as the Lord Jesus is the author of life, so Melchizedek is the author of righteousness and peace, because those who live through Christ are governed under the direction of righteousness and peace. He pours righteousness and peace into the hearts of God's servants to adorn the Lord's discipline. We read written in the eighty-fourth psalm that "righteousness and peace have embraced each other, and truth has sprung up from the earth"; and to show which righteousness he meant, it says that "righteousness has looked down from heaven." Scripture is pointing here to the time of the Saviour, when God's righteousness was given to the world through Christ in the knowledge of the mystery of the one God, which he had promised beforehand (for it is right that the creature should know the truth of its creator). This righteousness, made manifest on earth, removed the discord that had arisen from the unrighteousness of not knowing God. It made peaceable those who had been at variance, by establishing in one faith those who had long been divided. Thus "righteousness and peace embraced each other, and the truth of the one God sprang up from the earth," with righteousness as teacher. Christ's incarnation showed what truth was to be known about God himself. This, then, is certainly the righteousness of God. The same holds for peace, as the apostle says: "The God of peace himself will crush Satan."

I do not see how a distinction can be drawn here. The God of peace is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so is Christ himself, for he says, "My peace I give to you." Yet it is said of Melchizedek that he is king of righteousness and peace, and I do not understand on what principle he is set apart. I think that, as far as the reality goes, the king of peace differs in nothing from the God of peace. No one in the world ought to be called God, so that this name might be reserved for the one alone from whom all things come. God nevertheless appointed a king to bear his image, who would have all his power except the name of God. But because this king is earthly, he is king of men, not of peace and righteousness, since he too has righteousness as his guide, and he is not permitted to despise it. For him righteousness is God. Righteousness belongs to God, and whoever transgresses it becomes liable to God's judgement. Melchizedek, however, as we are given to understand, is not called king in the way men are, for he has under him righteousness, which rules over kings. No one can have righteousness under him unless he is of such a nature that he cannot sin. It is said to be under him because he devised it in the form of a law, by which those who can sin are to be governed. The king of righteousness, then, is the governor of the words he himself devised, words by which one may live and believe well and blessedly.

We labour long and hard and still say too little about Melchizedek, unless we return to scripture. Scripture itself has long been knocking and crying out to rouse those weighed down by heavy sleep to an understanding not of night but of day. It says, then, that Melchizedek is "without father, without mother, without genealogy," and so that he would not be understood otherwise than is fitting, it added: "having neither beginning of days nor end of life." By this it shows that Melchizedek was neither born nor died. What can human subtlety argue against things so plain? What crafty cleverness dares to resist what is manifest, and instead of drawing meaning from the reading, imposes a meaning on it? Violence is done to the Lord's scriptures, so that they find enemies even in those who appear to bow to their authority. Some say that we ought not to believe about Melchizedek what scripture relates, and so they bend the scriptures to their own meaning. It would be better for them to reject the scriptures openly than to work against them deceitfully, so that war is prepared in the name of peace and an enemy lurks under the cover of friendship.

They say, then, that his being described as without father and mother is a mark not of Melchizedek's noble birth but of his humble lineage. They claim that it was written this way to show that he was of foreign stock, not from the tribe from which Abraham sprang, because his lineage is not found in the law. "That is why," they say, "it also added 'and without genealogy': so that it would be understood that his origin is not recorded in the law at all, and so that he would be believed to have become a good man by his own effort, whatever kind of parents he had." How careless scripture must be, then, when it sets down in due order everything the case requires! First it says: "without father, without mother." Let us see whether the mothers of others are named in the law. We do not read who the wife of Nahor was, Abraham's grandmother and the mother of Terah, nor who Abraham's mother was, to say nothing of the rest. Are these to be said to have been without mothers? If it had said only "without father," would there not have been [?] some colour to their argument? Because the fathers of everyone who lived are given in the law, it adds: "and without genealogy." If it said these things to show that his lineage is not in the law, it would have been enough to say "without father," since if no one knows a man's father, much less does anyone know his grandfather.

To make it plain, it says: "having neither beginning of days nor end of life." Tell me, whoever you are who do violence to the text, how do you interpret this? What does it mean to have neither beginning of days nor end of life? Surely it would have been enough to say that his lineage was not written in the law, and so his origin would be believed to be among foreigners. It can be said that he was "translated" like Enoch and therefore did not die. Very well. But what does it mean to have no beginning of the days of life? Perhaps you will say that his birthday is not recorded. Whose birthday is recorded in the law? Is it reasonable that one whose birthday is not recorded should be said to have no beginning of the days of life? Then the same could have been said of all the others. And even if he had been translated as a man, he would still not have been without end of life, since whatever lives in expectation of death has an end.

Stop, whoever you are who are bent on contention. It is better to be conquered by the truth than to conquer the truth with falsehood. That is losing, not winning. Even if the truth seemed to lose in a man, it still wins before God, because its reasoning is invincible. So the mind must be conquered by the law and think what the law signifies. It must not give the law a meaning of its own choosing and so set itself up by force as law over the law. Hear Zerubbabel, who says: "Truth conquers above all things."

Melchizedek already shows the coming mystery of the Lord's incarnation and passion when he first hands to Abraham, as father of the faithful, the eucharist of the Lord's body and blood. In this way the truth that was to come in the sons was prefigured in the father. If he is thought to have been a man and a priest in the way Aaron was, or as priests are now, then let the place where he lived be shown or read. Let it be shown whether there was some temple or synagogue in which he gathered the people and offered their sacrifices, or what people assembled before him. If he was a priest on earth, he undoubtedly had a people. In that case there was a people serving God before Abraham, or at least in his time. How, then, was Abraham made the head, as it were, of faith, so that the people might have knowledge of God through him? Likewise, if Melchizedek existed to teach the fear of the one God on earth, Abraham was chosen in vain so that the people of God might be named after him. He could simply have been one of those who assembled before Melchizedek.

And what of the passage we read in the song of Deuteronomy: "When the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and his people Jacob became the Lord's portion"? If there was no people of God in the world apart from the sons of Abraham, on what ground is another people thought to have existed, descended from Melchizedek's teaching, when the prophet denies it? When he names all the nations in the world and says that no people is God's except the sons of Abraham, what follows except that, apart from these, the rest had no knowledge of God, since "God is known in Judah"? Melchizedek, "priest of God Most High," appeared to bless Abraham as a foreshadowing of the saints to come, because in the future the blessing was to be given to God's people through what is in effect God's prelate, whom we call a priest. This Melchizedek, then, appeared as forerunner of the sacrament of the Son of God who was to come, because the one who follows in rank goes ahead to serve. So the things we have said about Melchizedek should cause no astonishment, since scripture adds and says still more to confound those who clamour against them. After everything worthy of praise, it says, to confound the malicious: "but, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever."

Now see who it is you are so set on thinking ill of. If you do not revere him, at least fear Christ, whom scripture on its authority says he resembles. Step by step, in due order, scripture arrives at his natural dignity. Some may have been troubled by the earlier statements, which describe him as king of righteousness and peace and say that, though seen in the flesh, he had neither father nor mother, that is, he appeared unbegotten, having neither rising nor setting. By what it added last, scripture showed those earlier statements to be credible. Who but a madman would dare to say that all these lofty things are unsuited to one who is described as like the Son of God, remaining a priest for ever? He cannot be like the Son of God unless he is of the same nature. And what seems incredible in Melchizedek's appearing as a man, when he is understood to be the third person? Christ, the second person, was often seen in human form; why then doubt what has been said? We read in the psalm: "You are," it says, "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." None of us doubts that this refers to the person of Christ, because Christ is a priest for ever of the same kind as Melchizedek. Christ, however, is the high priest, and Melchizedek is second. If Melchizedek is a man, how could it be fitting for Christ to be a priest for ever after his order? Both are described as alike and as belonging to one dispensation precisely because they are also of one nature.

Since the authority of the one God must be preserved in every way, the second and third persons are placed under the Father's name. Christ is the Father's vicar and prelate, and for this reason he is also called priest. Likewise the Holy Spirit, being sent as a prelate, is called priest of God Most High, but not high priest, as our people presume to call him in the offering. For although Christ and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, the rank of each must be preserved. Priests or envoys are so called because they display in themselves the one whose envoys they are, since they are his image. Therefore Christ and the Holy Spirit, who bear God's image by nature, are called his priests. God is seen in them, as the Lord says: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also." If God was seen in the Lord's deeds, and the works are deeds of the Holy Spirit, as the Lord indicates when he says, "I cast out demons by the Spirit of God," then God was seen in the Holy Spirit as well.
110. On the First Psalm.

The prophet David signified spiritual meaning through the figure of carnal things. With an eager mind he uttered psalms of different kinds and merits for the praise of God and for his mystery. The first psalm he covered with no veil and assigned to no one in particular, but made it general, so that it belongs to those who have separated themselves from the wicked and fortified themselves with the company of the good. For the beginning, especially of this grace, ought not to be sung in obscurity — light comes before darkness, and the head of each thing is in plain view. So the question does not arise from the beginning but from what follows. He therefore began thus: “Blessed is the man who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly.” The counsel of the ungodly is the conspiracy of the wicked, which is to be understood in many ways. The ungodly differ from sinners — for ungodliness is the gravest sin — because every ungodliness is sin, but not every sin is ungodliness. How then does someone go into the counsel of the ungodly? Surely when he is called by it. In saying this he shows that as long as someone does not depart from his nature, he does not incur sin. That is why he says, “Blessed is the man who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly.” For ungodliness, which began with the devil, entices people through his consenting followers, so as to make them sharers in his ungodliness. He was the first to sin against God, when he wished to usurp sovereignty for himself by tyranny; and, cast down from the holy seats, he thought it a consolation if he could win many companions for his own ruin. And so he says, “Blessed is the man who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly.” For those who act under this prince and are our enemies are always enticing people, as the apostle says: “For your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers”; and in another epistle he says of their tyrant, among other things: “so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God.” Sinning seems sweet, and the evil is not felt until loss has come; and so deceivers do not show themselves for what they are while they are ensnaring, but are recognized only once they have deceived. For this reason he calls blessed the one who has not been lured into the counsel of the ungodly, so as to enter into the fellowship of their ungodliness.

This, then, is the first cause of ungodliness: by it they began to be rebels against God in a malicious conspiracy, and in imitation of it idolatry began. For the transgression that began on high came down to earth. Since people were not content to be subject to the one God and Creator, they became ungodly by sharing out his majesty among others, so that, despising him, they chose others for themselves to worship. This is the first cause of the offense of the human race, because of which, neglected by God, they are handed over to be mocked by various enticements and passions, as the apostle Paul teaches. For what work remains unharmed that has not acknowledged its maker? From there the evil, once sown, spurned all custom and spread in many directions like a vine stretching out its shoots, so that those who had not spared God rushed all the more readily into insulting and killing their parents. To say nothing of the rest — as the apostle says, “What have I to do with judging those outside?” — Reuben, to his father’s dishonor, committed adultery with his father’s concubine, and Absalom, against all right, presumed to seize the kingdom so as to deprive his father of his rule and his life.

Ungodliness has still other forms as well. To despise someone who pleads with you in danger when you could help him is ungodliness; and in a cruel and malicious affair, to give advice so that it can be carried out [?] … and other such things as could be found along these lines. Not without reason, then, is the man blessed who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly. For it is great ruin and an incurable wound for a person to join himself to these errors after coming to know God. Whoever turns from the truth to falsehood must necessarily be dealt with more severely; and blessed is the man who, having grasped the knowledge of the truth, flees the counsels of the ungodly, because ungodliness is the head of error.

And there follows: “and has not stood in the way of sinners.” For it is impossible not to sin, just as it is possible not to be ungodly: the gravest sin can be avoided, but there is no way [?] to keep the other sins from creeping in. For human life itself frequently [?] … While someone is not thinking of sinning, he falls into sin unexpectedly. And so blessed is he who does not go into the counsel of the ungodly, that is, who does not even begin evil. But since sin cannot help being begun, as I have said, he called blessed the one who does not remain in it; that is what it means not to stand in the way of sinners. For the way of sinners is a life spent in sins. Someone is said to walk badly who goes forward with the aim of seeking to sin. While his mind does not stand firm in God’s law but wanders, he is said to walk in the way of sinners, because this wandering seeks to sin. And so “blessed is he who does not stand in the way of sinners,” that is, who, with repentance following, grieves that he has been deceived and withdraws from the conspiracy of sinful people. Therefore, just as the man who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly is blessed, so if he has gone, he will be beyond amendment, as Solomon says: “The foot of the ungodly will perish”; and: “Blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners.” But if he has stood there, he is no longer blessed but guilty and deserving of blows. Yet he seems to have some hope of amendment, because he is not ungodly but a sinner. If, however, there is someone who has not gone into the counsel of the ungodly and does not stand in the way of sinners, he is blessed in a twofold way. For a person cannot be blessed if he does not go into the counsel of the ungodly yet stands in the way of sinners, because, even if he is not liable to perdition, he is still liable to punishment.

Then he added: “and has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” He says that this is blessedness: it consists of these three steps and is guarded by a threefold rule, namely, not to go into the counsel of the ungodly, not to stand in the way of sinners, and not to sit in the seat of pestilence. But since only two kinds, the ungodly and sinners, are named for reproach in what was said above, to whom did he mean to assign this third thing that he added, saying, “and has not sat in the seat of pestilence”? To the ungodly or to sinners? Let us see what it means to sit in the seat of pestilence, and then we will understand to which kind he assigns it. We call that the seat of pestilence which is outside God’s ordinance, which was devised precisely so that unjust judgments might come forth from it. That is why it is called the seat of pestilence: pestilence is a corruption that brings forth death, just as iniquity brings forth condemnation. The seat of death, then, is not from God; for Moses received a seat of life. It was given so that in it there might be the authority of the just Judge, that is, of God the Creator. Hence the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat”; and the apostle says: “There is no authority except from God; those that exist have been ordained by God.”

Hence he says to the leader of the people: “Do you sit judging according to the law, and against the law order me to be struck?” By saying “according to the law” he indicated the just and salutary authority of the seat. But by saying “against the law you order me to be struck,” he showed that the man himself was an unjust judge, since he sat in God’s seat and judged unjustly. This is why Daniel too says: “The kingdom is God’s, and he will give it to whom he wills.” Just as the authority of an earthly emperor runs through all, so that he is revered in all, so God has arranged that God’s authority should begin from the king himself and run through everyone. Although the world often does not understand this, and the one placed in power subjects himself to someone other than he ought, yet the order is that there should be One who is feared. Where this order does not exist, there the seat of pestilence is found. Nowhere is the authority of the one God rejected except among those who preach fear and reverence for many gods. These are the ones who sit in the seat of pestilence, because what their priests preach is death. For they teach that worshipers of the one God, as fools and enemies, should either be held in disgrace or be removed from this life. This is the very substance of ungodliness, and it extends into other areas as well, through which it displays the laws of its ungodliness. For at Jezebel’s command the officials of iniquity sat in the seat of pestilence: though they were not judges, they plotted evil against the innocent Naboth, suborned false witnesses, and passed sentence of death. Hence he says in another psalm: “And I will not sit with the ungodly.” For this is the judgment of the one whose seat is also the seat of pestilence. So if those who sit in God’s seat oppress the innocent, it is the judgment that will be unjust, not the seat. But where the seat of pestilence is, the judgment cannot help being unjust, even though they put certain veils over themselves to cover their ungodliness, so that onlookers are deceived. For ungodliness cannot be offered on its own, because it finds no buyer; and where the law of the devil holds, if he himself were named, people would shudder.

Just as something is mixed into poison so that it may lie hidden, so too they mix certain just things into the devil’s law and attach to it the name of truth. But the meaning of each thing must be judged, because he sometimes displays something true precisely in order to deceive, so that when he preaches malicious things they may be thought good. Since we have affirmed that the seat of pestilence is not of God’s ordaining, we say that the seats of those who have set up seats for themselves outside the Church or against the Church are also a seat of pestilence. For whoever presumes to take what has not been granted is guilty — how much more if he also corrupts the tradition of the one whose seat he usurps! For they disturb the order begun by the apostle Peter and preserved up to this time through the line of succeeding bishops, claiming for themselves an order without origin, that is, professing a body without a head. Hence it is fitting to call their seat too a seat of pestilence. Nor will they go unpunished because they do these things under the name of God. For it is clear that they pursue their own causes under the name of God. They do not do these things out of zeal for God, but from a wish to defend their own position, though we know that Korah and the two hundred and fifty men who presumed to make offerings to God were swallowed up when the earth opened, and that King Uzziah, when he had made an unlawful offering to God, was struck with leprosy on his forehead.

Since it has become clear that the seat of pestilence belongs to the ungodliness described above, let us go on to the rest. For he added: “but his will is in the law of the Lord.” He says that the will of that man is in the law of the Lord who has spurned the ungodly, abandoned sinners, refused the seat of pestilence, and set his will on God’s law. That is why he called him “blessed.”

And there follows: “and on his law he will meditate day and night.” It is plain that one who is free from all enticements and untouched by whatever is opposed to God’s law exercises himself in nothing else but God’s law. Strengthened by the sacraments of the Son of God, he applies himself to good works by day and to prayer by night. For this is the one of whom it is said in the Song of Songs that he sleeps and his heart keeps watch.

Hence he says: “And he will be like a tree planted beside the streams of water.” Who doubts that someone who meditates on God’s law has hope of receiving a reward? For just as a tree planted beside water cannot be barren, so too one who devotes himself constantly to God’s law cannot fail to have the fruit of his work.

And he added: “which will give its fruit in its season.” Every well-tended planting gives fruit at the proper time; so too this man, who obeys God’s law, will have fruit at the appointed time. For he will receive the reward of this devotion when the Lord Jesus Christ takes his seat to judge the living and the dead.

Then he added: “and its leaf will not fall.” It is plain that by a tree whose leaves do not fall he signified life. For a tree refreshed by the moisture of flowing water keeps its leaves. Indeed, the Lord Jesus says: “If they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” By the green wood he signified life and fruit. So just as a tree, helped by flowing water, does not suffer drought, so too this man, who devotes himself to God’s law, when temptation comes, is kept safe by God’s protection and does not lose salvation but gains it, as the apostle says: “For through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

And there follows: “and all that he has done will prosper.” What he says is clear: one who keeps faith with God’s law, eager for his commandments, becomes fortunate in all his actions; just as with Joseph, because he put the fear of God before this present life, God made everything he did prosper in his hands.

And he added: “Not so the ungodly, not so.” The repetition signifies that the future will be wholly otherwise than what is promised, because for the ungodly nothing will prosper in the future, but everything will go against them until their destruction.

Hence he says: “but like the dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth.” He says that the ungodly perish in the same way as dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth so that it perishes. For, lifted from its own substance and scattered through the air, it gradually wastes away. So too the ungodly, driven by the ministering angels from the face of God their maker, without whom there can be no life, will perish.

And there follows: “Therefore the ungodly do not rise again in the judgment.” What he says is fitting. For why should they rise in the judgment, when they preferred that no business of God be entrusted to them for which they would have to give an account? Since they spurned and denied God’s law, they have nothing on which to give an account, so that, when questioned in the judgment, they might answer according to the law entrusted to them. Found arrogant and rebellious against God, then, they will rise only to see that what they refused to believe is true, and to perish, because they judged God a liar.

And he added: “nor sinners in the counsel of the just.” In this psalm he indicates three kinds of people — the ungodly, sinners and the just — in the order in which error began. But the ungodly are strangers to these, because, as I said, they refused to live under God’s decree. Sinners, however, who live under God’s law, are to be set before the judgment seat of Christ, separated from the just, so that they may give an account of the law they received and be corrected in those matters where they did not take pains to earn more praise than blame. But the just, who have been found most zealous in the practice of fulfilling the law, are to be rewarded.

And he added: “For the Lord knows the way of the just.” God is said to know those who, mindful of his commandments, apply themselves to good works, so that, counted as just, they may be crowned. But to those who, forgetful of him, are careless about the care of their souls, he says this: “Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity.”

And there follows: “and the path of the ungodly will perish.” The psalm ends where it began, so that, once the case of the ungodly has been treated, they might be shown to be liable to nothing but perdition. For, as I said, God is said to know the way of the just because they walk in his law; but the path of the ungodly, because it lies outside God’s law, will perish, for “all the ways of the ungodly are dark,” says Solomon, but those of the godly are most bright, with Christ our Lord as their guide.
111. ON PSALM 23.

The psalm's title hints at its meaning. Since the prophet is about to speak of the mystery of Christ our Lord, he pointed to the Lord's day when he said: "To this David, on the first of the sabbath." When it says "to this David," it refers to the one whose image this David bears, the one of whom the prophet says: "And my servant David shall feed them." "The first of the sabbath" means the first day of the week, for the first day after the sabbath is the Lord's day. The gospel confirms this when it says: "On the first of the sabbath Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the tomb," and so on. So by the Lord's day he pointed to the mystery of the Saviour. But so that the psalm might be set out in proper order, he began with the person of God the Father, so that the mystery of the truth would be revealed to people in its right order. Anyone who wants to explain a matter cannot show its true nature or teach what its truth is unless he grasps its head and origin.

So the prophet began this way and said: "The earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it." In saying "The earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it," he held to the true faith about the world. He followed the authority of the holy men of old, who said that the earth and everything in it belong to the dominion of the Lord God.

And he added: "The whole world, and all who dwell in it." He had said that the earth and all that fills it are the Lord's, and so that no one would think he meant something less than everything, he made his meaning plain by saying: "The whole world, and all who dwell in it." He wanted to teach that absolutely all the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, so that nothing is excepted as not his. Some heretics think otherwise. As the apostle Peter said, they deny God his lordship, and the prophetic oracles condemn them by teaching that all things are God's.

And it continues: "He himself founded it upon the seas." This is what he indicated in another psalm when he said: "You established the earth upon the waters." So that evidence would follow the statement of faith, he shows how God did it. While everything was in confusion and neither earth nor water had its own form, at God's command the earth was gathered together and made firm upon the waters, so that earth and water would each have the distinct nature of its origin. That is why in Kings God's voice says: "Did I not make the waters?"

And he went on: "And upon the rivers he prepared it." It was prepared upon the rivers in this sense: it holds waters stored within it, which flow as if through pipes of veins and give it density, so that it would not be entirely dry, crumbling and useless for farming. These waters give life to the roots of growing things, and at the same time they relieve thirst in dry places.

And to show that profession of faith does not get far without a good life, he says: "Who shall go up the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?" He sets out what kind of person someone who professes God as Creator ought to be. He had shown that those who, as I said, deny God his lordship are to be punished, and he did not want those who confess him to think that they would escape punishment if they did not live rightly. By the mountain of the Lord he meant heaven. That is why he says in another psalm: "I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come." The Lord's place is where he appears. When the Lord appeared to Joshua son of Nun, Joshua was told: "The place where you stand is holy ground." And Jacob, where he saw the Lord, said: "This is the house of God."

And it continues: "The one innocent in hands and pure in heart." He says that a person is worthy to go up the mountain of the Lord, that is, into heaven, or to stand in his holy place, if he is innocent in his deeds and has a pure heart in the things of God, that is, in faith. Such a person can go up into heaven and stand in his holy place. When this life is over, he goes up to heaven. Then, at the Lord's coming, he will come down from heaven with the city of Jerusalem, worthy as an innocent man to stand where the Lord will judge the living and the dead. But the ungodly and sinners will be unworthy to stand in the holy place of God's judgment. They will rise again, the ungodly to destruction and sinners to punishment. For if the children of Israel could not look at the glorified face of Moses as he came down from the mountain because of their sin, how much more will a conscience burdened with offences dread to look upon the Lord of glory himself, seated on the throne of majesty! For they will hear: "I do not know you, you workers of iniquity."

And he added: "Who has not received his soul in vain." Now he touches on the kinds of sin themselves. In the first place, the one who is innocent and has a pure heart is the one who is free from the fornication of idolatry. For idolatry is that vanity, and whoever bows to it subjects his soul to corruption.

And it continues: "Nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbour." He has mentioned the two chief matters, God and neighbour, because whoever proves sound in these will no doubt be found approved in the rest as well. As the Lord says: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." Who, then, that loves the Lord with all his heart would fail to keep his law? Or who that has love for his neighbour would be eager to sin, since he loves his neighbour out of the fear of God?

And he went on: "He shall receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour." Now he shows the reward of one who has had faith and love in the matters of God and man, of the Creator and the neighbour. He will be blessed by the Lord, so that he may be seen to be approved, and he will obtain mercy in the things he could not fulfil. For no one can be so careful as never to go wrong. But because he was found diligent and faithful in great matters, in the smallest ones he will receive mercy from his God. God is called Saviour because he does not desire the death of one who is dying, but that he should turn back and live.

And it continues: "This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob." He said that there is one generation of those who seek God and who seek the face of the God of Jacob, and this is not said idly. Though both are good, these words point to two levels. It is good to seek God, but it is the fullness of good to seek the face of the God of Jacob, for those who stand before the judge's face are the worthier. This, then, is the generation of those with such merits. To arrive at this, innocence and purity of heart are what bring it about, just as, conversely, injustice and iniquity go before so that one may come to evil. For there are two generations: one on the side of iniquity, which is the mother of Cain, and the other on the side of justice, which is the mother of Abel. The one consists in faith and good conduct, the other in faithlessness and crooked deeds. These are the two laws, of good and of evil, of God and of the devil, and whichever a person has followed, he will be called its son. And so this is the generation of those who seek God: faith in God and love toward one's neighbour, as we said above. For whoever has faith in God will always seek his help, and whoever wants to have God gracious to him should not show himself unjust to people. The sign of this is when it says "the God of Jacob," because "God is known in Judah." But why are they said to seek the face of God, when Moses heard: "My face shall not be seen by you"? If Moses sought the face of God and could not see it, then these people are said to seek it in vain, since they are no better than Moses. Yet no one should be said to seek the face of God in vain. They are said to seek the face of God so that it may be known whom they are seeking, since they are also worthy to see. For anyone who is sought is recognized when his face is seen. But since the face of God cannot be seen by mortals, the phrase "the God of Jacob" stands as the sign in place of the face.

DIAPSALMA. Here the diapsalma marks a change of person. After what concerns the person of God the Father, he adds what concerns the mystery of the Son of God, so that the order of Father and Son is kept intact. For the law was given through Moses to be a kind of tutor to people. It instructed them and prepared them, with justice as their teacher, so that they might become worthy to receive the year of the Lord and the day of recompense. Then those who had been faithful in the hope of the Christ to come would receive him and could escape the sin of Adam, secure about their own sins, because the coming of the one they had hoped for would give them mercy for the things in which they had been led unawares into wrongdoing. This is what he mentioned above when he said: "He shall receive mercy from God his Saviour."

So he says: "Take away the gates of your prince." This is the voice of the holy angels, of whom it says in the gospel: "Angels came and ministered to him." They speak to the principalities and powers, against whom, the apostle says, we have our struggle, telling them to take away the gates of their prince, that is, the devil, who is the prince of the princes established in error. Through these gates one goes into Gehenna. These gates are faithlessness and the deceit of idolatry.

And it continues: "And be lifted up, you everlasting gates." Faith and hope, together with love, are the everlasting gates, because what is preached through the truth cannot be abolished. But those gates which I said are faithlessness and the deceit of idols are temporary, for no lie endures [?]: once the truth is revealed, it will perish. So they are taught to take away the gates of their prince, that is, to remove the error of many gods so that faith in the one God may be brought in through Christ. This is what the apostle testifies he was sent to teach: to show not only to people, but also to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, the mystery of the one God in Christ.

And he went on: "And the King of glory shall come in." He says that the deceitful gates built by the devil's cunning must be taken away. These are the presumption by which the devil thought himself God. They must be removed so that the King of glory may come in, who is Christ Jesus our Lord. Faith in God enters no one's mind unless he has removed from himself the error devised by the devil's transgression. And the princes mentioned above cannot receive Christ the King into faith in the one God unless they cast away from themselves the tradition by which slander is brought against the one God. This means not only the earthly tradition, but also the one usurped in the heavenly places by Satan, the prince of princes. For the error they plotted among themselves there, calling themselves gods at the devil's instigation, they also set up here on earth, so that the error here is an image of that one.

And it continues: "Who is this King of glory?" So that no one would think it idle to call Christ the King of glory, he introduces someone who asks: "Who is this King of glory?" This person speaks as if he were amazed, or wanted to be taught whether it is true and fitting to call Christ the King of glory.

So the answer comes to him: "The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle." With this added, he would learn that Christ is the King of glory not from bare words but with evidence. The strength and might by which he subdued and crushed the devil with his henchmen show that he is the King of glory.

And he added: "Take away the gates of your prince, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates." That is: since you have learned from the evidence of his power, which it is wicked to contradict, that Christ deserves to be called the King of glory, remove the error from your minds.

And he says: "And the King of glory shall come in." This shows that they cannot share in faith in Christ unless they have cleansed their hearts of all the filth of idolatry. For unless a person has been renewed, the Holy Spirit will not enter him.

And it continues: "Who is this King of glory?" This repetition gives confirmation. For anything heard as new is not taken into the heart unless it is repeated. Amazement causes astonishment when something is said that has never been heard.

And he added: "The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory." By repeating the same thing, he teaches that this one is rightly called the King of glory, since he is the Lord of hosts. It is not without reason that he who rules over the hosts is called the King of glory. That is why the apostle says: "For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty."
112. ON PSALM 50

This psalm has been placed fiftieth not because of the order of time but for a reason. Its title is governed not by its number but by that reason. As far as the history goes, it is earlier than the third psalm, since David was rebuked by the prophet Nathan for his offense before his son Absalom rose up against him, wanting to rob him of both life and kingdom. The reason it was placed fiftieth, then, plainly comes from the law, where it is laid down that the number fifty carries remission. After seven weeks it is the first day and is a type of the Lord's day. After seven days the first day is that very day which was made at the beginning, and which is always first when the week is over. In the same way, after seven weeks the fiftieth, counted in a mystery, is the first. It is called the Lord's day in two ways. First, it was made by the Lord in the beginning, and as it always comes round again through the cycles, it is first when the week is completed. Second, he rose again on it after triumphing over death, and so it is named the Lord's day. It is not without reason, then, that remission is contained in the number fifty, which we observe signifies the first in a mystery. Indeed, the law was given on the fiftieth day. On the forty-eighth day after the children of Israel set out from Egypt they are ordered to wash, so that after being purified for two days they would be ready on the third day to receive the law. What else does this washing indicate but a remission granted on the fiftieth day? Once purified, they would receive the law, and from then on, with the past wiped out, they would give an account of their actions according to the law entrusted to them. For the same reason the law commanded that a purchased possession must be released in the fiftieth year. This, then, is why this psalm too is entitled the fiftieth.

In this psalm King David asks for remission in the sense described above. So he says: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." Knowing that he had sinned gravely, King David makes his request in these words: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." For mercy is great when it pardons great sins.

And he added: "And according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity." To show that he had offended bitterly, he calls his sin iniquity, for iniquity is no light sin. Whoever blots out iniquity, that is, does not count it against a person, abounds in compassion. So he makes no attempt to excuse anything in his case. In this way he not only softens the judge's mind toward himself but even makes him share his grief. For the mind is moved to mercy when it sees a guilty man confess his sins in such a way as to show that he grieves for having sinned. A man who does not grieve seems to be mocking the judge, since he prays only so that he may escape for the time being, intending to do the same things afterward.

And there follows: "Wash me thoroughly from my injustice, and cleanse me from my offense." Since he proclaims God's great compassion, he prays to be cleansed completely, so that nothing of offense or injustice may remain in him to bring him under suspicion.

And so that he may obtain or win this very thing, he added: "For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is always before me." Because he knows that he has sinned gravely, he is anxious that it may not all be forgiven him. Considering the greatness of his sins, he is afraid, knowing that grave sins are not easily pardoned. And so with tears he confesses his sin, keeping it before his eyes, so that he may make the judge favorable to him from every side. For he knows that it is written: "Tell your iniquities first, so that you may be justified."

And there follows: "Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight." Now he looks for a remedy for his case from another side, so as to bring his petition to success. By this line of argument he declares himself innocent in the chief matter. Whoever sins toward another god is an enemy of God the Creator, for he chooses another in God's place and ascribes God's authority to him. So here, showing that he is free of this iniquity, he says: "Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight." That is: "Because I have sinned toward you and toward no other whom I might have called god through error, my case is lighter than that of the others who are liable to perdition. I am not impious but a sinner, because I sinned not against you but against your law. I did not deny you, but while confessing you as God and Lord I sinned against a man. So, since I am not guilty in the matter that is properly yours, forgive me for sinning against a fellow servant. For I sinned in such a way that I neither denied the honor of your name nor gave it to another." There was, then, something to move the judge to mercy. Many sin against him, and he even urges them to turn to him. So when those who do not sin against him nevertheless ask pardon for other causes, he gladly receives them. For the Lord always wants his servants to take refuge in his help.

So he added: "That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged." In asking for mercy he prays that God will not change his justice. Justice is normally impartial, the same toward those who sin and those who do not, rendering to each according to his works. But a man innocent in the mystery of God knows what he is asking for. He knows that the Lord often said in the law, "I the Lord your God am merciful." So he asks that this pledge may stand and that God may be justified in his words by holding to what he has said, and not be overcome by men's sins so as to withhold mercy. Those who sin know what God has promised to those who live well, yet because they persist in sin, they judge him a liar. Living wickedly, they do not believe that what he promised is true. Therefore King David asks that God may prevail over what men suppose, and give what he promised, so that those who do not keep his commandments, and so judge that he will not give it, may be put to shame.

And there follows: "For behold, I was conceived in iniquities." By adding this he now recalls the condition and weakness of the human race, since it is easy for a man to sin, so that he may soften the judge's scrutiny of him. He mentions the first cause, through which Adam by his transgression made the human race liable to sin. Persuaded and deceived by the enemy, Adam conceived iniquity and subjected all his seed to it, so that all born from him by descent would be liable to sin.

Therefore he added: "And in offenses my mother conceived me." Sin was passed down from Adam and hinders those conceived and born from leading a good life. For that reason mercy should not be denied to a suppliant, since he has an enemy planted within him who urges him to sin. For sin, which is the devil, once the first man had been made subject to him, received power to plant himself in his flesh and with a kind of subtlety to suggest the delights of offenses, by which he captures a man and strips him of life. The teacher of the Gentiles mentions this when he says: "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind." David says this so that the judge, seeing it, may stretch out his hand to a man who grieves at having been ensnared.

And there follows: "For behold, you have loved truth." "Since, then, you love truth," he says, "help one who asks, whom you know to be laying bare the true hindrances of his heart. Long ago, moved by mercy, you decreed to help every guilty man, so that heavenly providence might correct the error committed on earth."

For this reason he went on: "The uncertain and hidden things of the heart you have made known to me." By "the uncertain and hidden things of the heart" he means what God provided for the protection of the human race. So too the apostle says: "What eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." Who are those who love God, if not those who agree with his law by neither hiding nor excusing their sins? So these hidden things of the heart have been made known to those who love God. They grieved at being ensnared by offenses, and when rebuked they did not deny them but laid them to themselves and to their origin, [?] shifting onto God the Creator the sins they committed. Their hearts were enlightened by a spiritual flash, so that they might see God's providence in Christ, who was to come to condemn the sin that had ruled over the human race since Adam's transgression. This, then, is King David's prayer. God had foreseen that the human race would struggle and had decreed help for the future. David asks that God would help him beforehand, since he was caught in the same need in which God had decreed to help everyone. The gift was to be freely given in the future and could not be given before its time, but he asks that it be granted to him in answer to his prayer and tears.

He does not keep silent about how this is to come about, but says: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be clean." He rightly asks to be cleansed by a sprinkling of hyssop. With it the children of Israel smeared their doorposts with blood so that they would be kept safe from death. So here too he prays to be cleansed from his sins by a sprinkling of hyssop, so that death may not touch him.

And there follows: "You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Clearly what God does differs from what man does. So he says, "I shall be made whiter than snow," because what God has made is far better than what man has made. He asks to be cleansed by a sprinkling of hyssop for this reason: just as the bodily flesh is washed with water, so through what hyssop signifies the stains of souls may be washed away in a spiritual way. The sprinkling of hyssop is a kind of illumination, so that by means of what is visible a person may be cleansed invisibly.

And there follows: "To my hearing you will give joy and gladness." No doubt the voice of one proclaiming remission brings joy to sinners. Who would not rejoice on hearing that pardon is granted? For the one whom God forgives is safe both now and in the future.

Therefore, "the bones that have been humbled will rejoice." The bones were humbled in two ways. He was humbled by sinning, for no one is exalted by sinning, and he was humbled afterward when he begged for pardon as a suppliant. For he certainly rolled in sackcloth and ashes as he prayed for mercy. Having obtained it, he was lifted up with exultation of mind and refreshment of body.

And he went on: "Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities." He asks for remission in the form that had been appointed for the future through faith in Christ: that the Saviour, who had been specially promised to him, would begin with him to forgive all sins to those who turn to him. When someone's sins are not looked upon and all his iniquities are blotted out, there is nothing by which he can be declared guilty, and the mouths of his enemies are shut. Whoever does not look upon sins does not count them against the sinner. To turn one's face from someone's sins is to refuse to entertain an accusation against him. Why, then, though he was rebuked for two sins, does he add here that he accuses himself of many? And though he had heard from the prophet Nathan that he was forgiven, why does he plead so earnestly, as if he still had to reach pardon? It can only be that he is not pleading his own case alone. Taking his own sin as the occasion, he tells of the miseries of the whole people. For himself he prays for restoration, because a man who is forgiven is not free of shame unless he has been restored to his position, so that the dignity of his position may cover his shame. For the others he pointed to God's gift, which in Christ was to wash away all sins.

And there follows: "Create a clean heart in me, O God, and set a righteous spirit in my inmost parts." This is to plead for mercy with a good mind. He asks not only about the past but is also anxious not to sin in the future. By showing that he hates sinning, he seeks God's help through the spirit of righteousness, which he prays may be set in his inmost parts. That is, he asks that a new spirit be placed in him for this purpose, to guard him from sins, so that he may not be driven to do what he is known not to want. A person can have a clean heart if he does not offend either within or without, that is, neither in deed nor in thought. Since it is almost impossible to keep this in every respect, it must at least be kept in God's cause, which is the chief one: a clean heart must be kept in the mystery of God and of Christ by preserving faith in them unviolated. For in another psalm he says: "Who will boast that he has a clean heart, or that he is free from sins?" In the end King David had a clean heart in God's cause. He never sought help from vanity, that is, idolatry, and he never failed to carry out anything God commanded him.

As for the rest, you may judge. He added: "Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me." This is the sense I mentioned above: secure about pardon, he is anxious about restoration. One who is only pardoned is usually kept away from the face of the lord. Even if he is not punished, his crime has not been wiped out in the mind of the lord or judge. So he prays that his sin may be blotted out completely, and that he may be worthy to come before the face of the Lord and to prophesy again, which indeed happened. This is what he means by saying: "And do not take your Holy Spirit from me." This is the Spirit of the prophets.

And there follows: "Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with your sovereign Spirit." He asks to be given the joy that had been promised in Christ. Washed clean of every stain and restored, he would rejoice in the salvation he sought. He would not be removed but strengthened in his kingdom by the Holy Spirit. He called the Spirit sovereign because he is above all creation, and through him kings reign.

And he added: "I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will be converted to you." He says this so that through him the wicked may learn the kindness of God. God receives and advances sinners who confess to him, and he does not neglect the ungodly who are converted. Rather, he encourages them while he shows mercy to others.

And there follows: "Deliver me from blood, O God, the God of my salvation." By saying this he shows that his sin deserved death, and so he proclaims how great God's mercy is. In this way he also calls on others to take refuge in God's clemency.

So he went on: "My tongue will exult in your justice, O Lord." He says that he rejoices in the Lord's justice because the Lord holds to what he promised when he said: "But my mercy I will not take away from them." Glad and secure on this point, then, King David proclaims the justice of his God.

And there follows: "You will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise." God opens his lips by not allowing him to remain subject to the charge of sin. The mouth of one set free is open, but the sinner's mouth is shut. Gripped by shame and fear, he does not dare to speak. Once acquitted or set free, he dances for joy and proclaims the praise of the judge. So too the apostle, because he was free from all, as he himself testifies, says: "Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians."

And he added: "For if you had wanted sacrifice, I would certainly have given it." He speaks from what he knows. Holy Samuel said to King Saul, when Saul thought his sin could be wiped out not by grief of mind or by pitiful tears but by offering a sacrifice: "God does not want sacrifice so much as that his voice be obeyed." Sacrifices of this kind can cost a man loss, but they cannot appease God. God is appeased when a soul that remembers its sin weeps over what it has done in distress and sorrow of heart.

And there follows: "You will not delight in burnt offerings." God takes no delight in burnt offerings in cases of this kind. The soul itself must make satisfaction for itself and not buy itself off with something outside. Such things can lend help, but just as the soul took delight in sins, so it must be afflicted in penitence. Then it will delight God to blot out its sins.

So he went on: "A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise." He shows what kind of sacrifice God accepts for sins. No one can appease God unless he who rejoiced against his own salvation is afflicted in heart, so that he may be restored to life. Every restless or undisciplined person often ends up injuring the limbs of his body, and these certainly cannot receive the cure of health without pain. In the same way sinners cannot redeem their sins unless the soul that sinned has felt pain. It is just that since it rejoiced against reason, it should suffer sorrow according to reason.

And there follows: "Deal kindly, O Lord, with Sion in your good will." By saying Sion he means the church, so that our assertion may not seem improbable. He urges God to fulfill his promise to the church, knowing that he himself will receive full remission when God has fulfilled in Christ what he decreed. That is, those who hope in the promised salvation are to be freed from every sin, for through Christ they will be freed not only from their own sins but also from Adam's sin, which has passed down to all by descent.

And he added: "And let the walls of Jerusalem be built." Why does he say, "And let the walls of Jerusalem be built"? Had they been destroyed? No, by the walls of Jerusalem he means the church, which was to be built up through the faith that had been ordained in Christ. Its walls are understood to be holy men, as the Apocalypse of John the apostle teaches us, for both the city of Jerusalem and its walls are to be understood as the servants of God. King David knew the promise that was to be fulfilled through Christ for the deliverance of God's servants. So he prays that it may be fulfilled, that is, that the church may be built up through faith, and that those who hope for salvation from this faith may be set free.

And there follows: "Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings." He says this because offerings and burnt offerings would be accepted only when the church had been built. They would not be accepted at random or according to custom, but, he says, "you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness." A sacrifice is righteous when a worthy gift is offered, and nothing is so righteous and worthy as offering ourselves to God. Since God is spirit, spiritual sacrifices must be offered to him, so that a living victim may be offered to the living God. He had said that in the matter of sin God takes no delight in fleshly sacrifices. Now he shows that in the future offerings would be made to God spiritually and that God would accept them, because these are the sacrifices worthy of God. In the past, that is, they were lesser because they were fleshly; now they are greater because they are spiritual.

And he added: "Then they will lay calves upon your altar." If he meant that spiritual sacrifices would take the place of the former sacrifices when these ceased, why would he say, "Then they will lay calves upon your altar"? It can only be that through these bodily things he signifies spiritual ones, since he had said that God does not delight in fleshly sacrifices. So by speaking of calves he meant the new people reborn through faith in Christ, whose devotion is offered every day upon the altar of the Lord. Since he is understood to have spoken of the church, he must also be understood to have meant its spiritual sacrifices.
113. WHY THE SON OF GOD WAS SENT, AND NOT ANOTHER

Everything God does should be believed to have been done reasonably and with foresight. Still, I think it is better if, once we believe, we can also grasp the reason for what was done, so that what is believed is not left unknown. That is why the Lord says: "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." For first a thing must be believed, as the prophet said, and then what is believed must be known. The Holy Spirit helps someone who already believes and is diligent in this matter, so that by coming to know he understands the reason for the faith. Only then does he have the full joy of his belief, if he understands what he believes. This is the strength of faith, this its immovable foundation: to learn the mystery of what one believes. For where there is faith alone, devotion is not so pure, and deception may find a way in.

This is why the chosen vessel labours so that believers may learn the reason for their faith. For once they know how great he is to whom they have entrusted themselves, and what his power is, they will not allow themselves to be drawn away from their hope in him on any terms or for any reason. So we read the words: "Taste and see how sweet the Lord is," so that by deliberate effort they may come to know the savour of his divinity and understand that nothing is wiser than to believe in Christ. For this reason the teacher of the Gentiles himself says, among other things: "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge"; and again: "For I know whom I have believed, and that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him." So the person who understands that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the mystery of Christ's birth, passion and resurrection knows the reason for his faith and has no doubt about his power.

So, with my faith remaining firm, I long turned over in my mind why our Lord came down from the holy and heavenly seats to earth to become incarnate, and not someone else from among those whom the Lord himself calls holy angels. For it seems unfitting for one of his person to have undertaken this work, unless the reason for it is known. In fact this is what troubles many. God the Father in his providence could have carried out this task through another person: to show the truth to people caught in error, and to crush the devil, that presumptuous enemy of salvation, together with his followers, and to defeat and despoil him. For the obstinacy and insolence of those most wicked servants ought to have been checked by ministering servants, so that the Lord of all would not have to undergo something unworthy of him.

For Satan's force and power are not so great that he could not have been overcome by another power of the same rank, since it is clear that with God's help he is defeated even by human beings. And although the comparison is unequal if we take examples from earthly affairs, they will still fit the argument in some measure. When a servant rebelled against King David, Joab, his fellow servant, was sent to pursue and kill him; and the task of opposing Absalom, who had turned wickedly against his father, was entrusted to servants. How much more would the power of a single holy angel out of many have sufficed to overcome the devil's tyranny, since we read that when he fought against the angel Michael he could not hold out, but was thrown down to the earth!

As I often pondered these things, the only thing I knew was that he himself was sent by the Father so that it would not be an affront to him if the work made through him were restored through another. But knowing this was very little; it did not do justice to so great and wonderful a matter unless something more were grasped that would lead to a hidden understanding. So it came about that I perceived that the case itself demanded that the one who came should be the one to come. The matter touched him directly: he was to come to crush the one who had usurped his dignity and rank. For the devil wanted to be called god next after God the Father, and he still strives for this even now, although the title did not belong to him at all but to the Son of God, who is second after the Father, not in nature but in order.

So no one but Christ our Lord was fit to come and carry out this cause, because he came not only to crush the devil but also to reveal himself to all creation. Once the devil's person had been rejected, they would recognize that this was the one whose sovereignty and majesty Satan had presumed to claim. From then on, knowing the truth, they would abandon error and hold it as certain that Christ is the Son of God, who alone is God from God and the head or beginning of all things in heaven and on earth. For by the might and power with which he overcame the tyrant Satan, he was shown to be the one whose dominion the wicked devil, that is Satan, had presumed to seize.

For while he wickedly wants to be called god so that he may rule over the spiritual powers (for which the prophet rebukes him, saying: "For you said in your heart, I will set my dwelling in the clouds and I will be like the Most High"), he has deceived many, and by their conspiring together he has become the prince of error. In the psalm they are urged to reject the lie and receive the truth.
