For it is said to them: "Lift up the gates of your prince, and be lifted up, you eternal gates, and the King of glory shall come in." Unless error is removed from the minds of unbelievers, they will not be able to receive faith in the one God in Christ. They are taught this so that, once the gates are removed through which one goes to the second death (and these are the faithlessness begun by the devil), they may receive the sacraments of faith, through which one goes to life. That is what is meant by the eternal gates: the truth of faith is eternity, while faithlessness is temporal, because the lie is the devil's invention. For the devil, having begun his transgression in heaven, sowed it on earth by urging the worship of many gods, among whom he would hold the chief place. He wanted to be the head and beginning of the rest, a position that belonged not to him but to the Saviour. So the Saviour pursues him even to the earth, so that by crushing him he may expose the transgression of his error, once the truth has been revealed in himself. Hence it is said: "Truth has sprung from the earth." For when he was thrown down from heaven, he fled to the earth, so that he might accomplish in the lower regions the godhead he had plotted for in the heights. Hence the apostle says: "so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as if he were God." For he wants to fulfil his desire by any means, even at the cost of being condemned; being full of fury, he thinks it a lesser thing to be condemned than to fail to satisfy his craving for error.
114. AGAINST THE PAGANS.

I do not see how the pagans can make it plausible that they dare to take the field against us, or imagine they can attack our faith, since they have no proofs for their own claims, for what I would call their superstition rather than their religion. They bring forward things they have no warrant for, so that they themselves are the ones who should be regarded as the authors and defenders of novelties. In the first place, they claim to worship gods of whom they give no signs and no testimonies. They call gods those who never dared to give themselves that name, so that men are taken to be the authors of gods, when God ought to be the author of men; and for this reason their claim is empty and vain. For whatever is without God cannot stand firm. Their own books prove that what I say is plain. In them nothing divine is to be read, nothing established at a god's command. Instead they say that individual men, for various reasons, instituted the different sacrifices to the deities, and these were men who seemed to have no merit at all, though the aim was to show that what they had laid down had been laid down fittingly. Since, then, the ones they call gods are nowhere read to have commanded any of this, by what authority do these people act, or think their offerings are accepted, when they cannot prove that any command was given? And even if a command were proved, it ought first to have been examined whether it was right or proper to obey beings who had shown no signs or wonders in their deeds to recommend their divinity.

But when they are driven out of this position, they usually take refuge in the elements, saying that they worship these because human life is steered by their guidance. Of them we ask, as above, whether this was commanded or ordered by God, whom even they themselves confess to be great and supreme, and yet neglect. If it ought to be done, it should have been commanded by him who is called the author of the elements. But if he did not command it, it is presumption, and it will lead to punishment, not reward, because it is an insult to the Creator when the master is despised and the servants are worshipped, when the emperor is spurned and his officers are adored. How will this go unpunished, when we see such a thing punished, and harshly, even in this life?

But perhaps they will say that the command came from the elements themselves. Let them show a precept somewhere; let them read out something those elements once said. If they cannot show it, what punishment do they deserve, who are exposed as the authors of a presumptuous and made-up religion? The elements are free of this impiety. Indeed the very lights of the world will accuse them before God the Judge, for they show themselves in no way the authors of this empty scheme. In the same way those whom they call gods, though it is agreed that they were men, will, when they begin to be tormented for their own sins, plead that they are in no way guilty on this count, and will turn the charge back on those who began to worship them as gods without any command from them.

With what shame, then, do they think our faith should be criticized or laughed at, when they see that our law is supported by the testimony of mighty works, and when they read again the voice of our Lord and God himself, saying: "I am God, and there is no other besides me"? If he had said this in bare words, he should not have been believed, or we would seem like the pagans, who began to worship their gods without seeing any signs of majesty from them, and, what is worse, to worship them shamefully. For things are done there that it is shameful to reveal, and yet they call themselves wise, though they are made fools of by their own law as if by a conjurer.

Our God, on the other hand, commanded that he be worshipped with mighty works as his witness, and, to leave no room for suspicion, he handed down a law that was itself honorable and holy, as befits God. And we, whom the pagans call fools, would not have believed our God unless he had satisfied us with the testimony of mighty works, nor would we have accepted his law if we had not recognized it as pure and fully worthy of what it professes.

This is why nothing among us is done in darkness, nothing in secret. Whatever is known to be honorable has no fear of being made public; but what is shameful and dishonorable cannot be made public, because shame forbids it. That is why the pagans celebrate their mysteries in darkness: in this at least they are wise. They blush to be made fools of openly, and they do not want the shameful things done there in place of law to come to light, lest those who call themselves wise should appear dull to the very people they call fools.

But perhaps we seem fools to them because our law preaches chastity, mercy, and self-restraint. To them these things are foolish, because every good man is bad in the eyes of a bad one, and a wise man seems senseless to a fool. They so detest chastity that they even take delight in catamites, submitting themselves to the guidance of men who, unless they were such, would not themselves be fit [?], if it must be said, for their religion. For this is why they are castrated and change their dress: so that from men they may become, as it were, women, and, contrary to nature, submit to being used as women, and only then be fit and worthy ministers of their superstition. Can a man of this kind be blamed, when the law makes him what he is? He gives up both the conduct and the dress of a man and is changed into a woman precisely so that he may freely be used as a woman.

What sort of mysteries, then, are these supposed to be, in which the dishonored is made more dishonorable and the uncorrupted corrupted, when the true worship of religion is this: to make the shameful honorable and the undisciplined modest? How can their worshippers strive after a good life, when the mysteries of their law cannot be celebrated without catamites? If their law delights in these things, then whoever is not such will be a sinner and a fool. And so they call us fools. Those who practice these shameful things are judged wise by them, while those who avoid and flee them are fools. This indeed seems to have been cunningly and craftily arranged by them. They attach the name of wisdom to their law to cover up what deserves blame in it, since where there is wisdom there is no blame; but they call our law foolish to keep people away from it. But let the names of wisdom and folly be set aside, and let all the ill will that each side's defense produces be removed, and let the two laws contend with each other, so that it may appear where wisdom lies and where folly. Yet when the sign of the cross is present, paganism falls silent; and if that wisdom which they call folly is present, their sacred rites dare not give answers. Their entrails are held back, and they hide away in awe of Christian majesty. It is a great thing that what they call wisdom should fear what they call folly.

Let us now compare the substance of the laws. The pagans profess, even in writing, that they worship gods and goddesses; and what they say is true, for they worship both males and females. Janus and Saturn, Jupiter and Mercury and Apollo and the rest, and likewise Minerva and Isis, and that Frui [?], and Venus, and Flora the harlot, together with the others, are gods and goddesses, as the histories of both the Greeks and the Romans testify. Christians, on the other hand, poor as they are, the people they call fools, worship in mystery one God, from whom are all things, and they venerate nothing that he has created. For they know that he alone is sufficient for them, and more than enough for salvation, and they are not unaware that if they assign his glory and name to others they will offend him, since no emperor allows tribunes and officers to be adored under his name.

Let the laws now be compared, so that it may be seen where wisdom lies: with the one who worships the Creator or the one who worships the creature, the master or the servants? Can it happen that in a household someone other than the one master is called master? Yet the pagans, schooled in the literature of the courts, who think themselves wise, venerate many gods and goddesses in one world created by one God. They have given the stewards and agents of the world the names of lord and god, and so they are exposed as lacking foresight. To assert something that brings about destruction is the mark of a man without foresight, a fool, since God must avenge the wrong done to him on those who have shared out the name and glory of the Lord God among their fellow servants.

Next let the precepts be considered. Our law, the law of those they call fools, directs that bishops and ministers be ordained who are blameless, holy, and beyond reproach. Pagan tradition, on the contrary, holds that it cannot have suitable priests and ministers unless they are transformed from men into women, so that they may freely and publicly be used as women, and, tossing their hair shamelessly about in the water, give out a soft, quavering, and disgraceful voice. If they did this publicly outside their rites, they would be stoned by the whole people. And there is that Dog-head, who goes nodding about everywhere looking for the members of Osiris, the husband of Isis, the adulterer. See with what ministers, and without teachers [?], the pagans claim for themselves the name of wisdom, when this is not only folly but crime! For to love what is obscene and disgraceful is deadly. And what of the fact that they are made fools of in a cave with their eyes blindfolded? Their eyes are covered so that they will not shudder at being shamefully dishonored. Some flap their arms like wings, as birds do, imitating the cry of a raven; others roar like lions; still others, with their hands bound with chicken guts, are thrown over pits full of water, and then someone comes up with a sword and breaks the guts I mentioned, calling himself their liberator.

There are other things more shameful still. See in how many ways those who call themselves wise are shamefully made fools of! But because they undergo these things in darkness, they think they can remain unknown. Yet all these things, devised and arranged in secret by wicked and shameful men, the holy Christian faith has brought out and exposed. For when the faith was preached, those who heard it considered what goodness and holiness was being openly promised, and they came over to the faith, leaving behind those secret, dishonorable, and shameful things and confessing how they had been made fools of through ignorance. In earlier times nearly everyone was caught up in this error, and they thought themselves wise for this very reason: there was no one to rebuke them. For although all went astray under the one deceptive name of idolatry, each nevertheless arranged his worship according to his own character and way of life, so that the one error took on variety from the vileness and the way of life of its authors. Thus the rites they call those of Liber are dishonorable, utterly empty, and full of frenzy; for it is hard for an impure man not to be given to rage. And indeed he is seen painted everywhere with Priapus, with whom he lived shamefully.

Their other rites are of the same sort; but it was by Satan's subtlety and cunning that later generations came to be caught by these inventions. Although these things were not devised without his counsel, he sprinkled each invention with certain illusions by which he might lure people into error. And so it came about that deceit was recommended by being handed down from antiquity, and a shameful invention was excused. For through custom what was shameful ceased to seem shameful. When people are first dishonored, they blush; but afterwards, as custom flatters them, their shame recedes and their countenance changes, especially if a man sees many others like himself. And shamefulness profits most when those who are called noble are seen being dishonored; for dishonored nobility easily finds imitators.

If, then, in former times they thought themselves wise because there was no one whom this foul invention displeased, now that by God's mercy the human race has been enlightened, and it has been made plain that what passed for law was a crime, and that what was thought a wise invention was folly, they ought at least to give up that title, if they wish to remain in a crime that has been exposed, recognizing that the name of wisdom does not belong to them.

But to add to the heap of their own self-condemnation, having been caught in folly, they call those who refute them fools. Yet while they find fault with our faith and its posterity [?], they do not deny that nothing in our precepts can be criticized. Those who attack our faith take up the case not so much against us as against our author. For they declare that we are fools for having put our faith in something foolish, and that he is a liar, a deceiver, and malicious besides, for handing down a faith by which believers would be deceived. Let us therefore first prove that we did not believe foolishly, and then we will plead the case of our author.

When we lived in the error in which the pagans still remain, we were drawn by no signs of mighty works; on bare words we took up the things they call sacred, thinking them useful, not because divinity had recommended them but because old custom had handed them down. In that state, as is well known, we were made fools of by various vanities and recognized no hope of salvation; for what good could something invented by men do? But to come to faith in God and to believe that his Son was made flesh and crucified, we were persuaded not by words but by deeds. For we saw the dead raised, lepers cleansed, sight restored to one born blind, demons cast out, and every kind of illness healed.

Now let it be judged when we were fools: when we believed bare words, or when we believed deeds? Without doubt deeds come before words, since words were invented to signify things. If, then, we gave our faith to a human tradition, commended by no mighty work and invented to delude human minds, how much more should we give it to this faith, which all the signs worked by calling on God attest to be divine and making men divine! Would we not rightly be judged fools if we did not believe mighty works, we who had believed mere talk? Would we not reasonably be branded thoughtless and reckless if we did not follow a hope that called to us, we who had been bound over to despair?

"But," they say in reply, "what you believe is foolish; for it does not stand to reason that God has a Son, or that bodies that have died and decayed are restored to life again." All the philosophers and founders of schools pierced one another with their various disputations, and none went over to another, because each remained in what he had been schooled in. Since words are open to contradiction, no one got the better of another; there was nothing by which anyone could show himself the victor, but wearing one another out with contradictions, none of them persuaded the other.

Hence it came about that the providence of God, whose mind cannot be searched out, joined power to his preaching, so that the truth of the preaching might be proved by the testimony of power, and that those who were ready to contradict words would not dare to contradict when they saw power. For what greater testimony to the truth can there be than the working of power?

But if anyone denies the mighty works by attacking the Scriptures, how can he call our faith foolish when he denies the Scriptures? For where it is written of Christ that he is to be believed the Son of God, in that same place power is found as a witness. And if it seems absurd to anyone reading that Christ the Son of God was crucified, let him read on, and he will find that he rose from the dead; and let him understand that he who was able to rise did not die idly or unwillingly, but that there is a mystery here. Whoever he is, then, either he will keep silent about the cross, because if he calls the cross foolish he cannot call the resurrection foolish, since the resurrection vindicates the cross; or, if he does speak about the cross, he cannot deny that there is providence in it, since he sees it confirmed by the testimony of the resurrection. For either both are accepted or both are rejected, so that one who will not defend should not dare to accuse either.

Why he allowed himself to be crucified by his kinsmen is a mystery to be kept back. But he so commended this death that he testified that he would be glorified through it. For he says: "I have power to lay down my life," and: "I have power to take it up again." So he was not forced to die, who had power both to die and to rise again. Whoever rejects this power cannot say that death was inflicted on him by violence. For if he denies this, he cannot affirm that he died either, because these things are contained in the same place where we read that he was handed over to death. No one condemns the later parts on the basis of the earlier, or the earlier on the basis of the later, because what belongs to one body is not contradictory.

As for the dead rising again, they deceitfully say it is foolish to believe it. Yet they see examples by which it may be judged credible. For all the seeds needed for our use cannot spring up again unless they have decayed. If God ordained these things in the world for the sake of men, why do they think it foolish if he is believed to be going to grant the same to their very bodies, unless because they themselves are fools, who grant God no more than the world can do? Yet a shadow of the mighty works that were done still appears even now. For although this is not the time for working mighty works, since they had to be done at the beginning so that the seed of faith might grow through them, even now demons are terrified when the cross of Christ is named, and if it is done more earnestly they are put to flight; and the gods of the pagans, in dread and fear of the cross once it is named, cannot give oracles.

If the death of Christ is a disgrace, why does it cause terror? A thing that comes from a crime ought not to be feared but despised. Who would fear a man put to death for his own crime? And if he was innocent, he still cannot be feared, only mourned. So unless the demons, or the gods of the pagans, sensed that the cross of Christ was a sacrament, they would not be terrified when it is named; and, to put it more precisely, unless they were guilty, they would not be afraid. For all who are on the devil's side consented to the death of Christ. That is why all the demons, or gods of the nations, are shaken with terror when the cross of Christ is named. For anyone who is guilty of the death of an innocent man is seized by fear in his heart whenever that man's name is mentioned; the memory of his offense makes him see himself as guilty. How much more the demons, or gods of the nations, who are guilty of the slaying of the Lord and Savior of the world!

But the pagans contend that they hold the truth because of antiquity: "what is earlier," they say, "cannot be false," as if antiquity or old custom could prejudge the truth. By this reasoning murderers, the effeminate, adulterers, or other criminals could defend their unlawful acts, because they are ancient and began at the very beginning of the world. Rather, they ought to recognize their error from this very point: what is blameworthy and shameful is shown to have begun badly, while what is honorable and holy is rightly practiced; and what is shameful and blameworthy cannot come before what is holy and blameless.

Finally, it cannot be denied that the tradition of the pagans was invented by man, while it is evident that our law was given by God. For the majesty of God appeared on the mountain to give the law to men, and so that it might be believed, he sent ahead many signs and wonders performed in Egypt, as the books placed by Ptolemy in the library of Alexandria testify to this day. So he chose to give the law in such a way that no one could doubt that it was God who gave it. For the majesty of God was seen by all, openly and plainly, in such brightness and terror that no other god besides him would be believed in, and whatever he commanded would be held worthy of being kept in every respect.

And so that everything may be seen to fit a divine reckoning, let the law that was given be examined, to see whether there is anything unjust in it, anything dishonorable, anything ridiculous. This is how God had to make himself known: not appearing in a corner by trickery, he who cannot be shut in; nor in a cave, where alluring deceit is at work and things are other than they seem; nor handing down for observance things that would be done in darkness because they were dishonorable.

For when the knowledge of the one God had been blotted out in the world through the habit of sinning, because falsehood had drawn a veil over the truth, God, kind and merciful, unwilling that his work should be given over to destruction, chose to visit the human race. He did not appear as those who falsely wished to be called gods, but showed himself as he is, the truth of God, in order to take away the error that had corrupted the mind of the world through the preaching of false gods. And so more than six hundred thousand people who had come out of Egypt, seeing and recognizing from the appearance of his unspeakable glory that this was the Lord above all, were afraid to draw near to him, but worshipped him from afar on bended knee. Afterwards, as other signs followed, beyond those he had done in Egypt among all his wonders, he was made manifest as the one God.

These things became known in almost every language; these things struck terror into the neighboring nations. What is there like this among the gods of the nations? To what nation, to what people have they shown their glory? What signs or mighty works have they done as a testimony to their divinity? Where, or when, are they proved to have spoken?

But the unreasoning crowd began to worship as gods either apparitions of shadows, or demons, or images of the dead; and once this practice had been made into an ancient custom, they think the truth of their reasoning can be defended. Yet the reason of truth comes not from custom or antiquity but from God, who is proved to be God not by antiquity but by eternity. For this reason faith is not something that had a beginning; it is without beginning. Our believing in God has a beginning, but what is believed is eternal. How, then, do the pagans think themselves earlier, when what they worship comes after God? Does not the work come after the workman? The pagans worship the works, we the Workman; they the creature, we the Creator. Certainly God made the world: well then, did he not make himself known by what he made? Or did he make man and not want to be worshipped by the one he made? That is absurd.

So once man was made, he began to worship his maker, because it is fitting and the very nature of things requires it. When this worship had fallen into disuse through human neglect, God restored it in Abraham. The knowledge of God that had existed in Adam began again in Abraham, so that those born from him would be brought up in this knowledge, and so that, handed down from one generation to the next, it would not fail and there would never be a lack of people to worship God. People of foreign nations were also called to this knowledge of God. Whoever knows, then, is subject to a beginning; but the one who is known is above any beginning. On what grounds, then, do the pagans claim that their law existed before ours? If the world is older than God (God forbid!), then paganism might also be ranked ahead of Christianity.

No one should be surprised at the name of Christianity. It means worshipping one God in the mystery of the Trinity. Even if the name of Christ is thought to come from anointing, the reason for the name existed before creation. Among our forefathers, those who were anointed as kings were called christs, that is, anointed ones. They bore the image of the Christ who was to come, who, born of God the Father to be king, is rightly called Christ, because what anointing gave to them, his birth gave to him. As long as the pagans do not know him, they reject him. But once they have come to know him, they worship him more devotedly than others, rejoicing that they have passed from evil to good. If they were so stubborn in something so trivial and foolish, how much stronger and more ardent will they be once they know the truth! What kind of Christ, then, is ours, who is hated when he is unknown and loved when he is known! Every evil person is loved while unknown and hated once known. How many in the past hated Christ who now love him, and who grieve that they hated what they did not know! It is foolish to hate someone you do not know, because you must first test whether the thing deserves hatred. Indeed, those who oppose him today will defend him tomorrow, repenting that they came so late to know what is true. If the thing deserved hatred or contained any deceit, Christians would be turning into pagans every day. But because this is the truth, every day and every hour, without pause, people abandon Jupiter and take refuge in Christ. Among them are sophists and nobles of the world, the very ones who had made him up as a god. To Christ be honor and glory for ever and ever.
CXV. On Fate.

Nothing is so contrary to a Christian as to devote attention to the art of astrology, for it is known to be hostile to the law of God. If some people are born to be wicked and others, on the contrary, to be good, then the law will be said to have been given in vain. Worse, the lawgiver will be held unjust. Whoever gives a law and so compels people to act against what they were born for, knowing that nature cannot be changed, would surely seem to have given the law only to have a pretext for sating his cruelty with men's death. For why does he forbid what he knows cannot be averted? Or how does he condemn a man for not doing what he could not do?

But if he is seen to be just, as he is (for to think otherwise of God is wicked), then he gave the law rightly and for a saving purpose, knowing that man is able to restrain himself from what the law forbids. Therefore, since he gave the law justly, he is certainly not unjust when he punishes.

So if we are to put our faith in the law of God, because it is proved to have been given justly, the art of astrology must be avoided and shunned. It was devised by the cunning and subtlety of the devil. Since he does not dare to oppose the Creator openly, he works by evasion, so as both to do injury to God and to set man at enmity with the law and so punish him with the second death.

Whoever, then, yields to God's authority and holds it wicked to call his deeds into question obeys the law he gave. He applies himself to its study day and night and looks to nothing contrary to it, not doubting that man is able to keep God's commandments. For those who are eager to sin look for pretexts to make their sins not their own, so that, with the sins charged, as it were, to nature, the sinner may seem exempt from punishment. This is the aim of those who despair of the promised life and wish to enjoy present pleasure.

But those who rely on the confidence of faith and await the hope of things to come strive to fulfill what they promised at the beginning of their rebirth: to renounce the pomps and pleasures of Satan. How great was the subtlety Satan used, then, to make man readier to sin, so that through it he might satisfy the wickedness of his envy! When a man hears that he was born to sin, and knows well that God is most just, he believes he can sin with impunity. A just judge, he reasons, does not condemn one who sinned at nature's command, and a sin that another committed through him should not even be called his own, if man has been deceived; for, weighed down by sins, he has become liable to death. So whoever takes away evil takes away all man's good as well. For if the sinner has no punishment, neither does the righteous man have a crown. Why then are the good praised and the wicked reproached? If it is a man's nature that he cannot sin, what do you praise in him that is not his own? And why do you condemn the offense in the sinner, when you know that his sinning is not his own? Unless, that is, whoever praises good and accuses evil is to be unjust.

But perhaps someone will object: 'I praise a good nature in a man and condemn a bad one, just as good wine is praised though it is good by nature, and bad wine is rejected though nature equally makes it so.' If that were so, there would be nothing blameworthy in the matter. The righteous would be praised without being judged worthy of a crown, and the unrighteous would be blamed without being called deserving of punishment. But in fact we know and read that both now and in the future the righteous are rewarded and the unrighteous are subjected to punishment and burned. That would certainly seem unjust if one man suffered punishment in avenging fire for doing what his nature dictated, while another, likewise doing what his nature dictated, were granted rewards.

If the good man is to be praised because he did what belonged to his nature, the bad man should also be praised, because he too did what belonged to his nature. Each would then be praised for remaining what he was made. For if someone who remains as he was made is held blameworthy, the blame falls on the maker, who caused such a person to be born as would displease.

But if the righteous man is rightly to be rewarded and the unrighteous condemned, then the verdict answers not to nature but to the will. Nature is free; it is the will that is at issue, and the will admits approaches and withdrawals through the senses. So the unrighteous man, seeing the righteous crowned and himself condemned, must blame himself: he trusted his senses against the law and did evil when he could have done good. Can the sun be accused because it burns, or water because it chills? Must water be rewarded because it refreshes people suffering from thirst, or will the sun be given prizes because its heat restores people after the cold? They do what belongs to their nature, and so they are neither condemned nor praised, for they cannot do otherwise.

But that things are not as the star-gazers suppose is proved by the evidence of actions. No one can be found who always does good or always does evil. A man would seem to have been born to do good if he remained beyond reproach, and he would rightly be judged evil if he persisted in always doing evil. But you see the one you think was born good sometimes acting badly, and you sometimes see the one you call born bad doing good. How then do you prove that the bad man is bad and the good man good? Rather, this is most certain: a person makes progress in whatever he sets his mind to. There are also causes that give rise to sins, such as envy, quarreling, or becoming someone's enemy.

Moreover, people commit the things the law forbids not openly or manifestly but in secret. Why, unless they respect the law? But if, as they claim, they had been born to do evil, they would not look for hiding places or show any respect for the law; they would do everywhere whatever nature compelled. Yet you see sins being planned and ways devised to commit them secretly, for people choose places, persons and times to fulfill the wish of their evil purpose. In the same way the good also decide on their good works with a certain judgment, distributing their good according to the occasion and someone's need. This must surely be credited not to nature but to the will, which is part of nature. If it were natural, there would be no judgment.

If we examine the matter more fully, we shall show that those who are now righteous were formerly unrighteous and were changed by their own effort. We read that Abraham himself was made righteous through faith. He was not righteous before, since we understand that he worshiped idols under his father's lead. So too with Zacchaeus, to whom the Lord bears witness after a common life, and with the chosen vessel, who even confesses it, saying: "We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest." Since will takes the place of nature (for a person is judged by his will, not by his nature), without doubt all the martyrs and all the justified are good because they were not born faithful but reborn. And how many we know who led shameful lives and were prodigal devotees of luxury, and are now continent and holy! For when the fear of God comes, the vices that once ruled are overcome.

Let us see from this how much the fear of the law can do. Before Julian's edict, women could not divorce their husbands. But once they were given the power, they began to do what they could not do before, and every day they divorced their husbands freely. Where was fate hiding all that time? Hiding, I suppose, out of fear of the law.

And how did what Moses handed down slip in? While the fates were asleep, I suppose. So many commandments, and of such a kind, were handed down for them to keep as no other nation has. And lest anyone think this should be ascribed to their region of the sky, they keep the commandments of their law though scattered over almost the whole world. These precepts go against the fates. They did not exist for perhaps three thousand years and more from the founding of the world, but once given they endure to the end. How then did something that did not exist for so many thousands of years begin? For the course of the stars dates from the founding of the world.

And how is it that, with so great a multitude of Jews throughout the whole world, none of them changes and becomes a Gentile, while we see pagans becoming Jews, though rarely? You see that where the Jewish rite is concerned, fate is shut out, for they both began to stand outside fate and remain so.

What are we to make of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose end lies before our eyes as a punishment? It was such that all of them, stained with the infamy of filth, deserved to be consumed by divine fire. In the flood all had one fate, so that all perished by one death at one time, except the house of Noah. And will the whole army of Pharaoh be said to have been born under one decree, so that the foolish error of astrology may be upheld, just because they were drowned in the Red Sea with their king? There are many other examples, which we pass over; two examples are enough to satisfy, and three all the more!

Every nation has different institutions. What is permitted elsewhere is not permitted here, and what is permitted here is not permitted elsewhere. Here in the city of Rome and its territory, which is called most sacred, women are permitted to divorce their husbands, although divine law provides that not even husbands may use this power, except for fornication. See, in this matter the barbarians are better! It is not impossible to keep this rule here too, since it is shown to have been kept before. So fate has changed, because what was forbidden before has begun to be permitted.

Eunuchs may not be made in the Roman realm, though other peoples permit it. Yet it is plain that they could be made here too, for it is proved to have been done, though in secret. If fear ceased, it would be done openly. So fear restrains fate, for fate is overcome if it does not do what it wishes.

The Persians wear earrings like women, which here is shameful and unlawful. Yet the priests of the Mother called Great testify that it could be done here too. (And she truly was great, but a harlot. There is this difference, however: these men are catamites, while those are men.) What shall we say? Are these alone in the whole world born under such a fate that they are castrated and transformed into women, so that only these few are found in the whole world? It is well known that these wretches are ensnared and driven by promised rewards to this pain and disgrace. If they had been born for this, they would not need to be driven.

Persians are permitted to have intercourse with their daughters, and this is shown to be possible here too, since some are proved to have done it. But because punishment intervenes, fear restrains them from doing what can be done but is not lawful. Everything that is forbidden is forbidden precisely because it can be done, so that it may not be done. If it were a matter of fate, it could not be done, nor would it be forbidden. And if it is not a matter of fate and is forbidden, this shows that what is not of fate can be done. What wisdom would there be in forbidding what cannot be done? Would anyone forbid a person to fly from the city of Rome to Spain, or to carry a mountain on his shoulders? It is things that can be done but ought not to be that are forbidden.

It is a custom among the Moors for women to wear rings even in their noses. Is this a matter of fate? If it were, they would keep the custom when brought here, because if there is fate, each person carries his fate with him. But because it is not a matter of fate, all who come here from there change, seeing that what is thought becoming there is considered shameful here.

Certainly among all nations a number is a number, earth is earth, water is water, air is air and fire is fire. Can earth be found anywhere that is not dry, or air that can be touched, or water that is not flowing or cold, or fire that is cold? In the same way Jupiter is Jupiter everywhere, Saturn is Saturn and Venus is Venus, and so with the other signs. For that art is practiced everywhere by one and the same system.

But among all nations institutions endure not by the system of the fates, which, as the astrologers treat it, is the same everywhere, but by human invention. Whatever seemed reasonable and fitting to the man regarded as foremost among his people, he decreed for those he ruled. Hence each region or nation has its own customs to observe. Solon and Lycurgus, for example, had decreed many things for the Greeks to keep as law, and these were gradually blotted out as their power declined.

The kings of the Jews liked to ride mules; the kings of the Romans rode not mules but horses. The kings of the Garamantes, who live beyond African Tripoli, like to ride bulls. The kings of the Persians are carried in litters; indeed, the ancient kings of the Persians were not even seen by the people. The kings of Midian delight in riding camels and adorn their necks with golden collars. And throughout Africa people prefer to ride asses rather than horses.

Though all things exist everywhere, not all things please everyone, because each person chooses what finds more favor with him. We ourselves have varying tastes in clothes, in food, in other things we use, and in our very opinions. This cannot be called fate, since they assert that many people have different fates, because our will often changes. What we have loved for a long time we later despise, and we begin to love what we once did not like. Once a habit has formed, we remain changed.

They say the order of the fates is such that what the fates bring about at given times recurs at intervals as before: what they do today, for instance, they do again after a time. They are not said to stay fixed in one state, for they are overcome by discipline and habit.

For a long time Roman women did not know the use of wine. Discipline, once it had become habit, strengthened their resolve so that they kept what they had learned was beneficial. Were these the fates in those days, and did they die afterward, so that a good practice came to an end? No, it was not the fates but discipline that had discovered this. And when the habit was abandoned, the discipline perished.

The ancient Romans showed such restraint that they refused even gifts that were offered, regarding a good name as riches and preferring virtue to pleasures. Did other fates take the place of these, or did these fates die? It was not a matter of fate but of discipline, which is the tutor even of fate itself. How could something be a matter of fate that fate did not have before and does not have now?

I do not know why they lay so much blame on fate as to call it the author of every deed, when it both exists and does not exist. Where there is discipline, it does not exist; where there is habit, it does not exist; where there is chance, it does not exist. And where it seems to exist, it is overcome by fear of the law: lust is checked by fear, and monetary gain is rejected for the sake of winning God's favor. In this respect, then, its existence cannot be denied, since what is overcome cannot fail to exist. Yet it can rightly be said not to exist even in this very case, since what is overcome has no authority.

So whoever follows God's law and keeps to the habit of a good life finds that all the so-called fates yield to him. Habit is so powerful that it tames even beasts. Those who wish to live badly create fates for themselves. Luxury and pleasure produce intemperance and restlessness, which beget incontinence and anger. Knowing that this deserves punishment, and wanting to exempt themselves, they are ashamed and ascribe it to the fates. Meanwhile demons help those who brood on such things. Those beings stand ready to bring the plans of evil-minded people to success, and these people call them fates, not understanding that they are man's enemies.

If sins did not slip into the soul through the senses but were born from within, everything done wrong could rightly be said to be the [?] of the fates. But they see that the desire for sins is born through sight, hearing and the other senses, with the help of enemies who suggest what should be done. It is harmful, but is not thought so while it is being done, for it seems sweet while it is done or before it is done, and only once it is finished does it appear bitter. Why then do they blame the fates?

That it can be overcome we observe from this. When we are thinking about something and are concerned with some matter, the enemies are silent and lust subsides, for they cannot make suggestions to us while we are occupied. Does anyone suggest something else to a person absorbed in some task? He does not, knowing that either he will not be heard or he will be rebuffed for making an untimely suggestion. So it is with the enemies, who are clearly demons; for these are the gods of the pagans. If they see us occupied with divine things, they do not intrude to suggest the contrary, but lie in ambush looking for an opportunity to plunge in.

The defenses of the soul, then, are constant meditation on God's law and constant work, because if the demons see that we are idle in divine things, they are roused to tempt us. It is they who sow desires through flesh and blood. Although the flesh has its own impulse from its origin, since carnal birth is not idle, in this matter the help of demons is added toward the destruction of men.

Demons are of various kinds and have differing wills. Some disturb minds and dash bodies to the ground. Others mingle with the blood and beget desires in the soul. Others attach themselves to the human heart and suggest harmful things with flattery. And some only bind bodies with infirmities, like that daughter of Abraham whom the Lord healed.

Ignorant of all this, the pagans call it fate, though the causes are diverse and these things are brought about by enemies, so that a man, ensnared by one cause or another, may be subjected to passions. They call fate good when bodies are well tempered, or are commended by an affability that has a certain charm. They call fate bad if a body has too much heat or moisture, or lacks charm and is rather prone to misfortune; such people they call unfortunate.

Grant that these things are true. We see them even in animals, some of which have more heat. But animals are not rational like man, able to temper their bodies by taking care. The mind is the commander of the body precisely so that it may steer it with the reins of divine law. The divine law shows that what is suggested, whether by the impulse of the flesh or by the enemy, is not beneficial. God gave this law as a help, so that when the enemy dictates evil things as if they were good, we may look to the precepts of the law and understand that he is a seducer, because he urges something other than what the law teaches.

So the body is bridled in this way: because it runs hot, it is given less and kept from delicacies. Just as the heat of a feverish body increases if it takes food or drink, so bodies of this kind, burning with the heat of the blood, will blaze more fiercely unless they are governed. For if you give a fire no fuel, it dies down.

It is the mind's task to lead the body. If it lets the body go wherever it wants, the body throws it headlong, as a bridled horse throws a careless rider. The heat of the body flares up more when the enemies are at work to deceive the soul, for it is not the body that desires; rather, by its heat it generates desires in the soul. So we must implore the protection of our God to defend us and restrain these enemies, for our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers. Once they are removed, it will be easy to suppress the impulses of flesh and blood. A fire goes out if it lacks the material by which it lives.

What astrologers foretell happens to those who believe that what they say will come to pass. This is done through the cunning of demons, who bring about what their priests have foretold so that they will not be exposed as false. But their working has no power over those who give no credence to their responses. The demons are not so eager to satisfy those who do not believe them, and God does not allow them to do anything that might lead astray those who trust in God and do not believe the devil. For God has arranged everything so that it happens to each person according to his faith, and so free choice of the will remains. Therefore, whoever believes God and flees to his help, nothing can prevail against him. For the enemy knows for certain that the things God made are in God's power, and he does not dare to act against one whom he sees has the common God on his side.

Certainly God made the world and created the sun, moon and stars, setting their courses, by which the human race is governed. Does he not have the power to command them to do something at times other than what has been decreed for them? He made them so that they are subject to his will and follow their decreed courses only if he has commanded nothing else. So if those whom they serve ask him, because the rains come out of season or the crops fail from excessive drought, he may order the weather to be moderated. Or perhaps, as often happens, people live under God's anger, wandering astray through luxury and vanity and not doing what pleases God. Then he may hold back the rain for a very long time and stir up famine on the earth, as we read happened under Elijah and Elisha. Then, appeased by their atonement, he may grant that showers moisten the dry land.

For the world is ordered in the same way as an earthly empire. Some people, oppressed by provincial governors, run to the emperors for help to be raised up again. In the same way people who see hard times coming upon them should present themselves as suppliants to God, in whose power are all things.

But the astrologers do not see it this way. They say that nothing can happen except that the stars carry out the causes decreed for them. The stars, they claim, can neither be called back nor driven to do anything else; once their duties have been fixed, they keep to them. This is what the astrologers insist on: they say that the fates cannot be changed and that nothing can be obtained by prayer, because God, they say, fixed the order of the whole world once and for all and handed it over to the stars as his ministers, and the stars can be moved neither backward nor forward.

This is the astrologers' error, and by it they even attack God. By this claim they deny that anything can happen outside the order of the world. So whatever we read that God has done in the world, if it disagrees with the law of the world, they say must not be believed. They accept only the things said to have happened in keeping with the world's ordinances. On this view it could not be said that a virgin gave birth, or that Aaron's rod blossomed and bore fruit, or that the aged Sarah gave birth. The order of the world does not allow for these things, because we read that God did them outside the world's order. Yet what is surprising if the maker of the world did what the world cannot do?

'But he seems to have broken the order he himself laid down,' they say, 'since he is said to have acted otherwise than he decreed for the world.' Come now: he laid down for the world a law for making and begetting. Did he lay it down for himself? It would have been a lowering of himself if he acted in the same way as the world he founded. And how would anyone have understood that a thing was done by him if he had done it by the world's law? So that it might be understood as done by God and not by the world, it was done in a different order.

Certainly he decreed that the sun should run its appointed courses without ceasing and should have no freedom to stand still. Does it follow that, because he laid down this law for the sun, he himself is not free to make it stand still?

Certainly it is laid down for judges that they may not revoke a sentence once passed on a defendant. Is the emperor himself also under this law? On the contrary, he alone may revoke a sentence and pardon someone condemned to death. How much more must God be allowed what could not be granted to the world, since the world is the servant of its Creator! Indeed, by the law given to it the world can kill, but it cannot give life. Through imbalance it can make someone blind, but it cannot restore his eyes. It can make someone weak and sick, but it cannot heal him; this God has reserved for himself, so that it may be plain that he is Lord of all. And it serves to overturn fate that the dead have risen, that a man born blind had his eyes restored, that the sick and paralysed were made strong, and other such things that were done, so that, if there can be any such thing as fate, it can put no obstacle in the way of those who take refuge in God. For the apostle John says: "He who is in you is greater than he who is in this world."

When God is entreated, he sets aside even what he has decreed. He has certainly decreed that sinners are to be punished, and yet he pardons those who plead with him, because he alone may bind and loose. So although the sun is not permitted to stand still, under Joshua son of Nun it was ordered to stand, and it obeyed his command, contrary to what had been prescribed for it in the order of the world. Under Hezekiah we read that something greater was done. So that Hezekiah would not doubt that what had been promised him was true, he received a sign that was new and unheard of by human ears. The sun was not ordered to stand still, as before, but to go backward, so that, seeing this, Hezekiah would be sure that the One who had turned the ninth hour into the sixth could add fifteen years to his life. And because what was granted to Hezekiah goes against the astrologers (for they deny that anything can be added to a life), he received in this matter a sign that was itself against the astrologers. For they claim it is impossible for the stars to do anything other than what has been fixed for them.

They certainly say that whether one has a slave or not is a matter of fate. Very well. Where were these fates from the beginning of the world? Up to the flood, and for a long run of years after it, this condition of slavery did not exist. Or did these fates begin in the time of Ninus, who is said to have been the first to make war on his neighbours and to make his captives subject to slavery? You see, then, that this was invented later and is not a matter of fate but the work of demons. For if it were a matter of fate, it would have existed from the beginning of the world. They are the very same stars that were made in the beginning, and their course remains as it was.

Earlier, too, human life was rustic, and no one strove for riches. How, then, do the astrologers now say that people become rich and poor through the stars? Have the stars changed? Or is it the cunning and trickery of Satan, who says that things happen through the stars which he brings about through his angels and ministers? For as the time of his destruction draws near, he devises greater things through which people may sin.

We know that Italy and Africa, Sicily and Sardinia have suffered famine. Let the astrologers tell us whether all these people had one and the same fate, when they say that among a hundred people not even two can have matching fates. Let them blush and be silent, and stretch out suppliant hands to God, in whose power all things are. But perhaps in this case something slipped past the fates. What then shall we say of Pannonia, which has been so wiped out that it can have no remedy?

O the weakness of those who profess themselves Christians with a wavering faith! While they doubt the promises, they do not reflect on what has already been done. If they considered what the prophets and apostles did, they would never give a hearing to the astrologers' tales. They would know that all things are in God's power, and they would not be alarmed when evils befall good people, since the good will be rewarded at the coming judgment. They would remember the apostle, who says: "Through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." For whoever is content and waits for the judgment of his God will be rewarded and also avenged. But if he wants to be avenged in the present, or longs greedily to enjoy present wealth, he doubts the promised life, and for that reason in the future he will be counted among the faithless and judged worthy of punishment. God made the world as a place of training and adorned it with every kind of abundance, setting out two causes, the present and the future, the heavenly and the earthly, so that they might serve to test human beings. Whoever scorned the future life and chose the present would be assigned to the flesh. Whoever put the future before the present would be judged worthy of spiritual things. And whoever, unjustly oppressed by the power of the unjust, laid his complaints before God or kept them for the future judgment would there be relieved and honoured with spiritual glory. That is why none of the saints appeared glorious in the world or loved present pleasures. Hence the apostle says: "Having food and clothing, let us be content with these." Yet a Christian complains and grieves if someone seems prosperous in this age, although the dignity and happiness of Christians has been promised not on earth but in heaven. How then can he call himself a Christian who does not want to glory there, where it has been promised, but here, where it is forbidden? If it were good to enjoy present things, heavenly things would surely not have been promised to those who despise them.

With what hope, then, do Christians lend their ears to the astrologers, when they hear the apostle John crying out and saying: "Do not love this world or the things that are in the world"? If these are the precepts of our faith and our law, that neither the world nor the things in the world are to be loved, why do some of us complain, saddened at others' prosperity in the world, a prosperity which in God's eyes may be misfortune? They ought rather to rejoice that the world does not give them the things by which they would be bound and held fast, subject to human affairs.

For this prosperity, having gained the means to be secure, lacks concern for divine things. Someone who is supplied with every necessity and has nothing to worry about is bound to be careless about the oracles of God. People of this kind usually begin to labour under another worry: how to increase their standing in the world, which cannot be done without sin. If one looks more closely, the world will be seen to be rather the enemy of those it is said to make happy, for hardly any of them gives thought to heavenly things.

So Christians should rejoice when, living rightly, they are oppressed in this world. For he has overcome the world who, content with however things turn out for him in the world, gives thanks to his God, from whom he hopes that eternal things will be given back if temporal things seem to be denied him here. Why else did God establish the future judgment, if not so that those unjustly cast down for a time might be exalted in eternal life, while those are crushed who, through their power, despised God's future judgment or did not believe in it and supposed that crimes go unpunished?

But the defenders of fate deny the future judgment. For if some are born good and others, on the contrary, born bad, why do you praise or blame anyone, when the good man did not strive in the contest in order to win, nor was the bad man careless so as to lose? They peddle these tales among private people. But sinners brought before the courts have never dared to excuse their crimes by appeal to fate. Instead they confess themselves guilty and do not deny that they receive their sentence justly. So the authority of the law tramples on the theory of fate, so that once the law bestirs itself fate cannot even be mentioned.

How do those who have lived wickedly, and by some effort escape the severity of the law for a time, believe they will escape for ever, without considering that the author of the law cannot turn a blind eye to what happens here? Here there is an image of the law; there, the truth; and whoever mocks the image cannot mock the truth. Is there any place without God, or can anyone escape his hand? Yet they flatter themselves that whoever escapes here is now safe. And how do they think it just that others are condemned in such cases while they escape?

Certainly God established the world and showed it what law it was to follow. Loving his work, he showed it the way that leads to life and appointed leaders for people to follow, because there is also a way that leads to death. Must he not, then, inquire whether those he set as ministers of his kingdom governed his people by the law he established, and whether the people accepted his edict? Thus the ministers, if found faithful, may be worthy of praise, or, if unfaithful, be subjected to punishment; and likewise the people may be praised for keeping the law or condemned for despising it. This is just; this is what the case demands.

Why, then, are some unwilling to believe in a future judgment? This is something the madness of the astrologers invented. How could they accept a future judgment when they fight against the present one, since they contend that judgment takes place at birth? Yet because truth rises again when it is thought to be suppressed, these very people, who hold that by a kind of natural judgment the good and the bad are not made but born, themselves repay wrongdoers and do not let wrongs go unpunished. At home they punish with rods, the mill and chains those whom outside they declare were born incorrigible. Does any sensible person punish someone he knows cannot be corrected? That is the act either of a fool or of an unjust man.

But perhaps they will say that this too happens by fate, since one who is under fate does not do what he wishes, so that it is also in their nature to punish those they know remain unchangeable by nature. And truly so, for it has to be said that whatever is called fate must be counted as folly. How foolish it is that, while they say someone was born bad, they do not even prove good the one they claim was born good! How can a man be judged good when he is caught doing something unjust? And what is so unjust as for someone to be beaten who, it is claimed, could not have done otherwise than he did?

And if everything happens by fate, how did the law come in, which does not allow what is fated to happen? If the law were removed, forbidden things would be done openly everywhere; the powerful could not be endured, and there would be no freedom, because even someone who does not now contemplate evil would begin to be wicked once fear was removed. Indeed, we read that the law was given because of the wicked.

But perhaps this too was fated, that the law should be given. Then on what reasoning do the fates stand, if they give birth to something that destroys them, since the law declares that what is fated ought not to happen? They are irrational, then, if they produce things that contradict themselves; and they are unjust, because they cause people to be born for damnation. And if they are unjust, they ought to have no authority, since everything unjust is liable to punishment.

Or perhaps they will say that the law is of no use, because someone born to be bad cannot be changed by the law? If so, the law was given to no purpose. And how did the fates bring a useless thing into being, since 'nothing happens without fate'? So the fates act both for themselves and against themselves. And if that is so, what has no firmness, because its reasoning is inconsistent, cannot stand.

Or did the fates perhaps want the law to exist for this purpose, so that those whom the fates cause to be born bad should be condemned by the law, and fate and law might agree to punish them? What can be said to this, except that both the laws and the fates deserve to be condemned by their own judgment, if with equal injustice they work to have people killed who did evil not willingly but by the agency of the fates? Against this the law objects that the fates must be condemned by their own admission. For they do not deny that it is due to fate that the wicked are wicked. But the law is so opposed to the fates that it denies the wicked are wicked because of fate; it says they are wicked by their own will, and for that reason it rightly declares them guilty. So law and fate have nothing in common, since the law denies what the fates assert.

Under what reckoning will those be said to have been born who banned the astrologers from the city of Rome? This law is well known to have been enforced, and those who made it were certainly pagans. How can things that go against fate happen by fate? If there is such a thing as fate, it does not act against itself. Those who act against fate have no fate; and if they have no fate, there is no fate.

'But there is,' they say, 'a fate that determines for each person by what death he will die.' If so, a murderer is not to be accused. He will defend himself on two grounds: he did it by the agency of the fates, and the other man was killed by the agency of the fates. Meanwhile the law comes under attack, because it punishes the murderer brought before it. In the same way, someone is born to be an adulterer, and a woman to be an adulteress, and someone to be the victim of adultery. If this too is so, the law is again called into question, since it punishes adulterers. If it really were a matter of fate, the man whose fate it is to suffer adultery ought also to be punished. He too is found to be a party to it, because his fate allowed the adultery to take place. So it would be fair either to condemn them together or to acquit them together; and so the law appears unjust.

So if the fates come from God, the law will not be God's, because it befits not only God but even a sensible man not to condemn what he himself has done. But since no one has ever dared to speak against the law or to deny that it comes from God, the fates cannot be said to come from God, because God punishes these things through the law. For when what happens under the compulsion of the fates is condemned, the fates themselves are undoubtedly condemned.

'But bad souls,' they say, 'are born for this purpose, to do evil.' Very well. But then innocent people ought not to be born under such a fate that they could be killed by them. If those souls were bad, they ought not to be born but punished, so that they would not kill the innocent. But it is not the souls they imagine to be bad that kill the innocent; it is the fates, which cause people to be born in such a way that they are killed. And so it is not the souls but the fates that are unjust; and if they are unjust, they are not from God. Therefore they are from the devil and are to be condemned together with him.

And since the fates are said to decree for each person how he will die, whether by the sword, the noose, a fall, a shipwreck or some other way, they assign the same end to many. For no one can be alone in differing from everyone else's fate. If anyone is found to differ, it is no longer a matter of fate but of chance; and if chance is at work in the death of one, it will be at work in the deaths of many, and then it will no longer be a matter of fate. Anaxagoras was thrown into a mortar by order of a king and died crushed, which has happened to no other human being. And a woman drove a tent peg into the temple of Sisera, king of the foreigners, and so he gave up his spirit. No one else has died in this way. Formerly, too, people were nailed to crosses, which was afterwards prohibited by an edict that still stands. If it was a matter of fate, how did it stop? For when what is fated is prohibited and does not happen, fate is defeated. Or, if it was not a matter of fate, then people were not crucified by fate but by the judgment of the law. And so it is that people are condemned not by fate but because they are convicted by their own evil deeds.

Among the Etruscans, it is said, a man was born with a face more beautiful than any there has ever been. Because he was a good man, and so that he would not fall under suspicion with anyone, since he attracted the eyes even of respectable women, he wounded his face with seven cuts in order to condemn the beauty that everyone desires. See how the fates, if there are any, have been overcome! But perhaps someone will say: 'It was nature that he was born beautiful, but fate that his looks were wounded.' If that is so, fate is no longer something one is born with but a cause that befalls; and if it is something that befalls, it will not be a matter of fate but of deliberate choice, or at least of chance, so far as the other parts of the matter are concerned.

For what else is overcoming fate than changing nature? If nature were from God in this way, it could neither be changed nor overcome. We read it recorded in a certain law book that a woman once gave birth to five children at once. How did this slip past the fates, so that nature decreed for her alone what was not fated? If it had been fated, a good many women would have been burdened with this lot. Again, a certain man setting out for foreign parts entrusted his wife to a friend he knew to be faithful, not a boy but a man of mature age. To be a more careful guardian of her, this friend castrated himself, so that he could sleep near her safely without anyone's suspicion. What do we think: was this fate or deliberate choice? How could it be fate when it is the opposite? Whoever overcomes what was born in him makes fate void.

In learning, too, the question of fate certainly arises: whether someone is able to grasp something or not. Then all senators have one fate, since no senator lacks letters; and the peoples who lack letters have one fate; and all slaves are of one fate, since no slave is a senator.

But if you call what one is born with fate, whatever is added later will lie outside fate. Or if what is added comes from fate, why does it come through labour? It would be called fate if it happened to a person against his will. What befalls without foresight is said to belong to the fates; but why should something be called fate that is thought out, long weighed and acquired by means of practice?

One man is born a eunuch; others are made eunuchs. Where will fate be? In the one who was born so, I suppose. What are we to say of those who are made so? The cases are different. Or if these were made eunuchs by fate, then the other was born a eunuch against fate. And why is a eunuch so rarely born that it seems incredible? There was a woman in the city of Rome who is known to have had eleven husbands, and a man who had twelve wives. What fates decreed this for them? Again, in the time of the emperor Constantius it is well established that a girl in part of Campania was changed into a male and brought to Rome. What fates did this? Other ones, I suppose, that you know nothing about.

O if only you would be silent about this word, and leave some things to chance and accident, and grant some things to providence! For the strength and diligence of the mind can do so much that it not only resists nature but also amends itself or corrupts itself, since it has the power to judge itself.

It is recorded that the women of the Scythians, who were called Amazons, while their husbands were engaged in a distant war and long absent, slept with their slaves to have offspring. They killed every male child that was born and kept the females, so that none of them devoted herself to working wool; instead they were trained from early childhood in wrestling and arms. So great was their courage and energy in their exploits that they reigned for a long run of years, subdued a number of nations and made all Asia pay them tribute. What can be said to this? Were these things fated, which were carried on for so many years in such a way as to make void everything that is thought to be fated? First, that women, against nature, reigned and scorned men; next, that they slept with their own slaves; third, that all male children were killed and the females kept alive, and that such prosperity followed them that, without men, they extended the kingdom they had begun with great resources and over a long time. Certainly this has never happened since the foundation of the world except in Scythia alone. So they cannot claim that such things come about when the world is renewed after one thousand four hundred and sixty years, since the world is already in its six-thousandth year.

[?] and for how long a person does what he has set himself to imitate. Marcus Crassus was called 'Agelastus', because he is said to have laughed only once in his life. Gaius Junius was given the surname 'Brutus', because with shrewd foresight he pretended to be a fool so that King Tarquin the Proud would not kill him for his great wealth. And in the time of Constantine a man called Samsucius pretended to be a fool for thirty years, in order, as he himself said afterwards, to take the emperor's mind off his troubles. Where is the theory of the fates, when each person does what he wishes? It has been shut out.

And what about this: the defenders of fate are devoted to supplications, although these are contrary to fate? They commend their years, and they ask about marriages, journeys, purchases and offices. If something is fated, why do you pray, why do you make supplication for what is going to happen even against your will? 'But I am asking,' he says, 'whether I ought to buy.' Then what you say you ought to do once you have learned that it is advantageous does not depend on fate. For if it is fated, you ask in vain, since whether you want to or not, whether you ask or not, you are going to do it.

But because even among themselves this assertion is not firmly held, they hedge their bets in their uncertainty, in case the truth should turn out to be something other than what they argue. Those among them who seem wiser say: "We do not pray on account of the fates, since we know they cannot be changed at all, but on account of the things that lie near the fates, so that they may not do us any harm." Come now: suppose someone has a good fate, and next to it there is something that seems contrary to it. What can that be, since they deny that a good fate can be changed, just as they deny it of a bad one? Certainly people pray that this thing lying next to fate may not do harm, for it will do harm unless prayer is made. How, then, can they deny that the fate itself can be changed, when they fear what lies next to it? This would not be feared unless they believed the fate could be changed. But since the whole point for you is rather to avoid saying that fate is changed, you are without doubt praying for no reason.

But take care that your very praying is not also a matter of fate, since whatever you assign to fate tends to be witless. Praying is certainly not a bad thing; so why should it not be said to belong to fate? If, then, it is fate that a person prays, whose doing will it be that he prays and does not obtain? For if it was fate, he ought to obtain what he prays for. But if it is fate to pray and not obtain, fate is foolish, since it makes a person pray whom it knows will not obtain. And if it does not know whether the person it makes pray can obtain, then fate will be improvident and without reason, for all ignorance is lack of wisdom, and lack of wisdom is folly. Every argument of the pagans falls into this trap. Let the pagans see to it, who, wrapped in darkness, do not see the light. Ensnared by ancient error, they refuse to lend their ears to the truth that was formerly hidden.

What are we to say of certain Christians who, changed in name alone, uphold the vanity of their former error, and are so dull-witted that they claim the Lord himself acted under fate? They say: "He himself said, 'My hour has not yet come,'" as though this hour were not a matter of his will but a necessity imposed by fate, when in fact he meant the hour of his own will, in which he allowed himself to suffer. Indeed, he says: "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again." Where there is power of the will, then, the necessity of fate ceases.

And how is he called Savior by us, if what we do or what happens to us is a matter of fate? He is called Savior precisely because he showed us the way of salvation. So if it was shown by him, it was not a matter of fate, since it was formerly hidden, and they maintain that what is said to be fated comes about unexpectedly. Here lies the merit of faith, which cannot be said to come from fate, because what is believed was not heard of in other ages; for the fates are said to bestow only what falls within the ordinary course of human life.

But how can they be said to bestow what they are found not to know? This is why the apostle says: "whom none of the rulers of this age knew." These are the principalities and powers, which have evil angels under them, who under the name of the fates carry out their own pleasures as it suits them, as sorcerers commonly confess. For there are some whom they love, others they do not love, and some they hate. And each of them suggests to each person what he himself delights in, since they too have different pleasures: in some they stir up lust for various kinds of debauchery, in others lust for one thing, in others wanton indulgence, in others anger, in some avarice; for some they procure gain, for others loss, for some favor, for others hatred and also hindrances. Sometimes, at certain times, they are sated and rest at leisure; at other times they do not intrude upon a mind occupied with some purpose, because they do not rule but creep in, looking for an opportunity to take hold. The choice of the will is therefore free; but when through a certain sloth we grow careless about ourselves, they tempt us and urge us toward what is harmful. Above all, if they find us thinking of something contrary to the law, they will come and help us in that very thing, so that we carry out what the law forbids. For if the fear of God is in the soul, neither flesh nor blood nor principalities and powers prevail, because they are held in check by God's help, so that they are overcome without effort.

If we were not in our own power, how could the Lord say: "Ask, and it will be given to you; for everyone who asks will receive"? If, then, whoever wishes to ask will receive, the common saying no longer holds: "not what we want, but what has been given," because the will is roused by the Savior to ask and to receive what it has asked for. But they say that fate means this: whether a person asks or does not ask, he will still get what fate holds, whether evil or good. The Lord rules this out when he says: "Daughter, your faith has made you well," so that it is no longer a matter of fate, since it is faith that receives the benefit. And again he says: "If you believe, all things are possible to the one who believes." He clearly placed merit in the will, because the good belongs to faith, not to nature. Faith is something added, which rouses the will to action, so that, since faith is not in our nature, the will, which is in our nature, by taking up faith may lay up merit for itself with God. Human nature is like a stone, which does not have fire in its substance but has it in potential, so that by action it produces what it does not seem to have, because it does not yet exist except as in a seed. It exists in potential, so as to be brought forth through action; and if the action is lacking, it does not exist, just as a seed does not produce anything unless it is cultivated but remains only itself. It is the addition, then, that makes it produce. So too a human being does not have faith by nature, but has the seed of faith, which, unless it is stirred up and exercised, will bear no fruit, that is, he will not have faith. Those who believe the tales of the astrologers destroy the seed of faith, which bears witness both to the Creator and to his justice. For the work acknowledges its maker and testifies that he rightly loves what he has made.
