We therefore warn everyone to flee this art by every means. Its devotees are enemies of God and are never free from anxiety; they are always in suspense, waiting for what they know is uncertain. But we, who believe that all good things come from God and that any adversity that arises is held in check at his nod, should live simply, secure in his protection. Yet we know that even if some adversity befalls us while we are doing well, enduring it will gain us a crown.
CXVI. THE MEANING OF THE PASSOVER

The Passover, dearly beloved brothers, takes its name from the Passion, as we are taught by the prefiguring of this tradition that took place in Egypt through Moses, the servant of God, when Scripture says: “This is the sacrifice, the Passover of the Lord.” What, then, is the reason that the sacred mystery should be celebrated through blood, and the restoration of life brought about through death? It is so that death, when it thought it was gaining, would take the Savior’s blood and ebb away diminished, and, when it supposed it had acted with strength, would be weakened and perish. For by divine arrangement death was found for death through death’s own work. Because death always wills evil, it was given way to for a time, so that, justly destroyed by its own work, it could not complain that its kingdom had been taken from it. For although God can do all things, he does nothing that is contrary to reason. The justice he demands, he also practices himself, not presuming on his power.

Great, then, is his providence toward the human race: keeping justice, he undid what had been justly decreed and rescued man from death, although man was not undeservedly held by it. But because man had been deceived by the devil’s envy, it was just that he should be helped. He was held by God’s sentence, but it was Satan who had brought this about. So, just as it seemed just to rescue him, it would have been unjust to do so by sheer power, with justice set aside. For when man, overcome at the devil’s persuasion, was to receive mercy, the devil objected as his accuser. Therefore it was arranged that the one who gloried in man’s sin should himself be caught sinning, so that, having at last become guilty, he would not dare to object. So it came about that the Son of God was born as a man and, by preaching justice, provoked the devil, because he was keeping people from the devil’s vices, so that the devil even killed him who knew no sin.

Then the devil was found to have sinned, and more gravely than the man he was accusing. For while by God’s decree he claimed man for himself on account of sin, since whoever sins belongs to the devil, he was found to have sinned more when he killed one who had not sinned, in order to claim him for himself. So through death destruction crept in upon death, and blood was shed so that blood might be recovered. For, as I said, death, which is the devil, because it was found to have sinned in the death of the Savior, lost his blood together with that of all of us: just as through the one Adam who sinned it held all in death, so through the one who did not sin it lost all. The Savior’s blood, then, unjustly shed, obtained this by way of reward: triumphantly recovering the blood of its own origin, it restored it to its former state with its substance made better. For death, once conquered, could not object to the one who had conquered it. Blessed, therefore, is the mystery of the Passover, which wrought redemption through blood that is ours, death being overcome by death, just as poison is commonly overcome by poison.
CXVII. ON ABRAHAM

The faith of this patriarch was so outstanding and admirable that, by God’s judgment, all other righteous people acknowledge him as the father of belief, and no one is worthy of God and dear to him unless he is called Abraham’s son. For the distinction of his honor and merit is faith, which he did not hesitate to give even to things beyond belief. Among other things, he was found worthy to see the Savior in the form of the incarnation that was then still to come, as the Lord declared and confirmed to the Jews: “Your father Abraham longed to see my day; he saw it and was glad.” For it was fitting that he who had deservedly been made the father of faith should foresee the hope of his future children, a hope which, by the favor and foresight of God, would flow over by right of inheritance from a kindly and devout father to obedient sons.

Let us now see what this faith believed, that it should come by divine judgment to such honor and glory. We have praised his faith, but we have not yet said what he believed. The Lord brought him outside, showed him the stars of heaven and said: “Can you count them? So shall your offspring be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. It would not have been a great thing to believe God, except that what he believed the world judges unbelievable and foolish, because it lies outside what nature can be hoped to do. Therefore Abraham, alone out of the world, because he believed this, was set apart from worldly people and justified.

So it is the unbelief of worldly wisdom that makes it a great thing to have believed this; to have believed it against that wisdom’s expectation is of the highest merit. For the despair of worldly people is the merit and the hope of Christians. The reward of the good is produced by the case of the wicked, for faith is stronger and fuller the more it entrusts itself to what is beyond belief. A man already withered believed that from his aged wife he would have offspring too many to be counted, looking not so much at what was shown to him as at the one who showed it, whom he did not think capable of lying. And so it was credited to him as righteousness. For to believe something absurd and known to be impossible is the mark of a dullard, unless there is a person whose word makes it believable. Hence Abraham shows both admirable faith and a wise heart: he believes what is beyond belief, and he entrusts himself to one whom it is both foolish and dangerous not to believe.

This proves our faith reasonable: it believes of no one but God that he can do what he promises. This, then, is the bulwark of faith; this is its triumph. The wise of this world, looking at nature and seeing that nature cannot do this, say it is foolish to believe, not knowing that, according to the Apostle, the foolishness of God is wiser than men. They would rightly judge us foolish if we believed of nature something it is shown to be unable to do. But we believe that God will do, if he has promised, what nature cannot. What foolishness can be found in that? If the work that God is believed able to do were unworthy of him, faith might rightly be likened to dullness. But if it is worthy of him, precisely because it is impossible for the creature, why should faith not be praised, which grants the Creator as much as the creature is denied the power to do?

Great and admirable, then, is Abraham, who did not hesitate to believe God against the world’s opinion, because God is able to do what he promises. A Chaldean by birth, he appeared as a teacher of belief: although skilled in astrology, he set God above human counsel, thinking it fitting to believe of God something whose manner of happening cannot be searched out. He strengthened his own weakness with the power of God, for God had determined, in order to declare the unique greatness of his majesty, to do things impossible and unheard of in the world. By doing so he would show himself the Lord of creation, and creation would submit to him whose work seemed impossible to all others. Their unbelief exalts most faithful Abraham all the more. His faith is the punishment of unbelievers, and the unbelief of unbelievers is his glory; for he is the father of the faithful and the judge of the faithless. By his example the good are granted eternal life and the wicked will pay eternal punishment. At a time when the world was still a child in knowledge and not yet made bright by signs and wonders that might draw it to faith, he did not refuse God his faith, even against his own knowledge.

Holy Abraham, then, was given to the human race as an example of the greatest faithfulness. In him it was prefigured that all nations would come to salvation through faith. So that the overflowing growth of his faith might be known, he was tested and commanded to sacrifice his son to God, something that had never been done. He was neither disturbed by the strangeness of the thing nor did he argue whether the killing of his own child ought to be done at the command of God, who had threatened punishment so that murder would not be done. So, fearless and confident about God’s will, he did not hesitate to hold that what God commands is wise, and to offer [?] this son, whom two old people had received by promise, the reward of faith, the sign of merit, and the one in whom lay all hope of the promised offspring to come. To carry this out with complete devotion, he did not tell the boy’s mother, lest she put some obstacle in the way of his offering, knowing that mothers are more inclined to tender love toward their children. So he kept it from her, not doubting that what God commands must be fulfilled, so that by this example we might be taught to carry out God’s commandments with all care.

For if most faithful Abraham is found obedient in a matter so grave and harsh, how much more should we be, who are commanded things that can be borne! O faith dedicated to God and hope firm in the Lord, so dear and so sweet that it is put before the love of parents and children, as Scripture says: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is!”

Our patriarch, most faithful Abraham, being a prophet, knew what he ought to follow. So what the Lord has now said, he did then: he put God before his son, however dear, in his love, as the Lord says: “Whoever loves father or mother or children more than me is not worthy of me.” Therefore the patriarch, so as to be worthy of the Lord above all others, did not refuse even to kill his son.
CXVIII. ON JOB

Great, dearly beloved brothers, is the love of almighty God toward the human race. Understood, it leads to the heavenly kingdom; not understood, it leads down to hell. For God wants his kindness to be welcomed and fruitful, so that it may benefit us and it may delight him to show mercy.

Therefore, since he is good and wills all people to be saved, he has shown us an example of righteousness in his servant Job, as the present reading testifies, so that by following it we may both avoid evil and come to good, not only free from punishment but also rewarded.

How admirable, then, is most holy Job! Before the law was published in writing, he showed in his deeds a model of the law. He learned nothing of this from anyone’s teaching, but with nature itself as his guide, in which God decreed that the seeds of righteousness should naturally be present, he kept reverence for the Creator with devout devotion.

How much praise, then, does he deserve, and with what words should his deeds be extolled, since we can find no one equal to him either before the law or after it? Even if someone could admire his deeds and follow them, he would not for that reason be compared with him, nor could he rightly be called his like. For what that person had become would not be his own, since he would have followed someone else’s example. But holy Job, though he had seen nothing of the kind and read nothing of it in books, showed himself such that he owed nothing to anyone; rather, he gave to others, providing a pattern of wonderful deeds by which to win the Lord’s favor. That is why he is commended by the testimony of the Lord, who says: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a true worshiper of God.”

Who could earn so much, to whom could the Lord bear such testimony, except one who is found to be not an imitator but the originator of what he did? That is why he is declared a true worshiper of God. For no pretense of feigned truth can be seen in someone who had no one like himself before him. Everyone who pretends imitates what he sees.

Yet there are still greater things than all these to be told. In these praises there were no proofs by trials, only a purpose dedicated to God and grounded in practice and observances. Because this did not seem to the tempter enough to earn a crown of merit, he asked to be allowed to test Job’s righteousness with various temptations, so that, hemmed in on many sides, he might get stuck somewhere and go beyond bounds. For this is why various punishments are usually inflicted on wrongdoers: since no one can bear every torment, one of them may wring from him a confession of the truth.

So the tempter was allowed to wipe out and destroy everything Job had, even to the death of his children, so that if he bore the loss of his oxen, he might not bear that of his sheep; or if he bore that of his sheep too, he might not bear the loss of his camels, or of his servants, or of all his property; or if, because he was great of spirit and of pure enough devotion, he was not overcome by all these things, he would surely be broken by the force of love at the death of all his children at once. But because he had the law written in his heart before the law was published, no losses and no bereavements made him any less devoted to God, so that he gave a pattern of how God is to be loved with the whole heart above all things. How much glory, then, does he deserve, who kept the law before the law, showing how the law that was to come was to be kept, not in words but as a doer in deeds!

And because the tempter is shameless and did not think even this glory enough to prove the righteous man, unless he devised something else against him that he knew no human being could bear, he asked again to be allowed to strike Job himself with a cruel wound from head to toenails. When this was permitted, since he is not to be trusted, he was commanded to spare Job’s life for the sake of his free choice, so that he would not dare any violence against one whom he could not overcome by right of reason. Having received this power, his savage cruelty flared up again within him, and he struck the righteous man with an exceedingly great blow, so that there was nothing in his body free from wounds, something no human being could endure except Job alone, who was able to conquer Satan. And when even so the devil’s wickedness could draw nothing out of the righteous man against God, he remembered his old cunning, by which he deceived Adam, to see whether he could deceive this man too through a woman, since a person is easily deceived through a member of his household.

Yet in all this the utterly shameless Satan gained nothing; indeed, he suffered loss, finding God’s servant not only unmoved but even a teacher. Placed in that very distress, Job not only persevered in the fear of God but also, rebuking his wife when she urged the opposite, taught that everything that happens by God’s permission is to be borne bravely. This amounts to a double punishment for short-sighted Satan: he did not persuade Job of what he wanted, and in envying him he made others learn what he did not want even Job to know.

How much temptation benefits God’s servants and harms the devil we are taught more fully by this reading. For when he thinks he is harming them, he advances them, and when he persecutes one, he spurs on many. Seeing that this man was protected by God’s help, many become his imitators. So in wanting to make a gain he suffered a loss, for his fury always does him harm. While he will not let the righteous be righteous, so that they may not be rewarded, he makes them more worthy; and in his jealousy of holy Job he doubled his merit in heaven and on earth, for Job was both increased here and received into heaven with the Savior. So all these things serve the glory of the saints and the punishment of the devil.
CXIX. ON TOBIT

So great is the providence of the Lord God toward us that, not wanting us to go astray, he gave both the law and examples of good works, by which a modest and peaceful life may be led in the fear of God. For he who is the author of life certainly does not want his work to be subject to death. Although nature itself is not without law, yet because the Lord is good and merciful, he showed in writing and by examples what is to be followed and what is to be avoided, so that these might be better known, as the present reading testifies.

Holy Tobit, the servant of God, was therefore given to us after the law as an example, so that we may know how the things we read are carried out, and so that if temptations come we may not depart from the fear of God or hope for help from anyone but him, remembering that it is written: “I was young and have grown old, and I have never seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread.”

So whoever hopes in God with his whole mind can never be deceived. Even if troubles arise for a time through the snares of Satan, the examples of holy men teach us that God permits them only for the increase of our merits. If they are borne with an even mind, we will be given consolation here, with real effect, and in the future eternal life with glory. For our God, because he is just and shows no partiality, allows us to be tempted because he loves us, so that after our toil he can give us the richest rewards. Indeed, when the Apostle begged that temptations might depart from him, the Lord said: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” Following on from this he says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger,” and: “I rejoice in my troubles, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

How praiseworthy holy Tobit is, Scripture teaches us. Captivity did not lessen his devotion, the loss of his eyes did not persuade him to bless God any less, and the exhausting of his property did not turn him from the way of righteousness and truth. For hardship proves the righteous, and to keep fairness in poverty is true and perfect righteousness. What lessens some people’s devotion is the very thing by which Tobit, worthy of praise, grew. “Poverty,” it says, “humbles a man, and one who is humbled cannot keep righteousness.” But holy Tobit’s soul, lifted up to God, was neither broken by captivity nor humbled by poverty. Against the prohibition he committed the bodies of the slain to burial, and, confident in God’s bounty, he was merciful out of his little, knowing that the mercy that comes from little is more pleasing to God, as with that widow whom the Lord praised in the Gospel. For he is truly faithful, he does not doubt God’s promises, who gives generously out of little.

So, consoling his soul with the hope of things to come, Tobit, devoted to God, was found strong and steadfast in temptation, showing that in hardship one must be all the more watchful in the fear of God; for if hardship does not drive us to God’s help, how much less will security! Holy men, then, being certain that God has reserved to himself the judgment of everything that happens in this world, bore troubles, losses and other ruin or insults not with resentment but even with gladness, as did our apostles too, who, when they had been beaten, rejoiced that they had been counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of God. For the ruin unjustly inflicted on the faithful, whether in troubles or in insults, is a sign of merits to come.

So righteous Tobit pleased God so much that he received the reward of his merits in two ways. In the present life, through the ministry of an angel, he recovered the sight he had lost and was also enriched with the goods that belong to this present life; and in the future he was made an heir of the kingdom of heaven. By this we are taught that whoever obeys God’s law with his whole heart and does not doubt his promises is cared for by God in this world and is granted eternal life in the world to come.

There is something else, too, that invites us to the service of God. Holy Tobit not only obtained the merits of his own righteousness; his glory is heaped up still further by the good deeds of those who become his imitators. For examples are praised in their imitators, and this could happen for us too, if we live in such a way that we also are worthy to have imitators.
CXX. ON FASTING

It is fitting, dearest brothers, that a priest of God and overseer of Christ's people should most devoutly exhort the people placed under his care in sound doctrine, as the apostle commands, so that we may perform the work of faith as the season requires, with all care and diligence and with an eager and devout mind. The fasts that are now to be kept, as the feast day of Easter approaches, bring benefits that are no secret, but they still should not be passed over in silence. Devotion is stirred when things are reviewed again, even though they are already known. Such is the character of our nature that it grows sluggish if the practice of reading stops. Just as iron gathers rust unless it is used, so too sins will spring up in the soul unless it exercises itself often in divine readings. That is why in the psalm he calls blessed the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.

Indeed, although the divine words are known, yet when they are recalled from the sacred books the devout heart receives them as though they were new. The soul's desire for saving works is aroused. Hence the apostle says to Timothy, among other things: "that you rekindle the grace of God that is in you." Fasts, therefore, are as necessary to us as medicine is to wounds. They bring healing for eternal life, but only when they are commended by the witness of two things, namely prayer and mercy.

Fasts, then, temper the body's excess, check hostile impulses, and lift the burden from the soul, as the Lord says: "Do not give yourselves over to food and drunkenness, lest your hearts be weighed down." When the soul has been freed from food and drink, it recognizes itself better. Just as a person does not see himself as he is in a dirty mirror, so too, if he is weighed down with food and drunkenness, he perceives himself as other than he is. Then lust is aroused, anger kindled, pride inflamed, and debauchery born. Hence the apostle says: "Do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery." But if the body is tempered by a time of fasting, the soul regains knowledge of itself and understands with what devotion it ought to serve the Redeemer.

Fasts, therefore, are necessary in great measure. Under Queen Esther, when the Jewish people were in danger, they were delivered with the help of fasting. And the Ninevites, when they had heard from the prophet the day appointed for their overthrow, proclaimed a fast and were found worthy to escape. Our righteous men and prophets too, when they wished to obtain something from God, humbled themselves by fasting, as David says: "I humbled my soul with fasting." Even the Savior, who had no need of it, fasted in order to give us an example.

So no one doubts that fasts are beneficial. A person shows that he wishes to obtain what he asks for when he afflicts himself with fasting. Hence it is said: "Prayer is good with fasting." So that prayer may be acceptable, it wants to have the support of fasting. And since none of these is firm without piety, it added: "and almsgiving with righteousness," so that almsgiving, with righteousness preserved, may commend prayer joined with fasting. Thus Cornelius's mercy commended his prayer and fasting. He was rich, and he fasted, but he also fed those who had nothing, so that their being filled might make his fast acceptable. Fasting, then, needs some things and must be free of others, so that it may merit what it asks.
CXXI. THE PRAISE AND GLORY OF EASTER

O holy and saving day of Easter, worthy to be proclaimed with every praise! On this day death was conquered and the devil's kingdom taken from him; the mystery of God was made manifest, and the decree that stood against us was cancelled. The gates of hell were broken, the bound set free, the imprisoned released, the blind enlightened, the ignorant given knowledge, the ungodly made merciful, the unjust made just. Forgiveness of sins was granted, enemies were reconciled, error was corrected, truth was declared; sons were won for God from among the lost. Pride was brought low and humility exalted; the poor were enriched and the rich emptied; mountains were levelled, valleys filled and hills laid low. Shamelessness was trampled down and modesty strengthened. Souls were given access to heaven, freedom was restored, and captivity was broken and dissolved. Darkness grew numb, malice was confounded, filth was purified. Satan was cast down and hell emptied; our Lord Jesus Christ was proved to be the true Son of God; flesh was taken up into heaven, to the confusion of the wise of this world; and things in heaven, on earth and under the earth were shown to belong to the one God and Lord!

Therefore, dearest brothers, we ought to celebrate and revere this feast day in devotion to God, with moderation of life and gladness of heart, avoiding what is shameful and dishonorable, so that we may be found worthy to come to the fruit of Easter, through Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
CXXII. ON "IN THE BEGINNING"

"In the beginning was the Word." What does "in the beginning" mean? We also read in the old books: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." And in the epistle of the one whose gospel this is, whose "beginning" we are trying to say something about, the same meaning is expressed, for he says: "That which was from the beginning." So the epistle and the gospel have one meaning. But what is said in the Old Testament, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," is one thing. It is another when it says, "In the beginning was the Word," and "That which was from the beginning." To be "in the beginning" and to be "from the beginning" mean the same thing, since what was from the beginning did not begin to be. What begins to be was not from the beginning, and so it is placed under a "beginning": it is said to have begun to be in the beginning. That is, it is first in order among other things, because what was made in the beginning began to have others after it, which were made after it. So we read that "in the beginning God made heaven and earth." He did not say, "In the beginning were heaven and earth," because they did not yet exist when God was arranging to make the world. "In the beginning" means that among the things that went into building the world, "he first made heaven and earth." For a beginning is the start of someone undertaking something, that which is first in order.

But the saying that "in the beginning was" (that is, the Word) signifies that he existed before creation above and below began. So he would certainly not be understood as made first among the things that were created, since he was in the beginning, when God was arranging to make creation. If, then, he was in the beginning, that is, before all things, he always was; and so also "the Word was."

[?] "with God," he says, so that what was always with God would by no means be thought to be wrongly placed under a beginning. For it is fitting that what was with God before all things should be subject to no beginning.

Hence he also added: "and the Word was God." Now he shows openly that what was said above applies to the Word, for the Word, he says, is God. And one must not think of God in any other way than as one who is said always to have existed. If he began, he is a creature; if he is a creature, he is not God. Whatever exists is either God or creature, and so the name of God does not belong to a creature. But because he did not begin to be (for he "was"), he is rightly called God.

He is said always to have been with God because he is God not from himself but from God. For this reason his name is also given as "the Word of God," as the faith of the same evangelist shows in his Revelation. Among other things he says: "And his name is the Word of God." He was called "the Word of God" so that what is signified would be not the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom all things are; that is, not the Father but the Son. Since God cannot be without his Word, this one who is called "the Word of God" is believed always to have been with God. And since a word is not outside the one whose word it is, this Word which was with God is understood to be signified as coming not from elsewhere but from God; and since he is from God, it is not absurd for him to be called God.

So to say that God was with God does not make two gods. If there were two, they would differ in nature and would not have one will. If we humans, though we are of one nature, still have different wills, how much more where the nature also differs! Nor would God then be said to be with God. For the God who was and is with God does not have his being God from himself. Were it otherwise, God would not be said to be with God, nor would the "Word of God" be called God the Word. But since what is from God signifies nothing other than what God is, the "Word of God" has been named God. Because he is called "the Word of God," he is not referred to some other god; and he is called God lest it dishonor God if what was from God were not called God. Thus the unity of God has been preserved and due honor rendered, since he who is God from God has been received not in his own glory but in the glory of him from whom he is God.

That is why the gospel begins to speak about the Word before it speaks of God the Father: the questions are raised not about God but about the Word of God. No one has doubts about God, but about him who is God from God. Every tongue of those in heaven and on earth confesses one God, but is thrown into confusion by the mystery of the one God. It trembles when it hears the Word of God called God, for it is troubled by bodily ways of thinking, since a man's word cannot be called a man. Yet God is surely simple in nature. He is not composed of members; he has no inside and outside, no front and back, no top and bottom, but, if one may say so, he is wholly the same throughout, never varied or unlike. His brightness is one and immeasurable; for if fire has no front and back or inside and outside, how much more is this true of its creator! And so, since everything that God is, is wholly one, there is no discord when what is from God is called God.

In one respect, then, after a human pattern, and in another respect not after a human pattern, the Son of God, who is the Word of God, is God. In the same way that the sons of men are men, the Son of God is God. But the sons of men are men through intercourse, and the Son of God is not God after this pattern, for he was born simply from the simple God. And just as our word is from us, by this pattern the Word of God is understood to be from God. But because our word is not what we are, the Word of God is not from God in this way, for the Word of God is a reality, not a sound that dies away.

Just because certain words are used both of us and of God, it does not follow that what they describe happens in the same way for us and for God. We read: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." How did he make them? Was it with his hands, as we make things? And in what follows it says: "And God said, 'Let there be light'; and there was light." How do we think God spoke? He certainly did not speak to a man, but to one who was able to make things, who was also going to make man, as he did. Did he speak as we speak, with a bodily organ? Far from it. You see, then, that the words are indeed shared by us and God, but they differ in what they describe. God makes otherwise than we make, and he is said to speak, but not in our manner.

So too the Word of God is not a word like ours, which no longer exists once it has been spoken. That Word remains, because it is a Word that hears and speaks and acts. And this Son of God is not only "the Word of God" but also "the power and wisdom of God." As regards his being brought forth, he is called the Son of God. As regards the address by which God speaks to us through him, he is called the Word of God. As regards the wisdom by which God teaches us his mystery through him, he is called the Wisdom of God. And as regards working, since God made and makes all things through him, he is called the Power of God.

These titles could belong to no one but the Son of God. Because he is God from God, he is called everything that belongs to God, for by being born he obtained all that is God's. It would not have been fitting for one of a lesser kind to be called the Word of God and the Power and Wisdom of God, for this is what God is: Word, Power, Wisdom. But Christ, because he is God, wholly from the whole God, is called the Wisdom of God and the Power and the Word of God; that is, he is God from God and with God.

That is why he says: "He was in the beginning with God." To overcome the minds of unbelievers, Scripture was compelled to burst out and show that Christ is God. Everywhere else it wants Christ to be understood as God on account of the unity of God, but here it has said openly that he is God and has always been with God. In laying open the mystery of God, lest he be thought altogether solitary, it declared that God is not called one in order that he be considered solitary. Though there are two or three, they are still from one and do not prejudice the unity, because what is from one is referred back to that very one, since he is one.

All things are said to be from God, but it is one thing to have come forth from God in the proper sense and another to have been created outside him by God's command. That is, it is one thing to proceed from his substance and another to be created by his will when it did not exist at all. What proceeded from God's substance never [?] through substance, whereas what was created began to exist in substance when it was created. And therefore the Trinity alone has no beginning.

Disclosing the mystery, then, lessened the merits of faith. The more hidden what is believed, the greater the believer's reward and the lighter the punishment of the one who does not trust. And just as disclosing the mystery made believers merit less, so it brought greater punishments upon those who do not trust. A clearer law makes a man more guilty.

The Savior's testimony, in which he said that God was his own Father, would have been enough. For who among believers would doubt that the Son differs in no way from the Father in substance? But the perversity of heretics had begun to attack the laws of faith with inventions of unbelief, understanding the Son of God otherwise than he is proclaimed. So, to make the matter plain, it was added that he was with God before all things and is God. This declared openly what was contained in mystery in the idea of a true Son. In this the divine mercy seems to have provided for human weakness, by opening what it had kept closed for the merits of a stronger faith.

Hence he added: "All things were made through him." Human understanding is too narrow to grasp divine things, so if anyone was uncertain about any point in what came before, these words would enable him to grasp it. When he hears, "All things were made through him," he would certainly not think that the Word himself was a thing made, since he hears that all things were made by God through him. If he too were a thing made, it would not have said that all things were made by God through him, for he was not made through himself.

To convey this still more completely, he added: "and without him nothing was made." By saying this he shut out every dispute and earthly argument. Although there are [?] some who do not trust, yet by showing that nothing was made without him, he taught that one should in no way suspect him to be a thing made. How can he be said to be a thing made, when God is said to have made nothing without him? If God made him, Scripture lies. But far from it, for Scripture is faithful. To cut away error, it uses all the clarity it can to win back the salvation of humankind.

Then he went on: "What was made in him is life." "In him," that is, in the Word: he means that what was made is life. As the Lord himself says: "As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself." This is not because the Word was without life and afterwards life was given or made in him; rather, he wants the Word itself to be understood to be life. If it could be said of God the Father that he himself is one thing and has another thing in himself, then the same could be said of his Son, since "as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself."

Human speech is not adequate to explain divine things. So what is said seems faulty: though the Son of God is not a thing made, something is said to have been "made" in him. If he had said, "What was begotten in him," that too would have seemed faulty. But to show that his generation is substantial, he used the best language he could to point to the work done in it, through which he came to exist: his generation has life in itself.

We live, but we cannot give life to others, since that life is not in our power. He, however, is said to have life in himself because he is able to give life to and to create whatever he wills, so that it may exist and live. He is said to have been born for this, that he might be able to do all that the Father does, because he has life in himself just as the Father has. That is, the Father made all things through him and in him, and begot him in such a way that he would have life in himself, through which he could do all things. It is not that he is something other than life; rather, because his life is able both to live and to create other things that live, he is said to have life in himself. We live, but we do not have life in ourselves in such a way that we can give life to others. The apostle Paul also mentions this sense when he says, among other things: "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn before all creation, for in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him."

The gospels of the two apostles John and Paul agree, for they say the same thing: the Son of God was begotten before all creation in order to create the spiritual powers, the world, and the visible things in it. What John said, "What was made in him is life," Paul also meant when he said, "In him all things were created in heaven and on earth."

And in what follows: "All things were created through him and for him." He created "through him" because in substance he is the same God, that is, the Father in the Son. He created "for him" because he begot the Son in such a way that he had the power to make all things visible and invisible. This is what it meant to have made life in him: that he should both live and, as the image of God, grant to others, according to his will, the life of living, acting and understanding, and also grant life to the other living creatures.

For when he is called the image of God, this refers to both things. By a birth that expressed the Father exactly, he has in himself the full likeness of the Father, and he can do whatever the Father can do. So it is true that the Father is seen in the Son, who is the image of the invisible God.

Surely, by calling the Father invisible, he did not make the Son visible, since the Son is by nature what the Father is? And if the heavenly creation is invisible, how much more is its creator! But he meant what is in heaven, not what is on earth. Although the Son too is invisible, yet there, in the heavenly realm, he is seen by the apostles and by others like them. Of them he said: "Father, I want these also to be with me where I am, and to see my glory." And elsewhere he says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God"; that is, the Father in the Son, God in the image, which is God in God.

Just as a body is the image of a bodily being, so God is the image of God. For the Father is the exemplar, while the Son is an exemplar from the exemplar, and the Son shares this with the Holy Spirit: "for he will take from what is mine," he says. Therefore God is seen in the Son as in his own image. Just as no one was found worthy to open the book and its seals except the Word of God, so no one is worthy, either by nature or by merit, to see God the Father except his true Son. There is nothing standing between the Father and the Son, as he himself testifies to us when he says: "No one has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen God."

But if the Father is seen in the Son, why is no one said to be worthy to see God, when he is seen in the Son, since the Son differs in nothing from the Father? Plainly he differs in nothing in substance, because he is a true Son. But he differs in cause or rank, because all power in the Son comes from the Father. And though the Son is not less in substance, the Father is greater in authority, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: "If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."

The apostle Paul keeps to this order when he says: "There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him." So the first rank is the one from whom all things are, the second the one through whom all things are, and the third the one in whom all things are. And because none of these is of a lesser kind, they are signified in the unity of God, as the apostle says: "For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory."
CXXIII. DID ADAM HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT?

I have learned that some of our brothers have not examined the Scriptures thoroughly, but in simplicity of mind assert that Adam, when he was made, received the Holy Spirit, as it is now given to believers, and that he lost it by sinning. They are led to this by the argument that many commonly put forward: that through faith man has been restored in such a way that, returned to his original state, he received everything that Adam had obtained at the beginning. They also argue that man must be said to have been made perfect, and "if he did not have the Holy Spirit," they say, "he was imperfect."

I, however, say that not only man but all the things God made are perfect, although they cannot be said to have received the Holy Spirit. Every kind of animal is perfect in its own way, so that it fulfils the purpose for which it was made. So too man is perfect in his own way, able to tell evil from good and crooked from right. For he is a rational animal, perfect for the purpose for which he was made. He is capable of learning, of thinking things out and of making things, so that what he cannot accomplish by strength he accomplishes by understanding.

And how have they dared to say that man is born perfect and knows everything, when they see that he knows nothing beyond what he learns here? What he does not learn here, he does not know. Indeed, since he does not learn here what he himself is, he does not know it. So if he does not know what he himself is, how does he know all things, when knowing oneself is a smaller thing than knowing everything else? But because he learns about other things and does not learn about himself, he knows about others and does not know about himself: neither what he is, nor whether he existed before the body or only after it.

For if he had been made so perfect that he lacked nothing, he would not have been a man but God, and he would not have been deceived into transgression. To have the Holy Spirit, however, lies beyond man's nature and perfection, for it enables him to do the things of God. When the donkey spoke to Balaam, was that not beyond its own perfection? It received the power to do what belonged not to its nature but to ours.

So, because man is superior to the other animals, must they be called imperfect? Or are the holy angels imperfect because they are not what God is? Or are the lights and stars less perfect because they are lower than the angels above, or because the clouds hide the sun and moon behind their veil? And will the limbs be called imperfect because they need one another, since the feet cannot do what the hands can? Far from it. All things are sound and perfect in their own places and ranks, so that they fulfil the purpose for which they were made.

All things, then, are perfect, because their Creator is perfect; yet compared with him they are imperfect. For God is perfect in every respect, as the fount and origin of all things. The things that have been made are indeed perfect, but only for the purpose for which they were made, so that in another respect they are not perfect, because one needs another. Each is perfect in what it does not need, not in what it needs; and so all things are both perfect and imperfect. The hands need the feet, because unless the feet walk, the hands will be idle. Again, the feet need the hands, for they cannot put on their own shoes or tend themselves.

So although the body is perfect in its limbs, it still cannot fly, nor carry as much as a mule can. And although mules are perfect in these things, they do not know how to govern themselves, nor can they apply medicine to themselves. Hence it is said: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." Water and fire too, though they oppose each other, are perfect in their own way, for they fulfil the purpose for which they were made. Fire cooks and consumes, purifies and warms; water washes, cools, irrigates and refreshes the thirsty.

So although all things are perfect in their own way, without man they can do nothing; nor can man, though he is more perfect, do anything without them. This is why the apostle calls us both imperfect and perfect. Compared with unbelievers we are perfect, because we have come to know God; but because we know less than we ought about what has been promised, and because in this life we cannot grasp as much as there is to believe, we are imperfect. Since, then, they think that Adam's perfection is restored to believers, let us see whether this restoration carries no divine gift beyond what Adam had obtained.

When Adam was made, "he was placed in paradise to work there and to keep it": that is, to till the ground and to keep God's commandments, through which he would know that, though he had received dominion over all things, he himself still lived under the law of his Creator, so that his dominion would not exalt him and, puffed up with pride, he would not forget his Maker. He was placed there, then, so that his life might be sustained by food; but through Christ it has been granted that those who rise again need neither food nor drink, because what is mortal in man will be turned into life. Adam was made to dwell on earth; but faith has deigned to bestow on us a dwelling in heaven.

Scripture itself bears witness, saying: "The first man Adam was made a living soul, but the second man a life-giving spirit." "The first man," it says, "was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly one, so too are the earthly; as is the heavenly one, so too are the heavenly." What could be plainer proof that Adam did not have the Holy Spirit? He was made a living soul, but through Christ man is made into a life-giving spirit, so that man may in some way resemble his Creator and be what he believes. For since the mystery of faith, given for salvation, is threefold, man is made threefold: body, soul and Holy Spirit, through whom we are called sons of God, a name Adam is nowhere shown to have been given, for he was made earthly. But the sons of God, born not carnally but spiritually, are called heavenly.

See, it is established that God's gift granted far more grace in the time of the Savior than Adam had received, because man has not only been restored but also improved: restored in that he has been washed of his sins, improved in everything else. Both justice and reason demanded that God's mercy should be more abundant in bestowing benefits at the time when he chose to make the mystery of his divinity known to creation. Thus those who come to know what was unknown through ages and generations, that the sacrament of the one God consists in a Trinity, would, as a kind of dedication of this new thing, be washed of their sins and moreover justified, and, adopted by God, would receive the Holy Spirit, through whom they would be seen to bear the mark of adoption. For those adopted by God must bear the mark of God the Father, so that they may rightly be called sons of God.

This gift was promised through the prophets, to be given at the time when the mystery of God was to be declared in triumph over conquered death, so that creation might know that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God. This is why the evangelist says: "The Spirit had not been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified." For this is his glorification: when by his power he is recognized to be what he testified about himself. This glorification bestowed the gift that had been promised through the prophet Joel, for God says: "In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh," and so on. And the apostle says, among other things: "But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal, through the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Christ Jesus our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life." The apostle confirmed what had been promised through the prophet Joel: that after Jesus was glorified God fulfilled this, pouring out the Holy Spirit on those who believe in Christ, and that to receive the Holy Spirit is "to become an heir of eternal life," so that, since the Spirit is eternal, whoever has received him has eternal life. For he is the pledge of immortality.

Whoever has received him and remains in his love passes through this life and goes to heaven, to the one whose Spirit he has. It would be unfitting for someone who departs from here with the Holy Spirit to be held in the underworld. For his Spirit is the sign in man of Christ's victory, by which he conquered death, so that whoever has his Spirit cannot be held by the underworld. For this reason the Holy Spirit was not in the saints of old as he now is in the faithful, because when they left this world they were in the underworld. And it cannot be said that the Holy Spirit was held along with them under the sentence passed on Adam because of Adam's sin, which, passed down through the race, made all his offspring subject to the underworld.

There is no doubt, then, that the Holy Spirit was with the prophets and with righteous men: with the prophets for the sake of God's plan, with the righteous on account of their holiness. So we read of holy Simeon that "the Holy Spirit was with him," not as a mark of adoption in him but because of his merits. For believers began to be sons of God only when the Son of God was revealed to all creation by conquering death.

But if the Holy Spirit is said to have been in Adam or in others as he now is in the faithful, what new gifts did God give when he dedicated the kingdom of his Son in us? And how is the Savior's coming called a happy and blessed time above all others, if it granted what had already been granted? And what becomes of the Savior's words to his disciples: "Many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it"?

On what grounds, then, could it be said that the blessedness of this time conferred no greater gift than was conferred on those of old? This would be an insult to the Savior, as if he had nothing new to give to those who received him at the dawn of his reign, when even rich men make a point of giving their guests choice gifts to take home on the feast of their birthday. How great an insult to the Lord, then, to say that he had nothing untried to give to those he invited to a new and unheard-of feast, worthy of all praise! And what becomes of the words of John the evangelist: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but to all who received him he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God"? How, then, is what God gave to those who believe in Christ not something unprecedented, when he gave them power to become sons of God, that is, brothers of his own Son, born not of the will of flesh and blood or of man but of God, so that they might be born spiritually? Or if this grace is proved to have been granted earlier, then let it be said that Christ's coming brought nothing new.

Adam's making was certainly carnal and earthly, not spiritual. He was not born of God without flesh and blood, but was made by God from the earth. So he could not receive the Holy Spirit, since he was not spiritual and had not been granted the right to call God Father in prayer. For those who receive the Holy Spirit have been given the power, because they have the Spirit of God, to call him, the God of Christians, Father in prayer. Since this was not granted before, those of earlier times cannot be said to have had the Holy Spirit. Those, then, who think that Adam or others had the Holy Spirit do not know what kind of gift from God they possess, nor can they give him fitting thanks, since, though they have received more than the rest, they say they have obtained nothing more.
124. THAT ONE AND THE SAME DEED DIFFERS, WHETHER FOR PRAISE OR FOR CONDEMNATION, ACCORDING TO THE PERSON WHO DOES IT.

Mercy is one and the same in a rich man and in a poor man, but it is credited differently to the rich man and to the poor man, because it is more praiseworthy in the poor man than in the rich. For the poor man was not afraid to give out of his scanty means, hoping to be repaid by God both in the present and in the future. He believes the Scripture that says, "Whoever gives to the poor will not be in want." This is why that poor widow, while the rich were putting in a great deal, alone earned the Lord's praise, because she was not afraid to give out of her poverty. The rich give feeling secure in their riches, but the poor man feels secure in the Lord. So the rich do well when they give to the needy, but the poor do much better, and for this reason the poor man's reward is one thing and the rich man's another. For if the rich man does not do this, he will be beaten; but not so much is required of the poor man, and so the merciful poor man is praiseworthy.

Theft is one and the same sin in a poor man and in a rich man, but it makes the rich man more guilty, because the poor man steals out of want, while the rich man, though he has plenty, is not content with his own and takes what belongs to others. And, what is worse, they usually rob the poor. For this reason the punishment of the two differs.

Righteousness too is one and the same in a poor man and in a rich man, but it is more praiseworthy in the poor man. To keep to righteousness in poverty is a splendid thing; the rich man seems to keep to righteousness because he is a stranger to want. Both, then, are righteous, but it is greater to keep to righteousness in need.

Pride is one and the same, but it is more to be condemned in a poor man than in a rich man, because the rich man is puffed up by his abundance, whereas the poor man is proud in his poverty, which borders on madness. For this reason the poor man is more guilty.

Humility is one and the same, but it is more to be praised in a rich man. What is so great about a poor man appearing humble, when his very poverty makes him humble? But it is a splendid thing if a man distinguished by rank and wealth stoops down and does not claim for himself what he knows he deserves. Humility, then, is good in everyone, but much more so in a rich man.

Learning and study have the same purpose for both, but they are more praiseworthy in a rich man. The poor man, having no advantage to recommend him, worked to acquire something for which he might be sought out. But the rich man, though he did not lack things to recommend him, improved himself by hard work so as to be needed on two counts. He was not distracted by his wealth and did not hold back his mind from flourishing by its own efforts. So he is more worthy of praise than the poor man, who, had he not devoted himself to study, would have remained of no account in every way. The one was made eager for study by his will, the other by necessity.

Lust is the same in a poor man and in a rich man, but it is more damnable in the poor man than in the rich. Poverty itself ought to call the poor man back from the craving for luxury. He ought to reflect that he has no means of satisfying it, and that in hurrying to satisfy it he must necessarily commit many other wrongs, from which he may not escape even in the present; or at any rate, by spending what little he has, he will be left a beggar and disgraced besides. The rich, on the other hand, are provoked to the pleasure of lust by an abundance of luxuries, and besides they feel sure of going unpunished, knowing that the courts can be bought and that no one will rebuke them. For who would dare to reprove a rich man backed by high rank? So they are inflamed all the more, even to the point of acting with violence. Not only are they not reproached, but they are held in great honor, so that they can even boast of being what they are.

8. But if both, the poor man and the rich man, are chaste, the chastity of the rich man differs greatly from that of the poor man. The poor man may be held back by his lowly station from being able to do what he wants, or by fear of the laws; but the rich man, since many factors combine to lure him into pleasure, is praiseworthy if he turns his mind away from it. So the chaste rich man deserves one reward and the chaste poor man another. And if a king is chaste, that is very glorious: having everything in his power, he does not touch what he knows he could do with impunity. He truly fears God and truly keeps his commandments who, though he holds the laws in his power, keeps God's coming judgment before his eyes. So it is a great thing when someone who has no one to fear in the present conquers what delights him, since delight is so powerful that it does not fear even present things, let alone future ones. Hence those who overcome it earn great merit, but more so the one who in the present rules over laws and men. For others fear both men and laws, and that is why they hold to their resolve: to avoid being shamed before men they keep up what they have long maintained, and to avoid being condemned they abstain from what is forbidden. But this man, who by reason of his power neither fears the laws nor feels shame before men, wins great glory if he restrains himself.
125. AGAINST EUSEBIUS.

I remember reading in a little book by Eusebius, a man once distinguished in other respects, that not even the Holy Spirit knows the mystery of the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ. I am amazed that a man of such learning inflicted this stain on the Holy Spirit, for by saying this he implied that the Spirit is of an inferior kind. Someone who does not know the things of God cannot be said to be from God, because an inferior nature does not know what is in a superior one. But if he is of the same substance and divinity, how can he fail to know what is his own? Indeed the Son of God, having said, "I and the Father are one," because of their unity of substance, rightly added: "All that is the Father's is mine, and what is mine is the Father's."

So if the Holy Spirit is of the same divinity, on what grounds is he set apart and denied the same knowledge, when no one denies that he is of the same substance? You grant the greater thing and withhold the lesser. A creature learns, and begins to know some things about its maker, and what it has learned it would then share with its maker. But substance, or divinity, cannot be shared by God and a creature. God's substance has nothing to learn, because there is nothing it does not know. Human substance, on the other hand, does not have knowing in its nature, but learning. So knowledge is added to human nature, yet the substance is not changed, because human nature lacks knowledge. Its substance was created so that it acquires knowledge through practice.

Substance is therefore greater than knowledge, because knowledge does not acquire substance; substance acquires knowledge. Substance exists without knowledge, but knowledge cannot exist without substance. In God, however, knowledge is just as substance is. A substance that has nothing to learn is its own knowledge. That is why everything in God is called substantial. A substance that lacks nothing has all things substantially, because nothing has come to it through effort.

How then can it be said of the Holy Spirit that he does not know the birth of the Son of God, if he is consubstantial with him? Can one and the same substance both know and not know? Certainly the Son of God did not learn the mystery of his own birth; he knows it substantially, not by being taught. On what grounds, then, is the Holy Spirit said not to know, when he too has nothing to learn, because he knows all things through his substance?

Like the Son of God, the Holy Spirit too is the substance of God. The Lord says: "All that the Father has is mine," and by this he indicated that the substance of God the Father is his own substance. He also says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from what is his: "That is why I said, he will take from what is mine, because all that the Father has is mine." If the Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from the Son, how can he be ignorant of the Son's birth, when his substance is the Son's substance? For all that is the Father's is the Son's. Without doubt, then, the Father's substance is in the Holy Spirit. For the Son added: "And all that is mine is the Father's."

Why then is there any doubt about whether the Holy Spirit is of the same divinity, when he is of the same substance? Just as the Lord said of himself that he came forth from God, so he testifies of the Holy Spirit too. And so that this could not be interpreted otherwise, he says, "He proceeds from the Father," and, "He will take from what is mine," meaning that to proceed from the Father is to receive from Christ. When the Spirit is said to receive from the Son of God, there is no doubt that he himself is also from God, and so there can be no doubt that the substance and divinity of the Father are in the Holy Spirit.

So whoever says that the Spirit does not know the birth of the Son of God disparages the very one from whom the Spirit is said to have received. What he received is nothing other than what the one he received from is, because to have received from Christ means to have proceeded from God. He therefore cannot be ignorant of what the one he received from knows, and he must not be said to be ignorant of God, since he proceeded from God.

Certainly the Son of God, because he is from God the Father, knows all the things of God. Why then should it be denied that the Holy Spirit knows the things of Christ, when he has received from him? If the Son of God knows what is in God, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit also knows what is in the Son of God, and because he knows what is in the Son, he must not be said to be ignorant of what is in God. From the one from whom he received, he has knowledge of God.

But why are we laboring, when the apostle is our witness on this point, saying: "No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God"? See, what we have long sweated over we have completed with the apostle's help. And did he slight the Son of God by saying that no one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God? Far from it. In the same way the Son did not slight the Holy Spirit when he said: "No one knows the Father except the Son." He said that no one knows what is in God except the one who is from God, because everything that is from God knows God and what is in God. The nature of God knows itself. And once you understand that this nature is also in the Holy Spirit, since he proceeded from the Father and received from the Son, it is not safe to say that he does not know God the Father, whose nature you recognize in him.

And yet when the Savior said that no one knows God except the Son, he said it in a way that reserved this knowledge for another person too. He immediately added: "and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." To whom, do you suppose, does the Son choose to reveal him? No one can be dearer to him than his own Spirit, for "if anyone," he says, "does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." How then do you suppose God the Father is revealed by the Son to the Holy Spirit, if not in the way the Lord himself says: "He will take from what is mine"? God the Father cannot be revealed to a creature, because nothing can bear the nature of God unless it is of the same substance. For he dwells in unapproachable light, unapproachable, that is, to the creature.

But some think the Holy Spirit is rightly said not to know the mystery of the birth of the Son of God, because he is said to search all things, and, they argue, "one who searches certainly does not know." This must be understood in light of other passages. For God says, among other things: "I am God, who search minds and hearts"; and in the psalm: "God, who searches hearts and minds"; and the apostle says: "He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to the will of God."

From these examples it is clear that when the Spirit of God is said to search, it means that he is not ignorant. He is said to search "even the depths of God": and what are the depths of God that he is said to see into? To search means to penetrate hidden things, and so we should believe that nothing is hidden from him. The deep mysteries of God are God's inner things, which cannot be searched out by a creature. We also read that he intercedes for the saints according to the will of God, which the saints certainly do not know, as the apostle says: "For we do not know what to pray for as we ought." So to know the depths of God and to know the will of God mean the same thing. For what mystery is as deep as the will of God, which is known to the Holy Spirit but unknown to everyone else?

We should also consider how it is said that "no one knows what is in a man except the man's spirit that is within him." By "spirit" he meant the mind: no one knows what is in a man's mind except his own mind, which is his spirit. In the same way, no one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God, that is, God himself.

For one who is from God is understood to be nothing other than what God is. The Spirit of God knows what is in God precisely because he is from God. If no one but God knows human thoughts, how much more is it true that no one can know the secrets and will of God unless he is from God, that is, unless he is God himself! For God is known to himself alone.

Of course, there are no deliberations in God. He does not debate within himself what to do or not to do, weighing whether it is expedient, because everything in God is without hesitation, not by accident but by substance, not by effort but by nature, since he does not change. And so the Holy Spirit knows the mysteries of God in no other way than through substance, for one substance has one mind and one will.

He is speaking of God, who is always one and unchangeable, whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit. What the Father wills, the Son wills too, and what the Son wills, the Holy Spirit wills as well. That is why he is sometimes called the Spirit of God and sometimes the Spirit of Christ, because "he comes forth from God," he says, and: "he will take from what is mine."

This is why the apostle John says: "By this we know that God abides in us, by his Spirit whom he has given us." So if God is said to abide in us when the Spirit of God abides in us, this shows that the Spirit of God is God.

Indeed, this is the sign that believers are children of God: when they receive the Spirit, they dare to call themselves sons of God. Unless they have the sign of deity, they cannot be called sons of God. Since none of them is a true son of God, whole from whole, as Christ is, they become sons of God by adoption. Receiving the Spirit of Christ, they are called sons of God through him, because the Spirit they have within them is from God. For in sons, even adopted ones, something of the father's substance ought to be seen.

In the world, because things are imperfect, sons adopted by human beings receive no pledge, only the name. But God, because he is perfect, does more: he gives his Spirit to those he adopts, so that through the Spirit they may be seen to have some reality, since names without realities are empty.

Our apostle supports this claim of ours when he says: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!" How is it that elsewhere he says the depths of God, that is, his secrets, can be searched out, but here he denies it, calling them unsearchable? In this passage he was speaking of the creature: the secrets or judgments of God are unsearchable to it. But for the Holy Spirit, because he knows all the things of God, he said that everything in God can be searched out, so as to assert that what is unknown to the creature is not unknown to the Spirit of God. It cannot be denied, then, that a nature which knows what no creature can grasp is the nature of God.

Those who say that the Holy Spirit is of an inferior kind attack the purpose of God, who declared that the salvation of the whole creation rests on the divinity of the Trinity. If the Spirit is not consubstantial with God and Christ, it is absurd to count him with the Father and the Son, so that without him no one has either salvation or dignity. If he is not of the same divinity, this was done either foolishly or as a favor, which God forbid. What sensible person would deny that the Creator cannot be counted together with a creature, nor the eternal compared with one who had a beginning, nor the master made equal to the servant, nor the powerful set beside the powerless, nor the one who knows ranked with the one who does not?

But let the slander stop now. The Spirit is third in order, not in nature; in rank, not in divinity; in person, not in ignorance. Just as the Son of God is second after the Father and not less in divinity, so the Holy Spirit, who follows after the Son, is not unequal but equal in the divinity of the substance.

Indeed, what we read of the Son of God we also read of the Holy Spirit, as the Son himself testifies. He says: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth." By saying "another," he indicated that he himself is a Paraclete. The apostle John makes this clear when he says that the Son of God intercedes for our sins, and the apostle Paul says: "The Spirit of God himself intercedes for us." So Scripture shows that both are advocates. And by calling him the Spirit of truth, he showed that the Spirit differs from him in nothing, for he said: "I am the truth." He said that he was sent by the Father, and he himself promised to send the Holy Spirit. If he is not unequal to the one who sends him, neither is the Holy Spirit unequal to him. Because they are three, it does not follow that each is a part of the others, with different powers. The three have one power, so that nothing is lacking to any of them.
Let this be the end. The remaining matters, which concern the undivided unity of the Trinity, have already been treated in full in the little book written against the Arian impiety.
126. On the One Who Receives

It is written that a righteous man's righteousness will not help him on the day he goes astray, and that an unrighteous man's unrighteousness will not harm him once he has turned back. And the Lord says in the Gospel: "Whoever does not believe is already judged." By this he showed that whoever believes is not subject to judgment, waiting to receive a sentence, but will be worthy of praise because of the merit of his faith.

So the knowledge of God has this privilege: it obtains the forgiveness of sins. Whoever believes that Jesus is the Son of God becomes worthy to be set free from all his sins. Long led astray by error and tossed in many directions on the waves of ignorance, he has been enlightened by the flash of truth and has found a harbor where he may rest secure after so many storms. It is fitting, then, that once he has come to know God he should refrain from what he used to do while he lived in ignorance. What good is knowledge if his old way of life remains? For someone shows that he has come to know God when he changes his life and his conduct.

Once God is known, he must be feared, because he is proclaimed as the one who will judge, so that the faithful may receive the fruit of their righteousness and the ungodly, that is, the unbelievers, may pay the penalty their faithlessness deserves. It is fitting that the righteous should rejoice in the age to come, when Christ will reign with his own. In this world, whose prince is the devil, they suffer reproach and injury; in the kingdom of Christ they will appear in glory, since it was for his sake that worldly people judged them contemptible. It is equally fitting that the unrighteous, who only seem to flourish, and who resist the truth with lies, should be afflicted with punishment, so that those who looked glorious through pretense will be shown in truth to be despised and utterly humbled. Then the righteous will rejoice that they believed, when they see the faithless in torment. And the faithless will not regret their unbelief until they see their own punishment and the glory of those whom they thought foolish and contemptible for believing.

Therefore, because a person professes to be a Christian, he must strive not to sin. He must arm himself against the vices, and since it is impossible to win every time, if he is defeated he must grieve over it so that he is not defeated again, for whoever grieves at his defeat restores himself. So the one who fights back has an excuse if he is defeated, because he shows that he wanted to win but did not prevail. There is hope for such a person, since he can recover, so that with constant practice he may prove more skillful and stronger in the fight.

But whoever rises up for the very purpose of sinning has no excuse; his case is very serious. It is worse to live under the profession of God and still want to sin than to be ignorant of God and live a shameful and defiled life. The latter does not know whom he ought to fear; the former knows and despises him.

So believers receive the forgiveness of sins. Yet they will not be glorious unless, after receiving the faith, they live in the fear of God, so that, wrestling against the enemies of the Christian name, they win the victory and can earn the reward by winning more often than they are beaten.

Then there is the one who understands God but does not come to his faith, so as not to live as a Christian, and instead wants to receive the faith at the end, so as to die a Christian. Either he is ashamed to live as a Christian, or he is devoting himself to sins which he thinks can be forgiven him when he believes. I do not think such a person has a good case: so that he can keep sinning as long as he is in the world, he refuses to become and live as a Christian, or else he is embarrassed to be called a Christian. What kind of God does he expect, that he wants to receive wages from one in whose service he is ashamed to fight? A man like this is a mocker. Knowing that with death at hand he no longer has time to sin, he then wants to become a Christian. Because he can no longer sin, he says he believes in Christ, who abhors sin, so that it is not that he no longer wants to sin but that death has come first and he no longer can. To such people it must be read that God is not mocked.

Such people even tend to give instructions that the faith be given to them only when they are already failing, out of their senses and barely breathing, for fear that they might recover and be embarrassed at having become Christians. To them must be recited the words of the Gospel, which says: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this generation, the Son of Man will also put him to shame when he comes in the kingdom of his Father."

But perhaps they will say: "We know that the human race is frail, so we want to receive the faith at the end of life, so that we will not sin any more." But faith must be received in such a way that the one receiving it knows what he is receiving. He will have its benefit only if he understands and professes it, for "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." How, then, can someone be said to receive it when he no longer knows where he is? The one who has received it is the one who professes that he has received it, knowing that he has. If they believe that forgiveness of sins is given to believers, they ought to know that the one who believes is the one who believes with his own heart as witness, because God, who made the promise, searches the heart; he accepts the one whom he sees believing in his heart. So how will a person have the benefit of the faith if his heart does not take in the words of the faith?

Thus the one who can be seen to fear becoming a Christian by receiving the faith is the one who is evidently acting so that he will not sin lightly. But the one who is eager to sin refuses to receive the faith for this reason: so that he will not be compelled to live rightly, which he plainly does not want. Instead he wants to obtain impunity at death, hoping for forgiveness of his past wrongs, so that he will be secure about the past and about the future as well, since, being about to die, he certainly will not be able to sin any more.

But it is not done with good intent or a clean conscience when someone wants to receive the faith only when he is no longer able to sin, not when he is no longer willing to. That saying fits such people: "Let us do evil so that good may come," that is, "Let us sin now and believe at the very end, and it will be forgiven us." That is why he added: "Their condemnation is just." It is not right that forgiveness of sins be given to those who, though they already know that God does not want sin and hates sinners, still long to sin, and will not recognize that the gift of God benefits those who sin in ignorance of God, so that they do not know that God will judge. But when someone has heard and considered it within himself, and still wants to sin, not as one overcome under the pressure of some circumstance, but because he wishes to sin, it is hard for him to be pardoned.
