For there are two means that bring the forgiveness of sins: one is the gift, the other is repentance, so that whoever sins after the gift may be restored through repentance. Since he did not remain in the grace he received so as to continue in freedom, but subjected himself to sin again, he obtains the blotting out of his sin through lamentation and groaning. For he sinned knowingly and deliberately. It is not that anyone is ignorant of sin, but the one who does not know that God will judge thinks that his sinning will go unpunished.

For this reason, if a pagan falls ill and, in despair of his life, considers within himself the faith and the hope that is promised, his case is sound: if he believes, his sins are forgiven and he is not held in the underworld, since he carries with him the sign of death conquered and despoiled. Yet he will not have honor or reward, because there must be some difference between two men. One, moved by love for his lord, was not afraid to fight against his lord's enemies, arming himself with self-control and watchfulness against every vice so that he could resist evil, always concerned how to defend his lord's dominion. The other sided with his lord's enemies and supported them, and returned to his lord only at the end of his life, not to defend his lord's kingdom but to benefit himself alone, discharged before he was ever a soldier.

The one who prefers to live as a Christian, so as to be rewarded after death, knows that "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us." So, having taken up the weapons of faith, he does not hesitate to engage the principalities and powers, so that, proving victorious in this world, he may be crowned after it. It is right that the one who now bears witness to his lord's kingdom among the faithless and rebellious should receive the reward for this in the age to come. Then the enemies of God, seeing Christ's witness appear exalted in the kingdom of God because of the truth of his confession, will grieve in confusion that they thought false what has been shown to be true. And those too who believed late, confessing God not in life but in death, seeing how great is the glory of those who served under Christ's arms and fought their Emperor's wars devotedly and faithfully, will regret that they did not live as Christians but only died as Christians.

For a person who had no wish to live as a Christian can hardly seem fit to die as a Christian. Perhaps, being about to die, he wanted to be called a Christian simply because there was no more time for sinning. "In case," he says, "what is believed should be true, I want to become a Christian, since I lose nothing if what is believed is false." So, since at death it is not the will to sin that ceases but only the sinning, he tests whether faith can help him after death, when what would surely have been useful was for vices and sins to be corrected here, where they were committed.

A person proves that he has condemned his past when, following the line of faith, he is seen to change his conduct and his life. If he used to sin because he did not know God, then once he knows him he must sin no more, so that his knowing him is not in vain; some progress ought to come from the knowledge of God. A Christian should be recognized before he professes it: Christians are proved by their works more than by their name. That is why commandments were given that are purer than other laws and concerned with holiness, so that the worship of God might be evident from them. Otherwise they will hear: "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I say?" By this he showed that calling the Lord "Lord" is of benefit only if his commandments are kept; for whoever calls someone lord while despising his precepts seems to be mocking him. To such a person must be recited the words of the law that say God is not mocked. So whoever calls him Lord, while showing by his works that he hardly fears him, will be condemned by his own words.
127. ON THE SIN OF ADAM AND EVE.

I think no one doubts that this world was made for the sake of man. Although it consists of different substances, it is still one thing, fitted together from many members, so that by their working on one another the things man would need might be produced. A house was made for man, and his food with it, so that each of these things came to be on the earth according to its kind. That is, once made, they had this power planted in them: that the offspring of each of their kinds should be produced on the earth. For sources were established whose seed would go on to beget the kinds that were to multiply on the earth.

So Scripture testifies: "And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply upon the earth." The human race was blessed in the same way, a sense we see in the law, for we find it written: "The people increased and multiplied in Egypt." Man was blessed with the same blessing as the things created for his benefit, so that the offspring of the human race, from male and female alike, should grow and multiply on the earth. And just as seeds were to be improved by cultivation, so the human race, with care applied, was to strive to know its Creator and rein in its life in order to win his favour, so that all things together might advance to the praise and glory of the Creator.

The facts themselves show that these words mean nothing else. Everything that was made has multiplied and improved on the earth at God's command. Nor could it grow in any other way than God's will and blessing decreed for the seeds. How then can anyone say that something which increases by God's blessing and with his favour is done wickedly or is unlawful? The tradition of this practice remained in the synagogue and is now celebrated in the church: God's creature is joined under God's blessing. This is no presumption, for the pattern was given by the Author himself.

But if someone thinks it ought to cease, then it will have to cease when the other things that were blessed in the same way so that they would multiply also cease. If the begetting of human beings stops, what use is there in the birth of the things that were blessed on the earth? The world cannot be partly active and partly at rest. Either the whole of it works, or the whole of it rests idle. Is a body useful if some of its members are vigorous and others are numb?

Why then do some call a work that God has blessed sordid and defiled, unless in a sense they are laying hands on God himself? They would not condemn it unless they thought badly of God, the author of this work. Because they are afraid to disparage God openly, they accuse him through the work he devised. For when a work displeases, its maker is blamed.

If people like this read the Scriptures, or rather accepted them, they would remember Balaam saying: "How shall I curse," he says, "one whom God blesses?" It is useless to accuse someone whom the judge praises. In fact, whoever calls a man guilty when the laws defend him is his own accuser. Who are you, then, to propose condemning what you read that God has blessed, unless you either deny that this is God or accuse Scripture of being false?

There are some who think the old must be rejected, as if they were accepting the new. But the new commands that Christ made known to the nations do not disagree with the old. When he was invited to a wedding, he did not refuse to go. He not only honoured it with his presence but also supplied what was missing for its joy, for it is written that "wine gladdens the heart of man." To show that he had done this according to the will of God his Father, he answered the Jews who asked whether a man may put away his wife, saying among other things: "From the beginning God made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined together, therefore, let no man separate." This is why he went gladly when he was invited to a wedding, so that he would not seem to undermine what God his Father had done. Instead, he showed that the teaching of the old law and the new agree. He not only did not forbid marriage but was even willing to attend one, and so bore witness that God is its author. By a saving precept he showed that what God has joined must be neither forbidden nor separated.

Because birth is a benefit, when he was already leaving the world he entrusted his mother to John, his disciple. For this reason the commandments of both the old and the new law teach us to honour our parents, and the law warns that if we do not, we will bring a curse on ourselves.

What presumption is this, then, and from what law does it come, to block the way to marriage, when both the new law and the old clearly favour it in every respect? It is as we read: whatever goes beyond this comes from evil. That is why the apostle says that people like this, who forbid marriage and teach abstinence from foods that God created to be received, have a seared conscience. They are shown to be doing this out of hypocrisy and hostility, in order to bring charges against the law that God handed down.

Others are eager to promote the commands of a perverse doctrine, and so they raise their hands against saving precepts. For this reason they are said to have a seared conscience. With a corrupt mind they know one thing and profess another, like the Jews. These knew perfectly well that the Saviour's deeds were works of the Holy Spirit, but out of envy they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, in order to turn the people away from faith in him. The people mentioned above are just as cunning. To pass themselves off as lovers of chastity and holiness, they even say that marriage must be condemned, so that they will be admired for it and turn the people away from the truth. To pretend that they are devoted to abstinence, they teach that people must refrain from foods, and so present themselves as strangers to the world who are hurrying toward the kingdoms of heaven. With this they entice people's minds, and from then on they teach that unlawful things are lawful and condemn lawful things as forbidden.

These are Satan's tricks. He turns things upside down, so that by slipping in something supposedly new he may shut out the truth, in which nothing is new, because all of it is eternal. Who would fail to see that this view was devised by the adversary? Who would dare to reject what God devised, something that has never harmed anyone, except the adversary of the truth? To cover his own impurity he preaches a holiness he does not love, and while he uses it to look well-meaning, he urges unlawful things as if they were lawful. He makes himself attractive in order to deceive more easily. Once he has caught the unwary, he suggests things that will make them greater sinners. To find some remedy for his own case, he persuades people to sin gravely and takes great comfort from it, since he can show many partners in his crime. He reckons his punishment light, heavy as it is, if he sees many people with him in Gehenna. In their other sins people may look to themselves, when they are overcome by vices or through ignorance defend things as not deserving punishment here [?].

What contrary desire deceives them, or what darkness stands in their way, so that they do not see what is true! It is true that written words often seem to mean something else when they are read aloud badly or punctuated wrongly. But when we read "God made" and "he blessed what he had made," who could argue with that? Who could doubt it? Who would hear that something is blessed and think it cursed, unless he were driven by another spirit? If this were said to be the voice of a man, perhaps someone might suspect a deception. But God is said to speak, and you doubt? God blesses, and is it to be rejected?

But perhaps Moses brought in an error under God's name! Then let the signs and wonders that Moses performed in Egypt satisfy you. Let the miracles done at the Red Sea to set the children of Israel free persuade you. Listen to the magicians admitting, "This is the finger of God." Agree with the apostle when he says: "I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." On what grounds did the apostle say this? The Scripture is at hand, where we read that Christ our Lord said to the Jews: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me too, for Moses wrote about me." Who would refuse to believe in this harmony? Who would dare to say that what is one is at odds with itself? Whose mind is so bad that he would argue that undivided love looks like hostility? Here you have both the testimony of words and examples of mighty works to bring your mind under the truth, so that you will hold nothing to be true except what the books of the catholic church contain.

It has now been proved that the same God who is ours now was in the old law, and that many signs of his power show him to be true. His authority must therefore be put first, to the point that even something we think harsh and perhaps absurd must be accepted and understood differently from the way we suppose, if God's judgment commends it. We ought to believe God rather than ourselves. Our weakness and inexperience often judge harmful things to be useful and take false things for true. It is wicked even to suspect this of God, for his nature cannot be deceived. How much less, then, should anyone have doubts about marriage when God has spoken! The matter is plain and simple.

Every man certainly rejoices when he has received God's favour, and believes he is made better when he learns the mystery of the Creator. He could never have gained this unless he had been born. Why then does he lament what he rejoices in, and condemn what he boasts of having learned? If he rejoices because he has learned, and he would not have learned unless he had been born, then without doubt it is good to be born, for the fruit of birth is the knowledge of the truth. But if it is evil to be born, knowledge will not be good. What good will knowledge do if birth is condemned? If it is neither profitable nor right to be born, it is pointless for someone who is to be condemned to learn. But since no one is so dull as to deny that the knowledge of God benefits human beings, it is both good and useful. Through it birth is made better, so that it earns more than Adam was given. For believers will reign in heaven, not on earth, in the paradise of God the Father, not in the one where Adam had been ordered to work with his body.

If the Encaenia were celebrated at Jerusalem, that is, the festival of the dedication of the Lord's temple, how much more should we celebrate the birthday of man himself! He is more truly the temple of God, and a temple was even built by hands for him to give thanks to God in. Our body is the better temple, because it was built by God's work and the other by human labour, and our body is meant for eternity while the other is meant for destruction. So whoever knows that he was born by God's design, so that he may give thanks to God now that he knows his mystery, ought to rejoice on his birthday, seeing what his birth has gained. Truly, those who abandon their Creator and give his glory to others ought never to have been born. Their birth leads to punishment. Yet it is not birth that incurs guilt but the will.

But who are you, forbidding marriage? Perhaps you are Marcion, since you think the body was made not by God but by the devil, and you claim that the soul fell through some error and came into the regions of darkness where the world now is. How then could the soul be freed from here if begetting were forbidden? It was by being born that you learned of your fall, and you set yourself to return to your ancestral home and be restored to your source. You even say that you give thanks to Christ and congratulate yourself on gaining this knowledge through him. Come now: if you had not been born, there would be no knowledge and no freedom would follow. So if you are glad that the soul is set free, support birth. If you oppose birth, you are an enemy of souls.

Or if you are a Manichee and reject marriage as something hostile, I ask you this: if bodies were never begotten, how would the soul be rescued from here? You claim it was poured out into the region of darkness and clings to material things. Your own books say that it is freed through birth: souls leaving their bodies are received by the moon and handed on to the sun, which you claim is the god of your souls. You even rejoice when you are called Manichees, for through this name you lay claim to your liberation, and you certainly would not know about it unless you had been born. So it is plain to see that you condemn marriage out of hypocrisy. While you profess holiness, you secretly pursue uncleanness. This has been exposed not only in private but also in the emperors' edicts.

Now hear, catholic, how the gospel bears witness that human birth is a benefit. The righteous man Simeon wanted to leave the world, thinking it was enough for him to know the Creator without knowing his mystery. He was not allowed to do so until he had grown in his understanding of God, so that he might receive the full reward of his faith. At last he took the newborn Saviour in his arms, blessed God and said: "Lord, now let your servant depart in peace according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation." This plainly showed that God's kindness is found in human birth, when a righteous man who was thinking of death was told that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's Christ. He made such progress in life that he became worthy to see, even in this present life, the one he had hoped would be his deliverer after death. He was kept alive and not allowed to die until he had seen the fruit of his hope, so that he could be sure he was passing from life to life. How then can anyone say that birth did him no good?

If it were evil that we are born, we would not be promised paradise, eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, but punishment, Gehenna and destruction. Then anyone who knew he had been born for destruction would be afraid to beget another, and someone born unlawfully would not be allowed to beget.

But perhaps someone will say: "The kingdom of heaven was indeed promised, but to the faithful and to those who do good." Quite right. So you see that people do not become guilty because they were born, but because they lived badly. The kingdom of heaven was not promised to the unborn, so that those who will not receive it could blame their birth. It was promised to the born who do good, so that birth neither helps someone who does evil nor can harm someone who does good.

Birth is made better by the faithful and by those who do good, and made worse by unbelievers and those who do evil. Birth is like a tree that is grafted. If it is grafted with a good cutting, it will become better and be called good. If it is grafted with a bad cutting, it will become worse and will be called not good but bad. In the same way, if good teaching is added to birth, it will bear good fruit, but if bad teaching is added, it will bear bad fruit. A tree is needed so that there is something to graft onto, and in the same way birth is needed so that there is something in which progress can be made.

But someone objects: "If birth is useful, why are we born again?" We would not be born again unless birth were useful. To be born again is to be renewed, and what is renewed is restored. Rebirth does not accuse birth but reshapes it, and whatever is reshaped is shown to have been well made at the beginning. So when we are born again, our purpose is changed and the body receives its cleansing, so that we may be brought back to Adam's original state. The body was stained by the soul's sin, and once the purpose has been repaired and improved through faith, the body
is washed. Just as it had been polluted through contempt of God, it is washed through obedience, so that it may escape the sentence passed on Adam and be able to rise again.

So if sin began from the soul, why is the nature of the body blamed? Bodily desire was not the cause of Adam's sin. Rather, the soul, lured by the hope of becoming divine, "transgressed God's command," so that it subjected its own body to sin and human beings came to be born under sin. This does no harm at all to a person, provided that he obeys God's law, except that he dies. For this God in his kindness has promised a reward. Those who are found faithful in devotion to the Creator, yet were made subject to corruption and death through Adam's transgression, will for that reason receive from God the judge more than had been granted to Adam: in the age to come they will be glorious, will have eternal life, and will be called adopted sons of God. So it is a gain that they were born.

From here I will now return to the rest of the reading. When man had been placed in paradise, he received these commands: "Of every tree that is in paradise for food," it says, "you shall eat; but of the tree by which good and evil are known, you shall not eat of it." All the trees it mentions are fruit trees created for eating. In short, they are all called by one name, "trees," but they are understood to differ in their fruits. Still, all are trees, and eating is of one kind, even though the things eaten are different. For when he had created many fruit trees for man to eat, as I said, he forbade eating from one tree. Those who had received everything into their power were in this one respect to show reverence for the Creator: one tree was reserved, which they had no permission to touch, so that they would remember the law of their condition.

How could the kind of sin be understood from the sentence? This sentence fits a murderer, a sorcerer, an adulterer and a person of ill repute. Achan son of Carmi too, when he had sinned, was condemned to be destroyed with all his household. How can the kind of sin be understood from the sentence? One can tell that the offence was great, but one cannot understand what kind of offence it was. For we know that others were condemned by this same sentence, though they are known to have sinned in other ways. Both Haman and the people of Sodom are known to have perished with all who were theirs. So it happens that those guilty of a single sin are struck by different sentences, and sinners guilty of different crimes are punished in one and the same way. For this reason the kind of sin committed by Adam and Eve cannot be understood from the sentence that was given.

Although their sin was one, the man and the woman each received a sentence suited to their own person, and so did the serpent. The aim was not only that they should not remain as they had been made, but that toil should also be added to them as a punishment. For while all cattle and living creatures had been made subject to man, as we read, the serpent rose up against this order. It got round the man by deceit and trickery and made him subject to itself. Without doubt, whoever captures someone brings him under himself. Therefore the serpent was called back by God's sentence and pressed down lower than it had been made, so that it should not enjoy the fruit of its cunning and should not stand above man. In this way it was to grieve that its craftiness had not only gained it nothing but had even made it worse off. For whereas we read that it had been more cunning than the other beasts, after it deceived man it was made cursed above all the beasts of the earth.

After the sentence on the serpent, it follows that the woman also, whom the serpent had made its partner in despising God's law, receives her sentence. For he says: "I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sadness you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." No one confirms the very thing he rebukes. If children were granted because she had seized intercourse for herself, then seizing it brought her more. If you think that procreation took its beginning from the words "in sadness you shall bear children," what becomes of the earlier words, "Increase and multiply"? Understand, then, that this was added only as a punishment: what had earlier been granted with joy was now to have sadness placed beneath it as a penalty. And so that this sorrow, harsher and multiplied, might press on the woman continually, the turning to her husband is added, so that there would be a way for it to be renewed for her again and again.

If the Lord condemned intercourse in his servants, why did he add, "your turning shall be to your husband"? No one appoints as a punishment the very thing he condemns. A punishment is surely the opposite of the thing condemned, and it never comes from that same thing, but from its contrary. If they were the same, no one would fear condemnation. Again, would anyone sentence a person to the very thing in which he saw the law had been broken? That would be to confirm sin, not to punish it. If that were so, the woman's turning to her husband would come from her having had intercourse [?]. But the truth is that this turning, which had earlier been granted simply, should be believed to have been laid on her as a punishment, together with the utmost servitude. Through the woman the man had been brought into subjection. She had without doubt seemed the superior one, since he followed her advice and thought that what she urged would benefit him, and so God's work seemed to be undone by the serpent's subtlety. Therefore God's sentence restores the original arrangement: the woman returns to the subjection that belongs to her condition, humbled beneath her husband, as had been established. And what is added as punishment is added to her, when she hears: "I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sadness you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you."

Had it been decreed in any other way than that the woman should be subject to her husband's rule? From this it is clear that the woman was called back to what she had been made, with something added. That is why he says: "I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning." What does he multiply? He adds to something that already exists in a lesser measure. He is not seen to be working on something that does not exist. Here, then, the sentence does not begin procreation, for that had already been pronounced earlier: "Increase and multiply." Instead it brings harm to a procreation that had already been granted. Pain in bearing children is added to the woman and hardship is laid on her, but no new form of procreation is set up. For if procreation is rightly traced to this, then it could be understood that it came about by the serpent's will rather than the Lord's, and it would truly be, as he says, "a brood of vipers." But if anyone thinks he was born in this way, let him consider what he deserves. Because of sin, the pain of childbirth was increased for the woman: she who would have had only a little pain with her children had it increased because of the offence. For children are born with groaning and sorrow, and once born they are not kept without sadness.

Now, in the third place, this sentence is pronounced on the man: "Because," he says, "you listened to the voice of your wife and ate of the tree of which I had commanded you not to eat, and you ate of it, cursed is the ground in your works; in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you," and so on. Here too Adam is called back to that for which he had been made, but with loss. Before, he had been placed there to work the ground simply, so that the fruit of his labour would follow. But when he spurned God's command, believing that the serpent's advice would get him better things than God had made, he was called back to his original arrangement at the cost of toil. The ground, cursed not in itself but in his works, would yield him little in return for his labour. In this way it would be shown that God's purpose cannot be overturned and that no one can provide better than God. For no one can love another's work more than the one who made it, as the apostle says: "No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church."

Let us now see whether the later parts of the law agree with its beginnings. When Abraham had pleased God, among the other things that belonged to the reward of his faith, he was judged worthy, though old, to beget a son. How then can something be blamed that was evidently granted as a reward for merit? Because Abraham had done God's will, God fulfilled Abraham's will. It would not have been fulfilled at all unless it was innocent. God would not grant what he saw was asked for wickedly or foolishly, least of all by someone who pleased him; that would not befit even a man. Hannah, too, was barren and loved God. She asked to have a son, and she received one. If this had been wrong, she could have been warned by the one she loved not to ask for something harmful. And the most holy Samuel, who was born of her, fathered sons, yet this did not lessen the merits of his righteousness. From his earliest years he kept growing, so that in old age he was commended by an even richer testimony from God. Zechariah the priest, a righteous man, fathered a son in his old age by God's will, and at the birth he was found worthy to prophesy. On what grounds, then, is something blamed that is proved to do no harm at all? Who would deny that what harms no one should be called good?

And it strengthens the case to say something about the apostles at this point. Holy John certainly kept chastity. But his fellow disciple, the equally holy Peter, is known to have had a wife and children, and fathering children did not prevent him from receiving the primacy among the apostles. How then can something be thought worthy of condemnation when it is no hindrance to merit?

This is why the apostle shows that a man who has a wife can, and should, become a priest, provided he keeps the commandments in other respects. If marriage were unlawful, he certainly could not have said that a sinner ought to become a priest. What could be plainer? For the same apostle says: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord." The Corinthians were being troubled by heretics who hypocritically taught that marriage should be condemned, and they wrote to the apostle asking whether it was lawful to marry or to put away one's wife. The apostle then ruled that a wife ought not to leave her husband. He had every opportunity to say that a man may not marry in any way at all, if he had known that this was what should be taught. But he shows that he could not teach what he knew had not been handed down to him. Which of the disciples, then, would dare to teach what the master did not hand down, when he hears him preaching: "I want the young women to marry and to bear children"?

But perhaps someone will say: "If it is lawful and good to marry, why are priests not allowed to have wives, that is, why may those already ordained no longer come together with them?" Who does not know that each person has a law suited to his own station and dignity? There are things that are not lawful for anyone at all; there are things that are lawful for some and not for others; and there are things that are lawful at some times and not at others. Fornication is never lawful for anyone. Trading, however, is lawful at some times and not at others: before a man becomes a cleric he may trade, but once he has become one he may not. And for a Christian it is sometimes lawful to come together with his wife and sometimes not. On the days of the stations it is not lawful to come together, because one ought to abstain even from lawful things so that what is prayed for may be more readily obtained. That is why the apostle says that one should abstain by mutual consent for a time, "so that you may give yourselves to prayer." According to the law, too, it is not lawful to strike or quarrel during a fast, though afterwards it is, because greater reverence is owed to the things of God.

Is everything that is lawful among other people lawful in the emperor's presence? How much more so in the things of God! For this reason God's bishop ought to be purer than others, since he seems to bear God's very person. He is his vicar, so that what is lawful for others is not lawful for him, because every day he must act in Christ's place, whether praying for the people, offering the sacrifice, or baptizing. And this is not lawful for him alone but also for his minister, since he too ought to be cleaner, because the things he serves are holy. Compared with a lamp, darkness is not only dim but even dirty. Compared with the stars, a lamp is gloom. Compared with the sun, the stars are cloudy. And compared with God's brightness, the sun is night. In the same way, things that are lawful and clean for us are, compared with God's dignity, as good as unlawful and unclean. For although they are good, they do not befit God's person. Is not the tunic of an ordinary man, however clean, still dirty and unfit for the emperor? And is not the saxonicia [?] equally unfit for a senator? For this reason God's bishops ought to be purer than others, because they bear Christ's person, and God's ministers ought to be cleaner. No one serves the emperor unkempt; those who serve him do so dressed in bright, clean clothing. But since God is by nature supremely bright, his ministers ought to be clean in their nature rather than in their clothes.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS [OF SAINT AUGUSTINE]
I.
I of this recension = I of the recension of 127 questions.
II. Against those who deny that anything concerns God.

We greatly displease many people whom worldly life has blinded. They dislike it if we carefully keep God's commands, if we avoid occasions of sin, if we try with saving zeal to do every good thing, if we pay no heed to the seductive charms of temptations and vices, if we let no worldly sweetness ensnare us, if we willingly undergo torture and punishment for God's name, and if by the strength of the Spirit we despise death itself. These are the people whose mortal way of thinking has persuaded them that nothing that is done deserves either praise or blame. They do not want any of these things to concern God.

Indeed, some who want to defend their own crimes and wicked deeds say: "It makes no difference whether you live well or badly. God has no concern these days to hurry anxiously to watch you doing this and that according to your own bent and sickness, and to let his eyes mingle with your foul deeds now and then. Everything that people do as they please is vain. The one who is God is set apart and far removed from these human affairs, and so he is neither angered nor moved. He gives no attention to human affairs or to our actions. The whole course of the turning world, and a kind of endless rolling of the earthly sphere, so seizes everything, sweeps it along and casts it off, that anyone who thinks God can be brought back to caring is taken for a fool. Not even the spirit of the martyrs deserves approval, since they imagine that their God, whom they proclaim to be merciful, delights in the shedding of their blood. Nothing in us is dear to God, and nothing is hateful to him. He takes no pleasure in the manner of our death or in the soundness of our health, and he has no wish to know what is done where. It is not that the divine majesty cannot know nearly everything that has been done or is being done, but that he does not want to know the miseries of human beings and the vanities of the world. So indeed it is written: 'Vanity of the vain, all is vanity.'"

Their view rests on despair. It is refuted by the authority of the divine mind, and it is also defeated and overthrown by their own common religious language, which is in such wide use. When honesty and dishonesty clash in business and in people's various contracts, the deity is called on as witness, the very deity that is sometimes said not to know what we do. "God is witness," they say; "May God see, God judge, God act, God repay." When it comes to swearing an oath, the one who swears fears that something may befall him if he swears falsely, and the one who demands the oath trusts that whoever swears falsely to him can be paid back. When the health people longed for and their well-being are restored, thanks are given to the deity. When something falls and a person standing nearby happens to escape unhurt, people say that the good God granted it. And when contrary winds blow, the waves of the stirred-up sea rise, and the ship is battered and shaken on every side, the crowds on board stretch out their hands to heaven, beg God in pleading voices, and trust that they can be heard and saved. Where would all this come from, if God has no care for us and does not know what we do?

This belief, then, is empty: all things are known to God. Let no one flatter himself that his crimes will go unpunished. A good life brings the greatest reward; an evil life brings everlasting punishment and eternal torment. To us, therefore, who believe that God knows all things, and who hasten devoutly to martyrdom, a reward beyond reckoning will be granted, everlasting life. But for the wicked, who have taught that God does not know their crimes and the secrets of their misdeeds, there will be a devouring flame of fire and a burning that never fails.

XXXVII. Why did God say: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh, and their years shall be a hundred and twenty"?

In those days there were giants on the earth, destructive and proud. Puffed up by their great stature, they followed the desires of the flesh and were apostates from birth. Since this displeased God, he declared that he would destroy the human race by a flood, and he set a period of time. That way, if anyone heard of God's wrath and indignation over this and wished to correct himself, he would have time to mend his ways. This is why the ark appears to have been built over a hundred years. Twenty years are said to have passed before the ark was begun.

But what the narrative adds after giving the number of Noah's years seems to make this obscure, for this sentence is known to have been pronounced before Noah was five hundred years old. What does it say? "My spirit shall not remain in these men." And so it also added, because wickedness had increased on the earth: "I will destroy man from the face of the earth, even to the cattle." This was certainly fulfilled when the flood came. For we remember that people lived many years after the flood as well, and Aaron the brother of Moses is recorded to have lived a hundred and twenty-three years. As for Moses himself, the reason he could not live beyond a hundred and twenty years was that he did not glorify God at the waters of contradiction. He would have entered the promised land had sin not stood in his way. Some think that this saying applies to the time of Moses, though we find that Jehoiada the priest lived a hundred and thirty years.
XXXVIII. What the blessing that Jacob gave contains.

Jacob did not only foretell the future of each tribe from present circumstances. He also pointed to future things in the Jewish people that would come from other future things, of which there was as yet no shadow. He showed what each tribe would be like in its conduct, faith, discipline, luxury, insolence and contempt for faith, so that, though they came from one man, they did not all keep to one way. Some advanced to better things, others grew worse, and others stayed as they were. As a result, they could not claim for themselves the privilege of their descent. Jacob himself had foretold that some of them, though certainly of his own stock, would be rejected, and indeed that many would perish. And he signified that others would come in, to be grafted, to their shame and condemnation, into the stock from which they had fallen away. So he declared that in all the tribes there would be a mixed people, and this mixture was to be understood as including both the good, who are few, and the bad, who are many. And although he gave the sceptre for a time to his son Joseph, he set Judah over all. This was not because everyone from Judah would prove worthy, but because the Saviour, who is truly king, was to spring from that tribe according to the flesh.

XL. Was there no other sign for Moses to perform openly before Pharaoh than a serpent?

Let whoever thinks this blameworthy say what else should have been done. He made a serpent, of course, because it could strike terror and yet do no harm, since a kind of sluggishness makes it slower to do injury. If he had made a lion or a bear or some other such creature, how would those present have escaped? He did not want to kill anyone, only to instil fear and show his power. Since the first transgression began through a serpent, so too the remembrance of the knowledge of God and the amendment of conduct were to come through the sign of a serpent. In this way sin would be put right by the same means by which it was committed, just as the sin committed through a woman was taken away through a woman, namely Mary the mother of the Lord, from whom Christ was born and condemned sin. Eve was still a virgin when she transgressed, just as Mary too was a virgin. In this way what had been lost was called back to its original state. The kingdom, too, had been lost by tasting from a tree, and it was won back through a tree; for it says, "The Lord has reigned from the tree." In the same way the world was also renewed at the very time in which it was made, that is, at the beginning of the first month, which is the Passover. No nature, then, will be evil; only transgression is, since sin has been put right by the very means through which it was committed.

XLI. What is meant by the psalm, "Men and beasts you will save," and by the words to the prophet Jonah, "Shall I not spare the city in which a hundred and twenty thousand people live, and many cattle?", when the apostle says on the other hand, "Is it for oxen that God cares?"

As far as the words go, they seem contradictory. But if we consider the case of human beings and of cattle, it will become clear that they are consistent. God cares for all things as the maker of all things. Yet he does not preserve cattle for their own sake. He preserves cattle for the sake of human beings, not human beings for the sake of cattle. So when he cares for human beings, he protects the cattle, but his concern is not for oxen but for human beings. For what hope is there for cattle?
XLII. Did Adam, once made by God and given life, receive the Holy Spirit, since it is written: "God breathed into his face the spirit of life"?

It was not in the order of things that he should receive the Holy Spirit, because God reserved this for the future, so that in the last days, when the mystery of the one God had been made manifest, it would be given to believers. From the beginning, indeed, the Trinity was proclaimed, but the understanding of it lay as if under a veil. For the person of God the Father was proclaimed and made manifest first, without hesitation and without figure, because all things are from him. But the persons of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit were not passed over in silence, yet neither were they made manifest. Accordingly, the faithless raise questions about the Lord and about the Holy Spirit. For some madmen say that the Holy Spirit is himself the Father, just as Sabellius also says that the one who is the Father is also the Son. But about the person of God the Father no one has any doubt.

When, therefore, the Trinity is made manifest, then at last the Holy Spirit is given to believers, so that his person too may be manifest, and so that those who receive him may have a sign that they are sons of God, in that they have within them the Spirit of God, who is certainly from God. For this is what perfection means: to know that there is Father and Son and Holy Spirit. This perfection bestows this gift. For when the Son of God came and opened up and made these things manifest, he had to give something more, and it was fitting for him to bestow this perfection on believers, because perfection or salvation is not in the Son alone nor in the Father alone, but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Hence John the evangelist says that of his fullness we have all received, grace for grace, because the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through [?] Christ.

It is clear that with the Savior's coming the fullness of truth was achieved; for when what lay hidden and what was promised is revealed and made manifest, the fullness of truth comes about. Then believers, having received the Holy Spirit, become sons of God. For the inbreathing which we read that God performed in Adam is the bestowal of the soul. For “spirit” is frequently used for “soul,” as the Gospel says among other things: “And her spirit,” it says, “returned to her”; and in the psalm: “A troubled spirit,” it says, “and a contrite heart God does not despise.” Frequently, however, some manuscripts do not read “And God breathed into,” but “God blew into his face the spirit of life, and man became a living soul.” It is not because it said “spirit of life” that it therefore signified the Holy Spirit; for it speaks in the same way of the animals: “in which was the spirit of life.” It is called the spirit of life because it animates bodies to life.

XLV. “In the sun,” it says, “he has set his tabernacle,” that is, his body, in which Christ dwelt, since he was beaten with scourges by Pilate. How then does the psalm say of Christ, “The scourge shall not come near your tabernacle,” since he called his body a temple?

The body of the Son of Man and Son of God is understood to be a temple. Yet God, that is, the Son of God, although he came in the flesh, nevertheless dwelt in a soul; therefore both soul and body are the tabernacle of the Son of God, although the one God and man is both Son of God and Son of Man. So it is in this respect that the scourge is said not to have come near his tabernacle, that is, his soul, in which his divinity dwells: it was immune from the punishment of hell and of its princes. Here he was crucified as though a sinner, although he is innocent, and his flesh suffered some sorrow; lest it be thought that his soul suffered likewise in the underworld, Scripture shows that his soul could not be troubled in the underworld, since he descended for this very purpose — that is, he allowed himself to suffer — to confound the darkness and send its princes away dulled. Hence the Lord himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even to death.” For it was permitted, as belonged to its nature, to be sorrowful, and at once it brought back trophies and spoils from those by whom it had been made sorrowful even to death, being established after death in eternal joy. It can also be understood of the whole man, because he who knew no sin could not be scourged by the law.
XLVI. Why did Adam, when he was placed in the world, receive a command or law, when he himself had lordship over everything else?

Although Adam was placed in the world as lord, yet because he certainly did not have this from himself but received it from God, he had to receive an indication of this through a law. In this way he who seemed to be lord would, through the law, be subject to the one who had given him this power, and the Creator's authority would instill reverence in him through the law, lest such great dominion should puff him up and he forget God his maker.
XLVII. The old law asserts that God swore an oath — for it says: “Three times I have sworn by myself, says the Lord” — but the Savior forbade swearing. How then did he not destroy the old things?

Before there was knowledge of God on earth, there was no other way to rouse people to an unheard-of hope than for the promise to be made to them with an oath, especially since it came from one whom they did not know as they ought. But once he began to be known, there was certainly no need for him to swear, since it would be wrong to think he could lie. That is why the Lord commanded that not even his servants should swear any longer, but should so train themselves that their words would be believed. For the sacred bond of an oath is demanded either by faithlessness or by the deceit of the inconstant, so that, since people are prone to deceive, they may perhaps be restrained by the fear of God; or at any rate the one who is deceived will have satisfaction enough, since the deceiver incurs offense by it.

XLVIII. Why was even Aaron himself told in the law to offer burnt offerings for his sins, when David says: “For sins you did not require a burnt offering,” and further on: “You will not delight in burnt offerings”? How could he command to be offered that in which he does not delight?

It is clear that God does not delight in burnt offerings, but that pardon can be earned as satisfaction for sin through groaning and sorrow of heart. He wished the sacrifice, however, to be a testimony of sin, so that by offering the sacrifice the sinner would confess that he had sinned. How remission was to be obtained he himself shows in another place, saying: “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own seed”; or indeed: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.” So he first admonished that the offense must be confessed, then showed how it could be forgiven. For he never commanded sacrifice for an open offense, but for sins of ignorance, since a person sins even when he does not know it, and when he thinks he is acting rightly he goes wrong through some intention. Such a sin, he said, could be purged by sacrifice.
XLIX. Why did Solomon have the spirit of wisdom when he did not lead a clean life? For he took great delight in women, and thereby sinned.

At first he received the spirit of prudence by his own merit; but later, when he began to indulge excessively in women and thereby to sin, if he had the spirit of wisdom, he had it by merit of the kingship, just as Nebuchadnezzar too, by merit of the kingship, saw Christ in the furnace.
L. In Tobit it says: “It is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God”; yet the Savior, when doing a work of God, says: “Tell no one.”

The Savior did not say that the works of God ought to be concealed — for in another place he says: “Go and tell how much God has done for you” — but at times he rejected their testimony and suppressed boasting, lest he seem to bear witness to himself like a deceiver, which the wise regard as absurd.
LI. For what purpose were circumcision and the precepts given to the people, when they did not exist before and are not held authoritative now?

Circumcision is the sign of Abraham's faith, so that when this sign was seen in his sons, they would be known to be the sons of the man who had received this sign when he believed God. The precepts about sabbaths were given both as a testimony of things past and as a figure of things to come. For this sabbath, which came about at the completion of the week, is a figure of the future sabbath, which will give rest in eternity. The law about foods, however, was not given at the beginning of the law; but when, led by faithlessness, they refused to believe God's words and promises, they received, because of the hardness of their heart, precepts that were not good, as the prophet Jeremiah says. For this was done so that their neck might be pressed down for their own improvement — for the whole creation ought not to be made subject to proud and stubborn men. Afterward, however, when the mercy of God came, the freedom to eat was restored. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Why do you put a yoke on the neck of the brethren which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?”

LIV. In Wisdom it says: “He who created the world out of unseen matter”; and on the other hand: “For we were made out of nothing.”

The sense of the Scriptures declares that God created the substances together in a confused state. This confusion of things mixed with darkness — that is, air, water, and dark earth — it called unseen matter, as we read in Genesis: “But the earth,” it says, “was invisible and unformed.” Out of this confusion, then, he created the world by establishing the firmament, so that, once the waters were gathered into one place within it, a dwelling might be made for the human race. For when the substances had been distinguished and separated, he made a habitable home in the hollow.

III. Why were the deeds and words of the Lord set down in writing in four volumes and by four writers?

It was fitting that the acceptable year of the Lord, as the prophet calls it, should be contained in four volumes, as if in four seasons. For just as the year unfolds through four seasons, each needing the others, so too the deeds and words of the Lord were set out in four books, each needing the others; yet together they are complete in their fullness. And the reason they were arranged by four writers was this: since the seasons have different names, the Gospels too should have different titles. And if some things seem contradictory in their wording, they still do not disagree in sense, given an interpretation suited to the matter; just as the seasons, though they certainly seem different in name, in weather and in the course of the stars, still do not disagree in the effect of the things they bring forth.
IV. Since it is agreed that four books of the Lord's deeds and words were duly written, we must know what their order is.

The Gospel is put together by arrangement rather than by time. Matthew, then, must be placed first, because he took his beginning from the promise itself, that is, from Abraham, to whom the promise of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was made. After him comes Luke, because he narrates how this incarnation took place. Third is Mark, who testifies that the gospel preached by Christ was promised in the law. And fourth is John, because, speaking openly, he shows to be God the one who was promised to Abraham as one who would become incarnate, whose incarnation Luke described, and whose gospel Mark showed to have been preached in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah. For John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
V. Why does Matthew, in writing the gospel of Christ, say: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David,” when Abraham comes earlier?

He began this way so as to speak of Christ himself first, describing his genealogy from the promise of his incarnation, as the apostle says: “whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh.” He said “book of the generation” because Christ's incarnation is made up of many diverse people: since diverse peoples began from one, he would draw his bodily substance from them all — from Jews and Gentiles, from the worthy and the unworthy, for Ruth was a Moabitess, and Bathsheba was made a wife after being an adulteress — so that, drawing the flesh of all to himself, he might call them back to their native unity. And he said “of Jesus Christ the son of David,” although Abraham comes earlier, because Christ is specially called the son of David on account of the kingdom, so that, just as he is God from God, so also according to the flesh he might take his origin as a king from a king. For so it was said to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.”
VI. Why did the aforesaid apostle Matthew divide all the generations into three parts?

Causes create divisions and periods; that is why he marked off the period from Abraham to David. For the first section of the cause runs from Abraham to David, because Abraham is the father of faith and David the father of the kingdom — for Saul, having become unworthy, deprived himself of the kingdom. From David to the deportation is another section of the cause, in which the Jews, having become reprobate, lost the kingdom. After the Babylonian deportation, up to Christ, comes the third section, one of lamentation and misery, of their captivity and dispersion; for although after the Babylonian deportation and the period of seventy years they were released by Cyrus and returned to their own land, they never had any pause or rest. For Judea was never able to rule afterward, but they were always anxious and wandering. Indeed, at the time of Christ's birth they were captives, saying: “We have no king but Caesar.” For this reason, then, Matthew made three stages of the generation, to show the changes both of merits and of causes from the making of the promise up to Christ, but that the seasons of the year remain in one grace until the end.
VII. Why, when there are forty-one generations, does the evangelist seem to have counted forty-two? For what do three times fourteen make but forty-two?
By simple count forty-one generations are numbered, but by reckoning forty-two are established.

Jeconiah was begotten at the deportation — that is, made king, as is recorded in Chronicles — and he closed the second section; and because after the deportation he remained in the kingship with King Nebuchadnezzar's permission, the third section, which reaches to Christ, begins with him. So Jeconiah is counted twice, to conclude the second section and to begin the third. For it reads thus: “And after the Babylonian deportation Jeconiah begot Shealtiel.” Up to this Shealtiel, those of Judah reigned, but it is from their root that Joseph is born. For Jeconiah had a first son named Assir; but since Joseph traces his origin through the line of Shealtiel, Assir was passed over and Shealtiel was joined to his father Jeconiah, so as to arrive at Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed. Jeconiah also follows after Josiah; but because the line comes to Joseph through Jehoiakim, Jeconiah's father, he passed over him, that is, Jehoiakim, and set down Jeconiah, so as not to exceed the number of fourteen generations, and because after Jeconiah come Shealtiel and his son, through whom Joseph arises.

XVII. Why did the Savior fast forty days after his baptism and then become hungry? Could not someone who had fasted forty days by then be beyond hunger?

It is written: “Son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” And so the Savior fasted to give us a pattern, so that we too, persevering in fasting in the same way, may with God's help overcome every movement of the devil set against us, knowing from the Savior's example that the adversary's snares must be guarded against all the more when we approach the fear of God. For he grieves that we have withdrawn from him, and therefore rages against us all the more. The Savior did this for us, not for himself.

Likewise his hunger was not for his own sake but for ours. For when the devil's temptations had been overcome by fasting — temptations that were not written down because they do not serve our progress — afterward, that is, after forty days, he allowed himself to suffer hunger, so that he might endure hunger, which is proper to a man. In this way the devil, who had already been defeated, seeing the weakness of hunger in him, would be stirred up to tempt him again, seeing that the one by whom he was being defeated was a man.

For this was the Savior's mystery: since the devil insulted man and lorded it over him after defeating him, he would be defeated by a man, so that God's power might win the victory for man. In this way Satan was made all the more contemptible, since he both saw a man and perceived a power that was not man's. For, dulled with amazement, he wondered that there was a mystery present that was hidden from him, such that he had the power to approach but not to ensnare. He was tormented for two reasons: seeing weakness, he approached and found power, so that, though he saw a man, he suspected the power of God. So the Savior hungered for this purpose: to make a mockery of Satan's cunning. And he fasted no longer than this so as to agree with Moses and Elijah.
XVIII. If “the law and the prophets were until John,” from whose time the kingdom of heaven has been preached — for he is the initiator of the new preaching — why did his baptism cease?

The baptism John began did not cease; rather, what it lacked was added to it. For John only baptized; he did not give the Holy Spirit to believers, as he himself says of the Savior: “I baptize you in water for repentance, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.” This is what he means: “Through me there is remission of sins, but the Holy Spirit is not given, so that the purified may be called sons; for this was reserved for the Savior, as Lord, so that people would not become sons of God unless they had received the Holy Spirit from the Son of God.” So the effect of John's baptism, which worked silently without questioning, though not without mention of the Savior so that what he did might be firm, is the gift of the Trinity. The Savior's condescension revealed this when he gave the formula of the three names, which from the beginning, under the name or person of the one God, have worked one undivided work. So interpretation was added to John's baptism, together with the disclosure of the long-hidden mystery; and a greater gift was added too, that the baptized, having received the Holy Spirit, might be sons of God. So it was amplified, not made void.

XIX. Why are “the law and the prophets until John” rightly said to have ceased? Because the one of whom they prophesied had now come. But why “the law until John,” when the apostle says that we ought to be subject to the law? “The things that exist,” he says, “are ordained by God.”

The law has one name, but it has a threefold meaning. The first part of the law concerns God. For if “law” (lex) is named from “selection” (lectio), so that you may know what to choose from many things, then those who were placed among errors received it so that they might choose the truth, that is, reject the devil and choose God. The second part of the law is the one contained in six precepts, which begins thus: “Honor your father and mother.” The third concerns new moons and the sabbath, the distinguishing and choosing of foods, circumcision, and the offering of animal sacrifices. It is this law, then, that he says was to be kept until John and no further. For it was given so that it would cease when its time was fulfilled. Nor did it exist from the beginning; it was given for a reason and for a time, so that the law would cease at the Savior's coming. So both the law of the precepts and its nature remain from God; it is undoubtedly from him and cannot be abolished. For through it one advances toward the promised reward. For fear begets carefulness.

XXII. The sabbath is certainly law, or part of the law. How then was the law not made void when the sabbath was broken, as the evangelist says: “because he was not only breaking the sabbath,” and so on?

The Savior did indeed break the sabbath, but without prejudice to the sabbath that had been given. For when the time of the sabbath was already coming to an end, but the Jews still maintained that the sabbath remained in force, the Savior, by working on sabbaths and ordering the sick man to carry his bed on the sabbath, broke the sabbath according to the Jews' understanding. For in truth, to say this of something that had already ceased [?] is like saying, of someone who ought now to be called a former prefect and who has suffered an injury, that the prefecture has suffered injury. So the sabbath was not broken; rather, the people who imprudently claimed authority for the sabbath were made fools of, since a new law had already succeeded the sabbath.
XXIII. Why did the Savior call his disciples sons of thunder, when it would seem more fitting for them to be called sons of God? For thunder is said to arise from the collision of clouds.

Since thunder strikes terror, the Lord called his disciples sons of thunder for this reason, as if they were the sons of one who is to be feared. For although thunder arises from the collision of clouds, it still arises by the will of God and is terrifying.

XXVIII. It is evident that the Savior was called Son of God and Christ at his birth. Why then, after his baptism, did the tempter approach him saying: “If you are the Son of God,” and so on?

The Savior was born of the virgin in such a way that he was both Christ and Son of God, not by being made but by birth. But while he was still young, emptying himself of his power — that is, concealing his power — he did not provoke the devil's impudence. But when he was baptized and the Holy Spirit descended upon him, and the testimony of God the Father had shown people who he was, the enemy was driven by jealous rivalry to envy, seeing that this event worked against him; for he understood that the ordinance of baptism had been provided for the salvation of mankind. So he approaches the Savior, the author of this ordinance, not to test him with a view to approving him but to find an opening to overthrow him. For temptation sometimes serves to prove, and sometimes slyly to subvert. For he thought he might draw from the Savior an answer that suited the deceit of his own will, so that he would have his whole kingdom, confident that once the Savior, the leader of the teaching, was made subject to him, no one would escape death at his hands.
XXIX. Why did the Savior resist the devil, when the devil tempted him, with nothing but examples from the law?

"The Saviour answered not only the devil" who tempted him, but also the Jews, through whom the devil carried out his cruel impiety against the Saviour. For he foreknew that the Jews would call him an enemy of the law, so he silenced the impudence of their father, the devil, with testimonies from the law, in order to condemn the father in the sons and the sons in the father.

XXXII. The Gospel testifies that "no one has seen God"; yet Jacob, Moses and Isaiah declare that they saw God. But someone says: "No one has seen the Father." What has that to do with it? If the Son was seen, the Father was seen too, since the Father and the Son are both one God, in substance and in image, because the two have one image, and, as he himself says, "Whoever sees me sees the Father also." How then has no one seen God the Father, when the Son says that the Father is seen when he himself is seen, since he is not another God? So if he is not another, then he himself, being the same because he is one, is God, and he was seen.

As far as the evangelist is concerned, he said this about God the Father: that no one has seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known. Let us believe the Son, for he has declared that no one but he has seen God. He said this to teach that it was always he who appeared to the patriarchs and prophets. So this does not refer to the one God, but to the person of the Father, who cannot be spoken of otherwise than as God the Father. The Son, however, says that he was seen in such a way that he is nevertheless invisible even when he is thought to be seen. For "seen" here means "understood": he was certainly not seen with the eyes but understood with the mind, and to have seen was to have understood that God was present in what appeared there. And when the Saviour says, "Whoever sees me sees the Father also," he certainly did not mean the sight of the eyes but of the mind, so that no one would think there was any difference between the Father and the Son. Neither of them, then, was seen in his substance; but in appearance [?] the Son alone was seen, by the mind and not by fleshly eyes, because he is invisible as the Father is.

XXXIII. Why did the Saviour at first refuse mercy to a foreign woman, that is, the Canaanite, when he did not refuse the gift of healing to the foreign centurion or to the leper whom Jesus himself called a foreigner?

The circumstances themselves show that the Saviour acted fittingly. It would have been absurd, and an injury to the promise made to the fathers, if a woman who had not confessed the God of the Jews had received the gift promised to the nation that confessed God. That is why it was refused her at first. But once she bowed her neck and did not withhold her faith from the Saviour's words, and confessed that the believing Jews were the children while the Gentiles were dogs or servants, she joined herself by this to faith in the Lord; for servants point to a master, and a master is not without servants, and so a unity was formed between the one subjected and the one who subjects. This is why she was worthy to obtain what she asked for. The centurion, on the other hand, who received the gift from the Saviour without hesitation, had long ago steeped himself in the things of God. Indeed, the elders of the Jews say to the Lord: "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us." As for the leper, the Lord called him a "foreigner" not by faith but by nation. For he was a Samaritan, and the Samaritans are known to be of Babylonian origin. Yet even he did not obtain the gift without confession, because the Lord had told his disciples: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." That is, the gospel was not to be preached to the Samaritans and the Gentiles before the Jews, to whom this promise belonged. But once the Jews began to reject faith in Christ, the Saviour then offered himself to the Samaritan woman too, and after the cross to the centurion Cornelius. When the Canaanite woman sought him, however, he received her only after refusing at first, because the time had not yet come for salvation to be offered to her.
