XXXIX. The apostle Peter says, "Christ died for us," but the apostle Paul asserts that he also died for himself: "He became," he says, "obedient unto death; therefore God gave him the name that is above every name." If this is so, he will seem to have been imperfect, since he gained an increase through his own works.

None of the faithful doubts that the Son of God was born of God perfect. For in being born of God the Father he received everything belonging to the Father's divinity. It was then, therefore, that he received the name that is above every name, that is, to be called what the Father is called: God. For nothing is said to be future with him, since he has everything before him. He was born, then, to create and to restore all these things. For order and reason certainly require that every knee should bend to the Father's name. The Father gave this to the Son on account of what he was going to do; but he gave it when he begot him. For he begot him in such a way that he would be in the same honour as the Father himself.
XL.
XL = LXXII.
XLI.
XLI = LXXIII.
XLII. John to the Lord: "Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?"

Under his own person he pleads the case of his disciples. For John was not in doubt, since he had said, "Behold the Lamb of God, behold the one who takes away the sin of the world." But to satisfy his disciples he sends them with his own words, so that the Saviour's own mouth might confirm what John himself was teaching about him, and so that after his death his disciples would follow Christ without any doubt.
XLIII. Why, when the Saviour healed almost everyone by a word, did he restore the blind man's eyes with mud made from spittle?

The Saviour did this to confound those who find fault with the creation. For when he corrected a defect that had befallen the body in no other way than the Creator had made it, he commended the author of this work. He corrected it by the very means by which it had been made. For whatever is made, if after a lapse it is restored by the same means by which it was made, will be shown to have been made rightly. And if the Saviour proves himself God by this, that he corrected the injuries and defects of the body, how much more is he God who devised the body itself!
XLIV. When he was about to perform a wonderful and unheard-of act of power, namely raising Lazarus from the dead, why did he weep, or ask where he had been laid as if he did not know?

The Saviour is God and man, and so he always played both parts: because he had human feelings, he wept; but because he was also God, he raised the man he had wept for. One always goes from the least to the greater, so that, since he was seen to be a man, he proved himself to be what he appeared to be; but by his works he declared himself God.
XLV. Why do we read earlier that Herod died, but later, after many years, that Herod killed John, when John outlived the Herod who died earlier?

Herod was king of Judea. He had four sons: Archelaus, Herod, Philip and Lysanias. When their father Herod died, Archelaus succeeded him, and when he died the kingdom of the aforementioned Herod was divided into four parts, so that Pilate was admitted to a fourth part of the kingdom as governor, not as king, while Herod's sons were called kings. Then, when Philip in turn died, his brother Herod took his wife, and was rebuked by John the Baptist for her; for this reason Herod, son of the Herod mentioned above, killed him. What does the text say? "Herod the tetrarch," that is, the one set over a fourth part of his father Herod's kingdom. Why then is there any doubt, when the meaning of the added title shows that this is a different Herod? He is the one who also killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, and who afterwards was struck by an angel of God and died swarming with worms.
XLVI.
XLVI = LXXXVI.
XLVII.
XLVII = LXXV.
XLVIII. Why does the apostle say that he has become all things to all people, which seems the act of a flatterer and a hypocrite?

A flatterer is one who agrees so as not to offend someone whose favour he wants to keep. But one who, to avoid giving scandal, does something that is not dangerous but merely unnecessary is seeking the salvation of the person he does not want to see scandalized. When the apostle Paul circumcised Timothy on account of the Jews, and entered the temple after being purified, he certainly behaved this way so that those who were zealous for the tradition of their fathers would not be scandalized and either kill him or think our religion hostile to them. He was willing to allow something lesser in order to gain something greater. For he could have sinned gravely if he had not made himself a Jew by going into the temple to pray; so he submitted himself in order to benefit them. With those who were under the law, that is, the Samaritans, he agreed on the ground that they are known to confess rightly that the books of Moses are from God, and that circumcision and the Sabbaths were given by God. From these he showed them that the Christ they were hoping for was the one he was preaching. You have this in the Samaritan woman's words to the Lord: "I know that the Messiah is coming; when he comes, he will tell us everything." In line with this belief he followed up the words of the books of Moses, who said: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers." With those who were without the law he agreed on this point, that they say the world and the human race were made by God. For he says: "As some of your own have said, 'For we are his offspring.'" In this way, then, he became all things to all people, so as to further their salvation.
XLIX.
XLIX = LXXVI.
L. Since we profess that the Saviour was born, why does the apostle say that he was made of the seed of David, when to be made is one thing and to be born another?

In this passage "making" could be understood as birth, for making does differ from begetting, but in other matters, not where it is a question of flesh and body. Yet the apostle did not speak in these words without reason, since in another place too he says, "made of a woman." So he meant something by this expression. Because the Lord's flesh was not formed in the virgin's womb and made into a body from human seed, but by the working and power of the Holy Spirit, the apostle spoke this way. For it is one thing to make blood congeal and to beget by the mixing of seed, and another to bring forth not by mixing but by power. So he said "made" because he was not begotten.

LI. Why did the apostle say to the Galatians, whom he reproves and rebukes throughout the whole letter: "Be as I am, for I am as you are"? If he made himself such as they were, it was superfluous to say, "Be as I am." Or had he perhaps begun to imitate them in some things, and in others wants them to imitate him?

Which of them could imitate the apostle? Or what was lacking in the teacher of the Gentiles? But he urges them to imitate him, and since this is not impossible, he reproves them thus when he says: "For I am what you are. You are human beings, just as I am; so do what I do." It can also refer to this: he says he became all things to all people by agreeing with them in those matters in which they did not depart from the truth, especially the Gentiles. For none of their practices was of the kind that should no longer be done though formerly done rightly, such as circumcision and the observance of Sabbaths, new moons and foods. But whatever of the Gentiles' views he approved, he showed should not now cease. For they say that the world was made by God, and human beings too; this always stands. So if he agreed with them in these things and became as they were, he urges them in the same way to become as he is, agreeing with his teaching.

LII. How are we free in judgment and will, when the apostle says: "The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do what you want"? And if the flesh desires against the spirit, it is evil, for the spirit prompts what is good.

In this passage you are not to understand "flesh" as the substance of the flesh, but as evil acts and unbelief signified by the flesh. Because all error comes from visible and worldly things, and the flesh is akin to them, since it is made of the elements, he calls all error "flesh." He calls not only adulteries, fornications and debauchery works of the flesh, but also idolatry, sorcery, blasphemies and the like. Does the flesh compel blasphemy or idolatry? Are these not vices of the soul when it consents to error? Of those who act rightly, he says that they are not in the flesh but in the spirit, and yet they are certainly still in the body. So whoever walks well and does not lose confidence in the hope of the faithful is said not to be in the flesh, even though he is placed in the flesh; but whoever acts wickedly and blasphemes is said to be in the flesh, because just as those who act well are spiritual while still in the flesh, so those who live wickedly are carnal while still having a soul. For this is what is named by what he says [?]

This error, then, which he calls the flesh, desires against the spirit; that is, it prompts evil against the spirit, which is the law of God. For he introduces two laws, that of God and that of the devil. So he says that the spirit, because the law of God is spiritual, fights against the flesh, that is, against the vices, to keep a person for God; while the law of the devil, which is error, opposes it with the allurements of pleasure and worldly sweetness. Between these two warring powers stands the human being. When he consents to the spirit, the flesh does not want it; when he gives his hand to the flesh, he scorns the spirit, that is, he despises the law of God. So when he consents to the flesh, the spirit calls him back so that he does not do what he wants; and when he agrees with the spirit, the flesh tempts him so that he does not do what he thinks beneficial. But the spirit opposes and calls him back rightly and with foresight, to rescue him from the counsels of Satan, whereas the flesh, which is the opposing law, tempts him and resists the spirit of the law so as to deceive him by trickery.

The apostle makes these things known, then, to show human judgment to what it should commit its will; not to make the freedom of judgment void, but to teach judgment what it should join itself to. If there were no judgment of the will, neither the law of the devil, which is the flesh, nor the law of God, which is the spirit, would tempt a person with their counsels in opposition to each other. For whoever tempts, persuades; whoever persuades does not use force but gets round the person; and the one who is got round has his will changed by certain deceptions. If there were no free will, a person would be dragged unwillingly to what he does not want.
LIII. In what way is the wisdom of the flesh hostile to God, or what is this wisdom that is not subject to the law of God?

This question does not differ in meaning from the previous one. For it has been explained what is meant by "flesh," and from this its wisdom can easily be recognized. We said that all the elements, that is, the substances of visible things, are called flesh. Their reasoning is such that they think nothing can come about without mixture, abhorring the principle of a spiritual and simple power and judging it foolish. Those who distrust spiritual things and follow carnal things know nothing else and think nothing true except what the reasoning of the elements contains. So they believe neither that a virgin gave birth nor that the flesh rises again, because the reasoning of the flesh, that is, of the elements, does not admit it, since everything generated in time is produced by the working of mixture; and they believe that bodies that have died and decomposed cannot be restored to life again, because when the mixture is separated each element returns to its own nature. Puffed up by these arguments, they deny what we believe is to come or has already happened. And so their assertion is hostile to God, since it thinks foolish and empty what God has done and has promised to do.
LIV.
LIV = LXXVII.
LV. Why is it that John the Baptist, after first bearing witness to the Saviour, later doubted, saying through his disciples: "Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?"

Those who think that John doubted disparage the Saviour. For either they claim that John was right to doubt, or they certainly accuse the Saviour of lacking knowledge, because, as they think, he praised someone who had a poor opinion of him. But since it is impossible for the Saviour to be deceived, John was rightly praised by him. And if he was rightly praised, he did not doubt. For at the very time when John sent his disciples to Jesus from prison, saying, "Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?", Jesus answered his disciples, saying: "Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the lame walk, the dead rise; and blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me." And as John's messengers were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John the Baptist: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind, or a man dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, more than a prophet. This is the one of whom it is written: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way.'" Then even the tax collectors who had been baptized with John's baptism praised God.

How great was the praise given to John, that he should be called more than a prophet! And the Saviour calls blessed the one who is not scandalized in him: how could John be praised if he was scandalized by doubting? No, he certainly did not doubt. For the praise shows him to be blessed, because he was not scandalized. Indeed, the Saviour burst out in praise of John at that very moment precisely to show that John's mind was free of his disciples' doubt. John, wishing to strengthen his wavering disciples in faith in the Saviour, and knowing that his death was at hand, wanted what he had been saying about him to be confirmed by the Saviour's own mouth. So, to be a true witness, he calls on the testimony of one greater, so that their agreement might remove all uncertainty. This was John's device: to send the doubters as though with his own words, so that hearing from the Saviour the same things they had heard from John they might be made firm, knowing that the testimony of so reliable an agent and of the heavenly Lord could not be called into question. That is why the Saviour answered as if to John, so that between John asking and the Saviour answering they might learn the truth.
LVI.
LVI = LXXVIII.

LVII. What does the apostle mean when he says to the Galatians: "I am amazed that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in grace to another gospel, which is not another"? If it is certainly another, it is not the same; if it is not the same, how is it not another?

He called it "another gospel" than the one to which they had been called, because what the Galatians later began to follow was not this. Led away from the gospel of Christ, they had been drawn into Judaism under the name of Christ, as though this were what had to be followed, and they affirmed something other than what the apostle preached. Hence it follows: "as they persuade you." For the false apostles, when they deceived the believing Gentiles, said that what they themselves taught had been handed down by the Saviour, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." So the apostle, moved with grief at their overthrow, writes to them, saying: "I am amazed that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in grace to another gospel, which is not another."

He is amazed, then, that after something gentle and light they were eager for harshness and a burden; that is, that after the simplicity of faith they allowed themselves to be circumcised for the sake of the elements, and kept new moons and the Sabbath, subject to the elements. And so as not to seem to have given an opening to the false apostles, who said that what the Galatians had received was different from what the tradition of truth holds, he immediately added: "which is not another, except that there are some who are troubling you and want [?] to pervert the gospel of Christ." So the gospel to which they had been called by the apostle was different from what they had begun to follow at the urging of the false apostles; yet it was not different from what Christ had handed down. This was so that by this very fact they might recognize that they had been led into error, and might follow faith alone, confessing Christ as God, and that he is sufficient to grant salvation, he through whom, and not through the law, they had obtained the forgiveness of sins; for the grace of God forgives sins without the law.

LVIII. Many sins seem to be committed against the body, for anyone who does violence to himself in any part of his body certainly sins against his own body: one castrates himself, another ends his life with a noose, another drives a blade into himself. Why then does the apostle say: "Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body"?

Do you think the apostle was unskilled, or do you want the force of the saying explained? When the apostle said "body", he did not mean a single person. He included the woman as well, because the woman is a portion of the man. All the crimes mentioned above, which each person commits by violence against himself, do not defile the whole body. The individual sins, and so he alone becomes guilty. In fornication, however, the whole body is polluted, because consent to the defilement binds both the man and the woman. That is why fornication is a grave offence. A person sins most wickedly when he looks for a partner in his crime and leads that partner to perdition. One who lives well will also receive a reward for the person he has won over, and the wicked man likewise becomes guilty not only in himself but also in the one he wanted as a partner in damnation. How much more, then, is this true of the fornicator, who clearly defiles himself twice over, in a sense, by a single offence! For if he sins against the flesh that came from himself, he certainly corrupts himself twice.

Someone might think he can change the question by applying this saying either to the church or to the body of Christ, but that will not stand. It would be said improperly, and he would be like the Novatianists. To support their mad cause, they declare that the fornicator sins not against his own body but against Christ's, because Christians are members and the body of Christ. On this view fornication would be the same as sacrilege, and such a person would be said to sin against Christ just as one who denies Christ does. This argument is weak and fragile, because it is caught in a snare whichever way it turns and cannot escape. If the fornicator sins against the body of Christ, then other sins will not be committed against Christ, for example if a Christian kills a brother, or sacrifices to idols, or commits some other kind of sin, because every sin is outside the body except fornication. But if not every sin is outside the body, and every sin of whatever kind is committed against Christ, then whoever steals, perjures himself, lies, strikes a brother or does any such thing would be said to sin against Christ or against the Holy Spirit, which is quite absurd. And yet the apostle calls the church the members and body of Christ, so that we are members of one another. How then does the fornicator sin against his own body and not rather against Christ's? Because according to the mystery of the church we are called Christ's body, not our own, and that is far from the point at issue. The fornicator sins against his own body because the whole [?] is defiled.
LIX.
LIX = LXXIX

LX. Why did the apostle Paul rebuke his fellow apostle Peter because, "fearing those of the circumcision, he withdrew" from the Gentiles? Paul himself, fearing those of the circumcision, "took Timothy and circumcised him", which he forbade others to do. Is he not then to be rebuked as well?

It is incredible that so great an apostle would rebuke another for something he knew he had given way to himself. It is not right to believe that so great a man did this, for such behaviour belongs to those who live according to the flesh. The apostle Paul's action, therefore, is free from blame. He preached that people should not be circumcised. But he wanted to take Timothy with him, whose mother was Jewish and whose father was Greek, and it would have scandalized the Jews if he took on a man born of a Jewish woman who was uncircumcised. So for the moment he submitted himself to the situation and took Timothy and circumcised him. He did an unnecessary thing, then, with the permission of the one who underwent it. Timothy had a Jewish mother and had been taught the sacred writings in the synagogue from infancy, that is, the books of the Hebrews. So he allowed himself to be circumcised to remove a stumbling block for the Jews, who were zealous for their own race. Indeed Paul says, "Titus, being a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised." But Timothy, as I said, had a Jewish mother, and the Jews would not allow him to be taken on among the teachers uncircumcised. The apostle took him on so that he could ordain him a bishop, and that is what he did. Timothy was trained in the prophetic writings and proved a capable teacher for proclaiming Christ.

The apostle Peter would not have been rebuked if he had separated himself from the Gentiles out of fear of the Jews, so as not to be a stumbling block to them. What was rebuked in the apostle Peter was this. Before, he had lived like a Gentile among the Greek believers. But when Jews came from James, he gave way to fear and taught that those from among the Gentiles must live like Jews. Hence he hears: "If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" He had cast doubt on the teaching of the gospel, which is a crime, since he was tearing down what he had built. That is why the apostle Paul calls this dissimulation. It is clear that when Paul circumcised Timothy, he did not hide the fact that he was doing an unnecessary thing because of their scandal, and that he gave way because Timothy had a Jewish mother. The Jews would not have pressed the matter except on account of his Jewish mother [?], since they could not have found fault with this in Gentiles [?], nor would they easily take offence at those who were not of the race of Israel. So Paul did not do this out of dissimulation but under pressure. The case mentioned above, however, involved no small dissimulation. Many were rebuked in that affair, so much so that some of the Jews, and even Barnabas, joined in this dissimulation.
LXI. Which spirit does the apostle say is to be saved when he says that such a man is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh?

The destruction of the flesh happens when someone gives himself over to pleasures and carnal desires and so brings Gehenna upon himself, for he gains destruction from the works of the flesh. Through these he becomes wholly carnal. When a person lives according to the law, the whole person becomes spiritual, so that even the flesh is called what the soul is. In the same way, if he lives according to the desires of the world and the pleasures of lust, the whole person becomes flesh and advances to the destruction of the flesh. The flesh is fluid, corruptible and mortal, so when it loses the soul it becomes disfigured. Lacking form, it dissolves into destruction, for it perishes when it loses the vigour of all its members. So too the soul is disfigured by such a body. Having scorned its vigour [?], it is in punishment together with the flesh in which it stained itself with vices. So the flesh gains no advancement through the soul. Instead the soul is destroyed through the flesh, because it did not govern the body spiritually, though it was given to the flesh as its queen, but itself teaches the works of the flesh.

So when the church casts out such a man, it keeps the spirit safe, namely the Holy Spirit, who is the guardian of the church. Such a man defiled his father's wife with lust. If they allow him to stay among them, when they could compel him by the law so that he does not contaminate everyone, the Holy Spirit will depart from the church because of the polluted man, and the church will not have the spirit safe. What is lost is not safe on the day of the Lord either. Those found stripped of the Spirit cannot be counted among the children of God, for the Spirit bears witness that we are children of God.

The apostle says this to the people because bishops had not yet been ordained for the churches in every place. So he orders the people to do what he would have done if a bishop had been appointed there: to unite in one mind and expel that man from their assembly, so that they would not seem to consent to his deeds. Whoever does not rebuke a person when he can, but receives him as though he were not in error, gives him fuel for sinning. For that reason he too is defiled and drives the Holy Spirit away from himself.

To the Thessalonians, too, he says among other things in a similar way: "May your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord." The sense is the same, for to be "safe" is the same as to be "whole". The king says to Daniel: "Are the seals safe, Daniel?" And Daniel answers: "Safe, O king," that is, whole. So our spirit is whole when it does not abandon us. Those whom the Spirit abandons will no longer be whole as far as regeneration is concerned, because they do not have the one through whom they were called children of God. It is no contradiction if we say that the Spirit himself abandons us when we sin and is not whole. He is not whole when he abandons us, because he was our leader and guide. If he is our head, we are his members. But when we do something against him, it is not he who abandons us. Rather, we are seen to abandon him, and then he seems not to be whole, because he loses us. This is true and plain: it is not he who turns away from us, but we who turn away from him when we sin. And to the Colossians he says among other things: "from which the whole body, supplied and nourished [?], grows with the growth of the Lord." If we take this according to the sound of the words, it does not fit, for God lacks nothing that he should gain growth through us. Rather, when we return to the author of our life and confess him, he gains us for salvation and the Godhead produces growth in us. And so in those who depart from him there is loss. Not being whole, then, is the same as suffering loss.

LXII. Why does the Saviour say, "Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath", when the time of this persecution cannot be put off? The apostle says, "who will be revealed in his own time", and in the Acts of the Apostles it says, "determining the times and the boundaries of their dwelling". And why is it not permitted to flee in winter or to go out on the sabbath?

Flight is not safe in winter. It is cold, the rains are constant, it snows, it freezes, and the rivers overflow, so it is very hard for those who flee. They cannot hide in the woods, or in the mountains, or in caves. On the sabbath, according to the Jews, it is not permitted to go far from the city or to climb high ground, and so you cannot flee on the sabbath. These times make flight unsafe because of the obstacles mentioned above. In the same way our flight will not be safe if the foretold persecution finds us bound by the obstacles of the flesh. Worldly desires and earthly wealth hold people back like shackles, and they cannot escape the devil's seduction. So we must pray that when the time comes to flee, the condition of winter and sabbath will not be found in us. We must pray that God's help may keep us free from these obstacles, so that nothing may hold us captive by our desire for it and make us slaves of the world. The Saviour was speaking about the last persecution, which will come in the time of Antichrist. So he mentioned winter, which is the last season, and likewise the sabbath, which is the last day. Flight in these times is harsh and difficult, and in the same way he wanted to show that the persecutions and afflictions of that time will be so severe that hardly anyone will be able to escape them.
LXIII.
LXIII = LXXX
LXIV.
LXIV = LXXXI

LXV. What does the apostle mean when he says, "No one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit"? Can Photinus, then, who denies that Christ is God, confess our Lord Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit? Can Marcion and Mani, who deny that Christ came in the flesh, say "Lord Jesus Christ" in the Holy Spirit? Or can harlots and the unclean, since the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sin, and wisdom does not enter a malicious soul?

Truth is neither proved nor disproved by the person who speaks it. Whatever is said well and truly is without doubt said in the Holy Spirit. So if someone is guilty in other matters, he should not be ruled out in this, when he speaks the truth. In fact it is not he who is ruled out, but Christ the Lord who is contradicted, for whoever denies that this man speaks the truth does injury to Christ. Suppose the truth is spoken and someone denies that what is true is said in the Holy Spirit, even though Christ accepts it. (None of the good rebukes a person who speaks truly about him. And what is learned through tradition is not learned by revelation.) Even so, no one who speaks the truth can be proved wrong.

LXVI. If no one is justified before God by the law, why is it written: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them"? If people are justified by faith and not through the law, why is anyone who has not fulfilled the law cursed, since the law does not lead to righteousness?

The law given through Moses did contain righteousness, but an earthly righteousness. Those who kept the law were righteous for the present life and did not become guilty, for a person is righteous by the law if he harms no one. Hence the apostle says: "The law is not of faith, but whoever does these things will live by them." That is, whoever does the law will not die but will live for the present. But the righteousness that comes from faith justifies people before God, so that they are rewarded in the world to come. They added the righteousness of faith to temporal righteousness. For it is right to know from whom and through whom we exist, so that a true confession of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit may lead us to the heavenly kingdom. The ancients too, who not only kept the law of commandments but also loved God and had hope in the promise, were justified before God. So he says that the law alone does not justify people before God, just as faith alone does not commend them to God without good works. But when both earthly and divine righteousness are kept, they make people perfect. Hence the Lord says: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven."

LXVII. If all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, how can the same Saviour say that he does not know the day and hour of the coming judgment? And if he knows and says he does not know, he seems to be lying.

This saying has a double sense. First, he says that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ in this sense: whoever has Christ has him in place of all wisdom and knowledge, so that to know Christ is to know everything and to have grasped all wisdom. As he says to the Colossians: "Let no one deceive you through philosophy and empty seduction according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ, because in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily." That is, whoever believes in Christ lacks nothing for salvation, but has it in abundance, because the fullness of the Godhead is in faith in him. And again in the same letter he says among other things: "Let no one lead you astray with a lowly heart and the worship of angels, which he sees as he puffs himself up, vainly inflated by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from which the whole body, supplied and nourished [?], grows with the growth of God." So if those who believe in Christ revere the head of all rule and authority, they lack nothing but have everything needed for salvation. It will do them no harm not to know lesser things that contribute nothing to salvation, since they know what is necessary. People of this kind, then, should be said to know everything, because they know what will profit them for salvation.

There is also this second sense. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the Saviour, for all the Father's mysteries are known to him and he measures out the whole of creation. Further, the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, and no one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God, who is also the Spirit of Christ. How then can he be said not to know the day and hour of the coming judgment, when his Spirit knows what is in God, the Spirit of whom he said that he has received from what is his? If the one who received from what is his knows what is to come, how can Christ not know, who sent us the Holy Spirit? And can it be that the judge does not know the day of the coming judgment, when he has given all the signs of when it is to be expected? Perhaps, then, he will also be said truly not to know those to whom he will say, "Truly I tell you, I do not know you." Nor will he be said not to know the foolish and improvident virgins, though he also said to them, when they cried, "Lord, Lord, open to us": "Truly I tell you, I do not know you." So there is a reason for him to say that he does not know what he knows. Indeed he says: "Keep watch, therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come." So to make us careful and watchful, when he was asked he said that he did not know the day and hour of the coming judgment. He denied that he knew what he knew, for our benefit. We do not know what is good for us, for we want to know things that would harm us if we knew them. So Christ, who provides for our salvation, said that he did not know, so that we would not hear something that would work against us. Suppose a man in anguish asks for a sword to kill himself, and the one who has a sword answers that he has none. Is he to be convicted of lying for denying it, when he knows that if he did not deny it, the opposite of what is good would follow?
LXVIII.
LXVIII = LXXXII

LXIX. The Saviour says: "Whoever does not leave all his possessions" (that is, house and field and the rest) "cannot be my disciple." On the other hand, the evangelist says: "There came Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man, who was himself also a disciple of Jesus, waiting for the kingdom of God." Why does the evangelist declare him a disciple when the Saviour denied that such a man could be one? Zacchaeus too was rich, and so was Cornelius the centurion, and so were the women who provided for him from their means.

The apostle settles this question in a few words when he says: "Let those who have be as though they had not, those who use this world as though they did not use it, and those who buy as though they did not possess." So whoever has these things as though he did not have them is considered to have left them. He does not rely on them or boast of them, but walks humbly, not only in his dress but also in his mind, and understands that he has been made their steward and servant. Such a person is considered to have left all his possessions. For a thing is said to be left when it is withdrawn from desire and has no hold on one's affection.

LXX. Mary wanted to touch the Saviour out of joy. Why does he say to her, "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father", when we read that the other women both touched and worshipped him?

The words "Do not touch me" are spoken in indignation. Mary longed for the Saviour, yet while others believed in his resurrection, she stood weeping at the tomb when she should already have been rejoicing. She had heard from the apostles John and Peter that the Lord had risen. For this is what you have: "And he saw the linen cloths and the face-cloth in one place, and he believed; for they did not yet know the scriptures, that he must rise from the dead." But Mary did not believe, because she had not seen him risen. Her very great love made her doubt. After all, when those we love suffer some harm, we do not believe they will escape it; but when those we hate are already near death, we can hardly believe it. Mary was stunned and grieving because of her love, when she ought to have followed the faith of the disciples. So the Lord showed himself to her first, so that she would cease from grief, yet not without indignation. Hence she hears: "Do not touch me." That is: "You are following a carnal understanding. Hold back from it and follow spiritual things, which are not seen." "For I have not yet ascended to the Father," he says.

This is like the case of John the Baptist when he sent his disciples to Jesus and said: "Go and say: John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or should we wait for another?'" In his own person he was pleading his disciples' case. John was not in doubt, for he had said, "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world." But to satisfy his disciples, he sent them with his own words, so that the Saviour's mouth would confirm what John himself taught about him, and after his death his disciples would follow Christ without any doubt. In the same way the Saviour rebukes Mary with reference to himself when he says, "I have not yet ascended to the Father", that is: "Your heart is still pressed down to the earth, since you do not believe unless you see." If she had lifted her heart to God, she would have believed with the disciples that the Lord had risen.
LXXI. What does the Saviour mean when he says, "I am the door; those who came before me are thieves and robbers"? This saying seems to strike at the prophets.

No one comes to God the Father except through faith in Christ, and that is why the Saviour calls himself the door of the kingdom of heaven. If, then, he is speaking of a door, why did he need to speak of earlier people, saying, "All who came before me"? No question was being raised about the past; surely, since the door was present, the question concerned people who were present. The Saviour is in fact speaking of the Jews, who thought they would enter the kingdom of God not through faith but through the righteousness of the law. They came before the Saviour, that is, they stood before him and disparaged him by contradicting him, so as to turn others away from faith in him as well. That is why they are called thieves and robbers. These words were spoken at the time when the Pharisees were arguing with the man who had been blind, to whom the Saviour gave the eyes that nature had denied him. They wanted [to turn] him away from faith in the Saviour [?], saying that the kingdom of God could not be entered through him, because he broke the sabbath, but only through the righteousness of the law. Then the Saviour said: "I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved and will find pasture; but if anyone tries to enter by another way, he is a thief and a robber."

How does this apply to the prophets? Were the prophets thieves and robbers? Did the teaching of the prophets [?] say that God's favour could be earned through the righteousness of the law without faith, when they knew that Christ would come in the flesh? So he said this about people who were present, so that whoever stood or sat before him should be understood as thieves and robbers. They took aside the man who had been blind and wanted to turn him away from faith in the Saviour, saying: "Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner." He refuted them, saying: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing." So it was about this man, because he persevered in faith, and about those who said, "These are not the words of a man who has a demon; can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" that the Saviour said: "But the sheep did not listen to them." "Them" means precisely those he called thieves and robbers. For how could the sheep not have listened to the prophets, when the Scriptures make it clear that all good people obey the prophets and the wicked obey false prophets?

LXXII. THE APOSTLE SAYS THAT CHRIST DIED FOR ALL, FOR HE SAYS: "THEREFORE ALL HAVE DIED, AND HE DIED FOR ALL." BUT THE LORD HIMSELF SAYS: "THE SON OF MAN CAME TO GIVE HIS LIFE AS A RANSOM FOR MANY." IN THIS WAY THEY CONTRADICT EACH OTHER.

The words are indeed different, but the sense is one. In the same way, identical words can have different senses. For example: "Whatever is not of faith is sin"; and again, "The law is not of faith," yet the law is not sin. So the people the Saviour called "many" are the same people the apostle meant by "all." They are many, because the greatest part of every people and nation will believe in the Saviour. These believers the apostle called "all." Thus he says, among other things: "And he died for all," that is, for those who have believed and will believe. He also died for those who refuse to believe. But since they do not accept the benefit, they do not want Christ to have died for them. For this reason he does not seem to have died for those whom his death did not help at all, but rather harmed. He is properly said to have died for those for whom the victory was won, who understand the mystery and give thanks to God through Christ our Lord.

LXXIII. WHY DOES DAVID SAY, "LET THOSE WHO SAY TO ME, 'WELL DONE, WELL DONE,' BE CONFOUNDED AND PUT TO SHAME," WHILE THE LORD SAYS, "WELL DONE, GOOD AND FAITHFUL SERVANT," AND SO ON? WHAT DAVID TOOK AS A REPROACH AND AN EVIL, THE SAVIOUR PRESENTS AS SOMETHING DUE TO GOOD MERITS.

This is not very different from the previous question, for one word has different meanings, as I mentioned above. David's detractors, who wished for his ruin, rejoiced at his misfortunes. While he was suffering distress and hardship at the hands of Saul and his own son Absalom, they said it was right and good that it should happen to him. It is as if someone said of a person suffering injuries, "It is well for him; let him enjoy his troubles," meaning, "It serves him right; he deserves it." In a similar way the Saviour, glad at good works, declares a person's merit, saying: "Well done, good and faithful servant." He rejoices because the servant has made himself more worthy, and he says "Well done," meaning, "You have acted rightly, so as to store up greater merit." So one word is applied to two opposite cases. We often say of someone, "He has been adjudged," but the context, either what follows or what goes before, shows in what sense it is said. Sometimes it is said in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one, just as "desire" is sometimes applied to good and sometimes to evil.
LXXIIII.
LXXIIII = XCVIIII

LXXV. THE APOSTLE CALLS THE LAW GIVEN BY MOSES HOLY, JUST, GOOD AND SPIRITUAL, AND ELSEWHERE HE SAYS: "FOR THE LAW BRINGS WRATH," AND: "WHERE THERE IS NO LAW, THERE IS NO TRANSGRESSION." SO IT IS SAFE TO BE WITHOUT THESE THINGS.

By comparing these statements yourself you ought to have satisfied your own question. This is how doubters usually raise questions: they look for conflict and contradiction in the statements of one man, a man whom it is not right to censure. The apostle, a man outstanding in every kind of praise and fortified by truth on every side, calls the law holy, just, good and spiritual. That should be enough for faith, and what seems contrary to it should have been looked into without obstinacy.

Your proposition, in fact, wants sin to go unpunished. When the apostle was setting the law of faith above the other law, because of the merit of the time and grace, he was writing to the Romans, who under faith in Christ had been led into the law. By "the law" I do not mean the natural law. The Romans were certainly under a law: the one brought from Athens by ten men sent there, with two more added later, which was written on two tablets that were buried on the Capitol. I mean the law called the law of works: that they should be circumcised, keep the sabbath and the new moons, distinguish between foods, take care to purify vessels, and the other things of this kind contained in the law. It is this law, then, that he says brings wrath. These things were added when God was angry, to be a burden on the faithlessness of the Jews, for out of so many commands some must inevitably be neglected. Hence the apostle Peter says: "Why do you place on the necks of the brothers a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" And God says through the prophet Jeremiah: "I gave them commandments that were not [?] good." These things were given to them to observe after their many offences, after they had tempted God, insulted Moses and spoken against God. They were meant to weigh down their stiff necks, so that wherever they turned they would face the law and have no relief.

So, to free them from this law, the apostle says, "Where there is no law, there is no transgression," so that they could serve God spiritually and without anxiety by a shorter way. He means: "If you keep the law of the Jews, you will inevitably transgress, for its commandments are so many that it is impossible to fulfil them."

How could he say this of the natural law? Moses wrote that law down to confirm its authority, not because it did not exist before, since we read that wrongdoing was punished before Moses. Would he have said it in order to explain that the Romans should no longer live under law, when it was in their interest to live under law? They could not have kept righteousness in any other way. And indeed he says to them: "Do you want to have no fear of the authority? Do good," and: "Those who resist will bring condemnation on themselves."

So the law he calls spiritual, and also shows to be holy, just and good, is the one we have called natural, which forbids sin, for it is the guide to a good life. When the law of faith is added to it, it makes a person perfect. The natural law, as I have called it, and the one called the law of works go by a common name, so the apostle seems to speak against the law. But so that he would not seem to be setting aside this law, without which this life cannot be governed, he says: "We know that the law is spiritual." He says this so that the law he does set aside would be recognized as the law of the sabbath, circumcision, foods and new moons. The other law is called spiritual because it puts away all sins.
LXXVI. IF THE JEWS RECEIVED HARSH COMMANDMENTS BECAUSE OF THEIR UNBELIEF AND THEIR SLANDERS, WHAT SIN HAD THEIR CHILDREN COMMITTED, THAT THEY TOO SHOULD BE BOUND BY THESE COMMANDMENTS?

The law was given to the fathers so that it would be a burden on children who were like them. For afterwards the children sinned against God no less than their fathers, and perhaps more. God, knowing this in advance, gave this law chiefly for the children, since the fathers all died in the wilderness.

LXXVII. THE SAVIOUR SAYS: "I PRAY FOR THOSE WHOM YOU HAVE GIVEN ME; I DO NOT PRAY FOR THE WORLD." THE APOSTLE JOHN, ON THE OTHER HAND, SAYS: "WE HAVE AN ADVOCATE WITH THE FATHER, WHO INTERCEDES FOR OUR SINS, AND NOT FOR OURS ONLY, BUT FOR THE WHOLE WORLD." THIS SEEMS CONTRADICTORY.

Although the sense does not differ greatly, what the Saviour says is one thing and what the apostle John affirms is another. The Saviour prays for his disciples, that they may be kept safe from the attacks of evil. Indeed he says: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil." The apostle John, however, introduces another kind of prayer, for he says: "We have an advocate who intercedes for our sins and for those of the whole world." So for Christians he intercedes in two ways: he prays for their sins, and he prays that they may be kept safe from the attacks of the devil. For those who do not believe, however, there is only this one petition: that although they deserve to be punished for their sins and their faithlessness, God's goodness and patience may wait for them, in case they are willing to be corrected. He does not ask that their sins be forgiven while they remain unbelievers, but that they be granted a long delay, so that if they amend, their offences may be forgiven. This, as we have said, is what the Saviour asks for them.

LXXVIII. IN THE GOSPEL WE READ THAT THE ANGEL SAID TO MARY, THE MOTHER OF THE LORD, THAT "OF HIS KINGDOM," THAT IS, CHRIST'S, "THERE WILL BE NO END." DANIEL SAYS THE SAME ABOUT HIM: "THEN AN ETERNAL KINGDOM WILL ARISE, WHICH WILL NEVER BE DESTROYED." THE APOSTLE, ON THE OTHER HAND, SAYS OF THE LORD: "WHEN HE HANDS OVER THE KINGDOM TO GOD THE FATHER." HOW WILL HE HAVE AN ETERNAL KINGDOM IF HE IS SAID TO HAND IT OVER TO GOD THE FATHER?

Where the Father and the Son, that is, God and Christ, are concerned, "handing over" is to be understood as a transfer, not an abolition. Consider how the Father handed over the kingdom to the Son, as the Lord himself testifies: "All things have been handed over to me by my Father." If the Father ceased to have it when he handed it over, then it can also be said of the Saviour that he lost it when he handed it over. Yet the Son, after saying that the kingdom had been handed over to him by the Father, still gives the Father first place, saying: "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." In this sense, then, the Son does not lose the kingdom when he hands it over, so that both statements are true, and the angel and Daniel are not out of agreement with this sense. Anyone who thinks their testimony should be disparaged is full of faithlessness.

Now, holding to this faith, let us see what it means for the Son to hand over the kingdom to the Father. It is what the apostle says, among other things, in another place: "Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all." This subjection, then, is itself the handing over of the kingdom. An explanation therefore seems necessary here, so that the Son is not denied to be subject to the Father, and yet is still said to have an eternal kingdom. This is the Son's kingdom: at his name every knee bows, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. The apostle Peter affirms this too when he says: "There is no other name given under heaven by which we must be saved." And the Lord himself says to his disciples: "Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and I will do it." Thus the Son reigns, since all things are saved in his name and whatever is asked is given, until the end of the world.

But after all things have confessed Christ, whether by force or willingly, and have been subjected to the power they had resisted, the mystery of the one God will be revealed to all. All thanksgiving will be offered to the Father, from whom are all things, so that when preaching ceases, the one God may be known in the mystery of the Trinity. When all powers, principalities and dominions have bent the knee to Christ, the Son will then make clear that he is not the one from whom all things come, but his Son, and that the Father is seen in him. This is the subjection and the handing over of the kingdom. By showing that it is the Father from whom all things come, he subjects himself to him, since he says that he is from him. Such brightness and majesty will be seen at the coming of the Son that all the powers and the choirs of angels will think that he is the one and only God. But when the Saviour says that he is not the one called the Father but his Son, he hands over the kingdom to the Father while he reigns. In this both the subjection and the handing over of the kingdom are made plain: when he professes that he is from the Father, he acknowledges that whatever he has belongs to the Father, and he refers the whole sum of things to him.
LXXVIIII.
LXXVIIII = LXXXIII

LXXX. WHY DID THE APOSTLE, WHEN REBUKING THE GALATIANS, NEED TO INSERT THIS STATEMENT? AMONG OTHER THINGS HE SAYS TO THE GALATIANS, WHO HAD FLED BACK TO THE LAW AFTER THE GOSPEL: "A MEDIATOR IS NOT OF ONE, BUT GOD IS ONE." HE WRITES AS IF THE GALATIANS DENIED THAT GOD IS ONE. YET THEY HAD BEEN LED INTO THE LAW PRECISELY ON THESE GROUNDS: THAT THEY SHOULD BELIEVE IN ONE AND ONLY GOD, AND THAT CHRIST HAD COME, BY PREDESTINATION, ONLY AS A SERVANT TO DISPENSE THE GIFT OF GOD'S GRACE.

It is clear that the Galatians had been led into the law in such a way that they still professed Christ, but not as he deserves. They did so in the manner of Photinus: since the law proclaims one God, it would be against the law to call Christ God. This was a fabrication of the Jews who, overcome by mighty miracles, believed in Christ after the cross, but in such a way that while professing Christ they still kept the law, as if all hope were not to be placed in Christ. These are the people the apostle calls false brothers. After the tradition handed down by the apostles, these people had corrupted the minds of the Galatians, turning them into Jews under the Saviour's name. This is why the apostle says that Christ came as arbiter between circumcision and uncircumcision. As he says to the Ephesians: "making peace in one new man." So Christ came as arbiter. An arbiter makes peace between two parties by setting down a new rule: he takes away the claims of both and reconciles them, so that by following his judgement they give up their old quarrel. When the Jew insists on circumcision and the Gentile on uncircumcision, there is discord; but when this is taken away, there is peace.

"If this is so," he says, "how is it that you Galatians, having become Jews, are corrupting Christ's arbitration?" That is why he said to them: "You have been cut off from Christ." They despised the terms of reconciliation he had set between the parties and turned back to the old mindset of the Jews, accusing both themselves and the reconciler, for whatever displeases is accused. This was what had driven the Galatians to turn to the law: to confess one God without the mystery, as if it were hostile to the law for Christ to be called God. So he says: "An arbiter, that is, a mediator, is not of one," but of two, of course. "You, however, have turned to the law and rejected the arbiter. Yet God is one." With these words he declares that he does not proclaim Christ as God in such a way as to make another God or profess two gods, but that God is one, as the law also says. When Christ is proclaimed as God from God, this does not lead to another God, because what is from God does not allow itself to be called another God. Whether it is God or what is from God, there is one God. There is no difference at all between God and what is from God, yet he is another. He is another because of the person by which he is called the Son, but he is the same because of the unity of substance. Let no one find fault because I said "person"; some people object to the word. But let us follow the apostle, who says: "For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done for your sake in the person of Christ."

LXXXI. WHEN THE SAVIOUR SAID THAT HE WOULD SUFFER AND RISE AFTER THE THIRD DAY, HE ADDED: "AND AFTER I HAVE RISEN, I WILL GO BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE; THERE YOU WILL SEE ME." THE ANGEL SAID THE SAME TO THE WOMEN. YET HE IS FOUND TO HAVE BEEN SEEN BY THE WOMEN AND BY HIS DISCIPLES IN JERUSALEM.

To call the Saviour's words into question is the mark of an unbeliever. But I see that you are not doubting the Saviour's words. You are asking what they mean: why, when he was seen in Jerusalem after his passion, he said he would be seen by them in Galilee. He was seen in Jerusalem, but in part, to revive the spirits of the disciples; in Galilee he was seen by all of them together. So for those who were to see him in Jerusalem a few at a time, he appointed Galilee as the place where he would appear to all of them together and give them commandments for ordering their discipline.

LXXXII. THE APOSTLE PAUL INDICATES THAT WE SHOULD NOT GRIEVE OVER THE DEAD, FOR GRIEVING IS FOR THOSE WITHOUT HOPE. YET HE HIMSELF SAYS OF EPAPHRODITUS: "HE WAS ILL, NEAR TO DEATH. BUT GOD HAD MERCY ON HIM, AND NOT ON HIM ONLY BUT ON ME ALSO, SO THAT I WOULD NOT HAVE SORROW UPON SORROW." HOW CAN HE FORBID GRIEF, WHEN HE DECLARES THAT HE HIMSELF WOULD HAVE GRIEVED IF EPAPHRODITUS HAD DIED?

The apostle meant that he would have grieved over the death of Epaphroditus, had it happened, in one way, and he forbids grief in another. Here he said he would have grieved, if Epaphroditus had died, because he would have lost the comfort of his help, which he relied on in the work of the gospel. What he forbids us is to grieve in such a way that we mourn the departed as if they were extinguished and lost, despairing of the resurrection. So it is one thing to miss the comfort of someone who is absent, and another to lament the destruction of someone who will no longer exist. In the first case comfort is lacking; in the second, despair is ruled out.

LXXXIII. WHY IS IT THAT, ALTHOUGH THE APOSTLES HEALED ALL THE CASES BROUGHT TO THEM, THEY DID NOT GIVE A CURE TO THEIR OWN SICK? EPAPHRODITUS CERTAINLY WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN ILL TO THE POINT OF DEATH IF THE APOSTLE'S INTERCESSION HAD BEEN HEARD. WHO CAN DOUBT THAT THE APOSTLE OFTEN PRAYED FOR THIS AND DID NOT OBTAIN IT? IF HE HAD BEEN HEARD, THE ILLNESS WOULD HAVE BEEN TAKEN AWAY AT ONCE.

The apostles performed signs and miracles so that unbelief would be compelled to believe. Seeing deeds that are impossible for human beings, people would recognize from this that the preaching was from God, and the miracles would prove to them that faith has reason behind it. Words are always met with contradiction, so miraculous power was set up as a witness; when words give way to it, it shows that faith has a reason that cannot be expressed in words. Among believers, then, signs and wonders are no longer needed, but firm hope. Once the mind has learned that what has been promised is true, it arms itself to despise present things and become worthy of the things to come, storing up merit for itself through toil. Solomon testifies to this when he says: "My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation." These warnings were given because a person makes progress through temptations. Hence the apostle says: "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." These trials of tribulation come in various ways, so that the mind that perseveres in the faith it has received may be crowned. A person is tested not only in faith, but also in sickness, in loss, in persecution and in the death of loved ones. If in these sufferings he is not drawn away to seek the help of demons, he earns martyrdom without the price of blood. So when the apostle did not obtain what he asked for Epaphroditus, it was not to Epaphroditus's loss but to his advantage. The apostle too, when he made a request for himself, was told: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness."

XCII. ON THE ETERNITY OF THE SON.

There are some who have not yet shaken off the darkness of error, nor cleansed or wiped away the decay of a stale and aged life. Judging by earthly understanding, they are in doubt either about the Son of God or about how two can be one. (The faithless and stubborn nation of the Jews, to whom the fountain of the law and the treasuries of the sacraments lay open, does not merely doubt, but denies it outright with wicked words.) For their sake I will set the matter out briefly, as far as a rather compressed treatise allows. For the ignorant, hope is left whole, if they are willing to learn; for those who pretend not to know, everlasting punishment is appointed.

Since God almighty surpasses all in greatness and goodness, it was fitting that he should bring forth and display from himself something great and supremely good. But if he had brought forth anything that fell short of the measure of his own excellence, it would seem either that he could do no more, which cannot be said of the almighty, or that he did not wish to, which cannot be said of the most kind. Certainly it would have been no great thing for the supreme God to make something that, being placed beneath him, would not possess the power of full supremacy. Above himself, then, there was nothing, for there is nothing that surpasses God; below himself was too little, since what is less than the greatest was not fitting. So, creating a Son most like himself, he brought forth from himself as it were another self, and in this way that highest and greatest good which is supplied to us from God overflowed to us through his offspring.

Moreover, this reasoning must also be understood: God, who founded this world, and who among the other wonders of its beauty and order also gave it the power to create, so that it might supply offspring each of its own kind, must surely himself have first possessed what he gave. For no one gives what he does not himself have. He, then, who had a Son agreeing with him in every aspect of likeness (that is, the One an only one, the upright an upright one, the good a kindly one, the blessed a blessed one, the greatest the greatest, the everlasting an eternal one) surely held, before the world was created, the primacy of begetting offspring. From this he imparted a pattern to things coming into being, so that the shoots of all that beget should be bound to correspond to their own seeds. Indeed, the lawful order allowed nothing else than that he who was to be the Father of all things should first be a Father in his own right, that is, of his own offspring.

But when we say that the Son was brought forth, this must not be taken to mean that his origin is like ours, or that he was born in the way we see mortals born, when, as offspring burst forth, there come into existence things that did not exist before. For those beings are conceived from seeds implanted from elsewhere, and from differing elements they grow together into a union in the form of their own kind. But here God, divinely and with no help from any outside mixture, drew out and brought forth from himself what he had always had in himself and with himself. Suppose we say that light is born from the sun because it proceeds and flows from it. We certainly do not mean that the sun could ever be, or ever was, without light, as though it had begotten the light at some time later than itself. We mean that it has always held the light with itself, and that the light is born from it without any distinction of a beginning, because the sun always shines and always gives light from itself, as though renewing its gift. In the same way the Son of God, cleaving to the Father from eternity, has kept this likeness to him as well: he has neither rising nor setting. And as God is everlasting without origin, so the Son too is everlasting. And as God is one, simple and the same, so the Son is so blended with the Father that, though they are distinct in names and in affections, they are the same: one in both, and each in the one, continuous in inseparable majesty.

So God holds and embraces with himself the Son, not drawn from discordant materials but brought forth from the simple and single stock and seedbed of his own nature, always held within himself and never sent away from himself by any separation, in such a way that nothing of that unity is changed in the two of them.
